    Banking and NBFCs

    Banking and NBFCs — Complete Exam Reference

    Course faculty: Prof. M. Jayadev (IIM Bangalore) — Modules 1 & 2 Guest practitioners: Ashok Narain (ex-CGM, Dept. of Supervision, RBI — NBFC sector) · Mayank Jain (FinBox — credit programs) · Srinath Sridharan (FACE, the RBI-recognised FinTech SRO) · Anilkumar SG (Founder, Samunnati) · Hitesh Sachdev (ICICI Bank — startup partnerships) · Rahul Patidar (Chief Risk Officer, Money View — digital lending & credit risk)

    How to use this file. Sections 1–12 are Prof. Jayadev's two modules (deposits/payments, then credit). Sections 13–20 are the guest modules on NBFCs, the FinTech ecosystem and digital lending. Anything marked ← guaranteed MCQ is a number, date, threshold or definitional distinction that MCQ writers reach for. The Quick-fire revision table at the end is the single densest thing in this file — read it first if you are short on time.

    1. What a bank legally is
    1

    1.1 The statutory definition

    The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 defines banking as:

    "Accepting, for the purpose of lending or investment, of deposits of money from the public, repayable on demand or otherwise, and withdrawable by cheque, draft, order or otherwise."

    Three things to notice, because each is exam-friendly:

    Phrase Why it matters
    "for the purpose of lending or investment" A bank does not just hold your money — accepting deposits in order to lend or invest is what makes it a bank. An entity that only holds money is not banking.
    "from the public" Deposits must come from the general public, not from a closed group.
    "repayable on demand or otherwise" The "or otherwise" is the famous bit. In 1949 the drafters had no idea about ATMs, cards, internet banking or UPI. That single open-ended phrase is what has let the definition stretch across 75+ years of technology without amendment. guaranteed MCQ

    Trap: the definition contains both "repayable on demand or otherwise" and "withdrawable by cheque, draft, order or otherwise". An MCQ may quote only half and ask you to complete it.

    1.2 The three defining functions of a bank

    1. Accept deposits from the public
    2. Lend and invest those deposits
    3. Operate the payment and settlement system (issue cheques drawn on itself, participate in RTGS/NEFT/IMPS/UPI)

    Only banks do all three. This triad is the cleanest way to distinguish a bank from an NBFC.

    1. The six types of banks in India
    3

    # Type Key facts
    1 Public sector / nationalised banks Currently 12 after the merger waves. Government majority-owned. guaranteed MCQ
    2 Private sector banks Split into old private banks (pre-1994, mostly regional legacy institutions) and new private banks licensed from 1994 onwards after the Narasimham reforms (HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Axis, IndusInd etc.)
    3 Foreign banks ~40 operating in India, overwhelmingly through the branch model rather than as wholly-owned subsidiaries
    4 Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) Established 1975. Ownership split 50% Central Government / 35% sponsor bank / 15% State Government. Consolidated from 196 → ~28–29 guaranteed MCQ
    5 Small Finance Banks (SFBs) Licences issued 2015. Convert MFIs/local institutions into full banks with a priority-sector mandate
    6 Payments Banks Licences also 2015. Can take deposits and do payments but cannot lend

    Plus one failed experiment worth remembering: Local Area Banks (LABs), licensed in the mid-1990s. Ten were approved, six were set up, and the number fell to 4 → 2. They are the standard example of a licensing category that did not work. guaranteed MCQ

    2.1 Core functions banks perform

    Deposits · lending · investing in government securities (G-secs) · payments and settlements · custodial services · agency services (collecting dividends, paying taxes/utility bills on your behalf) · brokerage and third-party distribution (mutual funds, insurance, demat, even IRCTC tickets).

    1. The 1991–92 reforms — why Indian banking looks the way it does
    1

    The Narasimham Committee reforms of 1991/1992 are the hinge of the whole course. What changed:

    Reform What it did
    Prudential norms Income recognition, asset classification and provisioning rules — banks could no longer book interest on bad loans as income
    Capital adequacy Capital had to be held against risk-weighted assets
    Deregulation of interest rates Both deposit rates and lending rates were freed. Note: savings-account interest was deregulated only in 2011 — much later than the rest guaranteed MCQ
    Off-balance-sheet exposures Guarantees, LCs and derivatives brought into the supervisory net
    Three-in-one accounts Savings + demat + trading linked into one relationship
    Physical → virtual distribution Branch-centric banking gave way to ATMs, internet banking, mobile apps

    3.1 Democratisation of banking

    Four forces that pushed banking from the elite to the mass market:

    • JAM trinity — Jan Dhan accounts + Aadhaar + Mobile
    • CIBIL scores — a credit history for individuals, so lending stopped depending on who you knew
    • Mudra loans — small-ticket credit for micro-entrepreneurs
    • Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) — the rails that made all of the above cheap

    1. Deposit products — the full list
    8

    4.1 The four basic deposit types

    Product Key features
    Savings account Interest-bearing, for individuals/households. Rate deregulated in 2011
    Current account For businesses; unlimited transactions; pays NO interest guaranteed MCQ
    Term / fixed deposit Minimum tenure 7 days. Premature withdrawal permitted with a penalty of roughly 1% on the applicable rate
    Recurring deposit Fixed monthly contribution for a fixed term

    4.2 Special-purpose deposit schemes

    Scheme The point of it
    Capital Gains Account Scheme Park capital-gains proceeds so you retain the tax exemption until you reinvest
    Senior Citizen Savings Scheme (SCSS) Higher rate for those above the qualifying age
    Public Provident Fund (PPF) ₹1,50,000 maximum per year, 15-year lock-in guaranteed MCQ
    Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana For the girl child; rate around 8%+; part of "Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao" guaranteed MCQ
    Sweep-in / flexi deposit Balance above a threshold in the savings account automatically "sweeps" into a term deposit at the higher rate, and sweeps back out when you need it
    Certificate of Deposit (CD) A negotiable money-market instrument issued by a bank
    NRI accounts NRE (rupee, repatriable, from foreign earnings) · NRO (rupee, for Indian-source income, restricted repatriation) · FCNR (held in foreign currency, so no exchange risk to the depositor) guaranteed MCQ — expand all three
    PMJDY (Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana) Launched 2014; zero-balance basic savings account

    4.3 What determines the interest rate a bank pays you

    Four drivers: the REPO rate (RBI's policy rate) · liquidity conditions in the system · the maturity of the deposit · the size and standing of the bank (a bank desperate for deposits pays more).

    4.4 Tax on deposit interest

    • TDS at 10% is deducted if interest income exceeds ₹50,000 per annum
    • Senior citizens are exempt up to ₹50,000 of interest income guaranteed MCQ

    4.5 Deposit insurance — DICGC

    • DICGC = Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, a wholly-owned subsidiary of the RBI
    • Cover: ₹5,00,000 per depositor per bank (principal + interest combined)
    • The premium is paid by the bank, not by the depositor guaranteed MCQ
    • NBFC liabilities carry no such insurance. This is one of the sharpest bank-vs-NBFC distinctions.

    4.6 Nomination and unclaimed deposits

    • Every deposit account should carry a nomination
    • A deposit untouched for 10 years is classified as an unclaimed deposit and is transferred to the DEA Fund — Depositor Education and Awareness Fund guaranteed MCQ
    • The RBI's UDGAM portal lets the public search for unclaimed deposits across banks

    4.7 The risk ladder for a saver

    From safest to riskiest:

    Bank deposits → Urban cooperative bank deposits → NBFC deposits → Corporate fixed deposits guaranteed MCQ (ordering question) Higher promised return always corresponds to a step up this ladder.

    1. How a bank's own health is judged — CAMELS
    2

    Letter Stands for What it measures
    C Capital adequacy Capital against risk-weighted assets. Current minimum 11.5% (it was 8% under earlier norms) guaranteed MCQ
    A Asset quality NPAs, provisioning, concentration
    M Management Quality and integrity of the leadership
    E Earnings Profitability. ROA of 1% is considered good for a bank guaranteed MCQ
    L Liquidity Ability to meet obligations as they fall due
    S Systems (and controls) IT, internal controls, compliance

    1. Payment systems

    RTGS · NEFT · IMPS · UPI — all four are now available 24×7. RTGS settles gross and in real time (used for large values); NEFT settles in batches; IMPS and UPI are instant retail rails.

    1. Credit — the institutional landscape
    1

    Institutions that provide credit in India, beyond commercial banks:

    • State Financial Corporations (SFCs)
    • IFCI (Industrial Finance Corporation of India)
    • State Industrial Development Corporations
    • NBFCs
    • Microfinance companies
    • FinTechs (as originators/enablers rather than balance-sheet lenders)

    7.1 Priority Sector Lending (PSL)

    • 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit must go to the priority sector — a mandate that dates from around 1970 guaranteed MCQ
    • Agriculture, MSME, education, housing, export credit, renewable energy, weaker sections
    • MSME and retail lending carry a continuous policy push because MSMEs are treated as "the backbone of the country"

    1. Credit appraisal — how a bank decides to lend
    1

    8.1 The process

    1. Loan policy — every bank has one, framed within the RBI master circulars/directions. It is "a guideline for action of the credit managers at the branches."
    2. Business risk analysis — is the industry and the business model sound?
    3. Borrower analysis — who is behind it, what is their track record?
    4. Rating vs scoring — this distinction is a favourite:
    Used for Method
    Credit rating Businesses / corporates Judgemental + financial model, produces a grade
    Credit scoring Retail / individuals Statistical model producing a score (e.g. CIBIL)

    guaranteed MCQ — do not swap these 5. Tiered sanctioning authority — larger loans need higher approval levels

    8.2 The "C's of banking"

    The classic checklist, extended by Prof. Jayadev to eight:

    Character · Capacity · Capital · Collateral · Conditions · Competition · Complacency · Contingencies

    ← guaranteed MCQ. The traditional textbook list is the first five ("5 Cs"); the extended list adds Competition, Complacency, Contingencies. If a question asks "which of the following is NOT one of the C's", check against this list.

    1. Credit products
    1

    9.1 Fund-based vs non-fund-based

    Category Products
    Fund-based (money actually goes out) Cash credit · overdraft · bill discounting · term loans · bridge loans · credit cards · housing/mortgage loans · commercial property loans · demand loans
    Non-fund-based (a contingent obligation) Letter of Credit (LC) · Bank Guarantee (BG) guaranteed MCQ — LC and BG are NON-fund-based

    TReDS — Trade Receivables Discounting System — an electronic platform for discounting MSME receivables.

    9.2 Digital lending distribution channels

    Mobile app · DSA tablets (direct selling agents) · internet banking · partner marketplaces (e.g. BankBazaar) · branch.

    1. India's digital lending infrastructure
    1

    10.1 The India Stack layers as used in lending

    Layer What it is Examples
    Identity layer Establishes who the borrower is (KYC) Aadhaar · PAN · DigiLocker · GST returns · Udyam Registration Number (for MSMEs)
    Process layer NOT strictly part of India Stack — it is built by each bank itself: the workflow of who processes what, how fast, with what information guaranteed MCQ trap
    Payment layer Moves the money UPI
    Data layer Account Aggregators — one institution's data made available to another with consent (e.g. demat holdings, mutual fund investments used to support a loan)

    Exam point: the identity/process/payment triad is what Prof. Jayadev calls the "digital lending infrastructure", and the Account Aggregator is described as an additional data layer on top. If an option says "the process layer is a component of India Stack", it is wrong.

    10.2 Why it matters

    Digital lending now runs across banks and NBFCs, secured and unsecured, retail and small business — all four combinations.

    1. MSME lending
    2

    11.1 Who MSMEs are

    Sole proprietorships, partnerships, or private limited companies, operating in manufacturing, trading, services and more. They receive both term loans and working capital loans.

    11.2 The innovative MSME products (illustrative, not exhaustive)

    Product Basis of lending
    Financing against rent receivables A steady rental stream from a reliable tenant
    Transport operator finance Against the asset value of the vehicle
    Loans to practising professionals Doctors setting up clinics, CAs setting up offices
    Point-of-sale (POS) loans If given to the dealer/vendor → MSME loan. If given to the individual buyer → retail / consumer durable loan. guaranteed MCQ
    GST-return-based lending GST filings as proof the business is trading
    E-way-bill-based lending Goods physically moving between states as evidence of activity
    Rooftop solar loans Repaid partly from grid payments for surplus solar energy
    Street vendor / hawker loans Underwritten on payment and transaction data alone
    Commercial credit cards Credit cards issued for business use

    11.3 Mudra loans — PMMY

    Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana, up to ₹20 lakh, in three tiers:

    Tier Amount
    Shishu up to ₹50,000
    Kishore above ₹50,000 and up to ₹5 lakh
    Tarun ("term loan" in the transcript) above ₹5 lakh and up to ₹20 lakh

    guaranteed MCQ — the three names and their bands

    11.4 Targeted schemes

    • Nari Shakti loans — women borrowers
    • Startup loans — young graduates with a business idea
    • Stand-up loans — borrowers held back by weak social background / legacy disadvantage (SC/ST and women)

    11.5 What the bank checks for an MSME loan

    Purpose of the loan · business plan · customer orders · KYC · Udyam Registration Number · rating/scoring · collateral.

    Credit Guarantee Scheme: for collateral-free lending, the Central Government credit guarantee covers the bank's risk; the borrower pays a slightly higher charge (effectively an insurance premium). Such schemes exist worldwide precisely because small businesses carry borrower, business and cash-flow uncertainty.

    1. Retail lending in detail
    3

    12.1 Housing loan — the full processing sequence

    1. Personal information / KYC — identity, income tax returns, GST returns
    2. CIBIL score — Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited; the record of past loans and repayment guaranteed MCQ — expand the acronym
    3. Property information
    4. Legal verification / due diligence — current owner, chain of past owners, encumbrances. The bank needs a free and fair title, meaning "ownership of the property is established and it can be transferred without any difficulty"
    5. Financial information — what surplus is available to service the loan
    6. Loan amount decision
    7. Tenure decision — driven by age and remaining earning years. A 30-year-old may get 20 years; a 55–60-year-old will not
    8. Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratio — e.g. 80% of asset value
    9. Interest rate — see below
    10. Processing and administrative charges
    11. Documentation — contract, terms, creation of security in the bank's favour
    12. EMI fixed

    Top-up loan: after 5–10 years of servicing, the asset value has risen and the outstanding has fallen, so the borrower becomes eligible for additional borrowing against the same property.

    12.2 Interest rate types

    Type Behaviour
    Floating rate Linked to an external benchmark; moves with the benchmark. When rates rise, banks typically extend the tenure rather than raise the EMI; when rates fall, the tenure shortens. guaranteed MCQ
    Fixed rate Locked (e.g. 8% for 15 years). Borrower is protected if rates rise but gets no benefit if rates fall
    MCLR — Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate The bank computes: cost of the deposit + overheads + statutory obligations (CRR/SLR cost) + expected profit margin. Not applicable to every loan type

    12.3 Charges to look for

    Processing charges · administrative charges · legal verification expenses · penal charges for late payment · pre-closure / foreclosure charges · documentation charges. They may be levied separately (as a % of the loan) or built into the interest rate — the borrower must check which.

    12.4 Vehicle loan

    • Covers new and used vehicles
    • Repayment period up to 7 years
    • Loan is calculated on the on-road price (ex-showroom + registration + insurance)
    • Typically 80% of asset value financed; borrower deposits the remaining 20% first, then the bank pays 100% of the value by cheque directly to the dealer, not to the borrower guaranteed MCQ
    • Prepayment/foreclosure charges are generally waived now on vehicle loans as a marketing/competition measure

    12.5 The security distinction — mortgage vs hypothecation

    Loan Security created Meaning
    Housing loan Mortgage Charge over immovable property
    Vehicle loan Hypothecation The vehicle stays in the borrower's possession and use, but the bank holds the right to seize and sell it on default

    ← guaranteed MCQ — this is the single most likely definitional question in the retail section

    1. Working capital finance
    9

    13.1 The operating cycle

    Operating cycle = the number of days from raw material → work-in-progress → finished goods → credit sales (receivables) → cash collected → back to raw material. Working capital is the money needed to fund that cycle.

    Longer operating cycle → more working capital. Shorter cycle → less.

    The illustrative contrast (memorise it):

    Business Working capital position
    Railways / airlines / prepaid telecom & internet Customer pays in advance — the company receives working capital before delivering the service. Negative working capital need
    Automobile manufacturer Buys steel and components, assembles over 2–3 months, ships to dealer, then sells. Heavy working capital need
    Bakery Work-in-process period is a few hours — negligible WIP financing need
    Shoppers Stop (retailer) No raw material at all. Buys and holds finished goods for 30–40 days. Must hold heavy stock to attract customers
    Tata Steel (manufacturer) Must hold raw material inventory before it can process anything
    Build-to-order manufacturer Very short finished-goods holding period — goods are already sold before they are made

    ← guaranteed MCQ: "which business needs the least working capital?" → the one paid in advance

    13.2 The three holding periods that drive the requirement

    • Inventory holding period (or inventory turnover)
    • Debtors / receivables collection period
    • Creditors / payables period — how much credit the suppliers give

    The matching example: a trader who receives 30 days credit from the wholesaler and gives 25 days credit to customers collects before he must pay — a 5-day surplus, so no working capital gap at all. Reverse it (gives 60 days, gets 30 days) and he needs 30 days of funding. guaranteed MCQ Credit period is set by competition in the industry, and ranges from 3–4 days to 6 months. A business with several products/divisions has a different operating cycle for each.

    13.3 Innovations built on the operating cycle

    Channel finance · supply chain finance · invoice financing — all of them finance the supplier so the supplier stops pressuring the buyer for early payment.

    13.4 The three assessment methods

    # Method How it works
    1 Percentage of projected sales (turnover method) Used for traders, small businesses, MSMEs, services. Working capital ≈ (operating cycle in months ÷ 12) × projected sales
    2 Balance sheet method Working capital gap = projected current assets − projected current liabilities; the bank funds part of it
    3 Cash budget / cash flow method Gap between projected cash inflows and outflows over coming months

    Banks have full freedom to choose; the choice is written into the loan policy.

    13.5 The turnover-method worked example

    • Projected sales = 200
    • Operating cycle = 3 months → the cycle turns 4 times a year → working capital = 25% of sales = 50 guaranteed MCQ (the 3-month → 25% link)
    • Borrower's contribution (margin) = 20% of the estimated working capital = 10 (which is 5% of sales)
    • Bank finance = 40

    The 1-month variant: if the operating cycle is 1 month, the cycle turns 12 times a year, so working capital ≈ 1/12 ≈ 8–9% of sales; a liberal bank might allow 10%.

    Alternative using cost: sales 200, profit margin 10% → cost of goods sold 180; working capital = 2, 3 or 4 months of cost of sales depending on the cycle.

    Margin/contribution demanded from the borrower is typically 5%, 10% or 20% of estimated working capital, depending on the riskiness of the borrower.

    13.6 The balance sheet method

    Working capital gap = Current Assets − Current Liabilities

    The canonical worked figure:

    CA = 100, CL = 40 → working capital gap = 60. If the bank funds only 40, the borrower must bring 20 — that 20 is the Net Working Capital (NWC), i.e. the borrower's contribution.

    guaranteed MCQ Two sub-approaches within the balance sheet method:

    Approach Borrower's stipulated contribution Resulting current ratio
    A percentage of the working capital gap e.g. 25% of the gap around 1.17
    A percentage of total current assets 25% of current assets 1.33

    ← guaranteed MCQ: "25% of current assets brought by the promoter implies a current ratio of ___" → 1.33

    The key mechanical relationship, stated three ways: - More borrower contribution → less bank finance → higher current ratio - Less borrower contribution → more bank finance → lower current ratio - Current ratio falling ⇒ net working capital falling (and vice versa)

    A bank may levy a penalty if an agreed current ratio (e.g. 1.17) is breached over successive quarters.

    13.7 The ratios and concepts the bank actually computes

    Concept Definition / benchmark
    Current ratio CA ÷ CL. Banks typically want 1.3, 1.4 or 1.5 guaranteed MCQ
    Tangible net worth Share capital + reserves, excluding fictitious assets. Indicates solvency / financial soundness
    Quasi-equity Loans from directors, promoters or their family members. Accounting standards call it debt; the banker treats it as equity, which improves net worth and lowers assessed financial risk guaranteed MCQ
    Financial debt Borrowings from banks, FIs, NBFCs, lease finance companies, bonds, plus director/promoter loans
    Operating debt Sundry creditors / suppliers' credit — not money, but goods and services supplied on credit
    Debt-equity ratio Can be 1, 1.5, 2 or 3 depending on business and loan policy. Rising D/E → rising financial risk → borrower rating falls. Falling D/E → rating improves
    Working capital gap CA − CL
    Net working capital The borrower's own long-term money funding current assets. Positive and rising = safe; falling = warning; negative = serious risk
    Inventory turnover Textbook: sales ÷ inventory. In practice banks prefer cost of goods sold ÷ inventory, and for large firms they compute raw material, WIP and finished goods turnover separately
    Debtors collection period Benchmarked against industry and against firm size — small firms move goods slower and collect slower than large firms with scale economies

    13.8 Reclassification of current assets — a subtle, very examinable point

    Even though the borrower prepares accounts to accounting standards, the bank re-does the classification based on (a) true liquidity and (b) the source of funding:

    • A large deposit with the electricity distribution company is shown as a current asset under accounting standards, but it is long-term in nature and generates no liquidity → the bank excludes it from current assets, provided it was funded from long-term sources
    • A bank deposit sitting inside "cash" that cannot be withdrawn for operating expenses is similarly excluded — otherwise the bank would be financing its own deposit

    ← guaranteed MCQ: why does a bank reclassify current assets? → because accounting classification ≠ liquidity for lending purposes

    13.9 What the bank looks at in the income statement and cash flow statement

    Income statement: Is net sales growing? (No growth → no need for extra working capital.) The worked example uses a 35% projected sales increase over the previous year — and the bank must verify it against industry growth, comparable firms in the same and other regions, and the order book, because inflated projections invite diversion or siphoning of funds. guaranteed MCQ (35%) Cash flow statement: the most reliable statement for a banker, because accounting profit ≠ cash generated. The banker reads operating cash flow → how much was absorbed by working capital → what is left over for debt repayment or capex.

    Information demanded: typically 3–4 years of audited past financials plus 1–2 years of projections (sometimes quarter-wise). guaranteed MCQ

    13.10 Loan covenants / term sheet

    After sanction, the bank imposes covenants: D/E must not exceed X; interest coverage ratio must not fall below Y; current ratio must not fall below Z; monthly/quarterly income statements to be submitted.

    The contrast to remember: a car loan requires no further information after disbursement — the bank only cares that the EMI arrives. A business loan requires continuous post-sanction monitoring, because business risk is live and external. guaranteed MCQ

    13.11 Delivery — the loan is never handed over as one cheque

    Once the working capital number is fixed (e.g. 22,000 in the illustration), the bank splits it into products:

    Product Use
    Cash credit A running limit; the borrower withdraws as needed and must deposit sales proceeds into the same account. Interest is charged on the number of days the money is actually used
    Commercial credit card Cash-credit-like facility for small businesses, usable online
    Packing credit / pre-shipment finance Money advanced before shipment against an export order (raw material, packaging, shipping)
    Export bill purchase / discounting / advance against export bills Post-shipment finance against invoices
    Domestic bill discounting Against domestic invoices
    Import LC Where raw material is imported
    Demand loan A simple lump-sum drawdown
    Foreign-currency loan Where the exposure is in another currency

    The purpose of splitting is risk reduction plus borrower financial discipline. This is why banks want inventory broken into raw material (domestic vs imported) / WIP / finished goods and receivables broken into domestic vs export — each sub-category maps to a different product. guaranteed MCQ

    1. EMI calculation
    2

    14.1 The concept

    An EMI is the constant cash flow C of a present-value-of-annuity whose present value equals the loan amount.

    PV of annuity = C × [ 1/r − 1/(r(1+r)^t) ]

    Equivalently, solving for the instalment:

    EMI = P × [ r(1+r)^t ] / [ (1+r)^t − 1 ]

    where r = monthly interest rate and t = number of months.

    14.2 The worked example — memorise these numbers

    Input Value
    Loan (P) ₹50,00,000
    Annual rate 8%
    Tenure 15 years = 180 months
    Monthly rate (r) 8 ÷ 12 = 0.67%
    EMI ₹47,782.60 ≈ ₹47,783

    guaranteed MCQ Excel: =PMT(rate, nper, pv) — three inputs: interest rate, number of months, loan amount.

    14.3 Two conversion points that get tested

    • Banks convert the annual rate to monthly by simple division (8 ÷ 12), not by compounding — "none of the organisations are doing it on a compounding basis" guaranteed MCQ
    • The RBI requires banks and NBFCs to disclose how the EMI is calculated. It is the customer's right to ask.

    14.4 The amortisation schedule

    For each month: interest = outstanding × monthly rate; principal = EMI − interest; new outstanding = old outstanding − principal. Useful for taxation (interest and principal are treated differently under the Income Tax Act).

    14.5 Rate changes mid-loan

    Rate rises → tenure extended (EMI usually unchanged). Rate falls → tenure shortened. Prepayment and foreclosure are now generally charge-free on retail floating-rate products.

    1. Plastic money
    5

    15.1 Credit cards

    A credit card is a chip-bearing plastic card that represents a revolving loan limit.

    Types: individual · co-branded (bank + partner brand) · corporate (issued to employees of a corporate client) · Kisan Credit Card (for farmers, a Government of India push).

    The two limits — know the difference:

    Limit Meaning
    Credit limit Maximum outstanding merchant transactions at any time. It is revolving — the worked example: limit ₹2,00,000, ₹1,20,000 used → only ₹80,000 available; repay the ₹1,20,000 and the full limit is restored guaranteed MCQ
    Cash limit How much can be withdrawn as cash from an ATM using the credit card

    Controls the customer can set (risk management by the cardholder): enable/disable international transactions, point-of-sale transactions, online transactions, contactless transactions; and reduce the credit and cash limits. Reducing the cash limit is the specific protection against ATM misuse if the card is lost. guaranteed MCQ The full fee list — an MCQ favourite as a "which of these is NOT charged" question:

    joining fee (primary cardholder) · annual membership fee · cash advance fee · service charges on specific transactions · interest rate · finance charges · overdue interest · default charges/penalties.

    Grace period: 40 / 45 / 50 days, sometimes up to 2 months. Interest is charged only after it. Credit card interest rates are very high.

    The minimum-amount-due trap: bill of ₹1,00,000, minimum due ₹10,000. Pay only the minimum and interest runs on the remaining ₹90,000. Paying in full within the credit period means no charges at all and the limit is restored. guaranteed MCQ Billing date varies by issuer (1st, 15th, third week) — it determines which transactions fall into which bill.

    Security: PIN/passcode management via portal or app, grievance redressal mechanism, named officers, call-centre and toll-free numbers.

    15.2 Debit cards

    • The customer uses their own money — no loan is involved
    • Only a cash/transaction limit exists — per transaction, per day, per month; the number of ATM transactions per month is also capped
    • Typically 10 free transactions a month, charges apply beyond that guaranteed MCQ
    • Third-party benefits: merchant discounts, airport lounge access, hotel benefits, insurance cover (usually from a third-party insurer, with the bank charging a fee/premium)

    15.3 The risk comparison — the cleanest MCQ in this section

    Card Transaction risk Credit risk
    Debit card Yes No
    Credit card Yes Yes

    guaranteed MCQ

    1. Consumer protection in banking
    8

    16.1 The RBI's Charter of Customer Rights — five rights

    Right What it requires
    1. Right to Fair Treatment No discrimination on gender, age, religion, caste or physical ability. The RBI has specifically directed that branches be physically accessible — a branch on the first or second floor without a lift fails this test guaranteed MCQ (the lift example)
    2. Right to Transparency, Fair and Honest Dealing Interest rate calculation, charges, fees, associated risks and maximum liability in case of card loss must be disclosed; coercive contractual terms and unintelligible clauses must be explained
    3. Right to Suitability The product offered must be appropriate to the customer's needs, assessed against their financial circumstances and understanding. A bank cannot unilaterally convert a savings account into a term deposit guaranteed MCQ
    4. Right to Privacy Customer data — including credit information obtained from CIBIL — must not be disclosed to others through any channel
    5. Right to Grievance Redress and Compensation The bank must publish the process, the authority, the address, the email and phone. The bank remains responsible even for THIRD-PARTY products it distributes — insurance, mutual funds, stockbroking, even IRCTC tickets. It cannot disclaim responsibility by calling it a third-party product guaranteed MCQ

    These policies must be disclosed on the website, at branches, and on demand.

    16.2 The legal machinery — five instruments

    Instrument Year What it gives the customer
    Consumer Protection Act 2019 Defines a consumer as someone who avails a service for consideration but NOT for a commercial purpose; establishes a quasi-judicial machinery of consumer forums at district/state/national level guaranteed MCQ (the "not for commercial purpose" qualifier)
    Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 One of India's oldest commercial laws (the Indian Contract Act is 1872). Sets out the duties of the collecting banker and the paying banker for cheques, bills and promissory notes guaranteed MCQ (1881 vs 1872)
    NI Act Section 138 (amendment 1997) Cheque dishonour for insufficient funds is a criminal offence. Punishment: imprisonment up to 2 years and/or a fine up to twice the cheque amount. A recent Supreme Court ruling extended the protection to cheques issued to repay cash transactions guaranteed MCQ (2 years / twice the amount)
    Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 Established Lok Adalat, used by banks for small-value recoveries (₹20,000–₹30,000 range) from "soft defaulters" — those who defaulted through oversight or ignorance, not intent guaranteed MCQ
    SARFAESI Act 2002 Lets a bank enforce security and sell the collateral WITHOUT going to court. Full form: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act guaranteed MCQ

    The borrower's three rights under SARFAESI — a very likely question: 1. Right to receive a notice (a 60-day notice period) 2. Right to raise an objection within that period (and to settle by paying up) 3. Right to receive the surplus left after the loan is recovered from the sale proceeds

    16.3 Banking Ombudsman

    The RBI's Banking Ombudsman scheme handles grievances, disagreements, and excessive charges/penal interest. The Ombudsman mediates between the bank and the customer. Details and addresses are published on the RBI website. (For NBFCs, see §17.9 — the Integrated Ombudsman Scheme applies to NBFCs with asset size over ₹100 crore or that are customer-facing.)

    1. NBFCs — the sector
    32

    (Ashok Narain, ex-CGM, Department of Supervision, RBI)

    17.1 What an NBFC is

    Layman's definition: a financial institution that offers credit, investment and financial services without a full banking licence — it can lend, help you invest, invest itself — but it cannot accept demand deposits or issue cheques.

    Statutory definition: a company whose principal business is that of a non-banking financial institution, per the RBI Act, 1934.

    Section 45-IA of the RBI Act, 1934: no NBFC may commence or carry on business without (a) a Certificate of Registration (CoR) from the RBI and (b) the minimum Net Owned Fund prescribed by the RBI. guaranteed MCQ — Section 45-IA, RBI Act 1934

    17.2 The three registration conditions

    1. Registered as a company under the Companies Act (public or private limited)
    2. Minimum Net Owned Fund as prescribed by the RBI
    3. Principal Business Criteria — the 50-50 test: - Financial assets > 50% of total assets, AND - Income from those financial assets > 50% of gross income

    guaranteed MCQ — both conditions, both above 50% Definitional carve-out: "financial assets" includes all assets financial in nature EXCEPT cash, bank deposits, advance tax and deferred tax. guaranteed MCQ Excluded activities — an entity whose principal business is any of these cannot be an NBFC: - Agricultural activity - Industrial activity - Trading / purchase or sale of goods other than securities (shares, debentures etc.) - Providing services (e.g. running a hotel) - Purchase, sale or construction of immovable property

    guaranteed MCQ — a "which of these disqualifies" question

    17.3 Banks vs NBFCs — the full comparison table

    Dimension Banks NBFCs
    Governing statute Banking Regulation Act, 1949 RBI Act, 1934
    Prudential framework Basel III Scale-Based Regulation (SBR), introduced 2021; capital prescribed by RBI, not full Basel
    Demand deposits (CASA) Yes No (barring a small legacy subset)
    Funding source Public deposits Borrowings from banks, mutual funds and capital markets
    Deposit insurance DICGC, ₹5 lakh None
    Payment system access Full member; can issue cheques drawn on itself No such mandate
    Focus The broad economy Niches: vehicle finance, gold finance, MSME, affordable housing, microfinance, infrastructure
    Accounting standards IGAAP Ind AS (derived from IFRS) guaranteed MCQ — NBFCs are AHEAD of banks here
    FDI 74% (49% automatic, beyond that with approval); 100% not permitted 100% permitted guaranteed MCQ
    Ownership by business houses Not permitted Permitted — e.g. Tata Sons (the Tata group holding company) is an NBFC; Aditya Birla Capital is another guaranteed MCQ
    Character Broad, systemically protected Agile, lean, higher risk appetite

    Why banks are firewalled from business houses: banks live on public deposits and public trust, so they must be insulated from business-group interests.

    17.4 NBFC core strengths

    Strong customer relationships · deep understanding of regional/local dynamics · well-developed collection systems (banks are much less involved in collections) · personalised service.

    17.5 Why NBFCs are not allowed to take deposits

    This is a set-piece argument — expect a question on it.

    • Every NBFC CEO wants deposits because they are low-cost
    • But deposits would mean higher entry barriers, more regulation, stronger supervision, because public trust would be at stake
    • Without deposits, NBFCs enjoy operational agility, a lighter compliance burden, and the freedom to specialise in one sector
    • Without deposits, there is no need for deposit insurance and no need for a central bank liquidity backstop
    • Therefore: the RBI has not granted any fresh deposit-taking NBFC permission since 1997 guaranteed MCQ
    • Today 98–99% of NBFCs are non-deposit-taking (NBFC-ND)

    17.6 Size, growth and interconnectedness

    Metric Figure
    NBFC asset base over ₹50 lakh crore
    Credit disbursal exceeding ₹40 lakh crore
    NBFC credit as % of GDP (FY25) 26%
    Loan growth (FY25) 20% year-on-year
    AUM CAGR, 2005–2023 ~20%, even as the number of NBFCs shrank
    AUM expected to cross ₹50 lakh crore by FY27
    UBS report (Economic Times, 30 Aug 2025) NBFC loans growing at 1.4× the pace of banks; profits advancing 1.5× faster; NBFC profit CAGR 16% vs banks' 11% to 2030 guaranteed MCQ
    Government vision NBFCs equalling banks in credit disbursal by 2047 (Viksit Bharat 2047)

    Asset mix (pie chart): Personal loans 35% · MSME ~23% · Infrastructure finance ~23% · Housing finance 16% · Specialised (vehicle, MFI, gold) ~3% guaranteed MCQ Interconnectedness (as at 31 March 2024): - Borrowings from banks and FIs: ₹15 lakh crore - Borrowings from markets (debentures, commercial paper, inter-corporate deposits, subordinated debt): ₹15.2 lakh crore - Together ~85% of total borrowings - Other borrowings: ₹5.3 lakh crore

    Because NBFCs fund themselves from the rest of the financial system, their distress transmits systemically — which is why the regulator cares.

    17.7 The evolution of Indian NBFCs — the six phases

    Period What happened
    1960s–70s NBFCs operate on the fringes: hire purchase and equipment finance for those banks overlooked. RBI began regulating NBFCs in 1964 guaranteed MCQ
    1980s The James Raj and Chakravarty committees examine structural reform of the sector guaranteed MCQ (name both)
    1990s Liberalisation unlocks credit demand in housing, infrastructure and consumer finance. Banks are slow; NBFCs are nimble and carve out niches. Registration became mandatory in 1997. RBI introduces capital adequacy norms and credit concentration norms
    Early 2000s NBFCs mature into focused institutions able to underwrite semi-urban and rural risk, with unmatched customer-centricity
    2010–2018 Diversification and maturity — microfinance, vehicle lending, gold loans, infrastructure finance, MSME and the informal sector. HDFC and Bajaj Finance become household names. Digital lending pioneers appear
    2018 onwards IL&FS default halts the run; RBI strengthens supervision, introduces ALM norms, stress testing, mandatory disclosures, and in 2021 the Scale-Based Regulation framework

    Why 2015–18 was the NBFC boom: the RBI's Asset Quality Review (AQR) around 2014–15 exposed stressed corporate assets on bank balance sheets. Bank credit growth collapsed; NBFC credit growth shot up, and NBFCs became the growth engine of the economy. guaranteed MCQ — link the AQR to the NBFC boom

    17.8 The IL&FS case study — the defining crisis

    The setup: - IL&FS was no fly-by-night operator — shareholders included LIC and SBI - 348 subsidiaries, many abroad guaranteed MCQ - It was a Core Investment Company (CIC) - At default, liabilities had ballooned to ₹91,000 crore guaranteed MCQ What a Core Investment Company is (and why the structure mattered): - The vehicle a wealthy group uses for wealth management of the promoters and control over group companies - Owns the group companies; dividends and profits flow back up to the CIC's owners - Allowed to borrow from banks and markets and invest within the group - Exempt from the 15%-of-RWA CRAR requirement. Instead: Adjusted Net Worth must never be less than 30% of risk-weighted assets, and it may borrow up to 2.5× adjusted net worth guaranteed MCQ - Ordinary NBFCs investing more than 10% in group companies suffer a capital deduction; CICs do not — a CIC may invest any amount within the group guaranteed MCQ The mechanism of failure: 1. IL&FS held a large stake in ITNL (IL&FS Transportation Networks Ltd), the flagship road-building company 2. The same Key Management Personnel (KMPs) sat on both boards — so IL&FS "understood the problem more than it should have" and kept lending to ITNL when no arm's-length lender would 3. ITNL could not complete its road projects (land acquisition and legal glitches), but IL&FS kept funding it with short-term market borrowings 4. ITNL defaulted first; IL&FS followed when the market lost confidence and the short-term money vanished

    The six causal factors — memorise the list:

    # Factor Detail
    1 Complex layered group structure 4 layers: apex holding company → 10 key intermediate holding companies → business verticals → operating companies. The Companies Act's 2-layer limit did not apply to CICs guaranteed MCQ
    2 Common KMPs across entities Destroyed objectivity in decision-making; drove excessive exposure to non-performing group companies
    3 Exposure to unrated / sub-investment-grade group borrowers Another group NBFC (IFIN) lent to unrated borrowers who lent back into the group — circuitous funding
    4 Multiple gearing IL&FS could borrow 2.5× as a CIC and inject equity into group companies without capital deduction; those companies then borrowed against that capital again. Standalone leverage 2.5, but consolidated group leverage 16.8 guaranteed MCQ
    5 Opaque funding pattern IL&FS funded its subsidiaries vertically, not the projects/SPVs directly, destroying visibility on end use of funds
    6 Governance failures Risk management committee meetings were not convened for long periods; liquidity cover fell precariously with no management action

    The central learning: "No category of NBFC — particularly a large one — should remain unmonitored by chance or design; failing which the scope for perverse incentives gets enhanced."

    The aftermath and the silver lining: the crisis triggered a sector-wide liquidity crunch. NBFCs that had grown greedily on easy bank funding suffered most; NBFCs whose business models linked exposures to borrower cash flows survived and still got cheap funding. This differentiation brought market discipline to the sector. guaranteed MCQ

    17.9 The Altico Capital case study

    • A high-profile NBFC focused on real estate lending, backed by respected international investors, apparently well capitalised
    • A default on a modest ₹20 crore of interest put over ₹4,500 crore of public funds at risk and hit 27 lenders, including leading banks and mutual funds guaranteed MCQ — all three numbers The four things Altico exposed:
    Issue Detail
    Governance — CEO not on the board The CEO proposed the decisions but, not being a board member, carried no collective board responsibility or accountability guaranteed MCQ
    Governance — decisions on short video conferences Prevented deliberate thinking and objective analysis
    Business model — sector concentration Overdependence on one sector; concentrated exposure to high-risk developers
    Weak internal controls Hardly any stress testing was being done

    17.10 Scale-Based Regulation (SBR), 2021

    The old regime was effectively one-size-fits-all, which created regulatory arbitrage (light regulation for a large NBFC vs strong regulation for a small bank).

    RBI's philosophy: proportionality — the higher the risk, the tighter the regulation and supervision on governance standards, capital adequacy, disclosure and customer protection.

    The four layers:

    Base Layer → Middle Layer → Upper Layer → Top Layer

    Each step up reflects increasing systemic importance and therefore stricter supervision, capital adequacy and prudential expectations. guaranteed MCQ — get the order and all four names The hybrid approach — entity-based and activity-based:

    Approach Example Why
    Entity-based P2P platforms get light prudential norms — basic entry-level criteria only, because the platform carries no credit risk itself; it merely brings lender and borrower onto one platform guaranteed MCQ
    Activity-based MFIs get uniform prudential norms across all MFIs despite small ticket sizes, to ensure borrower protection and responsible lending guaranteed MCQ

    17.11 The types of NBFC

    • NBFC-D (deposit-taking, a small select set) vs NBFC-ND (non-deposit-taking, 98–99%)
    • By activity: Housing Finance Companies · Infrastructure Finance Companies (IFC) · Core Investment Companies (CIC) · Microfinance Institutions (MFI) · Factoring companies · Mortgage Guarantee companies · Account Aggregators (AA) · P2P platforms · Standalone Primary Dealers (SPD)

    Each has distinct licensing norms and RBI guidelines.

    17.12 NBFC business models

    Model Examples
    Secured / asset-backed Vehicle loans, gold loans, loan against property, housing finance, equipment finance
    Unsecured retail and MSME No collateral; underwritten on income or cash-flow assessment; merchant cash advances
    Microfinance and livelihood Joint Liability Group (JLG) lending, individual micro-enterprise loans, rural livelihood loans
    Digital-first and embedded partnership App-based lending, embedded finance (converting a purchase into EMI inside a shopping app), BNPL, co-lending, credit-as-a-service
    Wholesale / institutional Large project and infrastructure finance — IFC, CIC, SPD — for national economic development (a dam, a highway)

    17.13 Why NBFCs will keep growing — the USPs

    1. ~85% of Indians of productive age work in the informal sector; formal-sector employment is very low. NBFCs are better suited to serve the self-employed, MSMEs and borrowers without formal income proof guaranteed MCQ
    2. Higher cost of funds than banks, but higher yields and net interest margins to investors
    3. Lean, focused operating models
    4. Ability to innovate — digital-first and "bionic" NBFCs using alternate credit underwriting and AI
    5. The aspiring and middle class — India's largest income segment earns ₹1.25–5 lakh a year; these are the largest drivers of consumption and productive credit outside the top 10 cities guaranteed MCQ
    6. Two-thirds of Indians are under 35 — a digital-first generation for whom "the branch" is a fading concept

    17.14 NBFC compliance obligations

    Capital adequacy · provisioning · income recognition · exposure limits (segment-wise and product-wise) · loan-to-value ratios · KYC and AML · the Fair Practices Code. The RBI can inspect, penalise and even cancel the registration.

    17.15 Challenges facing the NBFC sector

    Challenge Detail
    Compliance and customer protection Stricter capital requirements · advanced fraud risk monitoring · the SBR framework · strict grievance redressal
    Concentration risk Vehicle finance or microfinance monolines are exposed to interest rate risk and ALM mismatches — when stress hits, funding stops and repayments stop simultaneously
    Asset quality Rapid expansion into unsecured credit (personal loans, credit cards, microfinance) — lucrative but higher default risk. Discernible NPA uptick; MFI and unsecured personal loans under recent stress
    Cyber and operational risk Heavy reliance on digital interfaces → cyber threats, data breaches, operational disruption. NBFCs must go beyond minimum regulatory requirements for IT governance
    Contagion A concentrated model in vehicle/MFI/real estate/personal loans transmits to its lenders if the segment falters
    Oversimplified underwriting A worrying recent trend: underwriting simplified to speed up onboarding, storing up asset-quality problems guaranteed MCQ
    Undiversified liability profile Structural weakness in funding sources

    17.16 The way forward — the four strategic imperatives

    1. Diversify funding — capital markets, retail bond markets, securitisation, co-lending, digital debt platforms, institutional partnerships
    2. Governance — ethical leadership, fit-and-proper management
    3. Digital innovation — AI, big data, API-based integrations; AI-driven early warning and fraud monitoring
    4. Sustainable business model and business plan

    Plus continuous upskilling of staff and attention to data privacy and cybersecurity.

    17.17 NBFC–FinTech collaboration

    FinTechs supply what NBFCs lack in-house: - Alternative credit scoring models → instant decisions for borrowers with no formal credit history - Predictive analytics — historical + real-time data to forecast borrower behaviour and creditworthiness - eKYC, e-signatures, AI chatbots - API integration with credit bureaus, GST systems and payment gateways - Blockchain-based securitisation and digital debt markets

    How blockchain securitisation works: the asset to be sold is represented as a token on a blockchain platform; the sale/purchase is recorded on a tamper-proof distributed ledger that is the single source of truth.

    Its benefits: transparency and immutability · reduced cost and operational risk · elimination of intermediaries · enhanced liquidity through tokenisation · efficient creation of asset pools and issuance of certificates via smart contracts · greater reach and investor confidence. guaranteed MCQ — list of benefits RBI's stance: encourage innovation while protecting stability and consumers; require full disclosure of the Lending Service Provider (LSP) relationship on both the platform and the NBFC's website.

    17.18 NBFC–bank co-lending

    The framing to remember: "banks act as anchors, FinTechs act as accelerators." guaranteed MCQ| The bank provides | The NBFC provides | |---|---| | Low-cost funding and a larger capital base | Last-mile reach | | Regulatory legitimacy and customer trust | Local credit expertise and credit assessment | | Digital rails — UPI, NEFT, RTGS for disbursement and repayment | Collections capability | | Capital stability | An asset-light model for itself plus non-interest (commission) income |

    17.19 Consumer protection in the NBFC sector

    • Code of conduct aligned to the RBI's Fair Practices Code and Digital Lending norms
    • Consent-based data usage
    • Guardrails for ethical recovery practices and regulated use of third-party recovery agents — "There was a time when NBFCs could claim they were not responsible for the poor behaviour of a recovery agent. Not any more."
    • RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme applies to NBFCs with asset size over ₹100 crore or that are customer-facing guaranteed MCQ

    17.20 SROs — and FACE

    • FACE is the only RBI-recognised SRO for FinTech; SROs are recognised only by the RBI guaranteed MCQ
    • What an SRO does: sets and enforces industry standards on governance, responsible lending and consumer protection; acts as a regulatory bridge — feeding sector-wide insight and emerging risks up to the regulator and pushing compliance standards down to the industry; capacity-building among members

    17.21 Future of NBFCs

    Data-driven and hyper-personalised lending · open banking and Account Aggregator · AI tools · lower cost of acquisition, lower cost of servicing, lower response time · stronger risk management · expansion of partnership ecosystems like OCEN and ULI (Unified Lending Interface).

    1. The FinTech ecosystem and credit programs
    11

    (Mayank Jain, FinBox)

    18.1 What a "credit program" is

    Any program that helps the last-mile user get credit from a bank or NBFC. It runs on a mesh of technology + risk + underwriting + backend operations + a regulatory layer above all of it.

    FinBox is a B2B infrastructure company — it supplies the technology that banks and NBFCs plug into. Example of an innovative product: Equated Daily Installments (EDI) — collection on a daily rather than monthly basis. guaranteed MCQ

    18.2 The four regulators

    Regulator Domain
    RBI Central bank, banking regulator, and guardian of the nascent FinTech industry
    SEBI — Securities and Exchange Board of India Financial markets; primary and secondary markets; raising money from the public
    IRDAI — Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India Insurance companies, policies, consumer protection in insurance
    PFRDA — Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority Government and private pension funds

    18.3 The five generations of lending in India guaranteed MCQ — this whole list| Gen | Name | Description |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | Branch banking | Customers visit branches for everything — cash, cheques, even getting a passport form attested | | 2 | DSA-led distribution | The era of the phone call pitching a credit card or personal loan. DSA = Direct Selling Agent, a channel partner of banks and lenders | | 3 | Digital banking | Banks build websites and mobile apps; smartphone proliferation moves transactions online. Took over India's banking scene in the early 2000s | | 4 | Partnership lending | Banks partner with FinTechs and digital platforms — Flipkart, Amazon, Google — reaching consumers where they already spend their time | | 5 | Digital Public Infrastructure | Government-built protocols: Account Aggregator, OCEN, ONDC |

    18.4 The RBI's dual role

    Watchdog and player — a rare combination.

    Role What it involves
    Monetary authority Meeting inflation and growth targets; prescribing key rates. Raise rates → credit becomes harder/costlier → demand falls. Cut rates → credit demand rises as borrowers rush for cheaper credit guaranteed MCQ
    Regulator of the financial ecosystem Balancing innovation and growth against consumer protection. Three objectives: maintain public confidence · ensure continuity and stability · ensure last-mile access guaranteed MCQ (the three objectives)
    Institutional watchdog Licensing and compliance; controlling instruments and interest rates; issuing directions, master guidelines, rules on cybersecurity, compliance, payments and credit flow
    Cybersecurity and compliance Stress testing, audits, fraud protocols and reporting systems, advance warning of fraud attacks
    Frameworks KYC, KYB (Know Your Business), ensuring consumer data held by banks and lenders is updated, correct and verifiable

    The instruments split into two kinds: rate-driven and regulation-driven. guaranteed MCQ

    18.5 The five credit gaps and how technology closes them guaranteed MCQ — all five| # | Gap | The problem | The technology fix |

    |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Access gap | Lenders have no data to trust new-to-credit or informal borrowers | Alternative data — device data, behavioural data, social media signals — to build a holistic profile | | 2 | Speed gap | Traditional institutions are slow | Automated decisioning and instant payments | | 3 | Customisation gap | One product does not fit all | Bank statements, bureau data, purchase propensity → tailored products offered when the customer is most likely to need credit | | 4 | Reach gap | Banks cannot scale beyond physical branches | Digital underwriting and digital credit reach anyone anywhere | | 5 | Efficiency gap | Underwriting is slow, expensive, manual and error-prone — a single error can cost millions if disbursed to the wrong person | Digital processes, automated verification, structured underwriting keeping frauds and bad actors out |

    18.6 The enablers of the FinTech ecosystem

    Enabler What they do Revenue model
    DSAs — Direct Selling Agents Reach new customers by direct calling, emailing and SMS; serve tier 2/3/4 cities where physical branches are uneconomic Partner-led commission model — commission per sale, so a direct incentive to push particular products guaranteed MCQ
    TSPs — Technology Service Providers Plug-and-play APIs for underwriting, risk, fraud management, consumer onboarding and collections. Examples: FinBox, Karza, Digio Cut the time from idea to launch through sandboxes and platforms

    Net effect of enablers: reduce go-to-market time, reduce operating cost, ensure compliance and regulatory management.

    18.7 The seven FinTech business models and how each makes money guaranteed MCQ — match model to revenue source| # | Model | Products | Revenue |

    |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Lending | BNPL, personal loans, instant credit; direct partnerships, co-lending with NBFCs, P2P | Interest sharing, commission, fees | | 2 | Payments | UPI, POS, wallets, digital payments | MDR, customer acquisition, payment partnerships | | 3 | Investing | Stocks, mutual funds, advisory; aggregation platforms, robo-advisors, direct MF distribution | Partner commissions, management and advisory fees | | 4 | Insurance | Micro-insurance, bundled insurance, API-led distribution, embedded finance | Float income, premium, commissions | | 5 | Data / financial inclusion | QR-code-based lending, telco-based credit, Banking-as-a-Service | Subscriptions, usage, transaction fees, commission on disbursements | | 6 | Embedded finance | A non-FinTech app embeds a FinTech product — a loan inside a grocery app, BNPL on e-commerce, credit on ride-hailing and gig platforms | Revenue share, fee per transaction, fee on disbursal | | 7 | RegTech | Regulatory compliance for banks and lenders — KYC and fraud analytics; SaaS, plug-and-play APIs for consent and compliance | Licensing, subscription, integration fees, usage fees |

    18.8 Partnership lending

    The division of labour: - FinTechs and platforms source the customer, handle onboarding, run risk checks using data and technology - Banks and NBFCs approve the credit and disburse the loan

    Benefits: higher reach at lower cost for both sides; contextual, tailored products at the last mile.

    Commercials: revenue sharing — interest and fees are split. Some models include FLDG — First Loss Default Guarantee: if the customer defaults, the platform reimburses the lender for the first loss, letting the lender tweak policies without absorbing all the credit cost. guaranteed MCQ — expand FLDG The EY survey numbers — a very likely MCQ set:

    Statistic Figure
    Banks expecting partnerships to be very important by 2025 55% (vs 32% as of 2024)
    Banks saying FinTech partnership would matter within three years 36%
    Lenders using partnerships to enhance digital products and reach 95%
    Lenders using partners to manage critical processes (risk, onboarding) 87%
    Banks using partners to save money and accelerate implementation 86%
    Banks viewing digital banking and data analytics as ripe for partnership-driven transformation 64%

    18.9 The partnership playbook — the four players guaranteed MCQ| # | Player | Role |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | Anchor platforms | Where the credit product is hosted — a grocery, e-commerce or shopping app | | 2 | FinTechs / technology providers (e.g. FinBox) | Build the infrastructure and plumbing — APIs for underwriting, onboarding, digital credit origination, collections | | 3 | Banks and NBFCs | Provide the funding | | 4 | Consumers | The beneficiaries — tailored, contextual credit |

    Real examples: Federal Bank, SBM Bank, ICICI, HDFC partnering with Zomato, Swiggy, Amazon to launch credit-card programs, co-branded cards, and use-specific cards (fuel cards, BookMyShow vouchers).

    18.10 Vision 2030

    • India's FinTech market to reach $1.5 trillion – $2.1 trillion by 2030 guaranteed MCQ
    • AI/ML in credit decisioning and fraud prevention
    • CBDCs and token-based digital currency models
    • Hyper-personalised financial journeys using real-time data
    • India as a global API-led FinTech infrastructure leader, with ESG and sustainability focus
    • "The next decade is going to be all about intelligent, inclusive and interconnected credit."

    1. Samunnati — the agri value-chain model
    14

    (Anilkumar SG, Founder)

    19.1 The name and the mission

    Samunnati = Collective Growth, Collective Prosperity, Collective Elevation.

    Mission: "to make markets work FOR the smallholder farmer" — the deliberate replacement of "markets have been working OFF the farmer" with "FOR". guaranteed MCQ (the off → for switch)

    19.2 The core underwriting insight

    Formal lending relies on bank statements, tax returns, financial statements — "the rear-view mirror of past performance". In informal spaces like agriculture the information exists but not in the form formal markets can use.

    Samunnati's two-capital underwriting model: guaranteed MCQ| Capital | What it determines | |---|---| | Social capital | WHOM to lend to | | Trade capital (transaction history) | HOW MUCH to lend |

    The custodians of that information are the aggregators in the value chain — the players who move goods and cash. Samunnati works with them and aligns incentives.

    19.3 The hierarchy of farmer needs (inspired by Maslow) guaranteed MCQ — the order| Level | Need |

    |---|---| | 1 (base) | Access to finance — largely addressed by Jan Dhan Yojana and the microfinance movement | | 2 | Access to CUSTOMISED finance — e.g. a paddy farmer needs working capital for 3–4 months, a sugarcane farmer for 9–12 months, matched to the crop cycle guaranteed MCQ| | 3 | Access to better, more remunerative markets | | 4 | Egocentric needs — becoming a progressive farmer | | 5 (top) | Self-actualisation — organising the farming community into collectives / FPOs (Farmer Producer Organizations) or cooperatives |

    19.4 The AMLA approach guaranteed MCQ — expand the acronym

    Aggregation → Market Linkage → Advisory services

    • Aggregation — farmers doing the same economic activity come together; their buying and selling needs are homogeneous, so they gain bargaining power
    • Market linkage — has two dimensions: the transaction and the working capital. "Market linkages without working capital would be incomplete" guaranteed MCQ
    • Advisory — how to cultivate, how to engage with larger markets, how to serve your own members if you are a collective

    19.5 The evolution of the model — four stages

    1. Lender — credit-first, working capital propositions
    2. + Market linkages (after ~1.5 years) → Samunnati Agro Solutions, mainly post-harvest linkages
    3. + Institutional capacity building → Samunnati Foundation, building leadership, process strength and technology for farmer collectives
    4. → Ecosystem orchestrator — engaging with agri start-ups and incubators post-COVID

    The insight that drove stage 2 (the Calvert Foundation validation): in an agri value chain, internal players (input dealers, aggregators, buyers within the market) get priority in cash flows over external players — and formal financial institutions are external players. So Samunnati deliberately became an internal player in the value chain to de-risk its own lending. guaranteed MCQ Today Samunnati addresses three dimensions of access: finance, markets and technology.

    19.6 The dual-engine business model

    Engine What it does
    Finance engine Removes the working capital constraint so value chains operate at a higher equilibrium. Principal product: short-term unsecured working capital
    Trade facilitation engine Brings buyers and sellers together, handles counterparty risk / credibility of new buyers and sellers, with Samunnati participating in the transaction

    Why working capital is acute in agriculture: the seller wants money immediately, the buyer wants to pay later — and agriculture is seasonal and cyclical, so everyone wants to buy and sell at the same time.

    The cotton worked example — memorise the arithmetic: guaranteed MCQ - Cotton is bought and sold in only 3–4 months of the year but processed across all 12 - With a 30-day trade cycle, a seller can do only ~4 transactions in a season - If it takes about a week to assemble a truckload, then with adequate working capital the same seller can do 4 transactions a month = 16 a year - The point: working capital multiplies throughput non-linearly

    19.7 Customer segments

    Segment Who
    Agri enterprises Large agri enterprises plus the MSMEs/SMEs around them — dealers, distributors, retailers, vendors, suppliers
    Farmer collectives (FPOs) and their members Called the "SOUL of Samunnati" guaranteed MCQ

    19.8 The technology architecture

    Two platforms: AE Next (agri enterprises) and FPO Next (farmer collectives)

    Four marketplaces underneath them: guaranteed MCQ — name all four| Marketplace | Purpose | |---|---| | Input marketplace | Direct access to input manufacturers; educating farmers to distinguish quality products from spurious products | | Output marketplace | Post-harvest; farm-gate procurement for enterprises; FPOs list quality, quantity and location to discover new buyers | | Credit marketplace | Not just Samunnati's own lending — brings in banks with priority sector lending targets | | Consumer marketplace | Focused on FPOs |

    19.9 The FPO underwriting insight

    An FPO is a member-owned, member-operated entity. Underwriting it on balance sheet strength alone gives only part of the story — the balance sheet may lack strength, track record or vintage.

    "The real capital of an FPO is the loyalty of their members and their connect with their communities." guaranteed MCQ

    19.10 The agri paradox and sustainability

    The paradox: a bumper harvest crashes prices; a failed harvest raises prices but there is nothing to sell. The farmer is always at the receiving end of demand-supply vagaries in both quantity and price. guaranteed MCQ On climate: agriculture is both a contributor of greenhouse gases (GHGs) and a victim of climate change ← guaranteed MCQ. Samunnati has a board-approved ESG policy.

    19.11 The six categories of the agri ecosystem guaranteed MCQ — all six

    1. Inputs — everything that goes into cultivation
    2. Output / post-harvest — everything after the harvest
    3. Financial sector players — especially banks
    4. Government — schemes and enablers
    5. Research and resource institutions
    6. Start-ups, agri-tech and agri-FinTech — "the green shoots"

    Banks engage this ecosystem to meet priority sector lending targets, via Kisan Credit Cards, agri value-chain players, traditional underwriting, partnerships, or land as collateral.

    The closing metaphor: "All the digital public good interventions — ONDC, ULI, UPI — are the highways. We as providers of service have to create the products and services, which are the vehicles that run on those highways." guaranteed MCQ

    1. Banks and startups — ICICI Bank

    (Hitesh Sachdev, Head of Startup Engagements and Investments, ICICI Bank)

    20.1 The context

    • India is the third largest startup ecosystem in the world, with more than 118 unicorns guaranteed MCQ
    • Two approaches to staying ahead in technology: (a) build in-house with large tech teams, or (b) partner with startups. ICICI Bank does both. guaranteed MCQ

    20.2 The five focus areas for startup partnership

    Lending · payments · customer experience · risk management · enabler ecosystem

    The four predefined objectives: additional business revenue · process efficiency (removing bottlenecks) · improved customer experience on digital properties · risk mitigation.

    Method: a problem statement repository built by talking to business teams, then matched against startup solutions, sourced through VCs, micro-VC funds, angel investors, incubators, accelerators and investment banks.

"I need enterprise backing and guidance to turn it into a product" 3. "I need a customer who will buy the product" — ICICI Bank itself Plus debt capital and equity capital
    • "Like it takes a village to raise a child" — tie-ups with serial entrepreneurs who share their early mistakes, and with ONDC and NPCI who contribute problem statements
