ICICI built a supply chain finance layer on top — dealers submit no extra documents | | AdvaRisk | An AI layer on digitised land records — accessing and monitoring properties against which loans were given; large reduction in turnaround time | | CarDekho | Largest online new and used car sales platform; ICICI built car financing on its data and customer profiles | | Fingpay | Advanced biometric technology to digitise business correspondent operations in tier-3/4 towns — the financial inclusion agenda | | PropertyPistol | Largest residential broking house; ICICI APIs embedded so customers can avail home loans while choosing the property | | SATSURE | Satellite data analytics — from a farmer's lat-long and land perimeter plus 4–5 years of satellite data, assess crop yield and farmer income for lending. Also used to map collection agents' routes to the harvest season → >20% collections efficiency gain guaranteed MCQ| | Fable FinTech | Powers the remittance platforms Money2India and Money2World | | Credgenics | Collections digitisation and automation — predicts delinquencies ahead of time and automates post-delinquency outreach | | Swirepay | Reconciliation of UPI, IMPS and NEFT — millions of transactions quickly | | MyClassboard | White-label school ERP; ICICI added a finance layer for students, parents, teachers and the school | | EQL FinTech | Compliance services for SMEs — incorporation, patents, trademarks, copyright, GST and income tax filing; financial products embedded into it | | Workapps | Video banking — video KYC and personal discussions | | SAMA | Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) — bank and borrower communicate online and resolve through arbitration, avoiding slow, expensive court recovery | | Karza Technologies | APIs for KYC, authentication and fraud checks during onboarding | | Perfious | Bank statement analyser — real-time insights into customer banking transactions | | IMPACTSURE | Trade finance — an AI model reads applications and guarantees, automates workflow; 60% of bank guarantees now processed online guaranteed MCQ| | skit.ai | Voice bots automating the call centre in multiple vernacular languages | | devnagri | Enterprise-grade translation of customer documents | | Bureau ID | Onboarding and fraud checks at onboarding | | OnFinance | Gen AI for credit note automation and compliance automation against RBI/SEBI circulars | | Vunet | Observability stack — pinpoints the exact reason and location of transaction failures, reducing failure rates | | PRACTICELEAGUE | Legal contract automation and digitisation of agreements |

    20.5 The four challenges of partnering with startups guaranteed MCQ| # | Challenge | Mitigation |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | Data security | Heavy data sharing with startups → repeated audits of their platforms and products | | 2 | Survival factor | Startup success ratio is low → partner with startups that are well funded, backed by reputed investors, with an experienced founding team that knows the domain | | 3 | Cybersecurity | Are the startup's platforms adequately protected? | | 4 | Low compliance and governance maturity | A structural weakness of early-stage companies |

    ICICI's answer: a developer portal with 300+ APIs, with clear documentation, sample journeys, and published API uptime — startups value the uptime measurement because it lets them guarantee their own customers' experience. guaranteed MCQ (300+ APIs)

    20.6 Digital public infrastructure initiatives

    Initiative Detail
    IBDIC — Indian Banks' Digital Infrastructure Company 18 banks; builds public infrastructure in trade finance. Products rolled out: Innovation Hub and Invoice Discounting Hub (which checks for de-duplication of invoice discounting). Also building a fraud registry guaranteed MCQ (18 banks)
    ONDC ICICI a founding promoter; democratising digital commerce for small shopkeepers and traders
    Sahamati Founding member; the coordinator for Account Aggregation in India; ICICI is helping it obtain SRO status guaranteed MCQ

    The three principles behind all Indian DPI: interoperability, trust and consent. guaranteed MCQ

    20.7 Acceleration programs

    Program Partners / focus
    FinXcelerate With RBI Innovation Hub and BITS Pilani — FinTech-focused acceleration, mentorship and POCs with the bank
    Hackathon With GIFT City — problem statements in blockchain, trade finance and global remittance
    Women-focused exploration program With AWS Tech Sparks — promoting women entrepreneurship
    BeyondXcelerate Acceleration for early-stage startups

    Investment criteria: (1) quality, professional ethics, attitude and domain knowledge of the team; (2) is the problem large enough and the societal impact big enough; (3) compliance and regulatory adherence — plus thorough financial and legal diligence.

    20.8 Advice to startups partnering with banks guaranteed MCQ

    1. Find a champion inside the bank — a team whose job is to work with startups
    2. Understand the bank's technology stack — makes integration far easier
    3. Adhere to compliance and regulation — banks are heavily regulated
    4. Be mindful of data security — protection against data breaches

    1. Digital lending and credit risk management
    13

    (Rahul Patidar, Chief Risk Officer, Money View; previously Capital One; 15 years in lending)

    21.1 The four things that make lending a unique industry guaranteed MCQ — this whole list| # | Peculiarity | Explanation |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | Demand is not the problem | Consumers always want money. The lender chooses whom to approve. You are solving for the right type of demand, not for demand | | 2 | A completed sale ≠ success | In normal B2C you profit almost immediately. In lending you only profit when the money returns with interest — so the feedback loop is very long | | 3 | Verification adds deliberate friction | Normal product companies minimise friction; lending adds it — KYC, verification documents, auto-debit (NACH) setup — to prevent fraud | | 4 | Heavy regulation | RBI is the primary regulator, but politics, the public and the media all watch lending. This creates high barriers to entry |

    21.2 The unit economics of a loan — the worked example

    Memorise this whole table; it is the single most examinable numeric block in the guest modules. guaranteed MCQ| Item | Assumption / value | |---|---| | Loan amount | ₹1,00,000 | | Tenure | 2 years | | Interest rate to customer | 18% | | Lender's cost of capital | 11% | | EMI | ~₹5,000 | | Total interest (as % of loan) | ~20% | | Cost of funds | ~12% | | Processing fee | ~3–4% | | Credit loss | ~5.5% | | Operations cost (collections the key component) | ~1.5% | | Net margin to the lender | ~3.7% |

    Credit loss of 5.5% means ₹5,500 of the ₹1,00,000 does not come back on an average loan.

    Sensitivity to memorise: in a bad downturn credit loss can easily reach 10%; in a very good environment it can fall to 2–3%. Credit loss is the biggest variable in the lending business model. guaranteed MCQ

    21.3 The four levers of profitability guaranteed MCQ| Lever | The trade-off |

    |---|---| | 1. Pricing | Price higher → more revenue, but price good customers too high and they will not apply to you | | 2. Cost of funds | Dictated by the capital structure. Banks fund from cheap customer deposits; NBFCs further down the value chain pay more, because they serve riskier customers | | 3. Credit cost | Driven by underwriting — which customers, how much | | 4. Operations cost | Dominated by collections. Traditional lenders physically visiting borrowers is expensive |

    21.4 What credit underwriting actually is

    Deeply understanding the customer through: - Bureau data — their loan history - Financial data — how much is in the bank account, how much they save, where they spend - Behavioural data — where they invest, what they purchase, where they live

    Pricing is inseparable from underwriting: you estimate the probability of default and set the interest rate accordingly — risk-based pricing.

    21.5 Digital lending platforms — what they do

    They connect consumers with lenders. There is no single place where all lender types can be found, and different lenders have different risk appetites, so the platform's real function is to identify the right match between borrower and lender. guaranteed MCQ Their four advantages, mapped to the four levers:

    Lever Digital advantage
    Underwriting & pricing Access to rich digital ecosystem data; can invoke additional data inputs on demand — e.g. if bureau history is thin, pull banking data through the Account Aggregator framework guaranteed MCQ
    Collections Built digitally → smooth journeys, online contact instead of offline presence → cost falls as you scale
    Capital structure Bring a diverse set of users and match them to lenders with different risk appetites — so most consumers can get some product

    21.6 Division of roles: digital lending platform vs bank/NBFC guaranteed MCQ — a very likely table question| Digital lending platform | Bank / NBFC |

    |---|---| | Acquire customers — tell them the products exist, bring them onto the platform, onboard them | The final lender — its capital is at risk | | Leverage digital data for credit scoring, supporting the lender's underwriting | Sets all guidelines, policies, KYC process, NACH (auto-debit) setup and fraud checks | | Operational support — completing the onboarding journey, collections, customer service, auto-debit setup | Underwrites the user and makes the offer — decides who gets a loan and how much | | | Oversees collections and customer service for compliance and smoothness | | Revenue: sourcing fee on each lead, plus extra for collection support; may provide up to 5% credit loss cover (of ₹100 lent, guarantees up to ₹5 of losses) guaranteed MCQ| Revenue: owns the asset and the net interest margin |

    21.7 The three tiers of data available to digital lenders guaranteed MCQ| Tier | Data sources |

    |---|---| | Available to app-based lenders | Credit bureau data (available to all lenders, but digital lenders build their own scoring frameworks on top) · SMS — with user permission, messages from banks and commerce institutions · bank statement data (similar content to SMS) · device data — with permission, which applications are on the device | | Available in a web-based context | The application form (also usable in app journeys) · third-party data aggregators · partner data — e.g. a commerce platform's own scoring data used in your underwriting | | Available only on the 2nd/3rd loan | Collections data — is the customer paying by auto-debit, debit card or UPI? When? How much delay? · Repayment refresh — bureau data taken as a time series, refreshed monthly, building a trend of the customer over time |

    The point of the whole list: the wealth of data is the crux of what digital lenders bring to the ecosystem, and it becomes richer the longer the user stays and the more products they take.

    21.8 From data to a credit decision

    Machine learning models — logistic regression, XGBoost or similar — convert data into a probability of default for each user. guaranteed MCQ (name the two algorithms) That probability rank-orders users from low risk to high risk. Then: - Low-risk users: more exposure, more of your eggs in that basket, more returns - High-risk users: higher interest rate to compensate for the risk and protect margins

    This is risk-based pricing — an old methodology; what is new is the granularity of segmentation digital lenders can achieve.

    21.9 Collections — where digital lenders add the second-biggest value

    • Payment experience — if paying is easy, users pay whenever they have money. This raises you up the "payment hierarchy" (which creditor gets paid first) guaranteed MCQ
    • Tech-enabled reminders and calling — reach out at the right time, save cost
    • Prioritisation — "not all users are likely to pay you in the next two days. If you know who will, your operations effort can be streamlined."
    • Customisation — some borrowers respond to email, some to WhatsApp, some to a phone call; a digital lender optimises which medium, what time, which day, and even which due date per customer

    21.10 The three pillars of credit risk management guaranteed MCQ| # | Pillar | Meaning |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | Maintaining resilient unit economics | Profitability must survive a credit-worsening environment — 2008, COVID, or any macro event where consumers struggle. Can the model sustain elevated credit risk and at least not lose money? | | 2 | Ensuring capital buffer | Enough capital that a bad year does not become a liquidity problem | | 3 | Managing losses within an agreed appetite | Set in combination with the board and the CEO — how much credit loss the institution is willing to run |

    "Credit risk management is not just looking at here and now, but understanding that business cycles and credit cycles come and go, and ensuring the business can survive those difficult periods."

    21.11 Money View — the company timeline guaranteed MCQ| Year | Milestone |

    |---|---| | 2014 | Founded as a personal finance manager app; vision: a personalised product for middle-income India | | 2017 | Launched personal loans, partnering with a few NBFCs | | 2019 | Received its own NBFC licence — to diversify capital sources and serve users who would struggle to borrow elsewhere | | Today | Pan-India, servicing almost all pin codes; one of the largest customer bases in the FinTech industry |

    Financial Inclusion and Regulations

    Financial Inclusion and Regulations — Complete Exam Guide

    Prof. M. S. Sriram · Intermediate Module

    Course shape: the concept of inclusion → why exclusion happens (credit and savings separately) → the role of financial services → the two market systems (informal vs formal) → the interest-rate conundrum → the two great innovations (SHG and Grameen/JLG) and their limits → policy interventions in two phases → the regulatory map → FinTech opportunity, JAM, and the "howevers".

    Exam note: this course is built on paired contrasts — informal vs formal, embeddedness vs codified embedding, trust vs fear/consequences, SHG vs JLG, phase 1 vs phase 2 policy, savings vs credit. Almost every MCQ will be "which of these belongs to X and not Y." Learn the contrast tables.

    1. What financial inclusion is
    7

    1.1 The four types of inclusion likely MCQ| Type | What it gives you |

    |---|---| | Political inclusion | Equality and the right to vote | | Economic inclusion | A way to carry out your livelihood | | Social inclusion | Equal opportunity in society | | Financial inclusion | Entry into the banking and financial sector |

    1.2 The "where do you keep your money?" test guaranteed MCQ

    The course opens by testing six or seven places to store surplus cash against three criteria: is it SAFE? · is it RELIABLE (will you get it back when you want)? · does it earn INTEREST?

    Where you keep it Safe? Reliable? Interest?
    In a box at home Possibly Yes No
    With a trusted person Yes Yes No
    Lent to a trusted person Yes Possibly not (timing mismatch) Usually no
    With a shopkeeper Possibly Possibly No
    In a chit fund / informal savings scheme Possibly Not really — "they're called blade companies" — not under a strong regulator Some return
    In a BANK ✓ ✓ ✓

    $$\boxed{\textbf{Only the BANK checks ALL THREE boxes. That is financial inclusion.}}$$

    The borrowing version tests three different criteria: easily available? · friendly repayment terms? · reasonable interest rate? — the money lender is easily available but has stringent terms and very high interest; the bank checks most boxes except easy availability ("banks do not easily lend — they do a lot of paperwork").

    1.3 The definitions guaranteed MCQ

    Rangarajan Committee on Financial Inclusion (set up 2005):

    "A process of ensuring access to financial services, timely and adequate credit for vulnerable groups such as weaker sections and low-income groups at an affordable price/cost."

    RBI's definition:

    "The process ensuring access to appropriate financial products and services needed by all sections of society in general and vulnerable groups such as weaker sections and low-income groups in particular, at an affordable, fair and transparent manner by regulated mainstream institutional players."

    Note the term "financial inclusion" was itself coined in 2005.

    1.4 The four RBI-specified inclusion products guaranteed MCQ

    1. A savings-cum-overdraft account (can go into negative balance)
    2. A pure savings account, ideally with a recurring or variable recurring deposit
    3. A REMITTANCE product to facilitate direct benefit transfers / money transfers
    4. Credit products for enterprise — the General Purpose Credit Card, Kisan Credit Card, artisan credit card

    1.5 Regulated vs informal — the two analogies memorable MCQ material

    "If there is a loan or a savings product, do you go to the RBI or do you go to the POLICE STATION?" A police station handles molestation, theft, traffic violations — a financial complaint is just one more; the RBI is a SPECIALISED institution with rules specific to that type of transaction.

    INFORMAL contract = the AUTO RICKSHAW FORMAL contract = the BUS
    Every ride is negotiated unless the meter is flagged The fare from A to B is pre-specified
    Escalating a complaint is cumbersome — it goes to the police You can identify the conductor and complain to the transport office

    What regulation actually buys you: banks are explicitly prohibited from visiting customers' homes between sunset and sunrise, from threatening customers, and from coercive mechanisms — a money lender faces no such rule.

    1.6 The unequal-contract argument likely MCQ

    "In a contract between the bank and the customer, the customer is always the more vulnerable party and the bank always the powerful one." The institution has bureaucracy, a balance sheet, institutional support, a panel of lawyers; the individual bears the full cost of litigation alone. Therefore the more vulnerable the customer, the stronger the protection the law must provide.

    1.7 The four financial-sector regulators guaranteed MCQ| Regulator | Domain |

    |---|---| | RBI | Banking and financial services (savings and credit) | | SEBI — Securities and Exchange Board of India | Capital markets — stock market, bond market, mutual funds | | IRDAI — Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India | Insurance | | PFRDA — Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority of India | Pensions |

    The scope note: the RBI definition of financial inclusion covers only savings and credit. A broader definition would also include social security (pensions), risk cover (insurance), and market-based products (mutual funds, SIPs) — this course focuses on the RBI-defined services.

    1.8 Why FinTech students must understand inclusion

    • The poor and vulnerable are the segment that benefits MOST from technological innovation — technology can handle small-ticket transactions and transaction trails that human intervention cannot
    • The services the poor need are NO DIFFERENT from those the rich need — savings, loans, pensions, housing, education. Only the SCALE is different. Therefore they can be served on market principles if products are designed appropriately
    • C. K. Prahalad's "Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid" ← guaranteed attribution MCQ: the poor need the same products in smaller packets and smaller use cases; because there are so many poor, the right approach can serve them profitably without subsidy. Prahalad's examples: shampoo sachets, the Jaipur Foot, Aravind Eye Care (cataract operations)

    1. Why the poor are excluded — CREDIT
    4

    2.1 The lender's two questions guaranteed MCQ

    1. ABILITY to repay — an objective assessment
    2. WILLINGNESS to repay — a second-order, BEHAVIOURAL, SUBJECTIVE judgement; "you look at the face, the interaction with the customer — it's like an interview process for a job". The course focuses on ability, not willingness.

    2.2 Why banks cannot assess the poor ← the core argument

    "Not only should I convince MYSELF that the customer can repay — I have to prove it to the SYSTEM, because the memory of the bank is not individual memory; it is the memory of the PAPER."

    The three things a bank asks for: 1. IDENTITY — Aadhaar, voter ID, driving licence — so the system knows who and where you are 2. A TRACK RECORD — passbook, balance sheet, account statement, salary statement — proving future repayment ability from past transactions 3. COLLATERAL — gold, house, car — encashable if you default

    Why the poor fail all three ← guaranteed MCQ: - Their transactions happen informally and in cash, so there is no transaction trail - The farm-labourer worked example: agreed wage ₹300/day × 20 days = ₹6,000 earned; the landlord deducts ₹1,000 for food and pays part in grain, leaving only ₹3,000 in cash — and even that is unrecorded. "You have nothing to show." - They have no collateral — and if they had a tractor and jewellery, would they even count as poor? - Even their assets are unusable: "we can't tie the goat in a bank and feed it"

    2.3 The two informal lending models guaranteed MCQ| | EMBEDDED model | COERCIVE model |

    |---|---|---| | Basis | The lender knows everything about you because he is part of the same community | The lender needs NO information — only a threat of consequences | | Analogy | An IPL cricket team travelling together for 3 months — you know who wakes late, who is a spendthrift, who is disciplined, without any investigation | "Parking a jeep in front of the customer's house"; taking away the door of the house; public shaming | | How it works | "By the time you go to the money lender, he already knows you're borrowing for the wedding — the whole village knows" ⇒ no invitation card needed | Consequences are deliberately not articulated — "the borrower keeps second-guessing" — like telling students "there will be consequences" without saying what they are | | Flexibility | Very flexible — uneven instalments, calibrated terms, high rates — because the lender is answerable only to himself | Standardised threat |

    Nuisance collateral ← likely MCQ: money lenders take the ration card, Aadhaar or voter ID. "It's not a collateral at all — you can't sell it. But getting a duplicate ration card is so bureaucratic and expensive that it's easier to repay and get the card back." Howard Jones's study in Dungarpur district, Rajasthan: people pledge utensils and small jewellery — not for market value but sentimental value, so they always come back.

    Why money lenders don't grow big ← likely MCQ: "their growth is restricted to the number of people they know." A study of a money lender's diary in Anantapur district shows they lend only within their own community or profession, operating in a niche market at a very high interest margin.

    2.4 The other reasons for exclusion likely list MCQ| Reason | Explanation |

    |---|---| | Mismatch in the credit ladder | The lender wants to fund growth and diversification (there's a track record); the vulnerable borrower needs consumption smoothing | | High TRANSACTION COSTS | The same paperwork is needed for a ₹10,000 loan and a ₹1,00,000 loan; a short-duration loan spreads that cost over less time; small transactions consume the same human time; more transactions to recover ⇒ "small customers are HIGH-COST customers" | | RELATIONSHIP vs TERMINATING transactions guaranteed MCQ| Buying a soap is a TERMINATING transaction — done. A loan is a RELATIONSHIP transaction — it terminates only when the last instalment is repaid, so you cannot walk away. Each recovery instalment is even SMALLER than the small loan | | Perceived high default | Uneven cash flows ⇒ higher default likelihood | | The interest-rate discourse | The only way to cover the above is a high rate — but "the big person gets 10% and you charge the poor 15% — you're sucking the blood of the poor" ⇒ it is easier not to lend at all than to lend at a cost-covering rate |

    1. Why the poor are excluded — SAVINGS likely MCQ
    1

    Savings should be easier (the customer is GIVING you money) — but they are not: 1. You are exposed to the whim of the customer — ₹100 one day, ₹1,000 the next, ₹50 the day after. Unlike a loan's predictable EMI, this upsets cash flow and adds accounting cost 2. You CANNOT pass the servicing cost back — with loans you can charge a risk premium (10% vs 15%), but "you can't say a large depositor gets 10% interest and a small one 6%". Deposit rates are pre-specified 3. Only BANKS (and cooperatives) may take savings — the RBI restricts deposit-taking because "there might be people who collect savings and run away." This limits the number of players, and, by limiting them, creates a large unregulated market — Ponzi schemes, shady companies, chit fund companies that disappear overnight

    The consequence ← the closing point of the course: "we have yet to see a huge TECH-LED BREAKTHROUGH INNOVATION in the arena of SAVINGS for the poor."

    1. The role of financial services
    2

    4.1 The core function

    $$\textbf{Managing the MISMATCH between the FREQUENCY of cash INFLOWS and the frequency of cash OUTFLOWS.}$$

    Inflow patterns likely MCQ| Person | Inflow pattern | |---|---| | Salaried employee | Once a month | | Farm worker | A token amount weekly, then the accumulated wage as a lump sum at the end of the harvest season (sometimes partly in grain) | | Agriculturist | Only cash OUTFLOW (sowing, irrigation, fertiliser, pesticide) until a lump sum at the harvest sale. Same for poultry — invest in day-old chicks, receive on culling | | Daily wage worker / auto driver | Per ride / per day | | Windfall | Inheritance, sale of assets, retirement benefits, lottery |

    Outflow patterns: daily (commute, snacks) · weekly/monthly (provisions, vegetables) · monthly bills (electricity, water, telephone, rent) · quarterly/annual (school fees, books, uniforms) · sporadic (holiday, pilgrimage) · social functions (birthdays, deaths, puja, weddings) · asset purchases (TV, fridge, car) · house construction · and periods when you CANNOT earn (retirement, illness, hospitalisation).

    4.2 The product that matches each need likely MCQ| Need | Product |

    |---|---| | Money needed soon, with multiple withdrawals | Savings bank account | | A planned, dated withdrawal for a known purpose (school fees in June) | Recurring deposit or a non-withdrawable/fixed deposit maturing then | | Managing adverse, unpredictable events (health, vehicle damage) | INSURANCE | | Income in a non-working period | Pension / retirement / provident fund |

    1. The two market systems guaranteed MCQ (this is the central table of the course)
    3

    SAVINGS CREDIT
    INFORMAL system runs on Embeddedness + TRUST Embeddedness + FEAR
    FORMAL system runs on Transaction cost + RELIABILITY Transaction cost + CODIFIED EMBEDDING + CONSEQUENCES

    Why "trust" for savings but "fear" for credit ← the exam-worthy nuance: in savings, the institution is more powerful than the saver, so the SAVER must trust. In credit, the lender is more powerful than the borrower, so the lender must be able to instil fear to extract repayment.

    Individual trait = TRUST. Organisational trait = RELIABILITY.

    5.1 The informal saver's sources of trust

    The local shopkeeper (static, regular transactions, gives provisions even without cash) · friends and relatives (trust learned "the hard way" by repeated withdrawal) · strangers with strong REFERRALS ("this is why chit funds and informal savings groups thrive") · solidarity/informal savings groups — chit funds, beeshees, self-help groups where 8–10 or 10–15 people pool money.

    5.2 Who the informal lender is likely MCQ

    Someone with a disproportionate amount of influence over the borrower: higher caste or higher standing, or a person of institutional power — a policeman, a priest, a school teacher, a postmaster, a dominant political person. They have regular cash flows and surpluses.

    5.3 CODIFIED EMBEDDING — the key formal-sector concept guaranteed MCQ

    "The formal system must replicate what a money lender does — but put that knowledge into PAPER and convert it into some kind of SCORE." "Even if the bank manager knows the customer, that knowledge must be committed, so that a manager who does NOT know the customer can take the same decision from the data."

    The money lender does not score — he knows. The bank cannot know — so it must score.

    5.4 Consequences in the formal sector

    • Mortgage / hypothecation — the borrower keeps the right of USE but loses the right to TRANSACT IN or SELL the asset. (Vehicle loan: you submit the registration certificate; on default the bank sells the vehicle and returns the residual.)
    • SOCIAL COLLATERAL — group guarantee, public shaming — used very effectively by microfinance institutions. "Things acceptable 10 years ago are no longer acceptable now."

    1. Protecting savers likely MCQ
    1

    The state protects savers by rationing who may accept savings: - Only BANKS may offer savings. Bank licences go only to those with deep pockets, adequate capitalisation, provable reliability, and scale, and they are closely and regularly supervised - NBFCs — even large ones — are PROHIBITED from taking savings, because they are not supervised in the same depth - DEPOSIT INSURANCE ← guaranteed MCQ: banks pay a premium to the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation of India (DICGC); savers are insured up to ₹5 lakh

    6.1 State interventions to push savings to the poor

    • Branch licensing policy — a metropolitan branch licence only if you open branches in unbanked/rural locations
    • Specialised institutions — regional rural banks, and later payments banks and small finance banks
    • Institutions run on MUTUALITY — cooperatives and self-help groups. "If you are operating in a closed loop — you save your money and one of you borrows it — there is internal oversight, so heavy external oversight is not needed"
    • The BSBD / "No Frills" account ← likely MCQ — Basic Savings Bank Deposit account: a stripped-down version for entry into the banking system. "You may not need foreign exchange access or payment system access". Jan Dhan accounts are simply BSBD/No Frills accounts under a new name

    1. The interest-rate conundrum guaranteed MCQ (the arithmetic is examinable)
    3

    7.1 The vegetable vendor example — memorise the numbers

    Item Value
    Loan taken ₹1,000, but the money lender cuts ₹50 interest UPFRONT ⇒ she receives ₹950
    Vegetables bought ₹950
    Gross revenue at end of day ₹1,250
    Margin ₹300 (≈ 30% on ₹950)
    Interest paid ₹50
    Daily interest rate ≈ 5.3%
    Annualised (× 365, NOT compounded) ≈ 1,921%

    The conclusion: "a daily return of 30% makes a daily interest of 5% perfectly reasonable." ₹50 out of a ₹300 margin leaves her ₹250.

    7.2 The three fallacies of the interest-rate discourse guaranteed MCQ

    1. Annualisation — "interest rates are ALWAYS articulated on an annual percentage rate basis, even when the loan is for a DAY." Comparing a very short-duration unsecured loan with a high-margin business against a long-duration secured loan with a transaction trail is unfair — they are completely different businesses and economics
    2. Interest is a naked GROSS MARGIN ← the best conceptual MCQ — "the principal comes back as is, so the interest IS the gross margin. In no other business is the price of the product a surrogate for the margin. Nobody writes on a packet of chips 'I'm making a gross margin of ₹8'."
    3. Reframing as a FEE — "if you call the ₹50 a FEE for use of a service, like a bus charge or rent, it doesn't look usurious at all"

    7.3 When high interest rates ARE and ARE NOT acceptable ← memorise

    Acceptable NOT acceptable
    Small transaction sizes · short repayment frequency · short overall loan tenor When there is COMPOUNDING — a 15–20 year housing loan at 18–20% is untenable because the principal reduces very slowly

    7.4 How the informal sector "cracked" articulation likely MCQ

    "The informal sector NEVER says 1,920% per annum. It says 5% per day or 3% per month — i.e. it articulates the rate on the frequency of repayment, which is the right thing to do." But formal transparency and regulatory requirements force the APR, which is precisely why formal institutions find it hard to enter this market.

    7.5 Why the model doesn't scale

    If the vendor doubles her turnover she needs another push cart and another person — and the original model never costed her own wage or rent. A temperature-controlled vegetable franchise has cold storage, stock-keeping and accounting software ⇒ much lower margins, but also a much lower interest rate on a longer-duration loan against physical infrastructure. Similarly, the money lender's model doesn't scale — how many people can he know personally?

    1. Innovation 1 — THE SELF-HELP GROUP (SHG) MODEL guaranteed MCQ
    4

    A very Indian model. Ideas emerged around 1985, rollout began around 1987. Promoted by NGOs frustrated at not getting mainstream finance for women's livelihood activities. The first SHGs were called "credit management groups." It works on cooperation and mutual benefit, and is focused on women.

    8.1 The design

    • 10 to 20 women, organised by an external agency called the PROMOTER (typically an NGO)
    • Members must be HOMOGENEOUS — same community, locality or area — "basically, they should know each other well"
    • They meet weekly (or fortnightly/monthly) and each pools a fixed savings amount. Worked example: ₹100 × 20 women = ₹2,000 per week**
    • The pooled GROUP FUND is available for members to borrow. The group decides who gets it, using embedded knowledge — "exactly like the money lender who knows everybody in the village"
    • Next cycle: another ₹2,000 plus repayments ⇒ the fund grows
    • Crucially, they RECORD everything — books of accounts, minutes of meetings ⇒ after 25 weeks they have a verifiable transaction trail

    The innovation in one line ← guaranteed MCQ: "They married the methods of the INFORMAL system to the recording requirements of the FORMAL system."

    8.2 The 1992 RBI landmark guaranteed MCQ

    In 1992 the RBI permitted SHGs to open bank accounts — even though a group has no identity and no address for KYC. The RBI used a reading of the Companies Act 1956 clause allowing an ASSOCIATION OF PERSONS of 20 OR FEWER people without incorporation.

    This is why SHG design caps membership at 20. The group signs an inter-se agreement on plain paper authorising 1–3 members to sign on its behalf.

    What it enabled: a safe place to park the group fund (otherwise it sits in a member's house — risk of theft or absconding) · interaction with banks improved the group's own bookkeeping · the bank now has its own record of how the group manages money, so it can lend to the group and leverage the group fund.

    8.3 Interest inside an SHG likely MCQ

    • No interest is paid on the weekly savings — "too complicated to calculate, the amounts are small, and the women save not for returns but for a safe place and to leverage a larger loan later"
    • Interest on loans is HIGH — deliberately set slightly BELOW the money lender's rate. Three justifications: (1) it must beat the alternative, since the bank was never actually an option; (2) it instils repayment discipline; (3) the accrued profit goes back to the group fund, which belongs to the same women — they are paying interest to themselves
    • It also creates self-filtration — "only serious people will borrow if the rate is high"
    • Accumulated profits are distributed as a bonus or as utensils/gifts during the festive season

    8.4 The EIGHT differences: traditional approach vs SHG guaranteed MCQ| # | Traditional approach | SHG approach |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | INSTITUTION-driven (a bank or cooperative pushes credit down) | COMMUNITY-based — informal groups; banks approached only for residual borrowing | | 2 | Oriented towards MEN, large livelihoods, agriculture | Fundamentally focused on WOMEN | | 3 | CREDIT FIRST — belief that the poor cannot save | SAVINGS FIRST — the poor CAN save; let them build their own capital and transaction trail | | 4 | Production/livelihood purposes only; consumption loans scoffed at | Tolerant of CONSUMPTION loans — e.g. the Rice Credit Loan in Andhra Pradesh (c. 2000–2006): buy the month's rice upfront, repay over the month ⇒ food security ⇒ better wage negotiation and nutrition | | 5 | PHYSICAL collateral — gold, tractor, property | SOCIAL collateral — group guarantee/solidarity; "social norms are much more powerful than legal norms" | | 6 | Belief that the poor cannot afford high rates ⇒ subsidised interest | Rates benchmarked to the INFORMAL sector; high rates are fine — they bring seriousness and discipline | | 7 | Transactions inside the bank's premises (banks also store cash, so they don't vacate) | Transactions in the open — temple premises, a school, someone's house; "they just needed a place for 15–20 people to sit for an hour" | | 8 | WALK-IN, random transactions — the counter clerk doesn't know what the customer wants | PLANNED transactions — fixed day, fixed time, fixed amount, 20 transactions aggregated into 20–30 minutes ⇒ great efficiency |

    1. Innovation 2 — THE GRAMEEN / JOINT LIABILITY GROUP (JLG) MODEL guaranteed MCQ
    5

    Drawn from the Grameen Bank of Bangladesh, started mid-1970s (1976) by Professor Yunus. Replicated in India in the late 1990s — i.e. about a decade AFTER the SHG model. Also women-oriented and also uses group guarantee — but fundamentally different.

    9.1 The structure guaranteed MCQ on the numbers

    $$\textbf{5 members per GROUP} \;\times\; \textbf{8 groups} \;=\; \textbf{40 members per CENTRE}$$ Members sit in 8 rows of 5, one behind the other. Each member pays her equal weekly instalment to the group leader → centre leader → credit officer. "It is very regimented. It doesn't tolerate any deviations."

    9.2 The 16 Decisions likely MCQ

    Recited every week and checked. Decision 1: "We shall follow and advance the four principles of DISCIPLINE, UNITY, COURAGE and HARD WORK in all walks of our lives."

    The rest cover: bring prosperity to our families · repair/build our homes · grow vegetables all year, eat plenty and sell the surplus · plant seedlings during the plantation season · keep our family small, minimise expenditure, look after our health · educate our children · keep our children and environment clean · build and use pit latrines · drink tube-well water, or boil it or use alum · take NO DOWRY at a son's wedding and give none at a daughter's · not practise child marriage · inflict no injustice nor allow it · collectively undertake bigger investments for higher incomes · always be ready to help each other · restore discipline at any centre where we see a breach · take part in all social activities collectively.

    The exam point: "While it looks like a social empowerment oath, every decision reinforces the repayment discipline of the loan" — health ⇒ no lost work days; small family and no dowry ⇒ no financial shock; unity ⇒ joint liability; clean water and latrines ⇒ fewer illnesses ⇒ more working days. (The only one that isn't directly repayment-linked is educating children — a long-duration project against short-duration loans; it is "facilitative".)

    9.3 SHG vs JLG — the master comparison guaranteed MCQ| Dimension | SHG | JLG / Grameen |

    |---|---|---| | Role of the external agency | PROMOTER — organises the group; the group manages its own finances | PROVIDER — forms the group AND directly dispenses credit | | Who borrows | The GROUP borrows from the bank, then lends to members ⇒ the member borrows indirectly | The agency lends to each INDIVIDUAL directly; the group exists only for guarantee | | Is the group an entity? | YES — autonomous, with a name, president, secretary, treasurer and bank account. A defunct group is isolated and doesn't affect others | NO — just a mechanism for transacting. A problem feeds back into the organisation's system and can SPREAD | | Norms | Evolved BY the group | Dictated by the PROVIDER (the 16 decisions were decided by Grameen Bank) | | Savings | SAVINGS FIRST | CREDIT ONLY in India — because the providers are not banks and are statutorily prohibited from taking savings. (In Bangladesh savings are possible) | | Loan amount | Based on need, decided collectively using embedded knowledge — 10,000 to one, 3,000 to another | UNIFORM — same amount, same instalments, same loan cycles for everyone; increases uniformly in the next cycle | | Group size | 10–20 | 5 per group, 40 per centre | | Default | Examined on circumstances — "she had a health event this week, that's genuine, we'll tolerate it" | ZERO DEFAULT POLICY — very low tolerance; another member pays or they go to the house. "It is extremely difficult NOT to repay a JLG loan" | | Underlying principle | TRUST and deep personal knowledge | COERCIVE — "there are CONSEQUENCES" | | Speed of formation | Slow — needs forming → storming → norming → performing, typically ~6 months | Fast — externally standardised: sit in 5×8, recite the oath, pass the group recognition test, get a loan |

    Similarities: (1) both deal only with women · (2) both use group meetings for transaction aggregation · (3) both document transactions · (4) both build a credit history · (5) both use a group guarantee.

    9.4 What happened to the two models guaranteed MCQ

    $$\textbf{SHG} \;\rightarrow\; \textbf{adopted by the STATE} \qquad\qquad \textbf{JLG} \;\rightarrow\; \textbf{adopted by the MARKET}$$

    • SHG: because it is democratic, participative, consultative and based on mutuality, it became the flagship of the Government of India's National Rural Livelihoods Mission (NRLM)
    • JLG: standardised and easily replicable, its growth outpaced the SHG's. Initially run by not-for-profits (so the interest-rate debate went away — "we reinvest the profits for the community"), it then converted to for-profit structures because grants dried up and NGOs couldn't raise enough capital. The operating model stayed intact; the ownership model changed. Later, new market-based players entered, some listed on the stock market; some became banks (Bandhan Bank) or small finance banks
    • Regulatory recognition: the RBI NBFC-MFI category allows registration and tolerates a somewhat higher interest rate, given the higher last-mile cost

    The paradigm shift ← the one-line summary: inclusive finance moved from a MANDATORY REQUIREMENT to a MARKET OPPORTUNITY — "from a supply-side space pushed by the state and not picked up, to one where markets have taken to it."

    1. Limitations of the two models likely MCQ
    1

    SHG limits: no sophisticated or long-horizon savings products (no pensions, no long fixed deposits) · cracks when loan amounts get BIGGER or durations get LONGER, because it rests on inter-personal trust. "If a friend asks for ₹5,000 you'd give it; at ₹50,000 you'd think twice even if you trust them." Both models are good bridging mechanisms but do not deepen the client relationship and do not meet the full bouquet of inclusion services (savings, loans, insurance, pensions).

    1. Policy interventions — PHASE 1 (institutional) guaranteed MCQ
    4

    $$\textbf{Phase 1 = INSTITUTIONAL intervention (independence} \rightarrow \textbf{1991)} \qquad \textbf{Phase 2 = POLICY \& REGULATORY (1991 onward)}$$

    The distinction: in Phase 2 new institutions still appear — but they are MARKET-driven, not STATE-driven.

    11.1 Cooperatives (the 1950s)

    • The All India Rural Credit Survey Committee — set up 1954, reported 1956 — recommended "STATE PARTNERSHIP WITH COOPERATIVES": the state provides promotional/seed capital but the cooperatives are ultimately autonomous
    • ~100,000 cooperatives were set up for ~600,000 villages ⇒ usually a cluster at block level covering 6–15 villages
    • Result: the informal sector's market share fell from over 80% at independence, with cooperatives capturing about 20–25% of rural indebtedness in two decades — "it did move people from informal to formal"

    The three-tier cooperative structure + a fourth refinance tier likely MCQ $$\textbf{Primary Agricultural Credit Cooperative Societies (PACCS)} \rightarrow \textbf{District Cooperative Banks (DCBs)} \rightarrow \textbf{State Cooperative Banks} \rightarrow \textbf{refinance (ARDD of the RBI, later NABARD)}$$

    Why cooperatives failed — four reasons: 1. Credit-only focus, no savings ⇒ highly leveraged, deposits had to be raised from urban areas by DCBs and state cooperative banks ⇒ members had no "skin in the game" 2. Single-product concentration risk — agriculture only. "If it doesn't rain and 80 of 100 borrowers default, the cooperative goes bust" 3. LOAN WAIVERS ← likely MCQ — "a third party enters a bilateral contract. Once a loan is waived, next time I'll wait for another waiver rather than repay" ⇒ destroys repayment discipline 4. Lack of professionalism and technical capability (They flourished in the first two decades partly because of the Green Revolution and a strong agricultural extension team, which later petered out.)

    11.2 Bank nationalisation guaranteed MCQ on the numbers| Round | Year | Banks nationalised |

    |---|---|---| | First | 1969 | 14 major private banks | | Second | 1980 | 6 more banks |

    The logic: private banks were not furthering the inclusion agenda — not lending to agriculture, not operating in rural areas. State ownership gave both strategic control (through the stake) and OPERATIONAL control (through ministry orders), and profit was not the primary concern because "the state will recapitalise you."

    Accompanying policy: priority sector lending targets · the LEAD BANK SCHEME · the BRANCH LICENSING POLICY — "a licence for an urban or metropolitan branch only if you open FOUR branches in rural areas" (the 1:4 rule).

    11.3 Regional Rural Banks guaranteed MCQ

    The intent: a blend of the LOCALISATION of cooperatives and the PROFESSIONALISM of banks, with a limited area of operation.

    Fact Value
    RRBs at launch 196 — roughly 1 RRB per 3 districts (India had 600+ districts)
    Ownership split Government of India 50% · SPONSOR BANK (a public sector bank) 35% · State government 15%
    RRBs today 28–29 — roughly 1 per state

    What RRBs achieved that branch licensing could not ← the exam point: the 1:4 rule fixed the RURAL:URBAN ratio but NOT the REGIONAL disparity — banks simply opened rural branches in areas where they already worked, i.e. south and west India. RRBs, headquartered in 196 different districts, actually penetrated the central, eastern, north-eastern and northern regions.

    Why RRBs weakened: "nobody's child" — the union government had 50% but no bandwidth; the sponsor bank (35%) appointed the chairman and general manager on deputation but didn't engage in detail; the state had only 15%. Then profitability considerations took over — "half of 196 are not making profits" — leading to amalgamation down to one per state, i.e. replacing the DECENTRALISATION argument with a PROFITABILITY and return lens rather than an INCLUSION lens.

    1. Policy interventions — PHASE 2 (policy and regulatory, 1991 onward) guaranteed MCQ
    1

    The defining feature: "post-1991 the government has NOT PROMOTED ANY NEW INSTITUTION itself. It has only performed a FACILITATION function."

    Year Intervention
    1994–96 ~10 new private sector bank licences granted. The 40% priority sector target was imposed on them, but the BRANCH LICENSING requirement was REMOVED for ALL banks ("open branches wherever you want")
    1998–99 LOCAL AREA BANKS — RRB-like banks with a limited area of operation, only one branch in the district headquarters, all others rural, higher PSL targets. 10 in-principle licences → 6 went live → 4 survived → only 2 still operate. "An experiment that did not gain traction"
    2005 Branch licensing REINTRODUCED — but REVERSED: instead of "4 rural branches to earn a metro branch", the rule became "25% of your branches must be in unbanked rural centres" (because adequate penetration had happened but white spaces remained)
    2010 The Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis — too many MFIs in one state, over-leveraging of borrowers, defaults, borrower distress and suicides ⇒ regulatory clampdown
    2011 The MALEGAM COMMITTEE (chaired by Y. H. Malegam) ⇒ creation of the NBFC-MFI category
    2015 10 SMALL FINANCE BANK licences and 11 in-principle PAYMENTS BANK licences

    The 2010 IPO: SKS Microfinance's IPO — "much celebrated as a commercial success of an inclusive finance agenda."

    The regulatory-enthusiasm warning ← likely MCQ: "When markets start performing, the regulatory architecture tends to encourage them, and in its enthusiasm sometimes forgets to notice that a bubble is building up. That happened both with the Indian MFI sector and with the US SUBPRIME sector in 2008 — though the MFI crisis was not so deep."

    12.1 Small finance banks

    • 8 of the 10 licences went to erstwhile MICROFINANCE INSTITUTIONS (NBFCs doing plain-vanilla JLG lending) — "now they got access to savings as well"
    • 72–73 applications were received
    • One merged with another ⇒ 9; RBI has since issued 2 more ⇒ ~11 today

    12.2 Payments banks

    • 11 in-principle licences → 3 surrendered before setting up → 1 surrendered later → 2 merged ⇒ 5 payments banks operating today
    • "Like the local area bank experiment, the payments bank experiment has not been a great success."

    1. The regulatory map guaranteed MCQ (memorise every number)
    3

    Institution Priority sector lending target Branch requirement Other key rules
    Commercial banks 40% of the book (with sub-targets for agriculture — within which small and marginal farmers — and MSMEs — within which micro enterprises; plus women and weaker sections) 25% of branches in unbanked rural centres Public sector banks carry a soft obligation to open Jan Dhan / BSBD accounts
    Small finance banks 75% 25% in unbanked rural locations Lower start-up capital but HIGHER capital adequacy (riskier loan book). 50% of the loan book must be loans of ≤ ₹25 lakh (₹2.5 million). May SELL but NOT BUY PSL certificates for the difficult sub-targets
    Regional rural banks 75% Yes —
    Urban cooperative banks Yes Yes No agriculture target — mainly micro and small enterprises
    Payments banks — — May take deposits up to ₹2,00,000 (originally ₹1,00,000). PROHIBITED FROM LENDING. Deposits must be placed entirely in government securities
    NBFC-MFIs — — See §13.2

    13.1 Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSLCs) guaranteed MCQ

    "If Bank A achieves only 38% and Bank B achieves 45%, B can SELL its overachievement to A." Only the OBLIGATION is traded — the underlying portfolio is NOT traded. The marketplace is the RBI's e-Kuber platform. If the whole banking system falls short and no PSLCs are available, the shortfall must be invested in bonds of NABARD or SIDBI at a low interest rate — "a carrot and stick policy."

    13.2 NBFC-MFI rules guaranteed MCQ on the numbers| Rule | Value |

    |---|---| | Minimum capital | ₹10 crore (₹100 million) | | Qualifying assets | 75% of loans must be microfinance loans | | Definition of a microfinance loan | A loan to a household with annual income below ₹3,00,000 (₹3 lakh) | | Customer protection cap | Total instalments across ALL lenders must be LESS THAN 50% of the borrower's income | | Credit bureau | Must UPLOAD borrower data to ALL credit bureaus (there are four, e.g. CIBIL), while taking membership of one for downloads ⇒ codified data at the SECTOR level, not just the institution level | | SRO membership | Mandatory. The two RBI-recognised SROs are MFIN (Microfinance Institutions Network) and Sa-Dhan |

    What SROs do: protect customer interests, set guardrails, ensure members don't exploit customers. They can take punitive measures through a collective member decision but do not have the RBI's punitive powers — they can complain to the regulator.

    13.3 Other regulated players in the inclusion ecosystem

    Wallets and payment apps (must register with the RBI) · P2P lending platforms · Account aggregators · Credit information companies (CIBIL and three others).

    1. The FIVE LEVELS of banking technology guaranteed MCQ
    3

    Level What happened Customer-facing?
    1 Digitisation of transaction recording — "computerisation". Slow in India because of union resistance over feared clerical job losses. Done branch by branch, decentralised, using "automatic ledger posting machines" as a euphemism for standalone computers — "computerisation by stealth" NO — entirely inward-facing
    2 Interoperability with other branches — for the bank's own benefit: inter-branch settlement, remittances, clearing houses, cheque truncation. Centralised servers, dial-up and VSAT NO — better housekeeping and data, but no consumer interface
    3 New private sector banks licensed (~1994), with modern technology as a licensing condition, becoming a benchmark for public sector banks and RRBs. The IDRBT (Institute for Development and Research in Banking Technology, an autonomous RBI institute) developed a SWITCH ⇒ the first consumer-facing interface: interoperable ATMs YES — ATMs
    4 Mission-mode completion of computerisation, driven also by international ANTI-MONEY-LAUNDERING requirements and Basel norms. By ~2010 the whole Indian banking system was computerised (core banking solutions, then RRBs). NEFT, RTGS, IMPS enabled seamless remittance. Customers could log in, check balances and transfer Partly — but only from a computer terminal, and the interface was ONE-SIDED: you could withdraw cash from an ATM, but depositing cash was still assisted
    5 UPI — mobile-based cash transactions. The IDRBT switch was corporatised into NPCI, which built UPI and BHIM (Bharat Interface for Money) YES — fully

    Why deposits are harder than withdrawals ← nice conceptual MCQ: when dispensing, the bank controls the currency type and denomination; when collecting, it must handle fake currency, soiled notes, and mismatches between what the customer entered and what was actually deposited.

    14.1 The Y2K "blessing in disguise" memorable MCQ

    Because dates were stored as DD-MM-YY to save premium storage space, 1999 → 00 would compute as −99 years. "Since India had NOT computerised early enough, this legacy problem did not affect it to a great extent. Sometimes being a laggard in adopting technology is good."

    14.2 The three inflection points for FinTech guaranteed MCQ

    1. DEMONETISATION (2016) — took cash out of the economy and forced people into digital payments. (Note: cash in circulation relative to GDP has NOT fallen, but the NUMBER of digital transactions has exploded.)
    2. RBI's ZERO INTERCHANGE / no-transaction-fee policy on UPI — "the entire architecture — your mobile, wallet, bank, the counterparty's bank and wallet, the telecom network, the internet, the API providers, the switch — is being borne by the economic system. Banks are possibly bleeding." This is the most important policy inflection point. (Contrast: cards carry an MDR — Merchant Discount Rate paid by the merchant.)
    3. Private equity and venture capital flowing in, even without a demonstrated viable business model — because "DATA IS THE NEW OIL"

    1. The JAM Trinity guaranteed MCQ
    3

    $$\textbf{J} = \textbf{Jan Dhan} \qquad \textbf{A} = \textbf{Aadhaar} \qquad \textbf{M} = \textbf{Mobile}$$

    15.1 J — Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY)

    • Introduced August 2014; goal: every household in the country has at least one account in a public or private commercial bank
    • The paradigm shift ← the exam point: "Until now the policy push was to set up a bank and make it accessible — a SUPPLY-SIDE solution. It never PULLED people into the bank. PMJDY was the first initiative to get DEMAND into the banking sector."
    • It persuaded banks to go BEYOND brick and mortar to customers' houses to run account-opening campaigns
    • Two SHG elements are embedded in it: (1) it starts with SAVINGS; (2) the bank goes to the customer
    • The account: a zero-balance No Frills / BSBD account + a debit card (usable at any ATM or POS) + insurance loaded onto the debit card by NPCI + an OVERDRAFT facility subject to regular transactions and balances
    • The carrot and the stick ← likely MCQ: the STICK was a target imposed on (mostly public sector) banks; the CARROT was that DIRECT BENEFIT TRANSFERS would flow through these accounts, generating transactions

    Why no other country could copy it ← good conceptual MCQ: PMJDY needed 50 years of prior building blocks — (1) the BUSINESS CORRESPONDENT (BC) regulation allowing agents to do withdrawals, deposits, account opening and Aadhaar work near the customer; (2) the branch network built by the 1:4 licensing rule (BCs themselves need a nearby branch to settle); (3) the levels 1–5 technology investment. (BCs are often part-time, co-located with photocopying shops or common service centres.)

    15.2 A — Aadhaar

    • Enrols the biometrics of residents and DE-DUPLICATES them, giving each a unique identity
    • Captures 10 fingerprints, iris, photograph, date of birth, address ⇒ a number
    • The crucial advance: earlier IDs (voter card, PAN, passport, driving licence) were NOT UNIQUE and NOT DE-DUPLICATED
    • Identity verification became technological — no attested photocopy; put your thumb on a scanner, hit the Aadhaar database, get yes/no ⇒ accounts can be opened OFFSITE by business correspondents

    The one weakness ← guaranteed MCQ: Aadhaar is a good IDENTITY document but a WEAK ADDRESS-PROOF document. Identity is permanent; address changes with migration and transfers. Aadhaar has no independent mechanism to update or verify an address — it relies on an existing address document. Current rule: if your claimed address matches the Aadhaar address it counts as address proof; on a mismatch you need an alternative document.

    15.3 M — Mobile, and the M-PESA contrast guaranteed MCQ| | M-PESA (Kenya) | UPI (India) |

    |---|---|---| | What moved | Only the MESSAGE — an encrypted message from sender's phone to recipient's | The MONEY itself, bank account to bank account | | Last-mile settlement | PHYSICAL CASH, dispensed by a mobile airtime/data agent for a fee | No physical cash anywhere in the chain | | Embedded in banking? | NO — a standalone network parallel to banking | YES | | Mode | Assisted | Self-serve | | Analogy given | The old MONEY ORDER — deposit at one post office, the message goes, the other post office settles | — |

    Why India could go further: "we came in a little late, but we came in with a big bang — converting the mobile itself into a wallet/bank."

    The mobile-as-POS point ← likely MCQ: a card reader costs ₹4–5,000 and does nothing but talk to the bank. A mobile is bought for calls, photographs, movies and maps — banking is merely an app on top, which is why acceptance scaled.

    15.4 What JAM + DBT achieved

    De-duplication ⇒ NO GHOST BENEFICIARIES · one Aadhaar can be mapped to only one benefit account · DBT added transactions to the bank, building a transaction history usable for overdrafts and loans · it familiarised the customer with the bank and its technology — "Jan Dhan DRAGGED the customer into the bank; DBT made them come NATURALLY."

    15.5 The five "HOWEVERS" guaranteed MCQ

    1. Beneficiary IDENTIFICATION was unchanged — Aadhaar de-duplicates identity, but deciding who is below the poverty line, a student, a widow, a farmer is done outside the Aadhaar system, so corruption there continues
    2. Jan Dhan is an INDIVIDUAL account, but some benefits are at the HOUSEHOLD level (e.g. rations) — Aadhaar has not mapped households to a common household ID
    3. BIOMETRICS FAIL for the poorest — manual workers' fingerprints are worn; cataract affects the iris
    4. CONNECTIVITY in remote areas — poor signal, poor net connections to the Aadhaar server
    5. Most transactions still happen in ASSIST MODE, and women lack AGENCY over the instrument — "a family of 4 or 5 poor people has ONE mobile", so the head of the family operates the account. "Women say: I have an account, but my husband or son operates it — I don't have a smartphone, I can't do UPI."

    1. FinTech's opportunity — the embedded model, digitised guaranteed MCQ
    3

    16.1 Why technology can serve small tickets

    "The most significant costs in technology are BACKEND INFRASTRUCTURE — CAPITAL costs: a tower, a server, a program, a switch. Once you have that architecture, the technology is AGNOSTIC as to whether you're doing a ₹1,00,000 transaction or a ₹10 transaction."

    Therefore the COLLATERAL BENEFICIARY of banking technology has been the small borrower and small saver.

    16.2 The three uses of transaction data

    1. Better and more customised products from data patterns over a month/six months/a year
    2. ANTICIPATING customer needs — "this person might be in a liquidity bind, so I'll offer a product now" (rather than merely triggering off a large transaction with "convert this to an EMI?")
    3. Going beyond transaction data — into what the course calls a grey zone

    16.3 The mobile as "intrusively embedded" the best conceptual MCQ in this course

    "The mobile phone is MORE EMBEDDED than the money lender. The money lender looks at what is happening externally to you; the mobile has access to far more."

    What a phone can capture: location and movement · shopping patterns · savings patterns · photographs · WhatsApp and other group memberships · the type and tone of conversations (profiling you as aggressive, passive, careful, risk-taking) · watch history · listen history · political orientation.

    $$\textbf{EMBEDDED} = \textbf{being around and watching you.} \qquad \textbf{INTRUSIVELY EMBEDDED} = \textbf{"you take it to your BED and your BATHROOM."}$$

    16.4 The four RED FLAGS guaranteed MCQ| # | Concern | Detail |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | PRIVACY | "When I eat a dosa I'm not conscious that data is being collected. A month later I get a message: 'last time you had a dosa here, want to go back?'" — data shared involuntarily used to push products predictably | | 2 | No HUMAN element / no moral fibre | A bank officer can say "you are technically eligible, but looking at your history, please don't take this loan." Technology has a single-pointed purpose and will PUSH products. Also, algorithms are built on and REINFORCE STEREOTYPES, so exceptions are always at the receiving end | | 3 | RECOURSE mechanisms | Automated bots, "press one, press two"; nuance in the customer's pain point is lost and escalation to a human is extremely difficult | | 4 | A potential SCANDAL or misstep | Exactly as in the 2010 microfinance crisis: standardised models ⇒ over-lending ⇒ deep indebtedness ⇒ debt trap ⇒ (with a consequences-based model) social boycott, threats and suicides ⇒ regulatory clampdown. "Every three or four years there is a crisis in the inclusive finance sector" |

    1. The FinTech ecosystem players likely MCQ
    4

    Player What it does
    Payment aggregators Provide the bridge/interface settling technology-enabled last-mile payments — mobile-to-mobile and internet transactions — plus redressal when a transaction fails
    UPI See §17.1
    Wallets CLOSED LOOP — usable only with one service provider (e.g. a cab aggregator's wallet). OPEN LOOP — usable anywhere. Advantage: transactions don't hit the bank server once the wallet is topped up; and you can cap the balance, protecting against the "FAT FINGER" error ("you meant ₹100 and pressed ₹1,000")
    Account aggregators Technology companies licensed to pull data from multiple sources with the customer's authorisation and present a consolidated financial history — "instead of running from pillar to post photocopying statements"
    ULI — Unified Lending Interface "As revolutionary as UPI" — a loan at the click of a button, based on data pulled from multiple sources, LENDER-AGNOSTIC, with no prior relationship required
    OCEN — Open Credit Enablement Network The RBI describes it as digital public infrastructure in the lending space, unlocking critical financial, non-financial and ALTERNATE data for informed credit decisions
    P2P lending platforms See §17.2
    Credit information companies CIBIL and three others — codified information from multiple sources

    17.1 UPI — the key facts in this course guaranteed MCQ| Fact | Value |

    |---|---| | You need only the recipient's MOBILE NUMBER — not the 12–16-digit account number, bank, branch or IFSC code | ✓ | | Transaction fee to the customer | ZERO — mandated by policy. No transaction charge, no GST cut | | Average UPI transaction size | ~₹1,800 | | Share of transactions under ₹500 | ~80% | | Share of transactions under ₹200 | ~75% (mobile-to-mobile) | | UPI vs RTGS/NEFT | UPI has the MAXIMUM number of transactions — but NOT the maximum VALUE. "Big money moves through RTGS and NEFT; small money moves through UPI" | | The stack | UPI is an architecture/stack built by NPCI; NPCI's own app on it is BHIM — Bharat Interface for Money; Paytm, PayU and others ride on the same stack |

    17.2 P2P lending platforms — why they haven't taken off likely MCQ

    • The analogy: like a stock market — borrowers and lenders on a common pedestal, matched when bid meets offer
    • But lending is far more nuanced than trading shares — you must judge whether the borrower will repay and at what rate
    • The platform does NOT take responsibility for non-repayment — "the lender parts with money into a black box"; the platform gives information but not risk-based support
    • The FLOAT problem: if lender money is not matched to a borrower, it lies idle in the platform's hands — "in a way it is equal to putting savings into a company", unless it is ring-fenced in an ESCROW account
    • Most existing platforms do salary-based lending, not inclusion lending

    17.3 The danger in ULI/OCEN likely MCQ

    "If the data shows a person upgrades his mobile every 6 months, you know he has a weakness for gadgets — so whenever a new model arrives you offer a loan and entice him before he had even thought about it. You are touching their vulnerability, and that leads to a DEBT TRAP."

    1. The course's closing assessment likely MCQ
    1

    Where innovation HAS happened Where it HAS NOT
    CREDIT — both technological and non-technological (SHG, JLG) SAVINGS — "we have yet to see a huge tech-led breakthrough innovation in savings for the poor"; cash still cannot be deposited without assistance
    PAYMENTS and settlements INSURANCE, PENSIONS and other social security — "innovations have been limited; you can compare products, but buying and servicing entirely on technology is still some way off"
    Transaction processing and data crunching

    The two savings-driven initiatives — PMJDY and the SHG programme — do NOT rely much on technology (PMJDY only for Aadhaar-based enrolment).

    The two phases of innovation: 1. Phase 1 addressed INFORMATION ASYMMETRY through groups, social collateral and contracts (SHG, JLG) 2. Phase 2 addressed the same issues through BETTER CAPTURE OF TRANSACTION DATA — digital-technology-led, gathering data involuntarily across a universal stack

    The two unresolved issues: customer VULNERABILITY and customer PRIVACY.

    The closing metaphor ← likely MCQ: "When we go to a doctor, the doctor depends on technology — MRI, X-ray, blood test. But ultimately she makes the decision in her mind after looking at your eyes, checking your pulse, looking at your tongue. It is not only technology, but TECHNOLOGY-AIDED SUPERIOR DECISION MAKING." Technology takes away human judgment and goes on stereotypes; human judgment can break stereotypes.
