    Securities and Markets

    Securities and Markets — Complete Exam Reference

    Course faculty: Prof. G. Sabarinathan (IIM Bangalore) Recommended texts (he names them explicitly — could be an MCQ): - Prasanna Chandra, Investment Analysis and Portfolio Management, 7th edition, McGraw Hill - Zvi Bodie, Alex Kane, Alan Marcus, Investments, 13th edition, McGraw Hill

    How to use this file. This course is arithmetic-heavy. Every worked example in the transcript is reproduced here with its exact numbers, because MCQ writers lift worked examples verbatim. Anything marked ← guaranteed MCQ is a number, formula, threshold or definitional distinction. The Quick-fire revision table at the end collects every formula and number in one place.

    The single sentence Prof. Sabarinathan says you must be able to give if woken from sleep:

    "The value of any asset is the present value of its cash flows."

    1. What securities markets are and why they exist
    3

    1.1 The basic definitions

    Term Definition
    Securities market The marketplace where companies and governments raise capital directly from investors, without an intermediary
    Issuers Companies and governments that issue securities — the securities are proof of having raised money
    Investors Those who provide capital and receive the securities as acknowledgement
    Security (formal) "The receipt which establishes the investor's right to receive funds back on agreed terms, to ensure funds are used for the purposes and in the manner originally intended, and to receive any interim payments such as interest or dividends"
    Security (working definition) A tradable financial asset guaranteed MCQ

    The key distinction that gets tested: a bank fixed deposit is a financial asset but NOT a security, because the rules of the deposit say only the depositor can receive the money back — it cannot be traded even if there is a willing buyer. A Maruti Suzuki share is a security, because you can sell it on the exchange and find plenty of buyers. guaranteed MCQ

    1.2 Real assets vs financial assets

    Definition Examples
    Real asset Any asset that can produce a tangible or intangible good or service Land, buildings, machines, intellectual property (his example: a lecture is an intangible output of a real asset)
    Financial asset A claim (once literally a piece of paper) representing the owner's right to receive cash flows Bank fixed deposit, shares/stocks, bonds, loans on a bank's books

    Note: the term "real" is the economists' usage — it does not mean other assets are unreal.

    1.3 The four benefits securities markets offer

    # Benefit Detail
    1 Potentially limitless capital Crores of individuals plus institutions participate
    2 Wide variety of maturities Commercial paper for as little as 3 months up to long-term bonds of 30, 50, 60, 90 years guaranteed MCQ
    3 Regulation Ensures issuers behave responsibly toward investors
    4 Liquidity You can encash a bond or share before maturity when you need cash
    5 Risk transfer Mechanisms to pass risk to someone willing to take it for a fee

    1. The Indian financial system
    11

    2.1 The three-box schematic

    SAVERS → INTERMEDIARIES → INVESTORS

    Careful with the vocabulary — this is a deliberate trap: in this schematic, "investors" means companies and governments that put money to work in real or financial assets, not the savers. guaranteed MCQ| Box | Who is in it | |---|---| | Savers | Households (earn more than they spend) · Companies (retained profits are savings) · Institutions (e.g. an insurance company collecting premia for health, accident, fire and death, which must invest to meet future claims) | | Investors | Firms (plant, machinery, factories, offices, patents, brands) · Government (law and order, healthcare, roads, infrastructure) | | Intermediaries | Banks · Mutual funds · Insurance companies · NBFCs guaranteed MCQ — the four named intermediaries|

    Note: "One of the biggest borrowers from the banking system in India is the government itself."

    2.2 Why intermediaries exist — the two economic reasons

    Reason Explanation
    1. Search and information costs Savers and investors would spend enormous time, effort and money finding and evaluating each other. Economists call these search and information costs guaranteed MCQ — know the term
    2. Diversification The wiper-blade example: put all ₹5 lakh in one wiper-blade manufacturer and you carry the whole risk; split it across five different businesses (wiper blades, ice cream, plastic buckets, a wedding hall, a car dealer) and the risk falls. A bank does both the evaluating and the diversifying for you

    2.3 Financial markets — the three types and three functions

    Types of market in a financial system: stock/securities exchange · currency market · commodity markets (crude oil, gold, copper, wheat, cotton).

    The three functions of a financial market ← guaranteed MCQ — he says the textbooks list five or six more, but names these three:

    # Function Explanation
    1 Bringing together large numbers of buyers and sellers → price discovery The orange-vendor example: with one buyer and one seller neither knows whether ₹100/kg is fair. With many, the true or intrinsic value is discovered
    2 Providing liquidity Converting an asset into cash — without incurring significant cost or delay. (Selling a ₹10,000 FD for ₹8,000 is liquidity, but at a 20% cost, so it doesn't count)
    3 Reducing the cost of transacting Cutting search and information costs

    2.4 The Urban Company example — the participants in a public issue

    Urban Company (formerly Urban Clap), a start-up of about 12 years, funded first by founders, then family and friends, then venture capital funds, decided to go public — meaning to list its shares on a stock exchange so they can be freely bought and sold.

    The IPO facts from the Economic Times advertisement: guaranteed MCQ| Item | Value | |---|---| | Price band | ₹98 – ₹103 per share | | Fresh offer (new shares, money to the company) | ₹4,720 million = ₹472 crore | | Offer for Sale (existing shareholders selling out) | ₹14,280 million = ₹1,428 crore | | Total issue size | ₹19,000 million = ₹1,900 crore | | Issue opens | 10 September | | Trading starts | around 17 September | | Listing on | BSE and NSE |

    Fresh offer vs Offer for Sale — a definitional distinction worth memorising: a fresh offer raises new money for the company; an offer for sale (OFS) simply lets existing shareholders convert their shares into cash. guaranteed MCQ

    2.5 The intermediaries in a public issue

    Intermediary What they do
    Merchant banker / BRLM (Book Running Lead Manager) The specialist advisor who knows how to take a company public — "like a Sherpa on a mountaineering expedition". It is NOT optional — the law requires every company going public to appoint one, so that companies do not make mistakes that harm small investors. Urban Company appointed four guaranteed MCQ
    Bankers to the issue Collect application money, keep it safe, set it off against shares allotted
    Registrars and Share Transfer Agents (RTAs) Transfer shares from seller's name to buyer's name
    Stock exchange The trading venue. BSE and NSE are the two biggest; there are three more that are relatively active
    Brokers Indian law requires that shares can be bought or sold ONLY through a licensed stock broker — even between two family friends guaranteed MCQ
    Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) Investors outside India who own Indian shares
    Underwriter Puts in funds in case of a shortfall in the public issue. (If the issue wanted ₹19,000 million but investors only wanted ₹17,000 million, the underwriter makes up the difference) guaranteed MCQ
    Custodian Safe-keeps shares and bonds for large institutional investors
    Depository The electronic bookkeeper for security ownership. India has a duopoly of exactly two: CDSL (Central Depository Services Limited) and NSDL (National Securities Depository Limited) guaranteed MCQ
    Credit rating agency Professionally assesses credit quality — whether a company has the capacity to repay what it borrows, as promised, on time. Works for a fee
    Clearing Corporation Guarantees that a seller gets paid and a buyer gets the shares

    2.6 Primary vs secondary market

    Market Definition
    Primary market Where securities are sold for the first time by an issuer. The first such offering is the IPO (Initial Public Offering); a later one is the FPO (Follow-on Public Offering) guaranteed MCQ
    Secondary market Where already-issued securities are bought and sold between investors, giving liquidity

    They are not physically different markets — they are parts of the same securities market.

    2.7 Clearing, settlement and T+1

    Term Definition
    Trading The process of buying and selling
    Clearing Determining who owes what and to whom in a trading transaction
    Settlement Fulfilling the obligations of the two parties to a transaction
    Clearing Corporation The institution guaranteeing both legs, so no investor loses faith in the market

    India settles on a T+1 basis — sell today, get cash tomorrow. "Which is as good as it gets in any market in the world." Many countries still take longer. guaranteed MCQ

    1. Trading vs investment vs speculation
    2

    3.1 The four-dimension comparison guaranteed MCQ — this whole table| Dimension | Investment | Speculation |

    |---|---|---| | Horizon | Longer — a year or more | Shorter — a few months, weeks or even days. Intraday / day traders buy in the morning and sell in the evening | | Risk tolerance | Lower | Higher | | Return expectation | Content with a return in line with the risk accepted; prefers less risky businesses | Willing to invest in high-risk businesses | | Basis of decision | Sound research into fundamentals | Hearsay and market psychology / sentiment — "the market is trending up, let's buy" |

    His business-risk examples: an advertising agency is inherently riskier than manufacturing steel or cars, because its revenue can vanish if clients switch. E-commerce is riskier than car-making, because a customer switches e-commerce sites with one click but does not switch from a Maruti to a Kia on a whim. guaranteed MCQ

    3.2 Three types of return-seekers

    Type Character
    Investor Careful with money, weighs pros and cons, takes risk commensurate with return
    Speculator Also careful, but a higher risk appetite (his example: buying gold today expecting 10% in one month)
    Gambler Loves risk for its own sake; knows the odds in a casino are loaded against the player and may lose the entire capital

    His point: these are not fixed identities. The same person can wear different hats at different times, setting aside a small part of capital for the "adrenaline rush".

    1. Classifying financial markets — the four bases
    5

    Basis Categories
    1. Type of money raised Debt (lending) vs Equity (ownership). "All these instruments — convertible debt, preference shares, convertible preference shares, debentures — fall into one of these two essential buckets." guaranteed MCQ
    2. Maturity Money market: less than 1 year. Capital market: more than 1 year guaranteed MCQ
    3. Stage of issue Primary vs Secondary
    4. Timing of payment Cash / spot market (pay now) vs Forward / futures market (pay later)

    Money market examples: the Overnight Call Money Market — a bank short of money at end of day borrows for one night from another bank (or, if no bank will lend, from the RBI) and repays the next day. "It's a huge market in India." Also commercial paper (3–6 months). guaranteed MCQ Capital market examples: a 5-year corporate bond; Urban Company's IPO (shares are treated as capital market instruments because the intent is long-term holding).

    4.1 Debt vs equity — the fundamental contrast

    Debt (lending / bonds) Equity (shares)
    Payments Interest + principal, both contractually assured. Indian law enforces it even without a written contract No obligation to pay anything. Dividends only if the company is profitable and the board so decides
    On losses "Sorry, that's not my problem — you promised." Lender can go to court Investor bears the loss, potentially down to zero
    Ownership No ownership relationship — "your job is to give money, our job is to give it back; the relationship cannot go beyond that" Fractional ownership of the company — share in both risk and reward
    Repayment Repaid on schedule Permanent capital — repaid only via a buyback of shares
    Suitable for Businesses with predictable cash flows. Start-ups rarely raise loans because sales and profits are unpredictable guaranteed MCQ Any business, especially those without predictable cash flow
    Fallback if cash flow fails Lender can seize and sell the assets (e.g. a housing loan lender takes a mortgage on the house) None

    The definition to memorise: A BOND IS A TRADABLE LOAN. A bank deposit is a non-tradable loan to the bank. guaranteed MCQ

    1. Bonds
    18

    5.1 The variants of debt

    Bonds · debentures · commercial paper · notes · fixed deposits — all borrowing mechanisms used by corporates and by central and state governments.

    5.2 The Indian bond market

    Issuer Instruments
    Central Government Treasury bills (T-bills) — maturity less than 1 year; long-term government bonds — 10, 20, 30, 40 years guaranteed MCQ
    State Governments Bonds of differing maturities
    Government-owned companies e.g. Indian Railway Finance Corporation
    Private sector e.g. HDB Financial Services (HDFC's financial services subsidiary)

    Why so many maturities? Because issuers match the maturity to the requirement — short-term borrowing for, say, festival advances to state employees (Pongal, Bihu, Baisakhi, Onam); long-term borrowing for highways and hospitals.

    5.3 The BHEL bond story (his running example — memorise the setup)

    BHEL = Bharat Heavy Electricals, a heavy engineering company making boilers and power generation equipment, needing working capital because a boiler takes many months to build and sell.

    Item Value
    Amount to raise ₹500 crore
    Split into 50 lakh bonds of ₹1,000 each guaranteed MCQ
    Face value ₹1,000
    Allotment date 1 April 2021
    Coupon 8% p.a., payable annually
    Maturity 5 years → redemption 31 March 2026
    Redemption At par (₹1,000)
    Listing BSE and NSE
    Document The prospectus, running into hundreds of pages

    5.4 The six bond terms you need in order to value a bond guaranteed MCQ| Term | Meaning |

    |---|---| | Face value / par value | The principal amount of the loan | | Allotment date | The date you officially become the owner and your rights begin. Decided by the board of directors | | Coupon (rate) | The interest rate. Called "coupon" because in the old American market investors received a book of coupons to surrender at a bank on each interest date guaranteed MCQ — know the etymology| | Periodicity of coupon | Quarterly / half-yearly / annual (monthly is technically possible but uncommon) | | Maturity | When the principal comes back | | Redemption amount | Usually the par value, but can be more or less depending on the terms — always disclosed upfront |

    5.5 Bond valuation — the formula and the worked example

    Value of a bond = PV(coupons) + PV(face value), both discounted at the opportunity cost of capital.

    Because the coupons are a constant cash flow at constant periodicity, they are an annuity, so:

    V = Coupon × PVIFA(r, n) + Face Value / (1 + r)ⁿ

    where PVIFA(r, n) = 1/r − 1/[r(1+r)ⁿ]

    The BHEL base case: coupon 8%, discount rate 8%, 5 years → PV of all cash flows = exactly ₹1,000.

    Total cash received = ₹80 × 5 = ₹400 of coupons + ₹1,000 face value = ₹1,400, but its present value is ₹1,000, so the NPV of the transaction is zero.

    The interpretive trap he flags ← guaranteed MCQ: NPV = 0 does not mean the investment is pointless. If you kept the ₹1,000 in your almirah you would still have ₹1,000 in 5 years. If you invest, you also have ₹400 of coupons which you can reinvest at 8%, so you end up with far more.

    5.6 What happens when the cost of capital moves — the three scenarios

    Cost of capital PV of the bond Name Market convention
    8.0% (= coupon) ₹1,000.00 Par bond 100%
    8.2% (> coupon) ₹992.06 Discount bond — a capital LOSS of ₹7.94 99.2%
    7.8% (< coupon) ₹1,008.03 Premium bond — a capital GAIN 100.8%

    guaranteed MCQ — all three numbers and all three names THE FUNDAMENTAL RULE: the value of a bond is INVERSELY related to the cost of capital. Rates up → bond prices down. Rates down → bond prices up. guaranteed MCQ Where does the discount rate come from? From the money market — the observable rate of return on similar instruments (other companies' bonds, bank deposits). "The price of money is determined in ways that are similar to the price of oranges, apples, tomatoes and onions — it is a result of demand and supply," and it shifts like a moving river.

    5.7 Yield to Maturity (YTM)

    Definition (his careful wording — note "expect to realise"):

    YTM is the rate of return investors EXPECT to REALISE, IF they hold a bond TO MATURITY, GIVEN THE PRICE at which they purchased the bond.

    guaranteed MCQ — all three qualifiers Mathematically, YTM = the Internal Rate of Return (IRR) of the bond. guaranteed MCQ The two uses of YTM: 1. Tells you the rate of return on that particular bond 2. Estimates the required rate of return on a comparable bond that has not been issued yet. His example: BEML (Bharat Earth Movers Limited) — also a government-owned engineering company — wants to know what rate it must offer. Answer: use BHEL's YTM as the proxy. (NTPC is mentioned as another comparable, but BEML is "even better than NTPC" as a comparable.) guaranteed MCQ — expand BEML

    5.8 YTM worked example 1 — solving for YTM

    A 5-year government bond carrying a coupon of 6% p.a. payable annually is selling for ₹98. Face value ₹100. The bond has 4 years left to maturity. What is the YTM?

    Reasoning before arithmetic: price (₹98) < face value (₹100), so the discount rate must be above 6%.

    Set up: 98 = 6/(1+y) + 6/(1+y)² + 6/(1+y)³ + 106/(1+y)⁴

    (the last cash flow is 106 = coupon 6 + principal 100)

    Answer: YTM = 6.58% guaranteed MCQ How to solve a 4th-power equation: the IRR function in a spreadsheet, a financial calculator, or an online YTM calculator applet.

    5.9 YTM worked example 2 — using YTM to find price

    A bond with face value ₹100 pays a 4.25% coupon annually, matures in 4 years, and the YTM on comparable bonds is 0.15%. What is the value of the bond?

    V = 4.25 × PVIFA(0.0015, 4) + 100/(1.0015)⁴ = ₹116.34 guaranteed MCQ Sense-check: the price (₹116.34) is above par because the coupon (4.25%) is far greater than the cost of capital (0.15%).

    5.10 Total return

    A bond paying a 6% coupon annually, face value ₹100, 5 years to maturity, trading at ₹98. If it is expected to be sold for ₹100.50 one year later, a day AFTER the interest was paid, what is the expected rate of return?

    Component Calculation Value
    Interest yield 6 ÷ 98 6.12%
    Capital gain (100.50 − 98) ÷ 98 = 2.50 ÷ 98 2.55%
    TOTAL RETURN (6 + 2.50) ÷ 98 = 8.50 ÷ 98 8.67% guaranteed MCQ

    Why "a day after the interest was paid" matters: the ₹100.50 is the present value of the cash flows occurring AFTER the interest has been paid. If interest had not yet been paid, the seller would demand a price that also compensates for it. guaranteed MCQ

    5.11 The three return measures for bonds — pulled together guaranteed MCQ| Measure | Definition |

    |---|---| | Yield to Maturity (YTM) | The rate of return realised if held to maturity = the IRR of the bond | | Current yield | Annual coupon ÷ price (6 ÷ 98 in the example) | | Total return | (Coupon + capital gain) ÷ purchase price |

    Term pairs he asks you to be able to distinguish: Bonds vs notes · YTM vs coupon · bid vs ask · current yield vs capital gain vs total return · par vs premium vs discount bonds · indexed vs non-indexed bonds · nominal vs real rate of return guaranteed MCQ

    5.12 Annualising a YTM — the bond market convention

    A 10-year bond carrying a coupon of 8% p.a. payable half-yearly, with 4 years to maturity, trading at ₹105. What is the half-yearly YTM? What is the annualised YTM?

    • 8 half-yearly interest payments of ₹4 each; at the 8th half-year you also get ₹100 back, so the final cash flow is ₹104
    • Equation: 105 = 4 × PVIFA(y, 8) + 100/(1+y)⁸ — note the power of 8, not 4 guaranteed MCQ
    • Half-yearly YTM = 3.28%

    THE CONVENTION: to annualise, simply MULTIPLY — do NOT compound.

    • Half-yearly YTM 3.28% × 2 = 6.56% annualised
    • Quarterly YTM 2% × 4 = 8% annualised

    "That's how the bond market has always done this calculation." ← guaranteed MCQ — this is a classic trap: the "correct" compounded answer (1.0328² − 1) is NOT the market convention

    5.13 Interest rate sensitivity — the duration idea

    Two bonds, both face value ₹1,000, both 8% coupon, both priced at ₹1,000 when YTM = 8%. TTM (time to maturity) = 4 years and 20 years. What happens when the YTM rises to 9%?

    Bond Price at 8% Price at 9% Drop Drop as % of face value
    4-year (TTM = 4) ₹1,000 ₹967.60 ₹32.40 3.24%
    20-year (TTM = 20) ₹1,000 ₹908.71 ₹91.29 9.13%

    guaranteed MCQ — all four numbers THE RULE: the longer the maturity, the MORE sensitive the bond price is to a change in interest rates. The reason is basic time-value arithmetic — the further out a cash flow, the more its present value is affected by a change in the discount rate. The textbook graph compares a 3-year and a 30-year bond and shows the same thing.

    And the identity to remember: "Rate of return and cost of capital are two sides of the same coin. The investor sees it as rate of return; the company sees it as cost of capital." guaranteed MCQ

    1. Inflation
    5

    6.1 The three components of a required rate of return guaranteed MCQ

    Investors expect a rate of return to compensate for: 1. Not having consumed the money immediately (the pure time value) 2. Inflation 3. Risk — the possibility they may never see the money again

    6.2 What inflation is

    The drop in purchasing power of a given currency. If a kilo of identical tomatoes costs ₹40 today and ₹45 a year from now, the rupee that bought 1/40th of a kilo now buys only 1/45th.

    6.3 The tomato worked example — memorise it

    Step Value
    Tomatoes today ₹20/kg
    Money lent ₹20
    Real required return 10% → I want to consume 1.1 kg in a year
    Without inflation Borrower repays ₹22, I buy 1.1 kg
    Inflation 5% → tomatoes become ₹21/kg
    To buy 1.1 kg now costs 1.1 × 21 = ₹23.10
    So the nominal return demanded (23.10 − 20)/20 = 15.5%

    The exact relationship: (1 + R_nominal) = (1 + R_real) × (1 + inflation) Check: 1.10 × 1.05 = 1.155 → 15.5% guaranteed MCQ

    6.4 Real vs nominal — the definitions and the shortcut

    Term Definition
    Real rate of return The rate in a world without inflation — pure compensation for deferring consumption
    Nominal rate of return Includes compensation for inflation on top of the real rate

    Exact: (1 + R_nom) = (1 + R_real)(1 + i) → R_real = (1 + R_nom)/(1 + i) − 1 Shortcut: R_nom ≈ R_real + i, so R_real ≈ R_nom − i

    The shortcut is only valid for SMALL real rates and LOW inflation. With high numbers it breaks down. guaranteed MCQ THE RULE TO MEMORISE: ALL rates quoted in the real world — FD rates, stock market returns, newspaper figures — are NOMINAL rates. guaranteed MCQ Worked check: stock market return 14% in 2025, inflation 5.5% → real return ≈ 8.5% by the shortcut, or 1.14/1.055 − 1 exactly.

    Why we use nominal rates in daily life: because inflation is a reality and is almost always positive — what people want to know is the return they will actually receive.

    6.5 Discounting a nominal cash flow — the two-step method

    ₹10,000 is due 1 year from now. Expected inflation 4%, required real rate of return 5%. What is the present value?

    Step Calculation Result
    1. Deflate to real terms 10,000 ÷ 1.04 ₹9,615
    2. Discount at the REAL rate 9,615 ÷ 1.05 ₹9,158
    One-step equivalent 10,000 ÷ (1.04 × 1.05) = 10,000 ÷ 1.092 ₹9,158 guaranteed MCQ

    The lesson: discounting a nominal cash flow at the nominal cost of capital gives the same answer as deflating to real terms and discounting at the real rate. Never mix — real cash flows with real rates, nominal with nominal.

    1. Equity — the fundamentals
    5

    7.1 Legal basis and scale

    • Companies Act 2013, Section 43 says a company can have share capital, of two kinds: Equity share capital and Preference share capital guaranteed MCQ| Statistic | Figure | |---|---| | Incorporated companies in India | ~28,00,000 | | Active companies | ~18,00,000 | | Listed on BSE | ~5,600 | | Listed on NSE | ~2,670 | | Combined market value of listed shares | ₹4,58,70,293 crore (458 lakh crore) |

    guaranteed MCQ (He also refers elsewhere to "about 7,000 companies listed across the two exchanges" and "6,000 shares in the market" when discussing indices — treat those as the working round numbers.)

    7.2 The four essential features of equity share capital guaranteed MCQ| # | Feature | Explanation |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | Ownership | Equity represents ownership of the company; a lender has no ownership relationship | | 2 | Voting rights | One share = one vote. Own 10,000 of 1,00,000 shares → 10% of votes; own 60,000 → 60%, a majority on any issue | | 3 | Limited liability | Your responsibility ends with the amount you promised — "not a rupee more." Considered one of the most important innovations in the history of commerce, because it lets entrepreneurs raise crores from thousands of strangers | | 4 | Residual claim | On winding up, the equity shareholder stands LAST in the queue — behind lenders, suppliers and employees. What remains may be many times the investment, a tiny fraction, or nothing at all |

    The contrast case — Joint and Several Liability: in a partnership, if your partner borrows ₹15 lakh telling lenders he is your partner and then absconds, you are legally liable for the whole amount — both partners are jointly liable for all claims and each is individually (severally) liable too. Unlimited liability. This is exactly what limited liability was invented to solve. guaranteed MCQ

    7.3 What equity investors get

    Two forms of return: dividends (periodic income) and capital gains (sale price − purchase price).

    7.4 The two rights of a share guaranteed MCQ| Right | Formal name | What it is |

    |---|---|---| | The ability to vote and thereby control the board and management | CONTROL RIGHTS | | | The right to participate in the wealth of the company | CASH FLOW RIGHTS (also "wealth rights") | Called cash flow rights because wealth is nothing but the present value of cash flows |

    1. Equity valuation
    13

    8.1 Holding period return — the Tunga Apparels example

    Tunga Apparels shares sell for ₹100 today, expected to sell for ₹110 in a year, dividend forecast ₹5.

    Component Calculation Value
    Dividend yield 5 ÷ 100 5%
    Capital gain 10 ÷ 100 10%
    Total return (5 + 110 − 100) ÷ 100 15% guaranteed MCQ

    The general formula:

    R = (D₁ + P₁ − P₀) / P₀

    8.2 Solving for price — the Mysore Steels example

    Mysore Steels is expected to sell for ₹120 in a year and pay a ₹6 dividend. The opportunity cost of capital for steel companies is 12%. What can you pay?

    P₀ = (6 + 120) / 1.12 = 126 / 1.12 = ₹112.50 guaranteed MCQ Where does the 12% come from? From comparable companies — "whatever rate of return I get from those steel companies, I should get from Mysore Steels. It should not be anything less." This is the opportunity cost of capital: the minimum rate of return expected from comparable investment opportunities. guaranteed MCQ The general one-period formula: P₀ = (D₁ + P₁) / (1 + r)

    This is the Dividend Discount Model (DDM), a DCF-based method of valuing shares.

    8.3 Two-period DDM — Tunga Apparels again

    D₁ = ₹5, D₂ = ₹5.50, P₂ = ₹121, cost of capital for apparel companies = 15%.

    V₀ = 5/1.15 + 5.50/1.15² + 121/1.15² = ₹100 guaranteed MCQ Decision rule: if the shares trade at ₹100 or less, buy; if more, wait.

    Note the deliberate teaching point: he uses 12% for steel and 15% for apparel to make you notice that cost of capital differs by industry. guaranteed MCQ

    8.4 The general DDM and the horizon price

    P₀ = D₁/(1+r) + D₂/(1+r)² + … + D_H/(1+r)^H + P_H/(1+r)^H

    and P_H itself is just the DDM applied from year H+1 onwards, i.e. P_H = D_{H+1} / (r − g). guaranteed MCQ

    8.5 The two perpetuity formulas — the heart of the course

    Case Value formula Cost of capital formula
    Constant dividend forever (no growth) P₀ = Div / r r = Div / P₀
    Dividend growing at constant g forever P₀ = D₁ / (r − g) r = D₁/P₀ + g = dividend yield + growth rate guaranteed MCQ

    A subtlety he explicitly flags: in the no-growth case the dividend has no subscript (it is constant). In the growth case it is D₁, and the 11th year's dividend is D₁ × (1+g)¹⁰, not (1+g)¹¹ — because growth applies from the second year onwards. guaranteed MCQ On plausible growth rates: "Don't assume even for an example that dividends will grow at a constant 10% — the number becomes too huge, like the chessboard-and-rice-grains story. 2–3% is a reasonable growth rate," because it is linked to population growth and GDP growth. guaranteed MCQ

    8.6 Coastal Power — the cost-of-capital worked example

    Price ₹47.30. Dividend at end of year 1 = ₹1.86. Thereafter dividends grow at 4.6% annually.

    Component Calculation Value
    Dividend yield 1.86 ÷ 47.30 3.93%
    Growth rate given 4.6%
    Cost of capital 3.93 + 4.6 8.53% guaranteed MCQ

    8.7 Vindhya Steels — the multi-stage DDM (the hardest worked example)

    Dividends of ₹0, ₹0.31, ₹0.65 at the end of years 1, 2, 3. Year 4 dividend ₹0.67. Perpetual growth of 4% from year 5 onwards. Discount rate 10%. What is the price?

    Year Cash flow Discounting
    1 0 0 / 1.1
    2 0.31 0.31 / 1.1²
    3 0.65 0.65 / 1.1³
    4 onwards The growing perpetuity, valued AT the end of year 4 [0.67 / (0.10 − 0.04)] / 1.1⁴

    Answer: ₹9.13 guaranteed MCQ THE CRITICAL TRAP: "The 4th year's dividend is the FIRST year of the perpetuity, because the perpetuity starts growing from year 5." So the perpetuity is valued at the end of year 4 and then discounted back 4 periods, not 3 or 5. guaranteed MCQ

    8.8 The buy/sell decision rule guaranteed MCQ

    Let V₀ = the value you calculate; P₀ = the market price.

    Condition Interpretation Action
    V₀ > P₀ Market is underpricing the share BUY (like finding a ₹3,50,000 car with a ₹3,00,000 sticker)
    V₀ < P₀ Share is overpriced SELL (or if you don't own it, stay away). Analysts may say "hold" if they believe it will recover
    V₀ = P₀ Neutral Hold if you believe it will improve; otherwise sell at the current price

    Notation point: he switches from P₀ to V₀ deliberately — P₀ is the market price, V₀ is your calculated value.

    1. Growth, ploughback and PVGO
    6

    9.1 The growth formula

    g = ROE × b

    where ROE = return on book equity and b = the ploughback (retention) ratio.

    Ajmeri Savouries worked example: ROE = 20%, ploughback = 50% → g = 0.20 × 0.50 = 10%

    (The transcript's dictation garbles this as "20 into 50 is 5%" — the formula and the method are what matters: g = ROE × b.) ← guaranteed MCQ — the formula is the single thing he says to remember if you remember nothing else from this section

    9.2 The supporting definitions

    Term Definition
    Earnings Profit After Tax (PAT)
    EPS PAT ÷ number of shares
    Payout ratio DPS ÷ EPS — the fraction of PAT paid out as dividend
    Ploughback (retention) ratio, b 1 − payout ratio = 1 − (DPS ÷ EPS)
    Book equity Share capital + reserves and surplus

    Why calculate EARNINGS growth when the formula needs DIVIDEND growth? Because if the payout ratio is held constant, earnings growth = dividend growth. guaranteed MCQ The economic chain: retained PAT increases book equity on the liability side → is used to buy assets on the asset side → assets produce returns → sales grow → earnings grow → dividends grow. guaranteed MCQ The summary chain he states: "Dividends grow with growth in earnings. Earnings grow from increase in sales. Sales grow with increase in assets. Increase in assets requires funding."

    9.3 Company Y — the PVGO worked example (memorise every number)

    Company Y planned to pay a dividend of ₹8.33 next year, being all of its earnings. Investors expect 15%. Instead, it now plans to plough back 40% at the firm's ROE of 25%. What is the stock value before and after?

    Scenario A — pay out everything (no growth):

    P₀ = 8.33 / 0.15 = ₹55.56

    Scenario B — plough back 40%:

    Step Calculation Result
    Growth rate g = ROE × b = 0.25 × 0.40 10%
    New dividend D₁ 8.33 × 0.60 (payout = 1 − 0.40) ₹5.00
    Price 5 / (0.15 − 0.10) ₹100.00

    PVGO = 100 − 55.56 = ₹44.44 guaranteed MCQ — every number in this box The general result:

    Value of a share with growth opportunities = Value without growth + PVGO

    PVGO = Present Value of Growth Opportunities

    Why it is called a present value: ₹44.44 is nothing but the present value of the higher future dividends created by the new assets.

    9.4 The three clarifications he insists on

    1. Both scenarios are perpetual policies, not one-off decisions
    2. Growth in earnings and dividends starts from YEAR 2, because the ₹8.33 of earnings arises over the next 12 months, the assets are created at the end of year 1, and they only generate additional profits from year 2. So D₁ = ₹5 and D₂ = 5 × 1.1 guaranteed MCQ
    3. The assumption that retained profit is the ONLY source of funding for new assets is a textbook simplification — in reality a business could borrow or issue new shares

    9.5 The exercise he sets — and the answer he later reveals guaranteed MCQ

    Redo the calculation with ROE = 10% instead of 25%, keeping b = 40% and r = 15%.

    g = 0.10 × 0.40 = 4%, D₁ = ₹5 → P₀ = 5/(0.15 − 0.04) = ₹45.45, which is LESS than ₹55.56.

    THE PRINCIPLE:

    If ROE > r (the shareholders' required return), reinvesting CREATES value. If ROE < r, reinvesting DESTROYS value — the company should pay the profits out as dividend instead.

    "By earning a rate of return of 10%, which is less than the 15% shareholders expect, the company is actually hurting shareholders financially — it is destroying value."

    9.6 The governance chain

    Shareholders appoint the board → the board appoints the CEO → the CEO's performance is measured by the impact on share price. guaranteed MCQ

    1. Relative valuation — accounting multiples
    8

    10.1 The method and its names

    Also called the accounting multiples method or the comparable firm method.

    Multiple Definition
    P/E (Price to Earnings) Price per share ÷ EPS — either the most recent EPS (more commonly used) or the forecast EPS for the year ahead
    P/B (Price to Book) Price per share ÷ book value per share
    Variants mentioned EV/EBITDA and EV/Sales guaranteed MCQ

    Book value = value of assets − value of liabilities = the money belonging to shareholders (the residual claim idea again). Divided by number of shares = book value per share.

    10.2 The interpretation of P/E guaranteed MCQ

    A P/E of 10 means you are paying ₹10 of price for every ₹1 of earnings. Inverted, E/P = 1/10 = 10% — the earnings return on the price you pay, which makes it a rough measure of the cost of capital for that industry.

    10.3 Trailing vs forward P/E guaranteed MCQ| Type | Uses |

    |---|---| | TTM (Trailing Twelve Months) P/E | The most recent EPS with the current price | | Forward P/E | The next year's forecast EPS | | P/B | No such distinction — book value per share is always a historical number from the balance sheet |

    10.4 The central empirical claim

    P/E and P/B ratios are INDUSTRY-LEVEL CHARACTERISTICS. Within an industry the values cluster around a mean; across industries they vary a lot. guaranteed MCQ The eight industries he tabulates: FMCG · auto parts · pharmaceuticals · cement · sugar · yarn spinning · public sector banks · private sector banks. (PSU and private banks are separated deliberately because "banks owned by the government work differently from banks owned by the private sector.") guaranteed MCQ The illustrative FMCG sample: Hindustan Unilever, Godrej Consumer, Marico Industries, Dabur India, Bajaj Consumer — P/E in the 25–57/69 range, P/B from 4.54 up to 12.4 and 20.

    The observed ordering: FMCG and pharma high · cement in the middle · sugar and spinning low. (Udaipur Cement is called out as an outlier.)

    10.5 The Good Heart Company — the comparables valuation worked example

    A privately held cardiac-drugs pharmaceutical company. The average pharmaceutical industry P/E is 37.79 ≈ 38. Good Heart's forecast EPS is ₹10.

    Value per share = 38 × 10 = ₹380 guaranteed MCQ The four-step comparables procedure: guaranteed MCQ 1. Estimate the forecast EPS of the target (EPS_T) 2. Identify comparable firms similar to T 3. Calculate their P/E ratios and take the average 4. Multiply the target's EPS by the average industry P/E

    When would you need this? When the shares are not traded on a stock exchange — e.g. (a) a family wants to sell the business, (b) the company wants to make an IPO and must price it.

    10.6 Which multiple for which industry

    P/B is used for: BANKS · PETROLEUM companies · SHIPPING companies. guaranteed MCQ

    1. Risk and return
    12

    11.1 The three ways of measuring historical return

    Measure Method
    Arithmetic mean return Simple average of the periodic returns — equally weighted
    Geometric mean return [(1+r₁)(1+r₂)…(1+rₙ)]^(1/n) − 1
    Compounded annual return (CAGR/CARR) (End value / Start value)^(1/n) − 1 — used when you know only the start and end values

    The worked series: 20%, 12%, −5%, 7%, −9% (5 years)

    Measure Value
    Arithmetic mean 5%
    Geometric mean 4.45%

    guaranteed MCQ THE RULE: the geometric mean is LESS than the arithmetic mean (almost always). guaranteed MCQ Compounded annual return worked example: initial value 100, value after 4 years = 200 → (200/100)^0.25 − 1 = 18.92% guaranteed MCQ Its real-life use: working out the implicit rate of return in schemes like Indira Vikas Patra or the National Savings Certificate, which tell you the maturity value but not the rate.

    11.2 Annualising a holding period return

    Buy a share for ₹40, sell for ₹42 after 6 months.

    Measure Value
    Holding period RETURN (rupees) ₹2
    Holding period RATE of return 2 ÷ 40 = 5%
    Annualised 1.05² − 1 = 10.25% guaranteed MCQ

    Note the distinction he draws carefully: "return" is the rupee amount; "rate of return" is the percentage. guaranteed MCQ Monthly example: a 0.5% monthly holding period return annualises to 1.005¹² − 1.

    Why annualise? Because the year is the common measurement period in finance — accounts, planning and management all run annually — so annualising lets you compare investments with different holding periods on one scale.

    The embedded assumption he flags: annualising assumes you replicate the same rate of return in every subsequent sub-period.

    11.3 The Dimson–Marsh 120-year evidence

    Source: two researchers named Dimson and Marsh, who published a celebrated book on 100+ years of investment history and keep updating the database.

    US securities markets, 1900 → 2019 — the value of $1 invested in 1900:

    Asset class Value in 2019 Nominal rate of return
    Equities (stocks) $58,190 11.5%
    Bonds $327 5.4%
    Bills (T-bills) $77 3.7%

    guaranteed MCQ — all six numbers The shape of the lines: the bills line is very smooth, the bonds line less so, the equities line is highly jagged — with a steep drop around 1930 and sharp rises and falls in the 1970s and 1980s.

    The conclusion: "Risk and return go hand in hand" — the higher wealth from equities is paid for by year-on-year variability. The same ordering holds for real rates of return as for nominal. guaranteed MCQ

    11.4 Risk = standard deviation

    In finance, RISK is measured as the STANDARD DEVIATION (or variance) of returns. guaranteed MCQ Standard deviation vs variance: both are used. Variance is preferred in some contexts because being a square it can never be negative; standard deviation is preferred when you want a number of the same order of magnitude as the mean, so you can compute the SD/mean ratio.

    His 10-year illustrative series: mean return 12.6%, standard deviation 14.3%, SD ÷ mean ≈ 1.14 — which he calls not a huge dispersion; real life shows much higher. guaranteed MCQ The opening-price subtlety he flags: in the table, year 1 closes at ₹12 but year 2 opens at ₹12.20. "The closing price for a period is rarely ever equal to the opening price for the next period." The calculation is always done as though you bought at the beginning of the period and sold at the end. guaranteed MCQ

    11.5 Using the past to forecast, and the normal distribution assumption

    Because nobody can predict the future in a vacuum, we use historical mean and standard deviation as estimates of the future.

    His worked illustration: if Infosys is expected to return 14% and the historical SD of Infosys returns is 16%, then "with 95% accuracy I can believe the future returns will be 14% plus or minus 3 standard deviations of 16%."

    The implicit assumption, which he states explicitly and endorses: returns are assumed to follow a NORMAL DISTRIBUTION. "Both academics and practitioners agree that the normal distribution is a reasonable approximation." guaranteed MCQ (Note for the exam: the "95%" figure conventionally corresponds to ±2 standard deviations, and ±3 covers 99.7%. The transcript says "95% ... plus or minus 3 standard deviations". If an MCQ tests the statistics, use the standard 68.3 / 95.4 / 99.7 convention from the analytics course.)

    11.6 Where returns come from

    Two sources: guaranteed MCQ 1. Periodic income — dividends (shares), interest (bonds), rent (real estate) 2. Capital appreciation — a future increase in price

    1. Diversification
    9

    12.1 The intuition

    Diversify across industries whose fortunes do NOT move together.

    His two examples:

    Pair Why they diversify each other
    Office real estate vs education/healthcare Office real estate depends on companies expanding; education and healthcare are largely unaffected by economic conditions — people study and fall ill regardless. (He even jokes both directions: a poor economy causes stress-related illness, a good one causes over-eating illness)
    BRICS vs continental Europe BRICS = Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa. When one bloc does well the other may not, so investing across countries reduces exposure guaranteed MCQ

    12.2 The two components of risk guaranteed MCQ — all the synonyms| | Component 1 | Component 2 |

    |---|---|---| | Primary name | Unique risk | Market risk | | Synonyms | Diversifiable risk · Idiosyncratic risk | Systematic risk · Non-diversifiable risk | | Source | Factors specific to a company, industry, country or region | Factors affecting the whole economy — his example: the price of oil/petrol, which affects education, healthcare, real estate, manufacturing, engineering and consumer goods alike | | Can it be diversified away? | Yes | No — no matter how much you diversify |

    "Systematic" is so called because it affects the entire system/universe of investing.

    12.3 The diversification graph

    X-axis: number of securities. Y-axis: portfolio standard deviation.

    • SD falls sharply from 1–2 securities down to a floor around 15, 16 or 17 securities
    • The curve is ASYMPTOTIC to the market-risk line — it never touches it, meaning some risk always remains guaranteed MCQ
    • The optimal number of securities is around 19 or 20 — beyond that, the marginal reduction in SD is less than the incremental cost guaranteed MCQ What the costs are: trading costs (every purchase or sale) plus research costs for informed trading decisions.

    A precision point he insists on: even at 19–20 securities you have not eliminated all unique risk — that is exactly why the curve never touches the market-risk line.

    12.4 The 11-company empirical study — the setup guaranteed MCQ| Detail | Value |

    |---|---| | Number of companies | 11 | | The companies | BHEL · HDFC Bank · Arvind · TCS · Infosys · Dr. Reddy's · Sun Pharma · Nahar Spinning · Maruti Suzuki · Tata Motors · Ashok Leyland | | Period | 1 January 2024 to 26 August 2025 | | Number of trading days | 410 | | Daily return formula | (P₂ − P₁)/P₁ | | Tool | Excel — no statistical package needed |

    Why so many observations? Because "the standard error of your estimate of the mean falls in inverse proportion to the number of observations" — more observations, lower standard error, more reliable mean. guaranteed MCQ Findings on standard deviation:

    Company Observation
    Nahar Spinning Standard deviation 2.95% — the highest
    BHEL Standard deviation 2.83%, with a very low mean-to-SD ratio — huge day-to-day fluctuation over this period
    Arvind Mean return 0%, SD still 2.62% — the returns cancelled out on average but varied a lot

    guaranteed MCQ A methodological caution he repeats: the results are specific to the period measured — a different 2-year window might show BHEL behaving quite differently.

    12.5 The correlation coefficient results guaranteed MCQ — memorise these five numbers| Pair | Correlation | Why |

    |---|---|---| | HDFC Bank ↔ Arvind | 0.14 | Bank vs textile — completely different drivers → excellent diversification | | Infosys ↔ TCS | 0.72 | Same business, same clients, same operating economics — poor diversification | | Maruti Suzuki ↔ Tata Motors | 0.37 | | | Maruti Suzuki ↔ Ashok Leyland | 0.35 | | | Tata Motors ↔ Ashok Leyland | 0.50 | | | Most other pairs | below 0.25–0.30 | Picking companies from different industries gives a more diversified portfolio |

    The automobile puzzle and its answer — a beautiful exam question:

    Why is Maruti's correlation with the other two (0.35–0.37) lower than Tata Motors ↔ Ashok Leyland (0.50), when all three are "automobile" companies?

    Maruti Suzuki makes ONLY passenger vehicles. Ashok Leyland is a commercial vehicle maker (trucks and buses) and Tata Motors is primarily a commercial vehicle maker which has moved into passenger vehicles (the Nano, then Jaguar Land Rover). Passenger vehicles are DISCRETIONARY spending — highly sensitive to the economy (witness the GST-cut-driven surge in Maruti and Hyundai sales) — whereas goods must be moved between towns regardless of the economy, so commercial vehicle demand is less susceptible to economic variation. guaranteed MCQ How he computed it: the Excel CORREL function on the two columns of daily returns.

    1. Portfolio arithmetic
    6

    13.1 The two formulas guaranteed MCQ

    Portfolio return (weighted average):

    R_p = x₁R₁ + x₂R₂

    Portfolio variance (NOT a simple weighted average):

    σ_p² = x₁²σ₁² + x₂²σ₂² + 2·x₁·x₂·σ₁·σ₂·ρ₁₂

    The whole point: the return formula is a simple weighted average, but the variance formula is not — it carries the correlation coefficient ρ₁₂ as a loading factor on the cross term. This is where diversification comes from. guaranteed MCQ Return sense-check (his worked verification): R₁ = 20%, R₂ = 10%, x₁ = 0.7, x₂ = 0.3 on ₹10,000 → ₹7,000 earns ₹1,400 and ₹3,000 earns ₹300, total ₹1,700 on ₹10,000 = 17%, which is exactly 0.7(0.2) + 0.3(0.1).

    13.2 The two-share illustration — Share A and Share B

    Share A Share B
    Expected return 15% 35%
    Standard deviation 22% 44%

    guaranteed MCQ Two scenarios: ρ = 0.1 (low) and ρ = 0.9 (high).

    Six portfolio weightings tested: 100/0, 80/20, 60/40, 40/60, 20/80, 10/90 (A/B).

    13.3 The results table — memorise these guaranteed MCQ| Weights (A/B) | Portfolio return | SD when ρ = 0.1 | SD when ρ = 0.9 |

    |---|---|---|---| | 100 / 0 | 15% | 22% | 22% | | 80 / 20 | 19% | 20% ← the minimum | 26% | | 60 / 40 | 23% | 22% | 31% | | 40 / 60 | 27% | 28% | rising | | 20 / 80 | 31% | rising | rising | | 10 / 90 | 33% | rising | rising |

    The three conclusions: guaranteed MCQ 1. At 80/20 with ρ = 0.1, the portfolio SD is 20% — LOWER than EITHER individual share (22% and 44%). "That's a remarkable bit of magic." 2. At 60/40 with ρ = 0.1, the return rises from 15% to 23% while the SD stays at 22% — the same as share A alone. "It's almost like a free lunch." This happens only because the two returns have a low correlation coefficient 3. With ρ = 0.9 the magic disappears — the lowest achievable SD is 22%, i.e. just share A's own SD, and it rises from there. High correlation destroys the diversification benefit

    The name for this whole process: MEAN VARIANCE OPTIMIZATION. guaranteed MCQ

    13.4 The 60/40, ρ = 0.1 calculation written out

    σ_p² = (0.6)²(0.22)² + (0.4)²(0.44)² + 2(0.6)(0.4)(0.22)(0.44)(0.1) → take the square root → σ_p = 22%

    Replace ρ = 0.1 with ρ = 0.9 and σ_p jumps to 31%.

    1. The efficient frontier and the market portfolio
    5

    14.1 The broken-eggshell diagram

    X-axis: portfolio variance (or SD). Y-axis: portfolio return. Each dot is a portfolio — a combination of assets with particular weights.

    Feature Meaning
    Global Minimum Variance Portfolio (GMVP) The leftmost point — that combination of assets, out of all possible combinations in the investible universe, which gives the LOWEST possible variance. No other portfolio has a lower variance guaranteed MCQ
    Upward-sloping arm = the EFFICIENT FRONTIER Every point on it gives either the highest return for a given variance or the lowest variance for a given return. Points below the line are feasible but inefficient
    Downward-sloping arm Not of interest — for every point on it there is a point on the upward arm with the same variance but a higher return. It exists only to complete the picture

    Efficiency here means return in relation to risk — the best return per unit of variance.

    How institutional investors use it: they state an objective — either "I need this expected return, give me the lowest possible variance" or "I will not tolerate variance above X, give me the best return" — and the answer is a point on the efficient frontier.

    14.2 Why the efficient frontier is impractical, and what to do instead

    The problem: building it requires price forecasts for every share, which needs high-quality information on sales, market share, profitability and cash flow prospects, plus a lot of judgement — and you may still get it wrong. Moreover, thousands of smart people are doing the same thing, so you are unlikely to out-guess them.

    The forward reference he makes: the Efficient Market Hypothesis — "markets generally get the price right and you can never out-guess the market in terms of asset valuation." guaranteed MCQ The solution: the MARKET PORTFOLIO — a combination of assets that represents the entire set of investment possibilities in the marketplace. guaranteed MCQ

    14.3 Indices as market portfolios

    Index Composition
    BSE Sensex (Bombay Sensitive Index) 30 shares, assembled to represent all 6,000+ listed shares — banking, oil and gas, manufacturing, chemicals, telecom, hotels, and Zomato as a representative of the new tech-enabled economy guaranteed MCQ
    NIFTY 50 The NSE's equivalent
    CRISIL 500 Another index he names

    Why you can't just buy the index yourself: with ₹10,000 you cannot own a fraction of HDFC Bank, Reliance Industries and TCS in the right proportions, and you would have to rebalance constantly as market capitalisations shift hour to hour.

    The practical answer: INDEX FUNDS.

    His closing statement: "The best optimised investment portfolio is the one that gives you the best return for the amount of risk you are willing to assume, and that is best captured through a market portfolio, because the market portfolio represents the collective wisdom of everyone in the market." guaranteed MCQ

    1. Mutual funds
    14

    15.1 The SEBI definition (three parts) guaranteed MCQ

    "A fund established in the form of a TRUST to raise monies through the sale of UNITS to the public or a section of the public under one or more schemes for investing in securities, money market instruments, gold or gold-related instruments, silver or silver-related instruments, real estate assets, and such other assets and instruments as may be specified by the Board from time to time."

    Part Content
    1 Must be established as a TRUST
    2 Raises money by selling UNITS to the public or a section of it
    3 Invests in: securities · money market instruments · gold · silver · real estate · other assets SEBI specifies

    Key implication: a mutual fund is a mechanism for the public to invest in a wide range of assets INDIRECTLY. guaranteed MCQ Other descriptors: a pooled investment vehicle; a mechanism for small investors to access securities markets and other asset classes.

    15.2 The six reasons investors use mutual funds guaranteed MCQ| # | Reason |

    |---|---| | 1 | Diversification across companies and asset classes | | 2 | Specialised knowledge of the fund managers — investing in gold or silver is a different skill from investing in shares | | 3 | Flexibility of ticket size — from a few hundred rupees to tens of crores in the same fund | | 4 | High liquidity — contrast with a plot of land, which you can neither sell in fractions nor sell quickly | | 5 | Falling fees, thanks to persistent SEBI effort: as little as 0.25%–0.5% for some fund types, up to about 2%, rarely above 2–2.5% guaranteed MCQ| | 6 | Intense competition producing schemes tailored to specific needs |

    15.3 The five broad categories of scheme guaranteed MCQ

    Equity-oriented · Debt-oriented · Hybrid (debt + equity) · Solution-oriented (e.g. pension, children's education) · Other schemes (a catch-all)

    15.4 Three vocabulary items

    Term Meaning
    Fund management organisation e.g. ICICI Prudential, HDFC Mutual Fund — manages dozens of schemes
    Scheme A specific fund offering put together for a specific purpose (e.g. a manufacturing-focused fund launched because the government announced manufacturing incentives)
    Market capitalisation Number of shares × market price. Example: 1 crore shares at ₹900 = ₹900 crore market cap

    15.5 Large / mid / small cap — the SEBI definitions guaranteed MCQ| Category | Rank by market capitalisation |

    |---|---| | Large cap | Top 100 companies | | Mid cap | 101 – 250 | | Small cap | 251 and below |

    "As you can see, it's fairly arbitrary" — and a company that slips from rank 78 to 114 moves from large cap to mid cap, which is bad news for everyone.

    15.6 SEBI's minimum allocation rules for equity schemes guaranteed MCQ| Scheme type | Minimum allocation |

    |---|---| | Multi cap fund | more than 60% of the corpus in large, mid and small cap equity | | Large cap fund | at least 80% in large cap equity | | Mid cap fund | at least 65% in mid cap | | Small cap fund | at least 65% in small cap | | Index fund | at least 90% invested in replicating or tracking the chosen index — and once an index is chosen it cannot be changed for the life of the fund |

    Why SEBI regulates this so tightly: because mutual fund investors are ordinary people who "should have a clear understanding of where our money would likely be invested." guaranteed MCQ

    15.7 Other equity scheme types

    Dividend yield funds (some companies yield under 2%, others 5–6%) · Sector/Thematic funds · ELSS — Equity Linked Savings Scheme, created by the government as a tax-saving mechanism ← guaranteed MCQ · Hybrid schemes.

    Risk matching by life stage: a young investor chasing high returns may choose small cap; a person nearing retirement wants the safety of large cap and prioritises capital preservation over high returns.

    15.8 Debt funds — classified by DURATION guaranteed MCQ

    The distinguishing point: equity funds are classified by theme and company size; DEBT funds are classified by the DURATION of the investment.

    Fund Maturity of securities it invests in
    Overnight fund 1 day — the same overnight market banks use to meet balance-sheet requirements
    Liquid fund 91 days guaranteed MCQ
    Money market fund 1 year
    Medium to long duration fund / long duration fund Progressively longer

    Who uses them: companies with a sudden large cash inflow, or start-ups that have just closed a funding round and need to spend some money now and some over 12–18 months.

    15.9 Solution-oriented schemes

    Designed to meet a predefined financial goal: a young parent saving for a child's college in 15 years; an older parent saving for a wedding in 5–7 years; a retiree needing steady income after the salary stops.

    15.10 Index funds and ETFs

    An index fund buys the constituent shares in proportion to their market capitalisation, so the portfolio mimics the index — if the Sensex rises 2% in a day, the portfolio rises 2%. Doing it yourself would require constant rebalancing. Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) are a special category of index fund.

    SEBI's definition of an index fund: an open-ended scheme with at least 90% of the funds invested in replicating or tracking an index.

    15.11 Fund of Funds

    A mutual fund that invests in other mutual funds. SEBI created the "Fund of Funds investing in foreign mutual funds" category so wealthy Indians can invest abroad (e.g. an Indian FoF investing in American mutual funds which in turn hold American shares and bonds). There are domestic FoFs too. guaranteed MCQ

    15.12 Open-ended vs closed-ended — the full comparison guaranteed MCQ — expect this table| Feature | Closed-ended fund | Open-ended fund |

    |---|---|---| | Subscription window | 1 to 3 months, then closed | Perennial — continuously open | | Units sold | Limited number of tranches (usually 2 or 3) | Ongoing | | Fund withdrawal (selling back to the fund) | NOT permitted | Permitted — the fund buys back | | How the investor gets liquidity | By selling on a stock exchange (requires listing and an actual buyer), or by redemption at the end of the fund's life | By selling the units back to the fund management organisation | | Maturity | Predefined / finite (e.g. 10 or 15 years) | Infinite — unless the organisation shuts the scheme |

    A precision point: "Simply because a unit is listed on a stock exchange does not mean a seller can find a buyer. Selling is possible only if there is a buyer on the other side" — that is what liquidity means. guaranteed MCQ

    15.13 Industry size data

    The industry table records, for each scheme type: number of schemes · number of FOLIOS (the number of investor accounts) · Assets Under Management (AUM = the value of all investments made). Growth was "very, very remarkable during the pandemic and post-pandemic." guaranteed MCQ — know what a "folio" is

    1. Investment plans
    3

    16.1 SIP — Systematic Investment Plan

    Definition: a mechanism by which investors invest a REGULAR, CONSTANT sum of money at PREDEFINED INTERVALS (monthly, quarterly, etc.).

    The two advantages: guaranteed MCQ 1. It induces a saving and investment habit, especially among younger investors 2. It averages out fluctuations in price — you buy some units when prices are low and some when they are high, so the gains offset the losses. Investing a lump sum at one moment exposes you fully to whatever the price happens to be that day

    16.2 STP — Systematic Transfer Plan

    For when you already have the lump sum (e.g. a gift from an elderly grandparent) but want SIP-style averaging.

    Mechanism: put the whole amount into a money market mutual fund, then instruct it to transfer 1/12th each month for 12 months into the target fund as an SIP. guaranteed MCQ

    16.3 SWP — Systematic Withdrawal Plan

    The opposite of an SIP — for retirees and pensioners. Put, say, ₹4–5 crore into a fund and receive ₹1 lakh a month by bank transfer for 15, 20 or 25 years.

    Its flexibility features: guaranteed MCQ - Can be for a finite period or for life (in which case, being uncertain for the fund, the monthly amount will be lower than for a fixed 15-year term) - Can continue to the spouse after the investor's death - Can carry an annual increment to compensate for inflation (₹1,00,000/month in year 1, ₹1,05,000/month in year 2, and so on)

    1. NAV and mutual fund performance
    7

    17.1 The concept

    Simple version: a fund raises ₹100 and issues 10 units of ₹10 each → NAV = 100/10 = ₹10. Over 5 years the investments grow to ₹150 → NAV = 150/10 = ₹15.

    17.2 The full NAV worked example — memorise every line guaranteed MCQ| Item | Value |

    |---|---| | Scheme size | ₹100 crore | | Face value per unit | ₹10 | | Number of units | 10 crore | | Value of investments | ₹180 crore | | + Receivables | ₹1 crore | | + Accrued income | ₹1 crore | | − Borrowings (liability) | ₹0.5 crore (50 lakh) | | − Accrued expenses | ₹0.5 crore (50 lakh) | | = Net assets | ₹181 crore | | NAV per unit | 181 ÷ 10 = ₹18.10 |

    The formula: NAV = (Value of investments + receivables + accrued income − liabilities − accrued expenses) ÷ Number of units

    17.3 The five pricing terms guaranteed MCQ| Term | Definition |

    |---|---| | Entry load | A small extra charged when the fund SELLS a unit to a new investor — a front-ended fee, collected before the service has been delivered | | Exit load | A small charge deducted from the NAV when the fund BUYS BACK a unit — a rear-ended fee, collected after the service was rendered | | Market price | The price at which units trade on a stock exchange (closed-ended funds). Very often LESS than the NAV, in which case the units trade at a DISCOUNT; the discount = NAV − market price guaranteed MCQ| | Repurchase price | The price at which an open-ended fund buys units back from a unit holder — linked to the NAV | | Reissue price | The price at which an open-ended fund issues new units — also linked to the NAV |

    Ideally the market price should equal the NAV, because the NAV represents the true value of assets backing each unit. In practice it usually does not.

    17.4 One-period fund return

    Opening NAV ₹16, closing NAV ₹17, dividend paid ₹1.

    Return = (17 − 16 + 1) / 16 = 2/16 = 12.5%

    (The transcript's dictation says "2.5%"; the arithmetic of 2 ÷ 16 is 12.5%. Use the formula.)

    The methodological point he stresses twice: this calculation is done as though the units were bought at the beginning of the period and sold at the end, even if the investor did neither — because the investor needs to review performance and compare it with alternatives. guaranteed MCQ

    17.5 CAGR / CARR — the Zeta MF worked example guaranteed MCQ

    ₹1,000 invested in Zeta MF on 31 March 2020. Value ₹4,000 on 31 March 2022. Value ₹6,000 on 31 March 2025.

    Period Calculation CARR
    2020 → 2022 (2 years) (4000/1000)^(1/2) − 1 100%
    2022 → 2025 (3 years) (6000/4000)^(1/3) − 1 14%
    2020 → 2025 (5 years) (6000/1000)^(1/5) − 1 43%

    The interpretation: the first 2 years were exceptional (100%); the last 3 years were much weaker (14%), which pulls the 5-year figure down to 43%. guaranteed MCQ The conceptual justification for using ₹4,000 as the starting value of the second period: "I may not have sold at the end of March 2022, but I had the CHOICE of selling. In exercising the choice not to sell, I am effectively making a new investment at ₹4,000." guaranteed MCQ (Note: the transcript at one point also reads out "43%" for the 3-year period before correcting to 14%. The three correct answers are 100% / 14% / 43%.)

    1. The Sharpe Ratio
    6

    18.1 The formula

    Sharpe Ratio = (Portfolio return − Risk-free rate) ÷ Standard deviation of portfolio return

    Named after the economist WILLIAM SHARPE. guaranteed MCQ

    18.2 The risk-free rate — and why it is risk-free guaranteed MCQ

    The risk-free rate is the return on an absolutely safe investment: CENTRAL GOVERNMENT BONDS.

    Why they are risk-free: the central government can print currency, so it will never default on rupee borrowing from its own citizens.

    The careful qualifier he adds: it could potentially default on foreign-currency borrowing — if the Government of India borrowed from US citizens it would have to repay in US dollars, which it cannot print. (India has never actually defaulted.)

    18.3 The worked example guaranteed MCQ

    Risk-free rate = 5% for all three funds.

    Fund Return Standard deviation Sharpe Ratio
    X 12% 6% (12 − 5)/6 = 1.17
    Y 18% 15% (18 − 5)/15 = 0.87
    Z 22% 18% (22 − 5)/18 = 0.94

    The results, and why they matter:

    Ranking by Best Worst
    RAW RETURN Z (22%) X (12%)
    SHARPE RATIO X (1.17) Y (0.87)

    ← guaranteed MCQ — note that Y is SECOND-highest on return but LAST on Sharpe Ratio

    18.4 The interpretation he insists on

    The Sharpe Ratio is NOT a verdict on the quality of a fund. It measures return in relation to risk, helping you choose the fund appropriate for your requirement and your stage of life:

    • A young professional building a corpus over many working years can afford the variability → may choose Z, because when it does well it delivers 22%
    • A person nearing retirement wants stability and less risk → may choose X

    guaranteed MCQ

    18.5 SEBI's role

    SEBI has been pushing for more disclosure and more performance measures, and is actively looking at requiring funds to disclose their Sharpe Ratio, so investors judge funds on return adjusted for risk, not return alone. guaranteed MCQ The principle the whole course closes on: "Risk and reward go hand in hand. As they say in economics, there is nothing like a free lunch in this world. Whenever there is an increase in return, there is a commensurate increase in risk as well — EXCEPT for the reduction in risk we achieve through systematic diversification." guaranteed MCQ

    Introduction to Insurance

    Introduction to Insurance — Complete Exam Reference

    Course faculty: Prof. Sankarshan Basu (IIM Bangalore, Finance & Accounting, 23+ years) Guest practitioner: Pradeep Yadav (BU Head, Term Insurance, PolicyBazaar)

    How to use this file. The course runs: what insurance is → classification → the legal framework → operations and claims → the India story (life and non-life) → products → intermediaries → IRDAI and regulation → underwriting → reinsurance → InsurTech. Anything marked ← guaranteed MCQ is a number, date, definition or distinction that MCQ writers reach for. The Quick-fire revision table at the end collects every figure in one place.

    The one sentence that runs through the whole course:

    "Insurance is RISK REDISTRIBUTION, not risk reduction. The risk in the SYSTEM does not fall; it moves from the individual to the insurer."

    1. What insurance is
    16

    1.1 Definitions

    Term Definition
    Insurance (broad) A method of handling risks that could result in potential losses
    Risk (in insurance) "A condition in which there is a possibility of an adverse deviation from the desired outcome" guaranteed MCQ
    Risk (economic) An EXPECTED loss — not yet a realised loss. "Risk may not always materialise"
    Insurance (contract form) In consideration of a specific payment (the PREMIUM) by the first party (the policy buyer), the second party (the insurer) agrees to indemnify the first party up to a certain limit for a specified loss that may or may not occur

    A crucial nuance on "deviation": deviation can be positive (actual return exceeds expectation — you're happy) or negative (adverse deviation → potential loss). Insurance is only concerned with the adverse side. guaranteed MCQ

    1.2 There is no risk-free environment

    His standing example: we assume a government borrowing in its own currency is risk-free because the Government of India can print money (the right of seigniorage). But globally there have been sovereign defaults on domestic borrowing, so "effectively there is nothing called a risk-free environment" — only a framework based on assumptions. guaranteed MCQ

    1.3 How insurance works — the economics

    Collection of small amounts of premium from many individuals, out of which the losses suffered by a few are reimbursed.

    Two conditions make it work:

    Condition Explanation
    A large, DIVERSIFIED policy base Deliberately spread across geographies and segments so that individual loss events are INDEPENDENT and concentration risk is low
    The LAW OF LARGE NUMBERS "The greater the number of observations of an event based on chance, the more likely the actual result will approximate the expected result." One or two observations may not map; ~300 observations will map closely guaranteed MCQ

    The statistical basis for pooling: if each risk has a probability of, say, 0.01 of materialising, and events are independent, the joint probability is the PRODUCT of the marginals — 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.0001. Multiplying numbers between 0 and 1 makes the joint probability smaller. guaranteed MCQ

    1.4 Why the premium must be a small fraction of the sum insured

    His argument, worked out fully:

    If the premium equalled the value of the asset, over a 10-year horizon you would pay the car's full value ten times over. In the one year you claim, you get back only what you paid that year, so your effective loss is unchanged. In the other nine years you paid for nothing. Therefore the premium must be a small proportion — typically 2% to 5% of the value of the asset — for the product to be attractive at all. guaranteed MCQ (the 2–5% figure) And the concentration counter-example: if an insurer covers all the cars in one residential complex next to a river that floods every year, one flood produces claims from every policyholder at once, and the premiums collected cannot cover them. guaranteed MCQ

    1.5 Pure risk vs speculative risk guaranteed MCQ| | Pure risk | Speculative risk |

    |---|---|---| | Outcomes | Loss or no loss | Loss OR gain | | Examples | Property, liabilities, life, health, associated loss of income | Business ventures, investments, financial risks | | Insurable? | YES — insurance covers ONLY pure risks | No |

    1.6 The risk management tools

    Tool Meaning
    Risk avoidance Don't take the risk. "Can we really avoid it? Effectively no."
    Risk reduction Lower the exposure, or take counterbalancing exposures
    Risk retention Hold the risk yourself and finance it
    RISK TRANSFER Pass the risk to someone with a greater appetite, for a consideration. This is the genesis of insurance guaranteed MCQ

    Note: "Insurance is only ONE of the approaches by which risk can be transferred."

    1.7 The risk management process — four steps guaranteed MCQ

    1. Identify the potential losses
    2. Evaluate those losses
    3. Select appropriate techniques for treating each loss exposure — "all exposures cannot be treated by the same technique"
    4. Implement and administer the programme on an ongoing, continuous basis — because "what holds good today may not hold good after 5 years"

    The risk manager's three questions: "What can go wrong? What can you do about it? How can you pay for it?" guaranteed MCQ

    1.8 The scope of risk management has widened

    Traditionally: pure loss exposures only → later extended to speculative financial risks → today ALL risks. This is the origin of Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) — a comprehensive programme covering pure and speculative risks, described as "a CEO addressing the risk issue" rather than cherry-picking one risk. guaranteed MCQ

    1.9 Premium components — what the premium is built from guaranteed MCQ| Component | Note |

    |---|---| | Claims (expected payouts) | The single biggest chunk. Risk becomes quantifiable only through the claims it generates | | Claims-handling expenses | | | Cost of acquiring business | | | Operational / management expense | | | Profit margin | | | Loading for contingencies | For what cannot be foreseen | | LESS: Investment income | The only NEGATIVE item — an income, not a cost |

    The relationship to remember: higher investment income → lower premium charged to policyholders, because part of the payout comes from investment returns rather than premiums. guaranteed MCQ

    1.10 The major risks (his list)

    Longevity is the first and most interesting: guaranteed MCQ

    Both dying too EARLY and living too LONG are risks. "Too short a longevity is a problem. Too long a longevity is also a problem."

    Others: financial market returns · protection of capital · divergence from the UN Sustainable Development Goals · new non-life product risks · delivery-channel risks · technology risk.

    Technology risk defined precisely: "Technology risk is NOT about today's technology. Technology risk is about the risk of the CHANGE in technology" — by the time you reverse-engineer and launch, new technology has arrived and your product finds no takers. guaranteed MCQ Delivery-channel risk: the move from direct agents → bancassurance → online buying removed the experienced agent's advice, created an information gap, and means "in a purely online product you do not know who your customers are."

    1. Why insurance matters — the catastrophe numbers
    3

    Event Year Loss
    September 11 (Twin Towers) 2001 Estimates range $15 billion to $80 billion (a band of more than 5×); economic loss ~$80bn; INSURED losses ~$50bn guaranteed MCQ
    Hurricane Andrew (USA) 1992 ~$20 billion
    South Asian tsunami 2004 over $13 billion
    Gujarat earthquake 2001 ~₹30,000 crore
    Bhopal Gas Tragedy ~40 years ago (1984) ~₹1,000 crore of measurable monetary loss

    And the headline statistic: "Insurance as an industry contributes about 15% of the country's GDP, particularly in DEVELOPED countries" (less in less-developed countries). guaranteed MCQ The oldest and most common form of insurance: MARINE INSURANCE — because global trade travelled by water and ships faced damage, pirates and destruction. "It has remained the cornerstone of international trade." guaranteed MCQ

    1. Classification of insurance
    5

    3.1 The basic split guaranteed MCQ| | LIFE insurance | NON-LIFE insurance |

    |---|---|---| | Subject | The individual | Property, and persons in the case of casualty/fortuity | | What is actually insured | NOT life — life cannot be insured or replaced. What is covered is the FINANCIAL LOSS arising from the absence of the individual | The VALUE of the asset, not the asset itself | | Name in the US | | Property and Casualty (P&C) | | Name in the UK / India | | General insurance |

    The definitional trap: "Life insurance is the name — but I can't really insure life. What I can insure is the financial loss that arises due to loss of life, or the impact if a person SURVIVES — the survivorship issue or survival benefit." guaranteed MCQ Life insurance covers TWO risks: guaranteed MCQ 1. Dying too early → the death benefit 2. Living too long → endowments, annuities, survival benefits

    3.2 HEALTH — the grey area guaranteed MCQ

    Health is on the individual, so logically it belongs with life. But what is reimbursed is the COST of treatment, not health itself — so in most markets including India, HEALTH INSURANCE IS CLASSIFIED AS A NON-LIFE PRODUCT.

    3.3 The corporate structure rule in India

    In India the SAME company cannot do both life and non-life. You may have a holding pattern across both, but they must be separate legal entities. Globally, companies on both sides run them as two separate divisions. guaranteed MCQ

    1. The pyramid: insurer → reinsurer → retrocessionaire → government
    3

    Term Definition
    Reinsurance (RI) Insurance for the insurer
    Ceding company The primary/direct insurer — it cedes part of its risk
    Line / Retention The portion of risk the ceding company KEEPS guaranteed MCQ
    Cession The portion passed on to the reinsurer guaranteed MCQ
    Retrocession The reinsurer ceding onward to a retrocessionaire
    The final backstop THE GOVERNMENT — because it has the right to seigniorage (printing money) and can revive the system if the whole market collapses guaranteed MCQ

    4.1 The structure of the insurance market

    Buyers (policyholders) → Intermediaries (brokers, agents) → Insurers → Reinsurers → (Retrocessionaires) → Government, all under a regulator.

    India is the EXACT OPPOSITE of the global pattern. And the historical irony: there was one life insurer (LIC) and FOUR non-life insurers, yet life did about three times the business of non-life.

The VOLUNTARY non-life market is still not a big element — whereas life insurance, which is predominantly a VOLUNTARY market, has taken off." guaranteed MCQ The implication: the greatest growth headroom in India is in NON-LIFE.
