    1. The legal framework
    22

    6.1 Insurance as a contract

    A contract between the INSURER and the INSURED whereby, for a consideration of payment of PREMIUM by the insured, the insurer agrees to MAKE GOOD ANY FINANCIAL LOSS the insured may suffer due to the operation of a PERIL that has been insured.

    The primary governing law is the INDIAN CONTRACT ACT, 1872 — because fundamentally it is a contract. guaranteed MCQ

    6.2 The specific statutes guaranteed MCQ — years and names| Act | Year | Scope |

    |---|---|---| | Indian Contract Act | 1872 | The base law for all contracts | | Indian Railways Act | 1890 | Carriage | | Carriers Act | 1865 | Carriage | | Indian Life Assurance Companies Act | 1912 | The FIRST effective insurance regulation in India (life only) | | Workmen's Compensation Act | 1923 | Non-life specific | | Indian Insurance Companies Act | 1928 | First to cover BOTH life and non-life | | INSURANCE ACT | 1938 | The primary legislation and "bulwark" of Indian insurance regulation to this day | | Marine Insurance Act | 1963 | Non-life specific | | Consumer Protection Act | 1986 | Consumer redress | | Motor Vehicles Act | 1988 | Non-life specific | | Public Liability Insurance Act | 1991 | Hazardous goods | | IRDA Act | 1999 | Created the regulator with statutory powers |

    A rule of legal citation he stresses twice: "An Act is ALWAYS characterised by the year in which it was FIRST formulated, no matter how many times it has been amended. The version enforced today is the latest amended version." guaranteed MCQ

    6.3 The standard contract requirements

    Offer · Acceptance · Consideration (the premium) · Lawful object · Competent parties · Consensus (meeting of minds)

    Plus, specific to insurance: guaranteed MCQ — the four insurance-specific principles 1. Insurable interest 2. Uberrimae Fidei (utmost good faith) 3. Indemnity 4. Subrogation and Contribution

    6.4 INSURABLE INTEREST

    Definition: the LEGAL RIGHT to insure, arising out of a financial relationship RECOGNISED BY LAW between the insured and the subject matter of insurance. guaranteed MCQ Its purpose: "It distinguishes insurance from pure betting." guaranteed MCQ The Tom worked example: Tom buys five fire policies — on his own house and on his office, two friends' and a neighbour's houses. A fire destroys a neighbour's house. Can Tom claim? NO — he has no insurable interest in someone else's house. guaranteed MCQ Where insurable interest exists: your own life · your own property · a mortgagee/lender over the borrower's property (because the lender must protect itself if something happens to the borrower) · relationships created by contract · relationships created by statute (e.g. compulsory motor insurance in India).

    WHEN insurable interest must exist — the three-way rule: guaranteed MCQ| Class | When it must exist | |---|---| | LIFE insurance | At the time of taking the policy (inception) ONLY | | MARINE and CARGO insurance | NOT necessarily at inception — but definitely BEFORE/AT THE TIME OF LOSS | | Other classes | At any point, or in some cases BOTH at inception AND at the time of claim |

    The television worked example: you hold a 1-year policy on your TV (1 Jan – 31 Dec). On 1 June you sell the TV to a friend and tell him not to buy insurance. On 15 June there is a claim. Result: the claim FAILS, because you no longer own the TV, so you no longer have an insurable interest. The fix would have been to ASSIGN the policy to the friend along with the TV. guaranteed MCQ ASSIGNMENT — transferring the rights/liabilities of an insured to a party who has acquired the insurable interest: guaranteed MCQ| Class | Assignment | |---|---| | Life insurance | Permitted | | Non-life insurance | Requires the insurer's EXPLICIT approval — except for marine cargo policies and transfer of interest by will or by operation of law | | Motor THIRD-PARTY | Assignment is allowed to the injured third party — the driver who caused the accident does not receive the third-party benefit; the person impacted does |

    6.5 UBERRIMAE FIDEI — utmost good faith

    Definition: the POSITIVE DUTY to VOLUNTARILY disclose, ACCURATELY and FULLY, all facts material to the risk being proposed — WHETHER OR NOT THE INSURER ASKS. guaranteed MCQ A MATERIAL FACT = information which, had it been known, would have changed the decision — either to reject the application or to issue on substantially different terms (higher cost, exclusions). guaranteed MCQ It binds BOTH parties. The insurer cannot hide behind fine print — everything must be in the document.

    The two worked examples — expect one of them: guaranteed MCQ| Case | Facts | Outcome | |---|---|---| | Harry | Takes a medical policy stating he is "perfectly healthy", though he has been diagnosed with hypertension and is on medication. 8 months later he suffers a stroke that the doctor links to the hypertension | CLAIM DISALLOWED — non-disclosure of a material fact that would have caused rejection or higher pricing | | David | Insures his car declaring nobody below age 25 will drive it, though it is extensively used by his 18-year-old son. The car is written off in an accident driven by the son | CLAIM NOT ENTERTAINED — the risk profile of an 18-year-old differs materially from a 25-year-old |

    Breach of utmost good faith arises from NON-DISCLOSURE or MISREPRESENTATION or both, and gives grounds for AVOIDANCE/NULLIFICATION of the contract by the insurer. guaranteed MCQ The cruel timing point he stresses: "The nullification does not come to life in the normal course. It is only when a CLAIM is made that these issues come to the fore" — so the policyholder discovers the problem exactly when they need the money.

    Duration of the disclosure duty: through the negotiation until the contract is concluded; again at each renewal of a non-life policy; and during the life of the policy when conditions change.

    The most important document: the PROPOSAL FORM and its declaration — "deemed to be a part of the policy." guaranteed MCQ

    6.6 WARRANTIES

    Undertakings by the insured, express or implied. Any breach of warranty makes the contract invalid or voidable.

    His laptop analogy: the sticker reading "warranty void if this seal is broken." A friend opens and repairs your laptop; months later the service centre sees the broken seal and refuses free repair — "though you might have had a protection, because that condition has been violated, it will not be honoured." guaranteed MCQ

    6.7 INDEMNITY

    The principle of indemnity ensures that an individual shall NOT be permitted to MAKE A PROFIT from the existence of an insurance contract. The insured should only be RESTORED TO THE SAME FINANCIAL CONDITION that existed PRIOR to the occurrence of the loss.

    guaranteed MCQ — this exact wording The Mr Smith worked example (know it both ways): guaranteed MCQ| Case | Property value | Policy limit | Loss | Payout | |---|---|---|---|---| | Over-insured | ₹5 lakh | ₹10 lakh | Total destruction by earthquake | ₹5 lakh — you cannot profit | | Under-insured | ₹10 lakh | ₹5 lakh | Total write-off | ₹5 lakh — capped at the sum insured |

    Four ways indemnity can be provided: guaranteed MCQ Cash payment · Repair · Replacement · Reinstatement

    Modifications to strict indemnity: agreed value policies · benefit policies · reinstatement value policies.

    Indemnity by class of non-life business:

    Class Basis
    Marine Commercial indemnity
    Liability (e.g. motor third party) The amount spent and awarded under the contract plus costs, subject to policy terms
    Fire and property Strict indemnity based on MARKET VALUE
    Benefit policies The specified amount

    Limitations on the amount payable: the total sum insured · average clause · excess · franchise · time excess · SALVAGE VALUE (the insurer compensates you, so if you can sell the damaged asset for scrap that salvage must be adjusted against the payout). guaranteed MCQ

    6.8 SUBROGATION and CONTRIBUTION guaranteed MCQ — do not swap these| Principle | Definition |

    |---|---| | SUBROGATION | Transferring the RIGHTS AND REMEDIES of the INSURED to the INSURER — the policyholder hands his legal rights to the insurance company after being paid | | CONTRIBUTION | The right of an insurer who has paid a loss to recover a PROPORTIONATE amount from ANOTHER INSURER who is also liable for the same loss |

    His two-car worked example: A and B collide; A is at fault. B's insurer pays B's repair. B's insurer then recovers that amount from A's insurer, because the liability sits with A. That recovery between insurers is the contribution process.

    6.9 CONTRA PROFERENTEM

    Policy documents are drafted by the INSURER, not the policyholder. Therefore ANY AMBIGUITY IS ALWAYS INTERPRETED IN FAVOUR OF THE INSURED, who is at the disadvantage.

    guaranteed MCQ — know the Latin name

    1. Insurance operations
    7

    7.1 The four things an insurance company actually does guaranteed MCQ

    1. Mitigate risk (transfer, not reduce)
    2. Earn a return on investments — because life insurance runs 25, 30, even 50–70 years, "the insurance company operates like an investment management firm"
    3. Provide risk cover — "this is what differentiates the insurance contract from all other financial services products"
    4. Provide additional benefits (optional riders, faster claims, etc.)

    7.2 The risk-redistribution point, stated precisely

    Risk reduction happens at the INDIVIDUAL level, NOT at the SYSTEMIC level. guaranteed MCQ| Example | Effect | |---|---| | Airbags, ABS, crash-protection in a car | Reduces the impact on the individual. Does NOT reduce the probability of accidents in the system | | Better transport containers for toxic material | Genuinely reduces systemic risk, because spillage becomes less likely for everyone |

    7.3 Why insurance is uniquely hard to market guaranteed MCQ

    "Insurance becomes valuable to a policyholder ONLY if there is a loss. If you ask a policyholder what they got at the end of a claim-free year, the honest answer is: nothing."

    You are selling a potential future NEGATIVE event for which you fund today — hence "probably the most difficult product to market in the whole universe of financial market products."

    7.4 The five risks an insurance company itself runs guaranteed MCQ| Risk | Definition and treatment |

    |---|---| | Market risk | The underlying price/value changes and you cannot control it. In insurance the primary source is INTEREST RATE RISK. Mitigated with forwards and options/derivatives. (His analogy: you can't control the weather, but you can wear a jacket or switch on the AC) | | Credit risk | The risk of DEFAULT. In insurance the default that matters is the INSURER failing to pay a valid claim. Mitigated with credit derivatives or, crudely, collateral | | Operational risk | Wrong payments, premium not collected, extra premium collected, wrong claims processed. The hardest to model — the events are "few and far between", so there is no pattern | | Reputational risk | Very important but essentially unquantifiable — "we don't have a model to quantify it" | | Legal risk | Disputes, contested claims, and — critically — the quantum of loss is often unknown/uncapped |

    The three operational-risk capital approaches (borrowed from banking): guaranteed MCQ| Approach | Method | Trade-off | |---|---|---| | BIA — Basic Indicator Approach | Track a few indicators; regulator sets the capital | Simplest | | Standardised Approach | A percentage of business size/profits per line | Simple to operate, but does NOT differentiate between firms — better firms get no credit | | AMA — Advanced Measurement Approach | Your own internal model, vetted by the regulator | Only very large global players can reach it; most use BIA or Standardised |

    7.5 The challenges an insurer faces guaranteed MCQ

    Data (the first THREE items on his list are all data): quality data, continuous data, authentic data. "Data is either not available, or not accurate, or too dated for any meaningful analysis" — and much of it is not properly archived. The Data Privacy Act adds the question of who owns the data and who may use it.

    People: the shortage of trained agents and staff, and especially ACTUARIES — "the number who graduate and practise as actuaries is minuscule compared with the number needed."

    The UK pension mis-selling case study: guaranteed MCQ

    Through the 1980s and early 1990s, UK pension funds mis-sold pension plans without giving full information. In the mid-1990s the UK regulator ordered the companies to correct it before writing new business. From roughly 1996–97 to 2005 — a good 7 to 8 years — that correction was the biggest problem for the UK insurance/pension industry, at huge cost. The lesson: having semi-informed or ill-informed personnel is a BIGGER problem than not having a person at all.

    Investment constraints: the regulator restricts where insurers may invest (to protect policyholders), yet they must still generate long-term returns — "the avenues of investment get challenged from both sides."

    Minimum guarantees in a volatile interest-rate regime are "extremely, extremely" difficult to promise.

    7.6 The five operational-efficiency issues

    Claims processing speed (the biggest one) · information flow from sales → underwriting → claims · information overload management · adapting to changing market demands — which requires LEARN → UNLEARN → RELEARN, and "UNLEARNING is the most difficult task" ← guaranteed MCQ · reducing leakages to generate surplus.

    1. Claims
    11

    8.1 What a claim is

    A DEMAND made against the occurrence of some event that has led to a financial loss. The exception is a life insurance survival/maturity claim, where no loss has occurred at all. guaranteed MCQ

    8.2 The sources of claims guaranteed MCQ| Class | Sources |

    |---|---| | LIFE | (1) DEATH of the policyholder → the DEATH BENEFIT. (2) MATURITY of the policy → the SURVIVAL BENEFIT | | NON-LIFE | The occurrence of a PREDEFINED EVENT |

    8.3 Life claim processing — the rules guaranteed MCQ| Situation | Rule |

    |---|---| | DEATH claim | Payable at ANY point during the valid policy life, and IRRESPECTIVE of how many premiums have been paid — even if only one has been paid. The FULL sum assured must be paid, unless death arose from an excluded cause (e.g. suicide in early years). The shortfall is met from the company's RESERVES AND SURPLUS | | SURVIVAL claim | Only on maturity, and only for term/endowment policies (not whole life). By definition all premiums have been collected. Payout = premiums + guaranteed bonus (+ possibly a loyalty bonus) |

    The rule of thumb: "Typically the sum assured is equal to the total value of the premium payable over the life of the contract" — though strictly it should be less, because the insurer earns interest on early premiums. guaranteed MCQ

    8.4 THE TWO-YEAR RULE — a certain MCQ

    In a LIFE insurance policy, non-disclosure or misrepresentation can be used as grounds to repudiate a claim ONLY within the FIRST TWO YEARS of the policy. Beyond two years the insurer has NO right to say information was suppressed.

    Why: "beyond two years, given the numbers are large, it all averages out" (the law of large numbers / central limit theorem).

    Why it doesn't matter for non-life: a non-life policy is at most one year, and each "renewal" is legally a NEW policy, so the two-year window never becomes relevant. guaranteed MCQ

    8.5 Health claim processing

    Benefit type Meaning
    Hospitalisation benefit Admission, procedures, room rent
    Non-hospitalisation / DOMICILIARY Doctor consultation, blood tests, ECG, X-ray, home-based treatment

    CASHLESS model: on admission the insurer is notified, sanctions the claim and tells the hospital the limit; the patient pays nothing up to that limit. Anything above it is paid by the patient. Otherwise it is a reimbursement model.

    THE 24-HOUR RULE: most policies require hospitalisation for 24 hours for the benefit to apply, except for specific conditions such as CHEMOTHERAPY and DIALYSIS. guaranteed MCQ The perverse consequence he flags: because the insurer will not pay for a stay shorter than 24 hours, hospital stays get artificially elongated, which adversely affects the healthcare system. guaranteed MCQ EXCESS / co-pay — "skin in the game": a stated percentage the policyholder must bear. Worked example: a ₹1,00,000 claim with a 10% excess → the policyholder pays the first ₹10,000 and the insurer pays ₹90,000. Its purpose is fraud reduction and shared responsibility. guaranteed MCQ TPA — Third Party Administrator: the interface between customer and insurer. They take NO risk and do NOT sell the policy — they simply administer it. Insurers outsource to them because "administering the payouts is not core; the risk mitigation is core." guaranteed MCQ

    8.6 NO CLAIMS DISCOUNT (NCD) — the two directions guaranteed MCQ

    The common logic: on day zero the insurer has no information about the individual. A claim-free year is information that lowers the assessed risk.

    Class How the NCD is applied Why
    MOTOR The PREMIUM falls Because the asset value DEPRECIATES each year, so the maximum payable falls anyway. Worked example: a ₹25 lakh car worth ₹20 lakh next year → premium X falls to X − A where A is the NCD
    HEALTH The premium is held CONSTANT and the COVER is INCREASED Because healthcare costs RISE with age. Worked example: ₹10 lakh cover → ₹12 lakh → ₹15 lakh, with no premium increase

    "Fundamentally the same thing, but operated in OPPOSITE directions."

    The equity rationale: without an NCD "the good people would be subsidising the bad people" — so the NCD incentivises being healthy / driving well.

    8.7 The insurer's three duties on claims

    Verify accuracy and validity before paying · Estimate the annual claims burden and make PROVISIONS through investment strategy and capital · Pay in an efficient, TRANSPARENT and TIMELY manner — "even if I have to reject a claim, it should be transparent."

    Non-payment of a valid claim — "whether it is a technical default can be questioned, but to the policyholder it IS a default." guaranteed MCQ
