    9.1 The global origins guaranteed MCQ — dates and names| Date | Event |

    |---|---| | ~1750 BC | The CODE OF HAMMURABI — a loan taken to buy/run a ship, secured by pledging the cargo. If the ship sank or the cargo was looted, the loan did not need repaying; if the cargo was delivered, the loan was repaid with interest — the interest being, in effect, the premium | | 1666 | THE GREAT FIRE OF LONDON — destroyed about 30,000 houses, changed London from wood to stone construction, and created the need for FIRE INSURANCE | | 1676 | HAMBURGER FEUERKASSE (Germany) — the oldest insurance company in the world that still exists, about 350 years old | | — | LLOYD'S OF LONDON — began in a COFFEE HOUSE where traders met to discuss sharing losses from piracy and natural disasters at sea. Today it is a MARKETPLACE for insurance and reinsurance, not an insurance company guaranteed MCQ|

    9.2 The Indian timeline guaranteed MCQ — this whole table| Year | Event |

    |---|---| | 1757 | Battle of Plassey; Calcutta becomes the key British trading post and eventually the second city of the British Empire | | 1818 | ORIENTAL INSURANCE COMPANY, CALCUTTA — the genesis of formal (life and non-life) insurance in India | | 1818–1871 | Indians ("natives") paid 20% MORE premium than a Britisher for the same product guaranteed MCQ| | 1850 | TRITON INSURANCE COMPANY LIMITED — the first separate, independent GENERAL insurance company in India | | 1871 | BOMBAY MUTUAL LIFE INSURANCE SOCIETY — its founding normalised the rates, ending the 20% discrimination after ~50 years | | 1912 | Indian Life Assurance Companies Act — the first effective insurance regulation | | 1928 | Indian Insurance Companies Act — covers life and non-life | | 1938 | THE INSURANCE ACT — the primary legislation for the next 60 years; its focus was monitoring activities and protecting the interests of the INSURERS (protecting the insured came later, with IRDA in 1999) guaranteed MCQ| | 1950 | First major amendment — equity capital requirements introduced for life insurance companies (until then there were none), investment controls, and the Office of the Controller of Insurance set up at SHIMLA guaranteed MCQ| | 1956 | NATIONALISATION OF LIFE INSURANCE → LIC (details below) | | 1972 | NATIONALISATION OF NON-LIFE → GIC and the four subsidiaries (details below) | | 1991 | The great liberalisation; financial markets at the forefront | | 1993 | The MALHOTRA COMMITTEE appointed under Mr R. N. Malhotra, a former RBI Governor — the "Committee for Reforms in the Insurance Sector"; reported in 1994 guaranteed MCQ| | 1996 | IRDA set up on an interim/temporary basis; the enabling amendment passed | | 1999 | The IRDA ACT gives the regulator statutory, quasi-judicial powers; the Insurance Act is amended and PRIVATE PLAYERS are allowed back in — "the single largest amendment" guaranteed MCQ| | 2000 | GIC becomes the official Indian reinsurer → GIC Re | | 2017 | IRDAI admitted to the IAIS | | 2025 | The Finance Minister removes the FDI cap — 100% foreign ownership permitted |

    9.3 The creation of LIC — the numbers guaranteed MCQ| Item | Detail |

    |---|---| | Statute | Life Insurance Corporation Act, passed by Parliament on 19 JUNE 1956, then presidential assent | | LIC physically established | 1 SEPTEMBER 1956 | | Entities amalgamated | 245 in total = 154 Indian insurers + 16 non-Indian insurers operating in India + 75 Provident Societies | | Seed capital from Government | ₹5 crore | | Objective | Spread awareness of life insurance especially to rural and semi-urban areas; "reach all insurable persons and provide adequate financial cover at a reasonable cost" — i.e. financial inclusion | | Side task | Initially also charged with promoting non-life/general insurance until GIC was created |

    9.4 The creation of GIC and the four companies — 1972 guaranteed MCQ

    Statute: the General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972. 107 insurers were nationalised and combined into FOUR geographic companies, with GIC created as the holding company:

    Company Headquarters Zone
    National Insurance Company Calcutta East
    New India Assurance Company Bombay West
    Oriental Insurance Company New Delhi North
    United India Insurance Company Madras / Chennai South

    Why four for non-life but only one for life? "The nature of the businesses was very different" — non-life is driven by industrialisation, which is geographically specific, so a company was placed in each of the four zones. guaranteed MCQ GIC's role: holding company for ~28 years; also did India's reinsurance business when the market was closed. In 2000 it became GIC Re, the designated national reinsurer, and the ownership of the four companies went to the Government directly — because IRDAI could now regulate them, so a holding company was no longer needed for oversight. guaranteed MCQ

    9.5 The FDI progression guaranteed MCQ

    100% domestic → 76% domestic / 24% foreign (1999) → 51% domestic / 49% foreign → 100% foreign permitted (2025 Budget)

    "So very soon major global players would want to come in and establish participation, because now they can own 100% and don't need an Indian partner."

    9.6 The players today guaranteed MCQ| Category | Number |

    |---|---| | Life insurance companies | 26 (LIC + 25 others) | | General (non-life) insurance companies | 27 — including the 4 public sector ones plus 2 other government entities: Agriculture Insurance Company and ECGC (Export Credit Guarantee Corporation) | | Standalone health insurers | 7 (e.g. Care, Niva Bupa) — companies whose ONLY business is health | | Reinsurers | 1 — GIC Re (public sector) | | Foreign reinsurer branches (FRBs) | 13 |

    Named private life insurers and their evolution: HDFC Standard Life → HDFC Life (bought out Standard Life) · ICICI Prudential · Max New York Life → Axis Max (Axis acquired the stake ~a year before recording) · SBI Life ("probably the only one who have done it themselves") · Bajaj Allianz · PNB MetLife. guaranteed MCQ Lloyd's India: the current regulation is the Registration and Operations of Foreign Insurers' Branches and Lloyd's India Regulations, 2024, which subsumed the earlier 2015 and 2016 regulations. "Lloyd's India is mentioned BY NAME in the title of the regulation" — a measure of its importance. guaranteed MCQ

    9.7 LIC's market position today guaranteed MCQ| Metric | LIC's share |

    |---|---| | Total life insurance market | over 75% — the other ~20+ firms share the remaining ~25% | | RENEWAL premium | ~80–85% — the source of its dominance | | NEW BUSINESS (first-time buyers) | ~48–50% — a much more even split | | LIC agents | over 14 LAKH — not employees; self-employed, commission-based guaranteed MCQ|

    1. How the Indian market evolved socially
    6

    10.1 From joint family to nuclear family

    In the joint family system only one or two people were economically active and the rest were carried, so the need for formal social security was never prominent. As India moved to nuclear families, collective accountability broke down and securing oneself became essential. guaranteed MCQ

    10.2 The three-stage evolution of WHY Indians buy insurance guaranteed MCQ| Stage | Driver |

    |---|---| | 1. Tax saving | Government tax incentives made insurance primarily a tax-saving instrument, with protection as a by-product | | 2. Investment | As incomes rose and other tax-saving instruments appeared, insurance came to be viewed as another investment opportunity | | 3. Wealth accumulation | The long-term, FORCED-SAVING character of life insurance makes it a wealth-accumulation vehicle — and the only genuinely LONG-TERM investment route (equity is short-term, bonds medium-term; pensions are the third leg) |

    The observable market consequence: until about 20 years ago, most Indian life policies were sold in the LAST QUARTER of the financial year (January–March) because that is the tax-saving window. As the motive shifted to investment, sales have evened out across the year with only minor bunching. guaranteed MCQ

    10.3 CREDIT LIFE INSURANCE — a recent Indian development

    The problem: a 20–30 year mortgage. If the borrower dies, the lender can theoretically seize and sell the house — but in India that is emotionally and legally extremely difficult, and the asset stays locked, adding no value. The alternative — charging very high rates — would itself push the loan toward default.

    The solution: the borrower takes a credit life policy linked to the mortgage's expected value, with a dual beneficiary condition: on default or death, the benefit accrues FIRST to the mortgage provider to clear the outstanding loan, and the balance goes to the insured's family. If the loan is fully repaid, the benefit reverts to the insured. guaranteed MCQ Its wider use: as a proxy guarantee to improve CREDIT SCORES, lower borrowing rates and improve market access.

    10.4 REVERSE MORTGAGE — why it works in the West and fails in India

    How it works: you agree to sell the house forward — on your (and possibly your spouse's) death the reverse mortgage company acquires it. They value it, compute the PRESENT VALUE of that future price, and pay you cash today. You continue to live in the house with full rights, use the cash to clear your mortgage, so your monthly liability falls and your disposable income and savings rise. Your heirs inherit liquid, geography-agnostic financial assets instead of a house in a remote town they don't want.

    The result: "A roaring success" in the West. A COMPLETE FAILURE in India and China — because in India a house is not treated as a mere financial asset but as a family heirloom to be retained for generations. guaranteed MCQ The mirror example: GOLD. India is "probably the highest consumer of gold in the world" because gold is a security mechanism, especially for women. In markets with developed financial inclusion, gold is not an important asset class. guaranteed MCQ The lesson: the principles of insurance are universal; the PRODUCTS must fit the society.

    1. Life insurance products
    10

    11.1 The main product types guaranteed MCQ| Product | Description |

    |---|---| | TERM insurance | A fixed term (5/10/15/20 years). If death occurs during the term, a fixed amount is paid. (In the traditional Indian variant described, on survival the premiums plus return plus loyalty bonus come back as a lump sum) | | ENDOWMENT insurance | You pay in instalments for a period, then a period of pure investment with no further input, then a payout. Open-ended closure date in the whole-life variant | | ANNUITY insurance | You pay the money UPFRONT in a SINGLE SHOT (the present value); it then pays you a fixed amount for a defined duration. This is THE difference from an endowment guaranteed MCQ| | WHOLE LIFE assurance | Cover for the entire life — completely open-ended | | Convertible whole life | Can be converted into something else later | | Anticipated endowment | How much do I need to put in for a given expected payout | | JOINT LIFE assurance | Not one life but two or more (e.g. self and spouse). Payout may be triggered on the first death or only when both have died | | GROUP life insurance | Cover for a number of persons under ONE contract | | ULIP — Unit Linked Insurance Plan | India's most popular type. Splits into an insurance component and units in the financial market (equity/bonds), so the corpus fluctuates with the market. A combined insurance + investment policy guaranteed MCQ| | Children's policies | Payouts timed to a child's life-cycle milestones (school, marriageable age). Government incentives often target the girl child. Their value over DIY saving is the enforced discipline — "the ability to keep the money there irrespective of any other demand" | | Money-back policy | Term assurance + pure endowment = endowment assurance, a variant of money-back: money comes back at several points, not only at the end | | Immediate vs Deferred annuity | Payments start now vs after a defined period (e.g. 5 years) |

    11.2 The advantage of joint life / group guaranteed MCQ

    When one insured life exits, the others in the group continue paying, so the insurer's loss is much lower — which lets the cost of insurance be brought down, making it affordable. In an individual policy, on the policyholder's death both the payout occurs AND the future income stream stops.

    Typical group types: employer–employee groups · borrower–depositor groups · affinity groups (a club, a friend circle). guaranteed MCQ The operational risk caveat — the 26/11 anecdote: guaranteed MCQ

    During the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks, one major company had its entire board and top ~30 executives at a dinner in the Taj/Oberoi. Pure luck kept the terrorists out of that room. Had they entered, "the survival of the organisation would have been brought into question." This is why organisations forbid the entire senior management flying together — a classic operational risk control.

    11.3 Premium payment structures guaranteed MCQ

    REGULAR PAY (annual or monthly — the most common) · SINGLE PAY (everything in one shot) · LIMITED PAY (a middle option — e.g. once every two or three years).

    11.4 Participating vs Non-Participating guaranteed MCQ| Type | Meaning |

    |---|---| | Non-participating | You do NOT share in the company's profits — your return is constant, unaffected by the firm's performance | | Participating | You share a portion of the profits, as either a CASH BONUS (paid to you in cash) or a REVERSIONARY BONUS (accrued annually and paid only on maturity — a loyalty bonus) |

    11.5 Pure risk vs savings-cum-risk contracts guaranteed MCQ| Type | Examples |

    |---|---| | Pure risk contract | Term policy, pure endowment. Two contingent events: death of the policyholder, or survival for the policy term | | Savings-cum-risk contract | ULIPs and similar — some risk benefit plus a savings component |

    11.6 The Swiss Re Sigma "product universe" framework guaranteed MCQ

    A two-dimensional map: from PURE RISK PROTECTION (left) through risk protection + accumulation (centre) to PURE SAVINGS/INVESTMENT (right).

    Row Left (risk protection) Centre Right (savings)
    Products Term insurance Whole life / term combinations Deferred, fixed and variable ANNUITIES
    Risks covered Mortality, longevity Mixed MARKET RISK
    Source of earnings Underwriting Mixed Market/investment returns and FEE income

    1. Non-life insurance
    10

    12.1 The three broad classes guaranteed MCQ

    FIRE · MARINE · MISCELLANEOUS (motor, liability, health, engineering, aviation, rural/agriculture)

    Within MARINE: guaranteed MCQ - HULL insurance = the SHIP/vessel itself - CARGO insurance = what it carries - They can be insured together or separately

    PACKAGE POLICIES: combine several aspects (fire + miscellaneous etc.) into one product.

    Recent additions to marine-linked business in India: guaranteed MCQ - TRADE CREDIT INSURANCE — introduced ~2021 - SURETY INSURANCE — introduced ~2022

    12.2 Motor insurance guaranteed MCQ — this is the most examinable non-life block

    Three vehicle categories: cars · two-wheelers (motorcycles and scooters) · commercial vehicles (taxis, buses, lorries, trucks, ambulances)

    Cover Compulsory?
    THIRD-PARTY LIABILITY — covers death or bodily injury to, or damage to the property of, a THIRD PARTY arising out of the use of a motor vehicle in a public place COMPULSORY BY LAW
    OWN DAMAGE — damage to your own vehicle VOLUNTARY
    COMPREHENSIVE — both Voluntary

    The mnemonic: "You may not want to protect YOURSELF — that you can live without. But the law requires you to cover the harm you may do to SOMEONE ELSE."

    Depreciation: the payout must reflect the depreciated value of a 5- or 10-year-old car, not a new one — hence the need for depreciation-based valuation models.

    Comprehensive cover typically includes: battery misfire damage, burglary, theft, riots, strikes, earthquakes, floods, typhoons, hurricanes, accidental damage by external or malicious means, terrorist attack, and damage in transit.

    12.3 Health insurance structures

    Structure Description
    Individual policy Reimbursement or cashless
    Corporate / GROUP medical claim A group of employees under one policy. Advantages: cross-subsidy (perhaps 10% claim in a year, 90% do not), lower marketing cost, lower administration cost
    FAMILY FLOATER A single total annual claim limit shared across the covered family members, whether one person or three uses it — avoids the administrative cost of separate policies guaranteed MCQ

    12.4 Personal lines vs Commercial lines guaranteed MCQ| | PERSONAL LINES ("mass risks") | COMMERCIAL LINES ("large risks" / industrialised insurance) |

    |---|---|---| | Bought by | Individuals | Businesses and organisations | | Examples | Fire insurance on a residence or its contents · motor insurance for private vehicles · health insurance · personal accident | Product liability (a mass-market product recall) · business interruption · large factory covers |

    Key distinction: personal lines are bought BY the individual but are NOT ON the individual — they are on the events and the assets.

    12.5 Compulsory (government-mandated) non-life policies guaranteed MCQ

    1. Motor third-party insurance
    2. Public liability insurance for HAZARDOUS GOODS — for storing or transporting hazardous chemicals, where a leak (a Bhopal-type event on a smaller scale) creates a liability too large for an individual player

    12.6 The Reliance Jamnagar case study guaranteed MCQ

    Shortly after the Jamnagar refinery was up and running in the early-to-mid/late 1990s, a massive flood hit — in a desert area of Gujarat bordering Rajasthan — and the factory was largely destroyed. They survived only because of the insurance cover; the insurers had to pay out to rebuild the factory and restart operations.

    And it introduces CONSEQUENTIAL LOSS: beyond the physical damage, Reliance also lost expected profits because it could not do business while the plant was down. Consequential loss insurance covers precisely this. guaranteed MCQ

    12.7 The breadth of the non-life product set

    "In the last count there are over 350, close to 400 different kinds of products" — from poultry farming and prawn cultivation to satellites and multi-million-dollar petroleum complexes. guaranteed MCQ

    1. LIFE vs NON-LIFE — the master comparison table
    5

    This is the single most likely table to be tested. Learn every row. guaranteed MCQ| Dimension | LIFE INSURANCE | NON-LIFE INSURANCE | |---|---|---| | Subject | The individual (financial loss from absence of life) | The asset / value of the asset; liability | | Global volume share | ~40% | ~60% (59.8%) | | India volume share | ~75% | ~25% | | Time horizon | LONG-TERM — decades; whole life can be 50–70 years | SHORT-TERM — no more than ONE YEAR, often less (e.g. travel insurance for a week) | | Renewal | A genuine renewal — the SAME contract runs across time. If you miss a premium you can revive the policy by paying arrears plus penalty | NOT a renewal — a FRESH CONTRACT every time. Terms can change | | Premium over the policy life | CANNOT be changed once fixed, even if the risk visibly changes | Changes every year as new risk information arrives | | Amount payable | KNOWN (the sum assured + defined bonus) | UNCERTAIN — the actual loss incurred, subject to a maximum cap | | Timing of payout | UNCERTAIN (death any time, or at maturity) | UNCERTAIN | | Number of claims per policy period | Effectively one | MULTIPLE claims possible in one period (several accidents, several events) | | Basis of the sum insured | HUMAN LIFE VALUE — set once and constant for the policy life | MAXIMUM LOSS from damage/write-off of the asset — readjusted every year (down for depreciation, up for healthcare inflation) | | Underwriting | A ONE-OFF exercise at inception (subject to the 2-year rule) | A CONTINUUM — reassessed every year | | Reinsurance use | Less common — individual life sums assured rarely exceed ₹5–15 crore | MORE common — industrial sums can be ₹50 crore, ₹100 crore, ₹1,000 crore | | Balance sheet — assets | LONG-TERM bonds (corporate and government) | SHORT-MATURITY, more LIQUID bonds — matched to the ~1-year payout horizon. The cost: liquid bonds yield less | | Balance sheet — liabilities | Policy reserves, subordinated long-term debt, equity capital | Same PLUS "UNEARNED PREMIUMS" and reinsurance premiums payable guaranteed MCQ| | Distribution | Sold personally, by agents in the social network | Much of it industrial/corporate, driven by corporate brokers | | Agent commission — 1st year | 35–40% of premium guaranteed MCQ| Much lower, but FLATTER | | Agent commission — renewals | Drops to ~5–6% | Remains constant or rises marginally | | Product design | STANDARDISED — commoditised | CUSTOMISED / tailor-made to specific requirements | | Valuation basis | Capitalisation of future earnings (human capital theory) | Market value of the asset, or per-event liability cost, or consequential loss | | Pricing inputs | Mortality/morbidity, cost of running the business, investment returns | File-and-use or tariff (standardised rate chart) |

    13.1 HUMAN LIFE VALUE — the life-insurance valuation method guaranteed MCQ

    An estimate of the actual future earnings, or the value of services, of an individual — CAPITALISED, net of maintenance costs.

    The worked logic: a 35-year-old in India, with superannuation at 60, has 25 more productive working years. Estimate the expected future earnings year by year, subtract the cost of survival/maintenance, and capitalise the net income. That is the individual's financial value.

    The stated caveat: "This is ONLY on a financial basis."

    13.2 The customer life-cycle "magic moments" (the BCG framework) guaranteed MCQ

    X-axis: age from ~20–22 (first independent decision) to ~75–80. Two curves: life (solid) and non-life (dotted), peaking at different points.

    The milestones: new job → first car → marriage → first child → house purchase → children's education → funding education → retirement planning → health issues → grandchildren → legacy.

    The marketing rule: match the product and the distribution channel to the life stage. "If I want to talk about retirement planning to a 25-year-old, it doesn't make sense. If I go to a 70-year-old and say 'that'll be your first car', it's unlikely."

    1. The insurance value chain guaranteed MCQ — the four links and their constraints
    8

    DISTRIBUTION → UNDERWRITING → OPERATIONS → ASSET MANAGEMENT

    Link What it does Its key constraint
    Distribution Acquiring customers Reach, cost to serve, channel effectiveness, and above all MIS-SELLING
    Underwriting Risk assessment; product development; accept or reject Availability and accuracy of information; actuarial competence — a scarce and expensive resource
    Operations Processing, customer service, claims management Cost to serve and the cost of maintaining service standards
    Asset management Where and how to invest Balancing risk and return — high returns are needed, but this is a social benefit product so high risk is not permitted

    14.1 MIS-SELLING — the deepest constraint guaranteed MCQ

    "Mis-selling is very difficult to understand the impact of in the short term. It's a long-term implication. I mis-sell today and offer a return higher than I could; the impact is 10, 15, 20 years down the line, at which point I do not have the ability to correct the process."

    The cartoon he uses: a business prices a $29 product at "$1,000,029 with a $1,000,000 discount" — the discount claimable only by filling in forms. It looks like a fantastic bargain; one customer forgetting to send the forms makes the seller a million dollars. Short-term growth, catastrophic long-term legal costs and reputational damage. guaranteed MCQ

    14.2 Distribution cost-benefit

    Cost side: recruitment costs · retention costs · transaction costs. Benefit side: dispersion · reach · volume of business.

    The optimisation rule: "We want to minimise cost and maximise benefit — but we cannot do both. So we FIX ONE and optimise the other." guaranteed MCQ

    14.3 The three key operational verticals guaranteed MCQ

    Policy administration (collection, processing, payments) → Claims management (verification, weeding out bogus claims, speed of payment) → Customer care and service (account monitoring, physical verification, customer response).

    14.4 Developmental challenges

    Low DIGITAL MATURITY on BOTH sides — customers and insurers alike · digital ambition not grounded in customer readiness · legacy and cultural internal constraints · customer retention ("acquiring customers is easy; RETAINING them is more difficult") · distributors are digital customers too · analytics is absolutely critical — a digital channel has no personal interaction, so data is the only substitute · insurers' failure to embrace social media in a landscape where platforms "evolve, live their life, die out".

    On technology: "Technology is like fire. Use it wrongly, it will burn you; use it appropriately, it helps in many ways. Technology is neither bad nor good — HOW you use it is the question." guaranteed MCQ

    14.5 Risk layering — frequency × severity guaranteed MCQ| Frequency | Severity | Example | Instrument |

    |---|---|---|---| | HIGH | LOW (minor) | Small scratches and dents driving on Indian streets | Contingency budgets — retain it | | LOW (rare) | HIGH (major) | Total write-off; earthquake; flood | Deposit/risk insurance, CAT BONDS | | Medium | Medium | | Contingent credit |

    The capital insight: "If it is unlikely to happen but has a major impact, I don't need a huge amount of capital blocked at all times — I need ACCESS to capital if needed. Liquidity is a cost." guaranteed MCQ

    14.6 The PROTECTION GAP — the "umbrella" slide

    "The biggest challenge and the biggest opportunity is to CLOSE THIS PROTECTION GAP" — the gap between the need for protection and the protection actually in place.

    1. Insurance intermediaries
    8

    15.1 Why intermediaries exist guaranteed MCQ

    An intermediary bridges/connects two counterparties. In a perfectly developed, fully financially literate market with complete information, an intermediary would NOT be needed. They exist because of INFORMATION ASYMMETRY and, crucially, because the ability to ANALYSE the available information is itself scarce — "it's not just knowing what product is there; the ability to analyse it is also a question."

    Their TWO roles: 1. Bring the counterparties together (the easier of the two) 2. Provide information and ADVICE on which policy actually suits the buyer — the more important role

    15.2 The three kinds of intermediary guaranteed MCQ| # | Intermediary | Character |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | AGENTS | "The bulwark and foot soldiers of the industry." Self-employed, commission-based, NOT employees. Part of the social/family network. HIGH VOLUME, LOW ticket size. Regulated since the IRDAI Insurance Agents Regulations, 2016, which set educational qualifications, recruitment, disciplinary action for mis-selling, and the roles of insurer and agent | | 2 | BROKERS | Negotiate with insurers on behalf of large customers — HNIs, large entities, corporates. LOW VOLUME, HIGH ticket size, high margin. Regulated by the 2018 regulations, amended 2019 (capital adequacy, qualifications, permitted products) | | 3 | IMFs — Insurance Marketing Firms | A distribution channel; a corporate entity; also referred to as corporate agents |

    THE FIVE TYPES OF BROKER PERMITTED BY IRDAI: guaranteed MCQ Direct LIFE broker · Direct NON-LIFE (general) broker · Direct REINSURANCE broker · COMPOSITE broker (all of them) · Direct life-and-general broker

    15.3 BROKER vs IMF — the comparison guaranteed MCQ| | BROKER | IMF (Insurance Marketing Firm) |

    |---|---|---| | Range | Works with a diverse range of customers and represents a very large range of products, across multiple companies | Operates for a GIVEN company — an HDFC Life IMF will not also be ICICI-approved | | Independence | Independent — offers customised, specialised solutions | Limited product portfolio; focused on selling that company's product | | Remuneration | Commission PLUS advisory FEES | Only the normal commission — NO advisory fees |

    Who can be a corporate agent: NBFCs, banks, firms, IMFs, NGOs, cooperative societies.

    ISP — Insurance Salesperson: an individual employed by a marketing firm. Tie-up limits: up to 2 life + 2 general (+2 health) insurers for an IMF; corporate agents up to 9 in each category = 27 in total. guaranteed MCQ

    15.4 The other intermediaries

    • Common Service Centres (CSCs) and village-level entrepreneurs — the channel for MICROINSURANCE, directed at the rural market, which is essential in India "because not everybody is able to take insurance at a large scale"
    • SURVEYOR / LOSS ASSESSOR — "the most understated but a very important cog in the wheel." Once a claim is made the agent is out of the picture; the surveyor determines the extent of damage and hence the validity and amount of the claim. Must be qualified in education and technical knowledge. guaranteed MCQ

    15.5 FINANCIAL CONSUMER PROTECTION — why it is harder guaranteed MCQ

    Buy a faulty phone → take it back next week → repaired or replaced. Your ability to correct is high and immediate. Buy a 15-year life policy → you only discover the mistake when the claim is made, 15 years later → you cannot go back in time. Therefore protecting the financial consumer is far more difficult, and the need to maintain standards is far greater.

    15.6 The bancassurance shift guaranteed MCQ

    The bank CANNOT be part of the insurance company — regulation forbids it. There may be common ownership at holding level, but it must be a SEPARATE LEGAL ENTITY. The bank sells the products.

    Current split: BANCASSURANCE ~60% of business; AGENTS ~40%.

    Gains Losses
    Bancassurance Organised, STANDARDISED — quality doesn't depend on which agent you got Loses the personal touch and personal information
    Agents Personal knowledge, tailored advice Quality depended entirely on your agent — "if not, it could be a disaster"

    1. IRDAI and regulation
    12

    16.1 What makes IRDAI unusual guaranteed MCQ

    IRDAI = Insurance Regulatory and DEVELOPMENT Authority of India.

    "Very rarely do regulators get into market DEVELOPMENT. And there are extremely rare instances where the NAME ITSELF incorporates the developmental agenda. Fundamentally these are OPPOSITE in nature — on one hand you control what the firm does; on the other you must push the boundaries and create new products."

    This model was later borrowed for the PFRDA (pension funds). guaranteed MCQ

    16.2 The statutory duty (the quoted section) guaranteed MCQ

    "Subject to the provisions of this Act and any other law for the time being in force, the Authority shall have the duty to REGULATE, PROMOTE AND ENSURE ORDERLY GROWTH of the insurance business and the reinsurance business."

    Powers include: certification/licensing of insurance companies · protecting policyholders' interests · quasi-judicial power to adjudicate disputes · governing life, non-life and reinsurance.

    Why an independent regulator was needed rather than the government: "With the government as regulator there is no LEVEL PLAYING FIELD. With an independent regulator, the government player and the non-government player are on an EQUAL FOOTING." guaranteed MCQ

    16.3 The licensing sequence guaranteed MCQ

    Round 1: apply → Round 2: verification and scrutiny → Round 3: Certificate of Registration granted → BUSINESS MUST COMMENCE WITHIN 12 MONTHS. "You can't take a certificate of registration and just sit on it."

    16.4 IAIS — the global alignment guaranteed MCQ| Item | Detail |

    |---|---| | IAIS | International Association of Insurance Supervisors | | Established | 1994 | | India (IRDAI) admitted | 2017, by cabinet approval | | Nature | A VOLUNTARY body — "like the Basel Committee in banking" | | Coverage | More than 200 jurisdictions, covering about 97% of global insurance premium | | Output | 26 ICPs — Insurance Core Principles | | Character of the ICPs | NOT a prescription — a FRAMEWORK. They set out what must be done, what is good to have, and what must be avoided; jurisdictions build their own regime within them |

    They also cover: supervision, market conduct, policyholder protection, risk management, control systems, reinsurance markets, legal issues — plus anti-money laundering (AML) and combating the financing of terrorism (CFT) through information-exchange MoUs.

    16.5 SOLVENCY — the most examinable regulation guaranteed MCQ

    Regulation: IRDA (Assets, Liabilities and Solvency Margin of Insurers) Regulations, 2000, amended in 2016 and 2022.

    Term Definition
    RSM — Required Solvency Margin The amount the regulator requires
    ASM — Available Solvency Margin The EXCESS of the insurer's ASSETS over the value of its LIABILITIES (including policyholder and shareholder liabilities) — effectively the free capital
    SOLVENCY RATIO ASM ÷ RSM

    The rules: - The solvency ratio MUST be greater than 1. If it falls below 1, the ability to service claims is not there - ASM must be ≥ 50% of the capital amount, or 100% of the RSM - The minimum/control level prescribed is 1.5 times, i.e. 150% guaranteed MCQ Why it matters so much: an insurance company's bankruptcy is not just a corporate cost but a SOCIAL cost — "the policyholder loses twice: they don't get the cover they banked on, AND the premiums they paid out of deferred consumption over the years are also gone." guaranteed MCQ

    16.6 The commission regulation guaranteed MCQ

    The Expenses of Management including Commission of Insurers Regulations, 2024, ABOLISHED the earlier CAP on commission.

    Why it was scrapped: under the cap, "people were figuring out other ways to make those payments" — leading to tax evasion and, more importantly, undercutting that was not financially sound.

    The self-correcting logic that replaces the cap: higher commission → lower income for the insurer → lower cover offered → the product becomes unattractive → fewer sales → less commission. "It becomes a chicken-and-egg scenario", so an optimal balance must be struck — now a business decision left to the companies.

    16.7 Advertisements and disclosures

    The purpose is to reduce information asymmetry (it can never be eliminated). No agent may issue an advertisement without the insurer's approval — the liability sits with the insurer. Nothing with a dual meaning may be published. guaranteed MCQ

    16.8 The REGULATORY SANDBOX guaranteed MCQ

    A segregated, controlled TEST ZONE in which new products and approaches are tried out without the full weight of market conditions, before being slowly rolled out.

    Why the regulator created it: "This is a market hugely based on TRUST. Building trust is easy; REBUILDING trust once broken is extremely difficult." The sandbox lets products be tested before they can shatter that trust and damage not just a company but "the whole financial infrastructure of the country."

    1. Underwriting
    30

    17.1 The definition guaranteed MCQ

    UNDERWRITING is the formal process of RISK ESTIMATION: the process by which you SELECT AND CLASSIFY risks — accepting or rejecting a proposal, and if accepting, on what TERMS AND CONDITIONS, and how much to RETAIN vs REINSURE.

    Stated in one line: "Underwriting is the process of choosing the RIGHT RISK." — the right risk being one you are willing to take at the price you are being compensated.

    The UNDERWRITER is "the person who signs at the bottom of the slip" — ultimately responsible for risk assessment and acceptance/rejection. guaranteed MCQ It is not insurance-specific: "It is relevant in ANY industry, any part of finance where a risk estimation is required" — a transferable skill.

    Can risk be estimated perfectly? NO — that would be equivalent to predicting the future with certainty. "Predictions could be 95%, 99%, 99.9% accurate, but there will always be that 0.1%." guaranteed MCQ

    17.2 The health-insurance illustration of terms and conditions

    A perfectly healthy young applicant is easy to accept. An applicant with an existing condition need not be rejected — but must not receive the same terms as a perfectly fit person. The insurer can: change the premium · add EXCLUSION clauses · impose conditions. guaranteed MCQ

    17.3 The documents of underwriting guaranteed MCQ — five documents| Document | Purpose |

    |---|---| | PROPOSAL FORM | Where the business starts — declaration of intent and of information. The DECLARATION FORMS THE BASIS OF THE CONTRACT — except in MARINE insurance, where the value is so high that other information must also be dug into guaranteed MCQ| | COVER NOTE | An INTERIM temporary certificate with basic particulars and limited validity — it lapses once the certificate of insurance is issued | | POLICY FORM | Payment structure, schedule, inclusions, exceptions, beneficiary, rules of interpretation and JURISDICTION | | ENDORSEMENTS / RIDERS | Modifications after issue. His example: you install a high-end stereo system in your car and, instead of buying a separate policy, get the existing policy endorsed to cover it for an additional premium | | CERTIFICATE OF INSURANCE | The policy itself — the valid contract |

    17.4 PHILOSOPHY vs POLICY — the vision/mission mapping guaranteed MCQ| Level | Set by | Content |

    |---|---|---| | UNDERWRITING PHILOSOPHY (= the VISION) | The BOARD and top management / CEO | High-level objectives in sync with strategic business goals: what risk level the company can live with; ability to absorb losses; which industries and geographies; what approach to REINSURANCE | | UNDERWRITING POLICY / GUIDELINES (= the MISSION) | The CHIEF UNDERWRITER / underwriting department | Converts the philosophy into rules, processes and SOPs: how applicants are assigned to risk classes; the rules for medical vs non-medical cases; the factors to be focused on |

    You never implement the philosophy directly — you implement the POLICY, which is the translated philosophy. guaranteed MCQ

    17.5 The actuarial premium components guaranteed MCQ

    Mortality / morbidity cost (the core actuarial cost) + office/operational expense costs (staff, electricity, establishment, marketing, transaction) + profit projection = the risk cost, i.e. the PREMIUM, then divided per individual.

    Why "mortality" even in non-life: "Don't think of mortality as the textbook definition of length of life — look at it as the LIFE OF THE RISK you are taking on." guaranteed MCQ

    17.6 SUBSTANDARD RISKS — the key underwriting principle guaranteed MCQ

    Rejecting all substandard risks "does not help the larger society and therefore indirectly impacts the very existence of the insurance company, because the market becomes much smaller." Instead: ACCEPT substandard risks, but on terms which are BALANCED AND EQUITABLE to the other policyholders. The good risk must NOT subsidise the bad risk: the bad risk comes in at a HIGHER price.**

    The lending analogy — the CIBIL score: guaranteed MCQ - CIBIL = Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited - Scale: 0 to 900, with 900 the best - Above 750, and especially 800+, is excellent creditworthiness - Below ~450–500 is high risk / substandard — such borrowers are not refused, they simply pay more

    And the definitional point: "There is NO objective definition of a substandard risk. It is substandard by YOUR OWN definition of what is acceptable — set by your philosophy." guaranteed MCQ

    17.7 RISK CLASSES guaranteed MCQ

    A risk class is a group of insureds with a very similar risk level. The design objective: VARIATION WITHIN a group as LOW as possible; ALL variation ACROSS groups.

    Class Definition
    PREFERRED class Anticipated average mortality LOWER than the population average
    STANDARD class Mortality AT the average
    SUBSTANDARD class (also called SPECIAL or IMPAIRED RISK) Mortality HIGHER than the average

    17.8 The risk assessment factors guaranteed MCQ — expect a "which is NOT" question| Category | Factors |

    |---|---| | CONCENTRATION RISK | "One of the biggest things to consider." Don't take everyone from one geography or one industry — e.g. all policyholders being coal miners gives no diversification. COVID-19 is his named exception, where "pretty much across the globe the impact was more or less uniform" — an "extremely weird and unique scenario" guaranteed MCQ| | MEDICAL risk factors | Build (obese / underweight) · personal medical history · FAMILY medical history (because some events are genetic) | | PERSONAL risk factors | Occupation (coal mining vs a desk job — "but a desk job has its own implications: no physical activity") · tobacco, alcohol and substance use · hobbies (car racing vs regular driving) · driving history · vocation | | FINANCIAL risk factors | Anti-selection bias · MORAL HAZARD · early lapsation |

    The INFOSYS concentration-risk parallel — an excellent MCQ: guaranteed MCQ

    Infosys has a definitive statement in its balance sheet every year that at no point may more than 10% of its revenues come from ONE organisation. If a client defaults, 90% of the business is safe. Avoiding concentration risk is a standard risk-assessment factor well beyond insurance.

    17.9 MORAL HAZARD — the cigar story guaranteed MCQ

    A man buys extremely expensive Cuban/Havana cigars, insures them against destruction by fire, then smokes them and claims — on the ground that fire destroyed them. The insurer had to pay (fire did destroy them) — but then had him prosecuted for ARSON. The lesson: because I have a cover, I may become less careful — and that itself creates risk.

    17.10 The underwriting decision — the possible outcomes guaranteed MCQ

    1. ACCEPT at normal rates
    2. MODIFY — offer a different product; change the term ("you want 50 years, I'll offer 20"); drop riders/add-ons; apply EXCLUSIONS
    3. Charge a HIGHER premium ("rate up") or impose LIENS
    4. POSTPONE pending further information
    5. DECLINE

    Exclusion example: "Accidental damage is covered, but accidental damage caused UNDER THE INFLUENCE OF ALCOHOL is NOT covered." guaranteed MCQ Restrictive clause example: COVID was not covered under original health policies, so early COVID death claims were refused or reduced.

    LIEN types: guaranteed MCQ - DECREASING lien — e.g. an underweight young person, where the lien reduces as they gain weight and age - CONSTANT lien — applied uniformly where extra premium would not compensate the risk (e.g. driving under the influence)

    17.11 The two methods of risk classification guaranteed MCQ| Method | Description | Limitation |

    |---|---|---| | JUDGEMENT method | The underwriter's experience creates a mental picture. Works when there are only one or two unfavourable factors or the decision is simple | UNIFORMITY is a challenge — different underwriters, or the same underwriter in different circumstances, decide differently | | NUMERICAL RATING method | Every risk parameter is assigned a NUMERICAL VALUE based on its probable impact on mortality: POSITIVE for an increase in mortality, NEGATIVE for a decrease. THE STANDARD MORTALITY IS REPRESENTED BY A BASE OF 100. | More scientific and objective, but NOT foolproof — borderline cases still need a human call |

    guaranteed MCQ — the base of 100

    17.12 FIELD underwriting vs JET underwriting guaranteed MCQ| | FIELD underwriting | JET (jet-speed / point-of-sale) underwriting |

    |---|---|---| | Key link | The AGENT, who has first-hand information | Automated processing | | Key document | The ACR — AGENT'S CONFIDENTIAL REPORT, a crucial document that helps resolve conflicts of interest between agent and underwriter | Not needed | | When used | Normal cases | "Mass production" — simple cases meeting STANDARD criteria, where the sum assured is not high and the risks are not complex |

    Managing the ACR: compare it against the proposal and any medical reports; build a reward-and-punishment system for agents' reports; train agents and treat them as PARTNERS, not just agents. guaranteed MCQ

    17.13 CLINICAL MEDICINE vs INSURANCE MEDICINE guaranteed MCQ

    A patient with borderline high blood pressure is told to change diet and lifestyle. After three months the doctor says "you're fine now, no medication needed." The patient is happy. THE INSURER SHOULD NOT BE. Clinical medicine asks: is the current problem resolved? INSURANCE MEDICINE asks: what is the PROGNOSIS — how likely is this to recur and how will it manifest in the future? (An appendix removal doesn't matter; borderline hypertension does.)

    This is why the underwriter must work closely with the CHIEF MEDICAL OFFICER — and with the CLAIMS MANAGER, because suspicious or eyebrow-raising claims give feedback on how good the risk assessment was.

    17.14 Centralised vs decentralised underwriting guaranteed MCQ| | Advantages | Disadvantages |

    |---|---|---| | CENTRALISED | Consistent policies and actions · lower overall administrative cost · easily managed when employees leave · better knowledge management | Cannot do customised solutions · COMMUNICATION GAP with the applicant · lack of involvement and enthusiasm among field units ("we don't have the authority; somebody else will approve it") |

    Ways to organise the department: by product category · by CHANNEL of delivery (online / bank / direct agent — each brings a different customer type and risk) · by strategic business · by geography · matrix.

    17.15 The three case-handling systems guaranteed MCQ — in escalating order| System | When used |

    |---|---| | CASE ASSIGNMENT SYSTEM | Simple cases; assigned by sum assured, application type, source, product | | TEAM UNDERWRITING | Senior and junior underwriters review together, depending on size | | COMMITTEE UNDERWRITING | Very large sums assured, complex products, multiple risk factors. The committee is INTERDEPARTMENTAL: underwriting + policy servicing + marketing + ACTUARIAL + LEGAL ("because non-payment of a claim goes into a legal issue") |

    The committee's four jobs: oversee overall underwriting practices · look into BORDERLINE cases with high commercial importance · create transparency · give FEEDBACK TO SALES — "you're getting me numbers, but you're not getting me the RIGHT numbers." guaranteed MCQ

    17.16 Technology in underwriting

    Expert systems · AI and machine-learning models · documentation and DATA MINING · e-learning and knowledge management · LIVE DATABASES to cross-check an application against the person's prior history.

    The career note he makes explicitly: "The market really has a SHORTAGE of good underwriters." guaranteed MCQ

    1. Reinsurance
    41

    18.1 The definition and the banking analogy guaranteed MCQ

    Reinsurance is insurance for the insurance companies. It involves transferring PART of the risk an insurer assumes to the next level — the reinsurer. THE REINSURER HAS NO DIRECT CONTRACTUAL RELATIONSHIP WITH THE INSURED.

    The analogy: "We all deal with banks. Banks deal with the RBI. But we cannot have a direct relationship with the RBI, and the RBI has no direct relationship with us." guaranteed MCQ Why the insurer cannot cede 100%: "Mathematically you can cede 100%. But then what is the role of the insurer who is just acquiring business and passing it on? The reinsurer could deal directly." guaranteed MCQ

    18.2 The vocabulary

    Ceding company (direct insurer) → LINE / RETENTION (kept) + CESSION (passed on) → Reinsurer → RETROCESSION → Retrocessionaire → ultimately the Government.

    The structure narrows into a PYRAMID: many buyers → fewer insurers → far fewer reinsurers.

    18.3 CO-INSURANCE vs REINSURANCE — the sharpest distinction guaranteed MCQ| | CO-INSURANCE | REINSURANCE |

    |---|---|---| | Liability to the insured | EACH insurer is DIRECTLY and individually liable to the insured | The reinsurer is NOT directly liable to the insured | | Who spreads the risk | THE INSURED spreads the risk among many insurers (e.g. buying 20% each from five companies) | THE INSURER obtains protection for its own liability | | The insured's protection | Direct, from each co-insurer | Only INDIRECTLY, through the insurer |

    18.4 Why reinsurance exists — functions guaranteed MCQ

    1. Limit FLUCTUATIONS in the losses the insurer bears on its own account — "any finance manager wants to avoid SPIKES; people are far more comfortable with a known flat level"
    2. Protection against CATASTROPHES
    3. Protect SOLVENCY
    4. Spread the risk of losses
    5. Stabilise operating results over time
    6. Increase UNDERWRITING FLEXIBILITY — the capital saved by not having to cover a once-in-100-years event can be used to expand the insurance base

    18.5 Advantages of reinsurance guaranteed MCQ

    • The ceding insurer's CAPACITY TO ACCEPT RISK INCREASES — the primary advantage
    • Stabilises financial ratios, profits and loss ratios
    • Allows an insurer to retire from or avoid underwriting a segment — "particularly relevant for GOVERNMENT insurance companies, which have to take care of the social impact and may not be able to say no to business"
    • Reinsurers are GLOBAL players — "a risk in India does not exist in the US, so it can average the whole thing out". This is one of the biggest advantages.

    18.6 The players guaranteed MCQ

    Global reinsurers named: Munich Re · Swiss Re · Employers Re · Zurich Re · Hannover Re · General Cologne Re · Berkshire Hathaway Re

    India: GIC (GIC Re) — "a unique proposition: General Insurance Corporation of India is a NON-LIFE insurance company but is ALSO the designated reinsurance company in the country", which he notes "is not really a very good idea, because if you're an insurance company doing reinsurance, you are not really spreading the risk." None of the global reinsurers listed do direct insurance. guaranteed MCQ Also: REINSURANCE BROKERS, who connect insurers to reinsurers.

    Market metric Figure
    Number of top-level global reinsurers ~200
    Global reinsurance capital ~$570–600 billion, growing rapidly

    18.7 RETENTION and PROBABLE MAXIMUM LOSS guaranteed MCQ

    RETENTION = how much risk (and hence loss) the insurer keeps on itself.

    What it depends on: the expected FREQUENCY of loss for that type of risk · the SIZE of losses likely to occur · the volume of business and premium earned · the TYPE of risk (property vs liability vs motor vs health).

    The two-dimensional rule: guaranteed MCQ - High frequency, small size → RETAIN it - Low frequency, very large size → CEDE it

    PML — PROBABLE MAXIMUM LOSS (also EML — ESTIMATED MAXIMUM LOSS): guaranteed MCQ Why those exact words: - "Probable/estimated" — because the event has not happened; we are protecting against a potential future loss - "Maximum" — "there is no point protecting against a minimum loss"

    Factors driving the PML for a building: size · height · area/zone (earthquake-prone? flood-prone?) · construction material and quality · contents and their value · internal protection systems · whether value is concentrated in one room or spread out · housekeeping standards.

    PML is expressed as a PERCENTAGE OF THE TOTAL SUM INSURED — so it is comparable across players and individuals. guaranteed MCQ

    18.8 FACULTATIVE vs TREATY guaranteed MCQ — the master distinction| | FACULTATIVE (FAC) | TREATY (OBLIGATORY) |

    |---|---|---| | Scope | SINGLE risks, on a CASE-BY-CASE basis | A PORTFOLIO or GROUP of risks | | Reinsurer's choice | HAS THE OPTION ("the FACULTY") to ACCEPT or DECLINE each risk — this is where the name comes from guaranteed MCQ| OBLIGED to accept ALL cessions within the scope of the treaty | | Detail supplied | Full details of EACH risk | NO individual details needed | | Number of risks | One at a time | Any number, within the limit | | Proportional / non-proportional | Typically PROPORTIONAL | Both | | Duration | Commences and ends WITH the original policy | Typically ANNUAL and renewable/continuing | | Age | The OLDEST form of reinsurance | Later | | Insurer's underwriting freedom | Constrained — the original contract cannot be changed without the reinsurer's explicit approval | Free — the reinsurer cannot intervene unless there is gross negligence or fraud | | Speed | SLOW and cumbersome; cover cannot be given immediately | Faster; immediate cover to the client | | Admin cost | HIGHER — effort is duplicated | LOWER |

    When facultative is used: guaranteed MCQ 1. When the direct insurer is left with a sum still needing reinsurance after both its retention AND the treaty capacity have been exhausted 2. When the policy contains risks EXCLUDED from the obligatory cover

    Popular facultative lines: AVIATION · HULL (marine) · SPACE · OIL risks. guaranteed MCQ Facultative advantages: - For the ceding company: maximum transfer of risk · increases capacity without upsetting its automatic treaties · can spread across many different reinsurers · finds a market for risks of varying quality · a loss on a facultative does not prejudice the ceding company's treaties - For the reinsurer: can select risks · underwriting safeguards · can advise the ceding company and demand a higher premium rate · can prevent accumulation of a particular risk · gains insight into the ceding company's underwriting

    Facultative disadvantages: higher administrative cost · slow · cover cannot be given immediately · the original contract cannot be changed without approval · the facultative reinsurer may demand a say in CLAIM SETTLEMENT — a potential interference in the insurer's business. guaranteed MCQ

    18.9 The documents

    Document Content
    REINSURANCE SLIP / RI SLIP A TERM SHEET: name of the insured · the risk · risks covered · premium · the ceding company's NET RETENTION · past history · estimated maximum loss · the facultative offer as a percentage · commissions and brokerage
    FAC SLIP For larger risks — a more detailed description including inspection reports
    BORDEREAUX Under treaties, individual cessions are not made — but sometimes a LIST of risks with full details (sum insured, retention, premium) is sent. This is AVOIDED in "BLIND TREATIES", where the reinsurer has explicit trust in the insurer, "follows the fortunes" of the insurer, and only annual statements need be submitted guaranteed MCQ

    18.10 PROPORTIONAL vs NON-PROPORTIONAL guaranteed MCQ| | PROPORTIONAL | NON-PROPORTIONAL |

    |---|---|---| | Basis | A PERCENTAGE of the risk | An ABSOLUTE AMOUNT | | Basis of the contract | The SUM INSURED | THE LOSS |

    The worked comparison — a certain MCQ: guaranteed MCQ

    Total expected loss 1,000, retention level 500. - Proportional (50%): if the actual loss turns out smaller — say 500 — you bear 250 and cede 250. Your share scales with the loss. - Non-proportional (₹500 absolute): if the maximum total loss is 500, the ENTIRE amount hits you and nothing can be transferred, even though you hold a reinsurance contract.

    18.11 QUOTA SHARE treaty (proportional) guaranteed MCQ

    Definition: fixed quotas agreed for ALL policies underwritten in the relevant area/class up to a limit. The quota determines how premium AND claims are shared.

    The worked example — memorise every number: guaranteed MCQ| Item | Value | |---|---| | Sum insured | 10 million | | Direct insurer's retention | 70% = 7 million | | Reinsurer's proportion | 30% = 3 million | | Premium | $2 per million × 10 million = $20,000 | | Insurer keeps | 70% = $14,000 | | Reinsurer gets | 30% = $6,000 | | A LOSS of 6 million occurs | | | Direct insurer bears | 70% = 4.2 million | | Reinsurer pays | 30% = 1.8 million |

    When quota share is used: guaranteed MCQ - The company is NEW to a particular market - Its surplus treaty experience has been poor - It wants to cut the administrative time spent on retention decisions

    Advantages Disadvantages
    Helps a small/new company build business safely · minimal reporting, simple administration · useful where there are statutory cession requirements · a strong partnership model Does NOT limit exposure to PEAK risks · provides reinsurance even when it is not needed · does not address the insurer's varied needs · profitable to the reinsurer because there is NO SELECTION against it (unlike a surplus treaty) · inflexible and high cost to the ceding company

    18.12 SURPLUS treaty (proportional, more sophisticated) guaranteed MCQ

    Definition: the ceding company decides a LIMIT OF LIABILITY it wishes to retain on any one risk (or class), and reinsures ONLY the amounts SURPLUS over and above that retention. If the sum insured is WITHIN the retention limit, there is NO cession at all.

    Arranged in terms of the number of LINES of the retention. A "LINE" = the amount retained for the insurer's own account (the NET RETENTION).

    WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — a 9-line surplus treaty with retention $300,000. Learn all three cases. guaranteed MCQ| Case | Sum insured | Premium | Loss | Retention | Cession | Split | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | A | $3 million | $4,500 | $1.5 million | $300,000 = 10% | $2.7 million = 90% (9 lines) | Premium: $450 / $4,050. Loss: $150,000 / $1.35 million | | B | $130,000 | $195 | $80,000 | ENTIRE amount — below the retention limit | NIL | Insurer keeps all premium and bears all ₹80,000 loss; reinsurer gets and pays NOTHING | | C | $3.5 million | $5,250 | $2 million | $800,000 = 22.86% | $2.7 million = 77.14% | Loss: $457,200 / $1,542,800 |

    (Case C: 9 lines × $300,000 = $2.7m is the maximum cession, so the insurer must retain the balance of $800,000 = 22.86% of $3.5m.)

    WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — multiple surplus treaties. Retention $100,000; first surplus of 10 lines; second surplus of 20 lines. guaranteed MCQ| Sum insured | Retained | 1st surplus | 2nd surplus | |---|---|---|---| | $800,000 | Nothing ceded — (within the first surplus capacity in the worked answer) | | | | $1.5 million | $100,000 | $1 million | $400,000 | | $3.1 million | $100,000 | $1 million | $2 million |

    If the sum insured exceeds both surpluses (e.g. $5 million), the direct insurer must either CARRY the balance itself or arrange a SEPARATE (facultative) contract. guaranteed MCQ A treaty may have a monetary limit as maximum liability — e.g. "a 30-line treaty with net retention of $100,000 may have $25 million as its limit."

    Other surplus features: guaranteed MCQ - Fire treaties are typically arranged on the basis of the maximum possible loss - All reinsurance under surplus is subject to the SAME rates, terms and conditions as the original policy - The reinsurer's liability begins AUTOMATICALLY AND SIMULTANEOUSLY with the direct insurer's, as soon as the retention is exceeded - Arranged for an indefinite period, cancellable on 3 to 6 months' notice - On cancellation — the "CLEAN CUT" METHOD: the portfolio may be run off or the liability withdrawn against a return of premium at about 35–40%, and outstanding losses withdrawn by debiting 90–100% of the estimated losses guaranteed MCQ| Surplus advantages | Surplus disadvantages | |---|---| | Unlike quota share, you do NOT give away premium on EVERY risk · automatic protection · retention can be VARIED by class of risk | Heavy administrative work fixing retentions and lines per risk · more complicated than quota share · needs technology · UNBALANCED risk distribution from the reinsurer's viewpoint, since risks are not uniformly shared |

    18.13 FACULTATIVE-OBLIGATORY cover guaranteed MCQ

    A hybrid: the CEDING COMPANY is NOT BOUND to cede (it retains the CHOICE), but the REINSURER MUST ACCEPT all cessions within a limit. It operates like a surplus treaty and is CHEAPER than a surplus treaty — which is what makes it attractive.

    18.14 NON-PROPORTIONAL structures guaranteed MCQ

    The basis is LOSS, not sum insured. The insurer sets a limit it is prepared to lose; the excess is transferred.

    Term Meaning
    STOP LOSS "This is the maximum loss I am ready to take; the excess is transferred." Used when an unforeseen surge in claims would leave a high claims ratio — the loss ratio is STOPPED at an agreed percentage and the reinsurer pays the balance
    DEDUCTIBLE What the insurer bears on its own — the retention level
    COVER LIMIT The maximum the reinsurer is liable for
    CAT XL — Catastrophe Excess of Loss Per-EVENT cover protecting against VERY LARGE losses — earthquake, flood, cyclone, tsunami
    WXL/R — Working Excess of Loss per Risk Protection where the loss is caused to ONE of the risks

    THE WORKED EXAMPLE — learn all three scenarios. guaranteed MCQ

    Setup: after all proportional arrangements, the direct insurer's retention is 8 million. It buys: - WXL/R: cover of 6 million in excess of 2 million - CAT XL: cover of 9 million in excess of 4 million

    Scenario Loss Who pays what
    1. A fire causes a 1 million loss 1 million Neither contract is triggered — it is below the 2 million WXL deductible
    2. A 7 million single-risk loss 7 million Direct insurer bears the first 2 million (the WXL deductible); the WXL reinsurer pays 5 million. The CAT XL does not come into the picture
    3. An EARTHQUAKE causing 9 million: risk A 1m, B 1m, C 1m, D 2m, E 4m 9 million Direct insurer takes the first 4 million (the CAT XL deductible) · the WXL takes 2 million in excess on risk E · the CAT XL pays the balance 3 million

    18.15 LAYERED REINSURANCE — the standard stack guaranteed MCQ| Layer | Instrument |

    |---|---| | Base — capital relief for shareholders | QUOTA SHARE | | Larger-than-run-of-the-mill risks | SURPLUS | | Catastrophic risks | EXCESS OF LOSS (XL) | | Exceptional cases where advice is needed | FACULTATIVE | | Stop loss | Not common — "it requires a large amount of TRUST" |

    18.16 REINSURANCE POOLS guaranteed MCQ

    Definition: instead of one risk line, MORE BUSINESS LINES are POOLED, and the pool is then RETROCEDED to the members in an AGREED PROPORTION of the volume of business.

    Origin: privately arranged or a government-initiated national pool.

    Typical purposes: special classes of risk — catastrophic risks, liabilities, and government risk insurance pools to INCREASE THE BUSINESS RETAINED WITHIN THE COUNTRY. "For a long time in India it was mandated that even an Indian direct insurer had to give 20% of its reinsurance business to GIC." guaranteed MCQ| Advantages | Disadvantages | |---|---| | Participants get a share of a wider section of business → lower and better-balanced risk · provides the COLLECTIVE CAPACITY of many · in less-developed insurance markets, helps fix premium rates and bring stability | More expense · can lead to ACCUMULATION of risks, which works against the interest of prudent, better insurers |

    A pool can itself buy an EXCESS OF LOSS COVER to protect the whole pool (a retrocession).

    THE FOUR INDIAN POOLS TO KNOW: guaranteed MCQ| Pool | Year | Managed by | Purpose | |---|---|---|---| | NUCLEAR INSURANCE POOL | 2015 | GIC Re | Catastrophic nuclear events — "no normal insurance product could ever cover a Fukushima-type loss" | | INDIAN MARKET TERRORISM RISK INSURANCE POOL | 2022 | Non-life insurers | Claims arising from terrorism | | Market FIRE pool | — | GIC | Retroceded in agreed proportions to members; has an excess-of-loss cover | | Market HULL pool | — | GIC | Same |

    The design principle behind pools: guaranteed MCQ

    Within a pool there must be HOMOGENEITY of risk — "the INTRA-CLASS variation is the lowest or non-existent; ALL variation is ACROSS classes." You do not mix flood risk with earthquake risk with nuclear risk, because investors have different risk preferences and a homogeneous pool can be targeted at investors who want that specific risk segment.

    18.17 CATASTROPHE BONDS (CAT BONDS) guaranteed MCQ

    How they work:

    Bonds are issued in the market. Investors buy them and earn interest at a rate TYPICALLY HIGHER THAN THE MARKET, until a disaster strikes. IF the disaster strikes, THE BONDS FORECLOSE and the money raised is used to cover the losses. IF NO disaster strikes during the term, the investors GET THEIR PRINCIPAL BACK like a normal bond.

    Why India needs them — the SBI report and the Sigma numbers: guaranteed MCQ| Statistic | Figure | |---|---| | India's rank among countries by natural disasters | THIRD (after the US and China) | | Global INSURED losses expected in 2025 (Swiss Re Sigma) | ~$145 billion | | Global UNINSURED losses — THE PROTECTION GAP | ~$181 billion — about $35bn MORE than the insured losses |

    The chain reaction if there is no cover: disaster → government must step in → pressure on public finances → deficit budgets → higher taxation.

    18.18 Reinsurance by class of business guaranteed MCQ| Class | Typical arrangement |

    |---|---| | LIFE | BOTH facultative and treaties; usually SURPLUS treaties; the original terms / risk premium are the basis. For GROUP policies, QUOTA SHARE. In some countries, POOLS for substandard risks | | PROPERTY | Treaties, with facultative for risks outside their scope. Mostly proportional SURPLUS; quota share also widely used; EXCESS OF LOSS for major catastrophes | | MARINE and AVIATION | Facultative, quota share, POOLS and excess of loss | | LIABILITY | Usually EXCESS OF LOSS |

    18.19 Direct insurer vs reinsurer — the comparison guaranteed MCQ| Dimension | DIRECT INSURER | REINSURER |

    |---|---|---| | Organisation of risk estimation | Both INTERNAL and EXTERNAL | INTERNAL only | | Risk assessment | Assesses DIRECTLY | Relies on the direct insurer under UBERRIMAE FIDEI | | Contractual obligation | To the POLICYHOLDER | Only to the INSURANCE COMPANY | | Underwriting policy | Directly influenced by individual risks | NO individual risk comes into the picture | | Loss process | Direct contact with the policyholder | Entirely reliant on the direct insurer |

    How reinsurers survive despite taking catastrophic risk: by exposure and ACCUMULATION CONTROL (avoiding concentration), so the joint probability of simultaneous losses stays low, plus long-term client relationships and stronger underwriting insight into the ceded portions of the direct insurer's book.

    1. ART — Alternative Risk Transfer
    5

    19.1 The four inefficiencies of traditional insurance guaranteed MCQ

    1. CREDIT RISK for the policyholder — will the insurer survive to pay?
    2. Little incentive to introduce LOSS PREVENTION measures — the MORAL HAZARD problem
    3. Insurance companies have LIMITED CAPACITY
    4. The good risks SUBSIDISE the poor risks — ADVERSE SELECTION

    19.2 What ART is

    An ambiguous umbrella term with no single definition. Common features: guaranteed MCQ - Tailored to CLIENT-SPECIFIC problems - Integrated, MULTI-LAYER, MULTI-LINE cover - Aimed at increasing the efficiency of risk transfer, broadening the spectrum of insurable risks, and TAPPING THE CAPITAL MARKETS for additional capacity - Its market share is still relatively small, but developing very fast

    19.3 The ART toolkit guaranteed MCQ| Tool | Definition |

    |---|---| | CAPTIVES | Insurance companies OWNED BY NON-INSURANCE FIRMS to accept the risks of the PARENT firm. Over 4,000 captives globally, with annual premium volume of about $21 BILLION (and note: "this is PREMIUM volume, not the sum insured — that will be many times this"). The critique of captives: transferring highly predictable payment flows generates little benefit while incurring substantial transaction costs guaranteed MCQ| | FINITE RISK (a.k.a. FINANCIAL INSURANCE) | Spreads risk OVER TIME rather than ACROSS A POOL — the defining contrast with traditional reinsurance. It smooths losses during the contract period and involves SHARING INVESTMENT RETURNS between insured and insurer guaranteed MCQ| | MULTI-LINE, MULTI-YEAR products | A bundle/portfolio across lines (marine + fire + liability) and across years | | MULTI-TRIGGER products | More than one trigger can activate the cover | | INSURANCE-LINKED SECURITIES | CAT bonds, earthquake bonds, insurance derivatives — SECURITIZATION as a complement and supplement to reinsurance |

    1. PolicyBazaar — InsurTech
    13

    (Pradeep Yadav, BU Head, Term Insurance)

    20.1 The four problems it set out to solve guaranteed MCQ

    1. The PROTECTION GAP — India is "a land of middle class", but insurance penetration is low; the middle class is "one incident away from derailing their entire lives"
    2. INFORMATION ASYMMETRY — hundreds of policies exist; customers don't know their options, and manufacturers don't know where their customers are searching
    3. DISCOVERY and awareness — insurance is "not a very exciting category; nobody gets up in the morning and says I'm going to go do insurance today", and is associated with being mandatory or a tax-saving instrument
    4. POST-SALE persistence — keeping the customer paying premiums and staying covered

    20.2 The company facts guaranteed MCQ| Item | Detail |

    |---|---| | Founded | 2008 | | Mission | "Protect the middle class through DEATH, DISEASE and DISABILITY — the 3 Ds" guaranteed MCQ| | The stated technology goal | "We are solving for the next 50 CRORE people" — a digital journey that works on an expensive device must work identically on an inexpensive phone, across devices and regions guaranteed MCQ| | The comparison drawn | "We want insurance democratised like JIO did for internet adoption" |

    20.3 The aggregator model guaranteed MCQ

    PolicyBazaar is an AGGREGATOR — "no different from Uber or Zomato."

    A traveller doesn't know where the cabs are; a cab owner doesn't know where the customers are. Put both on one platform with full visibility of options and the information asymmetry falls. (Zomato: diners vs restaurants. PolicyBazaar: 100s of policies vs customers who don't know they exist.)

    Market size he cites: 17–18 general insurance companies and 11–12+ life insurance companies, offering "all sorts of products" — so "for a customer it's quite overwhelming."

    20.4 The definition of insurance he gives guaranteed MCQ

    "A COLLECTIVE BARGAIN: a group of people all invest smaller amounts, so collectively they subsidise a huge amount withdrawn by 1%. The concept is very similar to a LOTTERY — except that NOBODY WANTS TO WIN this lottery, because to win it the event has to happen."

    20.5 The technology stack guaranteed MCQ| Layer | Use |

    |---|---| | Aadhaar and e-KYC | Seamless, less intrusive onboarding using government-exposed APIs | | UPI | Payments and RECURRING payments — "once in a lifetime kind of opportunity; India's skill here is unprecedented in the entire world" | | Big data, AI/ML, LLMs | Understanding what the customer needs from their actions and questions; VOICE ANALYTICS whose findings are fed back to INSURERS to shape future products guaranteed MCQ| | API integrations | Almost 400 API integrations — and some quotes are DYNAMIC and REAL-TIME (a car quote can differ between morning and evening) guaranteed MCQ| | AWS | Scalable architecture across devices, nodes and regions |

    20.6 Post-sale — the real differentiator guaranteed MCQ

    The CLAIMS ASSISTANCE PROGRAMME: in many cases the family does not even know the deceased held a policy, or doesn't know the process — and the claim is lost. Because of its deep API integrations with insurers, PolicyBazaar can go back to ALL insurers, find every cover the customer held, and pursue the claim to the end.

    FRAUD DETECTION: facial recognition · PIVC (pre-issuance video verification) to confirm the customer is alive and their statements true · predictive models flagging risky cases to the insurer for in-person verification.

    Motor claims: video verification of the incident to shorten the traditional wait for an inspection report while the car sits in the garage.

    The human element: "Even if we are a digital platform, that human touch or the HYBRID system has to continue." On a death claim they provide emotional counselling first, process in the background, and then guide the family on how to invest the money. guaranteed MCQ

    20.7 The LOW-COST ULIP argument guaranteed MCQ — the whole comparison

    Compare a 20-year investment in a PASSIVE mutual fund (Sensex/Nifty 50, expected to grow at 12–13% minimum) against a ULIP invested in the SAME passive fund.

    Mutual fund ULIP
    Return Same Same
    If the investor dies during the term Nothing extra The nominee IMMEDIATELY receives 10× the ANNUAL PREMIUM, AND the policy CONTINUES with the COMPANY paying the premiums on the customer's behalf
    Corpus at maturity TAXABLE ENTIRELY TAX-FREE
    The cap — Tax-free only up to ₹2.5 LAKH of premium per annum

    "Low cost" is a moniker for keeping the cost as low as possible so it competes as an offering for the middle class.

    20.8 The product bouquet

    Life: term insurance, ULIP, endowment, non-par/guaranteed products Health: family floater, individual, senior citizen Asset: motor (car, bike, commercial vehicles), travel, home Business lines: PB PARTNERS (a tech platform for listed agents selling digitally) and PB FOR BUSINESS (SMEs, institutions, corporates)

    The two products people most favour buying digitally: TERM and ULIP. guaranteed MCQ

    Item Answer
    Base contract law Indian Contract Act, 1872
    First insurance regulation in India Indian Life Assurance Companies Act, 1912
    First to cover life AND non-life Indian Insurance Companies Act, 1928
    The bulwark INSURANCE ACT, 1938 — protected the INSURERS; policyholder protection came with IRDA in 1999
    Other acts Carriers 1865 · Railways 1890 · Workmen's Compensation 1923 · Marine Insurance 1963 · Consumer Protection 1986 · Motor Vehicles 1988 · Public Liability Insurance 1991
    Rule of citation An Act is named by the year it was FIRST formulated; the amended version is what applies
    Four insurance-specific principles Insurable interest · Uberrimae fidei · Indemnity · Subrogation and contribution
    Insurable interest The LEGAL RIGHT to insure, from a financial relationship recognised by law — it distinguishes insurance from BETTING
    Tom's five policies No claim on the neighbour's house — NO insurable interest

    The TV example Sold the TV → claim fails; the fix was to ASSIGN the policy
    Assignment Life: permitted. Non-life: needs the insurer's approval (except marine cargo and transfer by will/law). Motor third party: assigned to the injured third party
    Uberrimae fidei The POSITIVE duty to disclose all material facts ACCURATELY and FULLY, WHETHER OR NOT ASKED
    Material fact One that, if known, would have caused rejection or different terms

    David Declared no driver under 25; his 18-year-old son wrote off the car → claim refused

    Indemnity You may NOT PROFIT from insurance; you are restored to the pre-loss financial condition

    Fire/property indemnity basis MARKET VALUE
    SUBROGATION Insured's rights transfer to the INSURER
    CONTRIBUTION One insurer recovers a proportionate amount from ANOTHER insurer also liable
    CONTRA PROFERENTEM Ambiguity is interpreted in favour of the INSURED, because the insurer drafted the document
