    Code of Hammurabi ~1750 BC — ship loan secured by cargo
    Great Fire of London 1666, ~30,000 houses, created fire insurance
    Oldest surviving insurer Hamburger Feuerkasse, 1676
    Lloyd's Began in a COFFEE HOUSE; today a MARKETPLACE, not an insurer
    First formal insurer in India Oriental Insurance Company, Calcutta, 1818
    Discrimination Indians paid 20% MORE than Britishers until 1871
    Ended by Bombay Mutual Life Insurance Society, 1871
    First separate general insurer Triton Insurance Company, 1850
    1950 amendment Equity capital required for life insurers; Controller of Insurance set up at SHIMLA
    LIC Act passed 19 June 1956; LIC established 1 September 1956
    Entities merged into LIC 245 = 154 Indian + 16 non-Indian + 75 Provident Societies
    LIC seed capital ₹5 crore
    GIC nationalisation 1972, 107 insurers → 4 companies + GIC as holding company
    The four National (Calcutta/East) · New India (Bombay/West) · Oriental (Delhi/North) · United India (Madras/South)
    Why four Non-life is driven by INDUSTRIALISATION, which is geography-specific
    GIC Re 2000 — GIC becomes the designated national reinsurer
    Malhotra Committee 1993 under R. N. Malhotra, a former RBI Governor; reported 1994
    IRDA interim 1996; IRDA Act 1999 giving statutory powers
    FDI progression 100% domestic → 24% foreign (1999) → 49% → 100% (2025 Budget)
    Players today 26 life · 27 general (4 PSU + Agri Insurance + ECGC) · 7 standalone health · 1 reinsurer (GIC Re) · 13 foreign reinsurer branches
    LIC share >75% of the life market; 80–85% of RENEWAL premium; ~48–50% of NEW business
    LIC agents over 14 lakh — self-employed, not employees
    Bancassurance vs agents ~60% vs ~40%
    Agent regulation IRDAI Insurance Agents Regulations, 2016
    Broker regulation 2018, amended 2019
    Lloyd's India regulation 2024 (subsuming 2015 and 2016)
    Three reasons Indians buy insurance (evolution) Tax saving → investment → wealth accumulation
    Sales bunching Historically Jan–March; now evened out
    Credit life insurance Benefit goes FIRST to the mortgage lender, balance to the family
    Reverse mortgage A roaring success in the West; a COMPLETE FAILURE in India and China — the house is a family heirloom, not a financial asset
    The mirror case GOLD — India the highest consumer, as a security mechanism, especially for women

    F. Products and life vs non-life

    Item Answer
    Life insurance covers Dying too early AND living too long
    What is actually insured The FINANCIAL LOSS from the absence of the individual — NOT life itself
    Health is classified as NON-LIFE (in India and most markets)
    In India, one company CANNOT do both life and non-life — only a holding pattern
    Endowment vs annuity Endowment: pay in instalments. Annuity: pay UPFRONT in a single shot
    ULIP Insurance + market-linked units — India's most popular product
    Joint life advantage Others keep paying when one exits → lower cost
    Group types Employer–employee · borrower–depositor · affinity groups
    Premium modes Regular · Single · Limited pay
    Participating vs non-participating Share in profits (cash bonus or REVERSIONARY bonus paid on maturity) vs constant returns
    Non-life three classes FIRE · MARINE · MISCELLANEOUS
    Marine sub-split HULL = the ship. CARGO = what it carries
    New Indian non-life covers Trade credit (2021) · Surety (2022)
    Motor compulsory cover THIRD-PARTY LIABILITY only. Own damage is voluntary
    Personal lines Bought by individuals — "mass risks"
    Commercial lines Bought by businesses — "large risks": product liability, business interruption
    Compulsory non-life Motor third party and public liability for HAZARDOUS GOODS
    Jamnagar Reliance refinery flooded in the 1990s; survived because of insurance; introduces CONSEQUENTIAL LOSS
    Number of non-life products 350–400
    Life vs non-life duration Life: decades, a SINGLE contract, revivable. Non-life: ≤1 YEAR, each "renewal" is a NEW contract
    Life vs non-life premium Life: FIXED for the policy life. Non-life: changes yearly
    Life vs non-life payout Life: amount KNOWN, timing uncertain. Non-life: BOTH uncertain
    Life vs non-life underwriting Life: one-off (2-year rule). Non-life: a CONTINUUM
    Life vs non-life investments Life: LONG-TERM bonds. Non-life: SHORT, LIQUID bonds (lower returns)
    Non-life extra balance sheet item UNEARNED PREMIUMS
    Life commission 35–40% in year 1, falling to 5–6% on renewals
    Non-life commission Lower but FLATTER, may rise slightly
    Life products are STANDARDISED/commoditised; non-life is CUSTOMISED
    Human Life Value Capitalised net future earnings (e.g. a 35-year-old with 25 working years to 60)
    Life-cycle framework BCG "magic moments" — match product and channel to life stage

    G. Value chain and intermediaries

    Item Answer
    The value chain DISTRIBUTION → UNDERWRITING → OPERATIONS → ASSET MANAGEMENT
    Distribution's key constraint MIS-SELLING — impact felt 10–20 years later
    Underwriting's key constraint Information accuracy + scarce ACTUARIAL competence
    Asset management's key constraint Balancing risk and return in a social-benefit product
    Risk layering High frequency/low severity → RETAIN. Low frequency/high severity → CAT bonds/insurance
    Liquidity Liquidity is a COST — hold access to capital, not idle capital
    Why intermediaries exist Information asymmetry + the scarce ability to ANALYSE information
    Three intermediaries AGENTS (high volume, low ticket) · BROKERS (low volume, high ticket) · IMFs
    Five broker types Direct life · direct general · direct reinsurance · composite · direct life-and-general
    Broker vs IMF Broker: many companies, customised, commission PLUS advisory FEES. IMF: one company, limited portfolio, commission ONLY
    Corporate agents NBFCs, banks, firms, NGOs, cooperative societies; up to 9 insurers per category = 27
    Microinsurance channel Common Service Centres and village-level entrepreneurs
    Surveyor / loss assessor Determines the extent of damage and hence the validity of the claim
    Why financial consumer protection is harder You discover the mistake only when you claim — 15 years later; you cannot go back in time
    Bank and insurer Must be SEPARATE LEGAL ENTITIES

    H. Regulation

    Item Answer
    IRDAI Insurance Regulatory and DEVELOPMENT Authority of India — development is in the name, which is "extremely rare"
    Model borrowed by PFRDA
    Statutory duty "REGULATE, PROMOTE AND ENSURE ORDERLY GROWTH" of insurance and reinsurance
    Licensing 3 rounds; business must commence within 12 MONTHS
    IAIS International Association of Insurance Supervisors, est. 1994; India joined 2017; 200+ jurisdictions, 97% of global premium; 26 ICPs; voluntary, "like the Basel Committee"
    Solvency regulation IRDA (Assets, Liabilities and Solvency Margin) Regulations, 2000, amended 2016 and 2022
    ASM Available Solvency Margin = assets MINUS liabilities
    RSM Required Solvency Margin
    Solvency ratio ASM ÷ RSM — must be GREATER THAN 1
    Minimum/control level 1.5 times = 150%; ASM ≥ 50% of capital or 100% of RSM
    Commission cap ABOLISHED by the 2024 Expenses of Management Regulations — because caps caused tax evasion and unsound undercutting
    Advertising No agent may advertise without the insurer's approval; the LIABILITY sits with the insurer
    Regulatory sandbox A segregated, controlled test zone — because "building trust is easy; REBUILDING it is extremely difficult"

    I. Underwriting

    Item Answer
    Underwriting The process of RISK ESTIMATION — selecting and classifying risk; "choosing the RIGHT RISK"
    The underwriter "The person who signs at the bottom of the slip"
    Can risk be perfectly estimated? NO — 99.9% at best
    Five documents Proposal form · cover note · policy form · endorsements/riders · certificate of insurance
    The declaration is the basis of the contract EXCEPT in MARINE, where the value is too high to rely on it alone
    Cover note An INTERIM certificate with limited validity
    Endorsement A post-issue modification (e.g. the car stereo)
    PHILOSOPHY The VISION — set by the BOARD/top management
    POLICY / guidelines The MISSION — set by the CHIEF UNDERWRITER
    Premium components Mortality/morbidity + operational costs + profit
    "Mortality" in non-life The LIFE OF THE RISK, not length of human life
    Substandard risks Accept them — but on terms EQUITABLE to the other policyholders. The good risk must NOT subsidise the bad
    CIBIL Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, scale 0–900; >750–800 excellent; <450–500 substandard
    Risk class design rule Minimise variation WITHIN a group; all variation ACROSS groups
    Three classes PREFERRED (below-average mortality) · STANDARD (at average) · SUBSTANDARD / SPECIAL / IMPAIRED (above average)
    Risk assessment factors CONCENTRATION · MEDICAL (build, personal history, FAMILY history) · PERSONAL (occupation, tobacco/alcohol, hobbies, driving) · FINANCIAL (anti-selection, MORAL HAZARD, early lapsation)
    COVID The named exception to the concentration-diversification principle
    Infosys parallel No more than 10% of revenues from ONE client
    Moral hazard story The Cuban cigars — insured against fire, smoked, claimed; paid, then prosecuted for ARSON
    Decision outcomes Accept · modify (exclusions, drop riders, change term) · rate up / impose liens · postpone · decline
    Standard exclusion example Damage under the influence of ALCOHOL
    Restrictive clause example COVID was not covered under original health policies
    Lien types DECREASING (underweight young person) and CONSTANT (where extra premium cannot compensate)
    Two classification methods JUDGEMENT (fails on uniformity) and NUMERICAL RATING (scientific but not foolproof)
    Standard mortality base 100
    Field underwriting The AGENT is the key link; the key document is the ACR — AGENT'S CONFIDENTIAL REPORT
    Jet underwriting "Mass production" for simple cases meeting standard criteria
    Clinical vs insurance medicine Clinical asks is it resolved; INSURANCE asks what is the PROGNOSIS
    Three case systems Case assignment → team underwriting → COMMITTEE underwriting
    Committee composition Underwriting + policy servicing + marketing + ACTUARIAL + LEGAL
    Committee duties Oversee practices · borderline high-value cases · transparency · feedback to SALES
    Market note A shortage of good underwriters — a transferable skill

    J. Reinsurance

    Item Answer
    Reinsurance Insurance for the insurer. The reinsurer has NO direct contractual relationship with the insured
    The analogy We deal with banks; banks deal with the RBI; we cannot deal with the RBI
    Ceding company The direct insurer
    LINE / RETENTION What the insurer KEEPS
    CESSION What is passed on
    RETROCESSION The reinsurer ceding onward, to a retrocessionaire
    Final backstop THE GOVERNMENT — the right of SEIGNIORAGE
    Co-insurance vs reinsurance Co-insurance: each insurer is DIRECTLY liable to the insured; the INSURED spreads the risk. Reinsurance: the reinsurer is NOT directly liable
    Reinsurance functions Limit fluctuations · protect against catastrophes · protect solvency · spread losses · stabilise results · increase underwriting flexibility
    Primary advantage The ceding insurer's CAPACITY TO ACCEPT RISK increases
    Global reinsurers Munich Re · Swiss Re · Employers Re · Zurich Re · Hannover Re · General Cologne Re · Berkshire Hathaway Re
    India GIC Re — unique in being both a non-life insurer and the national reinsurer
    Top-level reinsurers globally ~200; global reinsurance capital ~$570–600 billion
    Retention depends on Frequency × size of loss; volume/premium; type of risk
    Retention rule High frequency/small loss → RETAIN. Low frequency/large loss → CEDE
    PML / EML Probable / Estimated Maximum Loss — expressed as a PERCENTAGE OF THE SUM INSURED
    FACULTATIVE Single risk, case by case; the reinsurer has the OPTION (the "faculty") to accept or decline; full details supplied; the OLDEST form; ends with the original policy
    TREATY (obligatory) A portfolio of risks; the reinsurer MUST accept all cessions in scope; no individual details; annual and renewable
    Facultative used when Retention + treaty capacity are exhausted, or the risk is EXCLUDED from the treaty
    Facultative popular in Aviation · hull (marine) · space · oil
    Facultative disadvantage Slow, costly, and the reinsurer may demand a say in CLAIM SETTLEMENT
    RI slip / FAC slip A term sheet with the insured, risks, premium, net retention, history, EML, offer %, commissions
    BORDEREAUX A list of risks under a treaty — avoided in BLIND TREATIES, where the reinsurer "follows the fortunes"
    Proportional vs non-proportional A PERCENTAGE vs an ABSOLUTE AMOUNT; sum insured vs LOSS as the basis
    QUOTA SHARE example SI 10m, retention 70% (7m) / cession 30% (3m); premium $20,000 → $14,000 / $6,000; a 6m loss → 4.2m / 1.8m
    Quota share used when New company · poor surplus experience · to cut administrative time
    Quota share disadvantage Does NOT limit PEAK risks; reinsures even when not needed; no selection against the reinsurer
    SURPLUS treaty Reinsure only the SURPLUS above the retention; arranged in LINES; if the SI is within the retention, NO cession
    Surplus example (9 lines, $300k) SI 3m → 10%/90%, loss 1.5m → $150,000 / $1.35m · SI $130,000 → entirely retained, reinsurer gets nothing · SI 3.5m → retain $800,000 (22.86%) / cede $2.7m (77.14%), loss 2m → $457,200 / $1,542,800
    Multi-surplus example Retention $100k, 1st surplus 10 lines, 2nd 20 lines: SI 1.5m → 100k / 1m / 400k; SI 3.1m → 100k / 1m / 2m
    Beyond both surpluses Carry it yourself or arrange a separate (facultative) contract
    Clean cut cancellation 3–6 months' notice; premium returned at ~35–40%; outstanding losses debited at 90–100% of estimate
    Surplus advantage You do NOT give away premium on every risk; retention can vary by class
    Surplus disadvantage Heavy admin; UNBALANCED risk distribution for the reinsurer
    Facultative-obligatory The ceding company CHOOSES; the reinsurer MUST accept. Cheaper than a surplus treaty
    STOP LOSS Loss ratio stopped at an agreed percentage; the reinsurer pays the balance
    Deductible / cover limit What the insurer bears / the reinsurer's maximum
    CAT XL Catastrophe excess of loss — PER EVENT
    WXL/R Working excess of loss PER RISK
    The XL worked example Retention 8m; WXL 6m xs 2m; CAT XL 9m xs 4m. 1m loss → neither triggers. 7m single-risk loss → insurer 2m, WXL 5m. 9m earthquake (1+1+1+2+4) → insurer 4m, WXL 2m on risk E, CAT XL 3m
    Layered stack Quota share → surplus → excess of loss → facultative; stop loss is uncommon (needs trust)
    POOLS Business lines pooled and retroceded to members in agreed proportion
    Historic Indian mandate 20% of reinsurance business had to go to GIC
    Indian pools NUCLEAR pool (2015, GIC Re) · INDIAN MARKET TERRORISM RISK INSURANCE POOL (2022) · market FIRE pool · market HULL pool
    Pool design principle HOMOGENEITY — minimise intra-class variation
    CAT BONDS Investors earn above-market interest; if disaster strikes the bonds FORECLOSE and fund the losses; if not, principal is returned
    Reinsurance by class Life: surplus (quota share for groups; pools for substandard). Property: proportional surplus + quota share + XL for catastrophes. Marine/aviation: facultative, quota share, pools, XL. Liability: EXCESS OF LOSS
    Direct insurer vs reinsurer Risk estimation internal+external vs internal; assessment direct vs via UBERRIMAE FIDEI; obligation to the policyholder vs to the insurer

    K. ART and InsurTech

    Item Answer
    Four traditional inefficiencies Credit risk to the policyholder · little incentive for loss prevention (MORAL HAZARD) · limited capacity · good risks subsidise bad (ADVERSE SELECTION)
    ART Alternative Risk Transfer — tailored, multi-line, multi-layer; taps the capital markets
    CAPTIVES Insurers OWNED BY NON-INSURANCE firms for the parent's risks. >4,000 globally, ~$21 billion of premium
    FINITE RISK (financial insurance) Spreads risk OVER TIME rather than across a pool; shares investment returns
    Other ART tools Multi-line/multi-year · multi-trigger · securitisation (CAT and earthquake bonds, insurance derivatives)
    PolicyBazaar founded 2008
    Its mission Protect the middle class through the 3 Ds — DEATH, DISEASE, DISABILITY
    The model An AGGREGATOR — "no different from Uber or Zomato", closing information asymmetry
    Insurance defined "A COLLECTIVE BARGAIN … similar to a LOTTERY, except nobody wants to win"
    Technology stack Aadhaar/e-KYC · UPI (incl. recurring) · big data, AI/ML, LLMs, voice analytics · ~400 API integrations with real-time quotes · AWS
    The technology goal "Solving for the NEXT 50 CRORE people" — same journey on a cheap phone as an expensive one
    The analogy "Democratise insurance like JIO did the internet"
    Fraud tools Facial recognition · PIVC (pre-issuance video verification) · predictive risk flags
    Claims assistance Uses API integrations to find EVERY policy the deceased held and pursue the claim; plus emotional counselling
    Low-cost ULIP Same passive-fund return as a mutual fund, PLUS 10× annual premium on death with premiums waived and the policy continuing, AND a TAX-FREE corpus — capped at ₹2.5 LAKH of premium p.a.
    Most-bought digital products TERM and ULIP
    Business lines PB Partners (agent tech platform) and PB for Business (SMEs/corporates)

    End of Introduction to Insurance guide.

    Analytical Foundations for the FinTech Industry — II

    Analytical Foundations for the FinTech Industry — II — Complete Exam Reference

    Course faculty: Prof. Ananth Krishnamurthy (IIM Bangalore) Format: taught as a dialogue with two students, Tejas and Ashwini. All the examples are set in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka.

    How to use this file. The course is one continuous arc: linear combinations of normals → the three derived distributions (χ², t, F) → sampling and sampling distributions → the Central Limit Theorem → confidence intervals → hypothesis testing → covariance and correlation. Every worked example is reproduced with its exact numbers, because MCQ writers lift them verbatim. Anything marked ← guaranteed MCQ is a formula, threshold, definition or trap. The Quick-fire revision table at the end collects every formula and number in one place.

    1. Linear combinations of random variables
    12

    1.1 The general result (any distribution)

    For random variables X₁ … Xₙ and constants a₁ … aₙ, define Y = a₁X₁ + a₂X₂ + … + aₙXₙ:

    Quantity Result
    E(Y) a₁E(X₁) + a₂E(X₂) + … + aₙE(Xₙ) — always true, no independence needed
    Var(Y) if the Xᵢ are INDEPENDENT a₁²Var(X₁) + a₂²Var(X₂) + … + aₙ²Var(Xₙ)
    Var(Y) if the Xᵢ are CORRELATED The above PLUS the covariance terms: + Σ 2·aᵢ·aⱼ·Cov(Xᵢ, Xⱼ) over all pairs i ≠ j

    ← guaranteed MCQ — the expectation formula never needs independence; the variance formula does

    1.2 The special result for NORMALS guaranteed MCQ

    A LINEAR COMBINATION OF NORMAL RANDOM VARIABLES IS ITSELF NORMALLY DISTRIBUTED.

    "An attractive property or feature of the normal distribution." For any other distribution you can compute E(Y) and Var(Y), but you cannot say what the distribution of Y is. For normals, you can.

    1.3 The four special cases

    Case Y E(Y) Var(Y)
    Y = aX + b Linear transform of one normal aE(X) + b a²Var(X) — note b does NOT affect the variance guaranteed MCQ
    a = 1/σ, b = −μ/σ Y = (X − μ)/σ = Z — this IS the standard normal guaranteed MCQ 0 1
    Y = X₁ + X₂ (independent) Sum of two normals μ₁ + μ₂ σ₁² + σ₂² — (if NOT independent, still normal, but the variance includes the covariance)
    Y = ΣXᵢ, all aᵢ = 1, iid The SUM of n iid normals n·μ n·σ², so SD = √n · σ ← guaranteed MCQ — the MEANS add, but the standard deviations do NOT add directly
    Y = X̄, all aᵢ = 1/n, iid The AVERAGE of n iid normals μ σ²/n, so SD = σ/√n

    The insight from averaging: "Averaging REDUCES the variance to σ²/n, so the average X̄ tends to get closer and closer to μ. This tendency increases as n increases." guaranteed MCQ

    1.4 Worked examples on linear combinations

    (a) The piston-and-cylinder problem (Pankaj Vaghela, Jamnagar) guaranteed MCQ| Item | Value | |---|---| | Piston radius X₁ | Normal, mean 30 mm, SD 0.05 mm | | Cylinder inside radius X₂ | Normal, mean 30.25 mm, SD 0.06 mm | | Gap Y = X₂ − X₁ | Mean = 30.25 − 30 = 0.25 mm | | Var(Y) | 0.05² + 0.06² = 0.0061 → SD = 0.078 mm | | P(piston does NOT fit) = P(Y ≤ 0) | 0.0007 | | P(optimal, i.e. 0.1 ≤ Y ≤ 0.35) | 0.872 |

    Note the key step: for a DIFFERENCE, the VARIANCES still ADD.

    (b) Cotton plants (Chirag Heera, Rajkot) guaranteed MCQ Individual plant height: normal, mean 29.4 cm, SD 2.1 cm (variance 4.41). n = 20 plants. X̄ is normal, mean 29.4, variance 4.41/20 = 0.2205, SD = 0.469. - 95th percentile of the average: 30.17 cm - 95% of the time the average exceeds: 28.63 cm - 95% of the time the average lies between: 28.47 and 30.32

    The teaching point: the SD of the AVERAGE (0.47 cm) is far smaller than the SD of an INDIVIDUAL plant (2.1 cm).

    (c) Two stocks (Munaf Khan, Bharuch) guaranteed MCQ — a very likely exam item| | Stock A | Stock B | |---|---|---| | Mean return | 8% | 9.5% | | SD | 1.5% | 2% |

    Classification: excellent > 10% · moderate 5%–10% · unsatisfactory < 5%

    Question Answer
    P(A is moderate, i.e. 5% ≤ X_A ≤ 10%) 0.886
    P(B is excellent, i.e. X_B ≥ 10%) 0.4013
    Y = X_B − X_A Mean 1.5, Var = 4 + 2.25 = 6.25, SD = 2.5
    P(B outperforms A) = P(Y ≥ 0) 0.726 (73%)
    P(B beats A by at least 2 points) = P(Y ≥ 2) 0.421 (42%)

    (d) Nine investments (Nilesh Desai) guaranteed MCQ Nine independent investments, each normal with mean ₹50,000, SD ₹10,000. Total Y: mean = 9 × 50,000 = ₹4,50,000; SD = √9 × 10,000 = ₹30,000 - Value below which there is a 1% chance: 4,50,000 − 1.28 × 30,000 = ₹4,11,533 - P(₹4,00,000 ≤ Y ≤ ₹5,20,000) = P(−1.67 ≤ Z ≤ 2.33) = 0.9901 − 0.953 = 0.037 (3.7%)

    (e) Three weeks of inventory (Naman Lakhani, Bayer Chemical, Vapi) guaranteed MCQ — includes a deliberate trap| Week | Mean | SD | |---|---|---| | 1 | 50 | 10 | | 2 | 45 | 5 | | 3 | 65 | 15 |

    THE TRAP Ashwini falls into: she says SD(Y) = √(10 + 5 + 15). WRONG. Correct: Var(Y) = 100 + 25 + 225 = 350 → SD = √350 = 18.71. Mean = 160. guaranteed MCQ - Current stock 180 tons. P(run out) = P(Y > 180) = P(Z > 1.07) = 0.142 (~14%), so he is safe 86% of the time - To be 98% sure: stock = 160 + 2.05 × 18.71 = 198.4 → 199 tons

    1.5 Two pure normal-distribution worked examples

    (a) Pawn brokers (Ramesh bhai Shah, Nadiad) guaranteed MCQ — the inverse-calculation pattern X = number of people bringing items to pawn shops per day, normal, mean 658. Given P(X ≤ 610) = 0.03.

    Step Working
    Find the z P(Z < −1.88) = 0.03
    Solve for σ (610 − 658)/σ = −1.88 → σ = 25.52
    P(600 ≤ X ≤ 700) P(−2.27 ≤ Z ≤ 1.65) = 0.9505 − 0.0116 = 0.9389 (~94%)
    Busiest 3% of days 658 + 1.88 × 25.52 = 706 or more people

    (b) Chaas bottles (Suresh Pandya, Gujarat) guaranteed MCQ Amount per 12-oz bottle: normal with adjustable mean μ, fixed SD 0.05 oz. Regulation: at least 11.9 oz, met 99.5% of the time.

    • P(Z > −2.57) = 0.995 → (11.9 − μ)/0.05 = −2.57 → μ = 12.03 oz
    • P(X ≥ 12) = P(Z > (12 − 12.03)/0.05) = P(Z > −0.6) = 0.726 (73%)

    1. The three distributions derived from the normal
    20

    Why we study them: "These distributions will be very useful when we are looking at STATISTICAL INFERENCE and its applications in later modules." guaranteed MCQ

    2.1 CHI-SQUARE (χ²) guaranteed MCQ

    Definition:

    If Z is standard normal, then X = Z² has a chi-square distribution with ONE degree of freedom. More generally, if Z₁ … Zₙ are independent standard normals, then X = Z₁² + Z₂² + … + Zₙ² has a chi-square distribution with n degrees of freedom.

    Degrees of freedom = the NUMBER OF SQUARED STANDARD NORMALS BEING ADDED.

    Properties:

    Property Value
    Range Defined ONLY for POSITIVE values
    Number of parameters ONE — the degrees of freedom
    MEAN = the degrees of freedom, k
    VARIANCE = 2 × the degrees of freedom = 2k
    Shape as k increases Skewness REDUCES; converges to a symmetric, bell-shaped NORMAL (a consequence of the CLT)

    Uses: many non-parametric hypothesis tests · feature selection and classification · logistic regression tests of independence of variables · the GOODNESS-OF-FIT test — "one of the more popular hypothesis tests, used to check whether a data set follows a particular distribution." guaranteed MCQ Excel: CHISQ.DIST(x, k, TRUE/FALSE) — TRUE gives the CDF, FALSE gives the PDF.

    Critical value notation: χ²(α, k) is the value for which the upper-tail probability = α, i.e. P(X ≥ χ²(α,k)) = α.

    THE CRITICAL VALUE TABLE (from the Excel template) guaranteed MCQ| df (k) | α = 0.2 | α = 0.1 | α = 0.05 | α = 0.01 | |---|---|---|---|---| | 5 | 7.3 | 9.2 | 11.1 | 15.1 | | 10 | 13.4 | 16.0 | 18.3 | 23.2 | | 15 | 19.3 | 22.3 | 25.0 | — | | 20 | 25.0 | 28.4 | 31.4 | 37.6 |

    Two observations: as df increases, the critical values INCREASE (the distribution has a higher SD and is flatter); and the skewness reduces as df increases.

    Chi-square TABLE lookups worked in class guaranteed MCQ| df | Upper tail | Critical value | |---|---|---| | 5 | 0.05 | 11.07 | | 15 | 0.025 | 27.49 | | 20 | 0.975 | 9.59 | | 10 | 0.1 | 15.99 | | 18 | 0.95 | 9.39 |

    Interpretation he asks to be repeated: χ²(5 df) = 11.07 at an upper tail of 0.05 means "this random variable will take a value greater than 11.07 only 5% of the time — in other words, 95% of the time it takes a value ≤ 11.07."

    2.2 STUDENT'S t guaranteed MCQ

    Definition:

    A standard normal Z divided by the square root of an INDEPENDENT chi-square with k degrees of freedom divided by k: t_k = Z / √(χ²_k / k)

    THE STORY — a near-certain MCQ: guaranteed MCQ

    The t distribution was discovered by WILLIAM SEALY GOSSET. He studied mathematics and chemistry at Oxford; in 1899 he moved to Dublin, Ireland, to work as a statistician for the GUINNESS BREWERY. Working on the quality of barley and hops, he proposed the t distribution, and in 1908 published under the pseudonym "Student", because Guinness did not allow its employees to publish their own research. Hence "Student's t distribution."

    Properties:

    Property Value
    Shape Symmetric, bell-shaped, centred at ZERO — like the standard normal, but FLATTER
    MEAN 0 (for 2 or more degrees of freedom)
    VARIANCE k / (k − 2), for k > 2 guaranteed MCQ
    Limiting case The STANDARD NORMAL is the limit of the t as k → ∞

    Uses: hypothesis tests about means of a population, especially for SMALL SAMPLE SIZES · comparing the means of two populations · hypothesis testing and diagnostics of LINEAR REGRESSION models. guaranteed MCQ Excel: T.DIST(x, k, TRUE/FALSE)

    THE CRITICAL VALUE TABLE t(α/2, k) guaranteed MCQ| df (k) | α/2 = 0.1 | α/2 = 0.05 | α/2 = 0.025 | α/2 = 0.005 | |---|---|---|---|---| | 5 | 1.48 | 2.02 | 2.57 | 4.03 | | 10 | 1.37 | 1.81 | 2.23 | 3.17 | | 15 | 1.34 | 1.75 | 2.13 | 2.95 | | 20 | 1.33 | 1.73 | 2.09 | 2.85 |

    2.3 F DISTRIBUTION guaranteed MCQ

    Definition:

    F is short for FISHER, named after the statistician RONALD FISHER. F(k₁, k₂) = [χ²(k₁)/k₁] ÷ [χ²(k₂)/k₂] — the ratio of two independent chi-squares each divided by its own degrees of freedom. k₁ = numerator df; k₂ = denominator df.

    THE ORDER MATTERS: F(k₁, k₂) is NOT the same as F(k₂, k₁). guaranteed MCQ Properties:

    Property Value
    Range Only POSITIVE values
    Shape Unimodal, long right tail, SKEWED
    MEAN k₂ / (k₂ − 2), for k₂ ≥ 2 guaranteed MCQ
    SD DECREASES as k₂ increases
    As k₁ and k₂ both grow The PDF becomes more sharply spiked about the value 1

    Uses: ANALYSIS OF VARIANCE (ANOVA) — used heavily · feature selection in machine learning · testing the OVERALL FITNESS of multiple linear regression models. guaranteed MCQ Excel: F.DIST(x, k₁, k₂, TRUE/FALSE) — four parameters.

    THE CRITICAL VALUE TABLE F(α, k₁, k₂) guaranteed MCQ — note especially the asymmetry| (k₁, k₂) | α = 0.2 | α = 0.1 | α = 0.05 | α = 0.01 | |---|---|---|---|---| | (5, 5) | 2.23 | 3.45 | 5.05 | 10.97 | | (5, 10) | 1.80 | 2.52 | 3.33 | 5.64 | | (10, 5) | 2.19 | 3.30 | 4.74 | 10.05 | | (20, 20) | 1.47 | 1.79 | 2.21 | 2.94 |

    Two observations: swapping k₁ and k₂ changes the critical values — "we must be careful"; and as k₂ increases, the critical values SHRINK toward 1.

    How the F tables are laid out: guaranteed MCQ

    ROWS = denominator degrees of freedom (k₂). COLUMNS = numerator degrees of freedom (k₁). EACH SEPARATE TABLE corresponds to one upper-tail probability — the tables provided are for 0.05, 0.025, 0.01 and 0.005. Anything else must be interpolated.

    1. Sampling
    8

    3.1 The vocabulary

    Term Definition
    Sampling The process of selecting a SUBSET of observations from a population
    Element An entity for which data is collected
    Population The collection of all elements of interest
    Sample A subset of the population
    Sample STATISTIC A quantity computed from the sample (x̄, s, p̄)
    Population PARAMETER The corresponding true value in the population (μ, σ, p)

    The purpose: "We collect this data not just to analyse the sample, but as an efficient way to make INFERENCE about population parameters. Therefore an INCORRECT SAMPLE may lead to WRONG INFERENCE about the population." guaranteed MCQ

    3.2 The two motivating examples

    Case Detail
    Viren Agarwal (Jaipur, elections) Sample of 400 registered voters; 160 favour a candidate → p̄ = 160/400 = 40%. The population is over 4 crore registered voters
    Manoj Choudhury (Kota, HR at a power plant) Sample of 120 migrant temporary workers; average salary ₹36,500/year. The problem: "it is even hard to identify the composition of the entire population"

    (He also notes what Kota is famous for: coaching classes and entrance exam preparation.)

    3.3 The FOUR STEPS of the sampling process guaranteed MCQ| # | Step | Content |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | Identify the TARGET POPULATION | Put boundaries on parameters — e.g. age, gender, type of work for "migrant workers" | | 2 | Decide the SAMPLING FRAME | "The source, method or procedure used to IDENTIFY the elements of the target population." Viren can use census data or voter registration data; Manoj has no pre-built database of migrant workers, so his frame is much harder | | 3 | Determine the SAMPLE SIZE | Bigger is better, but data collection is expensive in cost and time; an insufficient sample means lack of precision. Sample size affects the confidence level and margin of error | | 4 | Choose the SAMPLING METHOD | Split into PROBABILISTIC and NON-PROBABILISTIC |

    3.4 PROBABILISTIC sampling methods guaranteed MCQ| Method | Definition | When to use / notes |

    |---|---|---| | RANDOM sampling | Every subject has an EQUAL probability of selection | Ideal when the population is HOMOGENEOUS. Execution: label all cases 1 … N, generate uniform random numbers (Excel RAND() or RANDBETWEEN()) | | STRATIFIED sampling | Divide the population into mutually exclusive AND collectively exhaustive groups called STRATA (by age, gender, marital status, income, demography), then random sample WITHIN each stratum | Use when the population is HETEROGENEOUS. The sample size in each stratum should be PROPORTIONAL to the size of that stratum in the population — if women are 40% of the population, they should be 40% of the sample. If the strata are homogeneous, stratified sampling gives results as precise as simple random sampling with a SMALLER sample size guaranteed MCQ| | CLUSTER sampling | Divide into groups called CLUSTERS; each element belongs to one and only one cluster; take a simple random sample OF CLUSTERS, then take ALL elements within each selected cluster | Ideal case: each cluster is a SMALL-SCALE REPLICA of the entire population. A common form is AREA SAMPLING (districts, municipalities, wards). Generally requires a LARGER sample size than random or stratified sampling, but can save cost and time |

    THE STRATA vs CLUSTER DISTINCTION — a certain MCQ: guaranteed MCQ

    We want STRATA to be HOMOGENEOUS (alike within). We want CLUSTERS to be HETEROGENEOUS (diverse within, each a mini-population).

    (His illustration of cluster sampling: a bank talking to students at one college to infer the credit-card preferences of all college students.)

    3.5 NON-PROBABILISTIC sampling methods guaranteed MCQ| Method | Definition | Example / limitation |

    |---|---|---| | SYSTEMATIC sampling | Randomly select ONE element from the first k, then take every kth element thereafter. Worked example: 400 from 4 crore → 1 in every 1,00,000: randomly pick one of the first 1,00,000, then every 1,00,000th after it | Used when simple random sampling is time-consuming. Because the first element is a random choice, it is usually assumed to have some properties of simple random sampling | | CONVENIENCE sampling | Elements included by convenience, with no pre-specified or known probabilities of selection | Manoj surveying only workers he met at his plant last month; traffic inspectors pulling over the next passing motorist. Easy and cheap — but it is IMPOSSIBLE to evaluate how well it represents the population, and NO statistically robust inference is available | | JUDGMENT sampling | The most knowledgeable person selects the elements he or she feels are most representative | The TV panel expressing opinions on a political issue. Quality depends entirely on the judgement of the selector | | VOLUNTARY sampling | Data collected from people who VOLUNTEER | Customer surveys — "primarily customers with BAD experiences respond; those with good experiences do not bother" — and clinical trials seeking volunteers. Inherently BIASED |

    Basavaraju runs a Chroma store in Ballari and surveyed customers about their laptop purchase, recording brand, price, RAM, hard disk, OS and a satisfaction score out of 100.

    Sample size n 36

    3.7 Point estimators

    x̄ estimates μ · s estimates σ · p̄ estimates p. These numerical values are called POINT ESTIMATES.

    The key conceptual point: "Our x̄ of 57.31 is but ONE out of MANY possible point estimates for the unknown μ. If Basavaraju, or you, or I did a similar survey on the same population, we would perhaps get a DIFFERENT x̄." guaranteed MCQ

    1. Sampling distributions
    27

    4.1 The central idea guaranteed MCQ

    If we consider the process of selecting a simple random sample from a population as an EXPERIMENT, then the sample mean x̄ is a NUMERICAL DESCRIPTION OF THE OUTCOME of that experiment — and therefore x̄ IS A RANDOM VARIABLE.

    The probability distribution of x̄ is called the SAMPLING DISTRIBUTION OF x̄.

    Ashwini's die analogy: "If you toss a die 500 times you get 3, 1, 6 …; if you conduct the survey 500 times you get x̄ values of 57.31, 56.63, 58.02 …" — but in practice Basavaraju has only ONE outcome, like tossing a die once.

    x̄, p̄ and s are all CONTINUOUS random variables (they can take fractional values).

    4.2 The sampling distribution of x̄ — the three properties guaranteed MCQ| Property | Result |

    |---|---| | EXPECTED VALUE | E(x̄) = μ. Because the expected value of the estimator equals the population parameter, x̄ is an UNBIASED estimator of μ | | STANDARD DEVIATION (the STANDARD ERROR) | σ_x̄ = σ / √n — for an infinite/large population relative to n | | SHAPE | If the POPULATION is normal, x̄ is normal for ANY n. If not, see the CLT |

    WHY "STANDARD ERROR"? guaranteed MCQ

    "The term STANDARD ERROR is used throughout statistical inference to refer to the standard deviation of a POINT ESTIMATOR. The reason for this new term is so we do not confuse it with the standard deviation of the POPULATION."

    The finite-population caveat he explicitly sets aside: when the sample size n is comparable in order of magnitude to the population size N, the expression for σ_x̄ needs a finite population correction. He assumes throughout that N is large enough relative to n that the infinite-population formula applies. guaranteed MCQ Basavaraju's numbers: with σ = 6 and n = 36, σ_x̄ = 6/√36 = 1. With σ = 5, σ_x̄ = 5/6 = 0.833.

    The die illustration of why n matters: the true μ of a fair die is 3.5. Toss twice and get {1, 2} → x̄ = 1.5; get {5, 6} → x̄ = 5.5. Both far from 3.5 because n = 2. Toss 100 times and both x̄ values will be close to 3.5. guaranteed MCQ

    4.3 THE CENTRAL LIMIT THEOREM guaranteed MCQ — the exact wording

    "When you select random samples of size n from a population, the SAMPLING DISTRIBUTION OF THE SAMPLE MEAN x̄ can be APPROXIMATED BY THE NORMAL DISTRIBUTION if the sample size becomes large."

    THE RULE OF THUMB: n ≥ 30. guaranteed MCQ Three precision points he hammers:

    Point Detail
    1. It is about x̄, NOT the population "The Central Limit Theorem is talking about the DISTRIBUTION OF x̄, and NOT of the population. Just because you sample more than 30 from a population, the DISTRIBUTION OF THE POPULATION CANNOT CHANGE." This is tested repeatedly — the tax-consultant example below is built to catch it guaranteed MCQ
    2. n = 30 is EMPIRICAL, not theoretical "It is theoretically proved that the distribution of x̄ converges to the normal as n → ∞, but it has been EMPIRICALLY OBSERVED that even at n = 30 it starts to look like the normal in most cases."
    3. Highly skewed populations need more "You can always find distributions, especially ones with HIGH SKEWNESS, where even with n MORE THAN 150 the sampling distribution may not appear normal."

    The four-population picture: the top row shows four population distributions — normal · uniform · skewed (exponential) · an arbitrary "purple" distribution. The bottom row shows the sampling distribution of x̄. At n = 2 it looks like neither the population nor the normal; beyond n = 30 all four look normal. guaranteed MCQ

    4.4 The effect of n on the standard error guaranteed MCQ

    E(x̄) = μ regardless of n. But σ_x̄ = σ/√n falls as n rises.

    | n | σ_x̄ (with σ = 6) | P(|x̄ − μ| ≤ 2) | |---|---|---| | 36 | 1.0 | ~0.95 (95%) | | 100 | 0.6 | P(−3.33 ≤ Z ≤ 3.33) > 0.999 (99.9%) |

    (The transcript's dictation garbles 6/√100 as "0.1"; the correct value is 0.6, which is what the 3.33 z-score uses.)

    4.6 The sampling distribution of the proportion p̄ guaranteed MCQ

    p̄ = x/n, where x = the number of elements in the sample possessing the characteristic of interest.

    Property Result
    E(p̄) = p → p̄ is an UNBIASED estimator of p
    STANDARD ERROR σ_p̄ √[ p(1−p)/n ]
    SHAPE Approximately NORMAL, provided np ≥ 5 AND n(1−p) ≥ 5

    THE DERIVATION he walks through — a likely conceptual MCQ: guaranteed MCQ

    x is a BINOMIAL random variable (counting "successes" in n trials), with mean np and variance np(1−p). If np ≥ 5 and nq ≥ 5, the binomial is approximated by a normal. Dividing a normal by the constant n keeps it normal, with mean np/n = p and variance np(1−p)/n² = p(1−p)/n, giving SD = √[p(1−p)/n] — exactly the standard error of p̄.

    Basavaraju's application: assume p = 0.5. Then σ_p̄ = √(0.25/36) = 0.0833.

    n σ_p̄ P(0.45 ≤ p̄ ≤ 0.55)
    36 0.0833 0.452
    100 √(0.25/100) = 0.05 0.683

    4.8 The sampling distribution of the SAMPLE VARIANCE guaranteed MCQ

    s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1)

    WHY DIVIDE BY n − 1 — the degrees-of-freedom argument he gives: guaranteed MCQ

    "If I told you the average of THREE numbers is 10, and two of them are 1 and 2, what is the third? It HAS to be 30 − 1 − 2 = 27. So when we fix the sample average, NOT ALL n numbers are free — only n − 1 are. We have LOST ONE DEGREE OF FREEDOM."

    THE KEY RESULT: guaranteed MCQ

    If x₁ … xₙ are independently selected from a NORMALLY DISTRIBUTED population with variance σ², then

    (n − 1)s² / σ² has a CHI-SQUARE distribution with (n − 1) degrees of freedom.

    THE CRITICAL CAVEAT: "For sample variance, UNFORTUNATELY, WITHOUT KNOWING THAT THE POPULATION IS NORMALLY DISTRIBUTED, WE ARE NOT ABLE TO SAY MUCH — NOT EVEN APPROXIMATELY. THERE IS NO CLT-LIKE RESULT FOR SAMPLE VARIANCE." guaranteed MCQ — this is the single biggest asymmetry in the course And a second precision point: the result gives you the distribution of (n−1)s²/σ², NOT the sampling distribution of s² directly — a quantity involving both the estimator and the population parameter.

    4.9 Using the chi-square result — Basavaraju, n = 36, s² = 40.73, df = 35 guaranteed MCQ| Step | Working | Result |

    |---|---|---| | χ²₃₅ with cumulative probability 0.9 | | 46.06 | | So (n−1)s²/σ² < 46.06, 90% of the time | σ² > 35 × 40.73 / 46.06 | σ² > 30.92 → σ > 5.56 | | χ²₃₅ with tail probability 0.9 | | 24.8 | | So (n−1)s²/σ² > 24.8, 90% of the time | σ² < 35 × 40.73 / 24.8 | σ² < 57.44 → σ < 7.6 |

    Conclusion: from one sample of 36 with s = 6.38, the population σ is more than 5.56 (90% of the time) and less than 7.6 (90% of the time).

    Note the direction reversal: because you DIVIDE by the chi-square value, a LARGER chi-square gives a SMALLER σ² and vice versa. guaranteed MCQ

    1. Properties of point estimators guaranteed MCQ — all four
    4

    Notation: θ = the population parameter; θ̄ = the sample statistic / point estimator.

    Property Definition Application
    1. UNBIASED E(θ̄) = θ — "the estimation errors BALANCE OUT." If E(θ̄) ≠ θ, the estimator is biased, and the gap is the amount of BIAS x̄ is unbiased for μ; p̄ is unbiased for p; s² is unbiased for σ² — and this is exactly why we divide by n − 1 guaranteed MCQ
    2. EFFICIENT When two unbiased estimators exist for the same θ, the one with the SMALLER STANDARD ERROR has GREATER RELATIVE EFFICIENCY Even sampling from a normal population, the standard error of the sample MEAN is much LESS than that of the sample MEDIAN — so the sample MEAN is MORE EFFICIENT than the sample MEDIAN guaranteed MCQ
    3. CONSISTENT The values of the estimator tend to be CLOSER to the parameter as the SAMPLE SIZE GROWS Both σ_x̄ = σ/√n and σ_p̄ = √[p(1−p)/n] have n in the denominator, so x̄ and p̄ are both consistent
    4. SUFFICIENT The estimator contains ALL the information in the data about the parameter — it uses ALL n data points x̄ and p̄ are sufficient (both use the entire data set). The sample MEDIAN is NOT sufficient guaranteed MCQ

    On bias: "Having a biased estimator is not necessarily insurmountable. If the bias CAN BE QUANTIFIED, a BIAS CORRECTION can be done — but people usually prefer to work with an unbiased estimator."

    Why the median is not used despite being robust to outliers: it is less efficient and not sufficient.

    1. Sampling errors vs non-sampling errors guaranteed MCQ
    3

    6.1 SAMPLING ERROR

    Deviations of the sample from the population that occur due to the RANDOM NATURE of the sample collected. "Sampling error is UNAVOIDABLE — this is the risk we must accept when we collect a simple random sample." We quantify it using STANDARD ERRORS, and a very large sample leaves very little potential for sampling error.

    6.2 NON-SAMPLING ERRORS — the three types guaranteed MCQ| Type | Definition | Basavaraju example |

    |---|---|---| | 1. COVERAGE ERROR | The RESEARCH OBJECTIVE and the POPULATION from which the sample is drawn are NOT ALIGNED | His objective is to grow sales revenue, but he surveys only his current customers — missing his competitors' dissatisfied customers and the untapped market | | 2. NON-RESPONSE ERROR | Some segments of the target population are systematically UNDER- or OVER-represented because they are more or less likely to respond | Handing out forms in the store ignores online customers; a purely online survey ignores in-store customers; even doing both may give response rates that don't match the real mix | | 3. MEASUREMENT ERROR | The data collection instrument is ambiguous, difficult, or distorting, so responses don't reflect what respondents intended | A non-anonymous in-store form; store staff looking over the customer's shoulder; a form that is too long or confusing; poor recollection, unwillingness to be honest, or rushing |

    6.3 The FOUR steps to reduce non-sampling errors guaranteed MCQ

    1. Carefully define the target population before collecting data
    2. Carefully design the data collection process and TRAIN the data collectors
    3. PRE-TEST the procedure using a PILOT to identify and correct sources of error before final collection
    4. Choose the appropriate method — stratified, cluster or systematic — so the variables of interest are adequately reflected

    1. Confidence intervals
    35

    7.1 The general form

    INTERVAL ESTIMATE = POINT ESTIMATE ± MARGIN OF ERROR

    Parameter Form
    Population mean μ x̄ ± margin of error
    Population proportion p p̄ ± margin of error
    Population variance σ² NOT a ± form — a direct lower and upper limit (because the chi-square is not symmetric) guaranteed MCQ

    7.2 The logical derivation — why the interval "contains μ 95% of the time" guaranteed MCQ

    95% of all normal values lie within ±1.96 SD of the mean. For Basavaraju: σ_x̄ = 5/6 = 0.833, so 1.96 × 0.833 = 1.63.

    95% of all x̄ values obtained from n = 36 lie within ±1.63 of μ. Therefore, any x̄ that lies within 1.63 of μ creates an interval x̄ ± 1.63 that CONTAINS μ. Since 95% of all x̄ values satisfy that, 95% of all such intervals contain μ.

    We say: "we are 95% CONFIDENT that the interval 55.68 to 58.94 includes μ."

    The three-sample picture: intervals built around x̄₁ and x̄₂ contain μ; the interval built around x̄₃, which fell in the upper tail more than 1.63 from μ, does NOT.

    Vocabulary: 1 − α is the CONFIDENCE COEFFICIENT (0.95); the interval is the CONFIDENCE INTERVAL; α/2 is the tail probability.

    7.3 CI for the mean, σ KNOWN guaranteed MCQ — the definition

    x̄ ± z_{α/2} · σ/√n

    where 1 − α is the confidence coefficient and z_{α/2} is the z value with an area of α/2 in the UPPER TAIL of the standard normal.

    Why z is legitimate: x̄ is normal with mean μ and SD σ/√n, so (x̄ − μ)/σ_x̄ is STANDARD NORMAL.

    7.4 THE FOUR z VALUES — memorise them guaranteed MCQ| Confidence coefficient (1 − α) | z_{α/2} |

    |---|---| | 0.80 | 1.28 | | 0.90 | 1.64 | | 0.95 | 1.96 | | 0.99 | 2.58 |

    7.5 Basavaraju's four confidence intervals — the master worked example guaranteed MCQ

    x̄ = 57.31, σ = 5, n = 36, so σ/√n = 0.833

    Confidence z_{α/2} Margin of error Interval
    80% 1.28 1.28 × 0.833 = 1.07 56.24 to 58.38
    90% 1.64 1.64 × 0.833 = 1.37 55.94 to 58.68
    95% 1.96 1.96 × 0.833 = 1.63 55.68 to 58.94
    99% 2.58 2.58 × 0.833 = 2.15 55.16 to 59.46

    7.6 The effect of α and n on the interval guaranteed MCQ| Change | Effect on the margin of error |

    |---|---| | Higher confidence coefficient | WIDER interval — "if you want to be more confident, the band increases, because we cannot escape the randomness" | | Larger sample size n | NARROWER interval — n is under a square root in the denominator |

    THE 100% CONFIDENCE INTERVAL TRAP: guaranteed MCQ

    A confidence coefficient of 1 gives z_{α/2} = INFINITY, so the margin of error is infinite and the interval is (−∞, +∞) — "even without statistics we know the score lies between 0 and 100. If you are too greedy, the interval becomes useless."

    How to CHOOSE the confidence coefficient: guaranteed MCQ - Sometimes it is specified by a regulator — "in critical applications such as FDA approvals for the pharma industry, the FDA might specify 99% or 95%" - Otherwise, the decision maker chooses by asking: "WHAT IS THE COST OF BEING WRONG?" — an opportunity cost or risk assessment, not a literal cost. High cost of being wrong → use 99%; low cost → 80% may be acceptable - CRITICAL RULE: do NOT keep changing the confidence coefficient while comparing different decision options. Pick one and use it consistently.

    7.7 CI for the mean, σ known — worked examples guaranteed MCQ

    (a) Amit Mishra, Thaggu Ke Laddu, Swaroop Nagar, Kanpur — famous for laddus and badam kulfi

    n = 50, x̄ = ₹2,200, σ = ₹84 → σ_x̄ = 84/√50 = 11.88

    Confidence Margin of error Interval
    80% 1.28 × 11.88 = 15.22 ₹2,184.78 to ₹2,215.22
    95% 1.96 × 11.88 = 23.28 ₹2,176.72 to ₹2,223.28

    (b) Puneet Prasad, Swan Spa, Gomti Nagar, Lucknow — the SMALL-SAMPLE assumption question guaranteed MCQ n = 10, x̄ = ₹3,600, σ = ₹500 → σ_x̄ = 500/√10 = 158.11

    THE ASSUMPTION QUESTION: "The sample size is less than 30, so can we approximate the distribution of x̄ as normal? NO, we cannot. But IF WE ASSUME THE POPULATION IS NORMAL, then x̄ WILL ALREADY have a normal distribution."

    Confidence Margin of error Interval
    95% 1.96 × 158.11 = 309.90 ₹3,290.10 to ₹3,909.90
    99% 2.58 × 158.11 = 407.27 ₹3,192.73 to ₹4,007.27

    (Ashwini's practical suggestion: just take a larger sample — there is not much cost or time involved.)

    7.8 CI for the mean, σ UNKNOWN — the t distribution guaranteed MCQ

    This is "the more common case." When σ is unknown we must use the SAME sample to estimate both μ and σ.

    WHY WE CANNOT JUST SWAP s FOR σ AND KEEP USING z — the key conceptual point: guaranteed MCQ

    "When we divide by s/√n instead of σ/√n, we are no longer dividing by a constant — s is itself a RANDOM VARIABLE, because it comes from the sample. So we are dividing one random variable (x̄ − μ) by another (s/√n). And that is exactly the definition of the STUDENT'S t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom."

    CI for μ, σ unknown: x̄ ± t_{α/2, n−1} · s/√n

    Technically this is exact only when the sample is drawn from a NORMAL population.

    7.9 The practical guidelines for using the t interval guaranteed MCQ — expect a question| Population | Guidance |

    |---|---| | Normal | The t interval is EXACT for ANY sample size | | Not normal, but roughly symmetric / bell-shaped | Even n as small as 15 gives good approximations | | Not normal, general case | n of 30 or more is more than adequate | | Highly SKEWED or containing OUTLIERS (e.g. Dr Sachdev) | Increase the sample size to 50 OR MORE | | Small samples generally | Only use the t formula if you are willing to assume the population is approximately normal |

    7.10 CI with σ unknown — worked examples guaranteed MCQ

    (a) Jyoti Hegde (Head of Placement and Alumni Relations, IIT Dharwad) — salary data

    n = 103, x̄ = ₹25.92 lakh, s = ₹3.66 lakh → s/√n = 0.361; df = 102

    Confidence t_{α/2, 102} Margin of error Interval
    90% 1.66 1.66 × 0.361 = 0.60 ₹25.32 to ₹26.52 lakh
    95% 1.98 1.98 × 0.361 = 0.72 ₹25.20 to ₹26.64 lakh

    (b) Hanumantha Pai (Canara Bank, Mysore) — monthly credit card spend

    n = 55, x̄ = ₹3,852.11, s = ₹1,454.23 → s/√n = 196.09; df = 54

    Confidence t_{α/2, 54} Margin of error Interval
    80% 1.30 254.41 ₹3,597.70 to ₹4,106.52
    95% 2.00 393.13 ₹3,458.98 to ₹4,245.24

    (c) Arvind Anand (ABM FinTech, Ghaziabad) — 15 corporate bonds guaranteed MCQ n = 15, df = 14, t_{0.025, 14} = 2.145

    Variable x̄ s s/√n Margin of error 95% CI
    Years to maturity 7.567 3.146 0.813 2.145 × 0.813 = 1.743 5.824 to 9.309
    Yield 3.552 0.931 0.240 2.145 × 0.240 = 0.516 3.036 to 4.067

    (d) Sumit Kumar (Suri Automobiles, Jhokan Bagh, Jhansi) — motor insurance premium guaranteed MCQ — the "does it include the national average" question National annual average premium = ₹21,115. Sample: n = 20, x̄ = ₹19,215.7, s = ₹3,588.15; df = 19; margin of error = ₹1,679.3 95% CI: ₹17,536.4 to ₹20,895.0

    The conclusion: the national average of ₹21,115 does NOT lie in the interval → there is evidence that the average premium in Jhansi is different from (lower than) the national average.

    AND THE CRUCIAL INTERPRETATION WARNING: guaranteed MCQ

    "We are NOT claiming that 95% of the sample data, or 95% of the population data, lies in the interval. What we are claiming is that the MEAN OF THE POPULATION will lie in the interval we calculated, 95% of the time."

    A practical table note: if your df (say 34) isn't in the table, you may use the critical value for 35 or for 30 — interpolation or the nearer entry is acceptable.

    7.11 DETERMINING THE SAMPLE SIZE for the mean guaranteed MCQ

    The decision is taken BEFORE collecting the data.

    Set E = the desired margin of error. Then E = z_{α/2}·σ/√n, so:

    n = ( z_{α/2} · σ / E )²

    THE THREE WAYS TO GET A PLANNING VALUE FOR σ: guaranteed MCQ 1. An estimate from a PREVIOUS study (as Basavaraju had σ = 5 from last year) 2. A PILOT STUDY — use the sample SD from a preliminary sample 3. Judgment / best guess — e.g. take the RANGE (largest − smallest) and DIVIDE BY 4 as a crude approximation of σ

    Worked example (Basavaraju): 99% confidence (z = 2.58), σ = 5, desired E = 1 n = (2.58 × 5 / 1)² = 165.8 → 166 guaranteed MCQ Worked example (Sangita Sharma, HDFC ERGO General Insurance, Moradabad) — planning value σ = 4 minutes = 240 seconds, 95% confidence (z = 1.96) guaranteed MCQ| Desired margin of error E | Calculation | n | |---|---|---| | 75 seconds | (240 × 1.96 / 75)² | ≈ 40 | | 60 seconds (1 minute) | (240 × 1.96 / 60)² | ≈ 62 |

    7.12 CI for the PROPORTION guaranteed MCQ

    The problem: σ_p̄ = √[p(1−p)/n] contains p — the very thing we are estimating. The solution: substitute p̄ for p.

    CI for p: p̄ ± z_{α/2} · √[ p̄(1 − p̄) / n ]

    Worked example (Basavaraju): p̄ = 0.47, n = 36 √(0.47 × 0.53 / 36) = 0.08; margin of error = 1.96 × 0.08 = 0.16 95% CI: 0.47 ± 0.16 → 0.31 to 0.64 guaranteed MCQ Worked example (Hanumantha): customers spending less than ₹3,000/month — x = 16, n = 55, p̄ = 0.29 √(0.29 × 0.71 / 55) = 0.06

    Confidence z Margin of error Interval
    80% 1.28 0.08 0.21 to 0.37
    99% 2.58 0.16 0.13 to 0.45

    Tejas's valid objection: "These intervals are far too WIDE to be useful for decision-making." → which motivates sample size determination.

    7.13 DETERMINING THE SAMPLE SIZE for a proportion guaranteed MCQ

    n = z²_{α/2} · p(1 − p) / E²

    THE FOUR WAYS TO GET THE PLANNING VALUE p*: guaranteed MCQ 1. The sample proportion from a PREVIOUS study 2. A PILOT STUDY 3. Judgment / best guess 4. If none of these work, USE p* = 0.5 — the conservative choice, which maximises p(1−p) and therefore gives the LARGEST (safest) n

    Worked example (Hanumantha, 99% confidence, desired E = 0.05, p* = 0.5): n = 2.58² × 0.25 / 0.05² = 665.64 → 666 — "a lot higher than the 55 Hanumantha collected" guaranteed MCQ Worked example (Anil Sharma, SBI, Ayodhya — cashback credit card): desired E = 0.03, 98% confidence → z = 2.33 (upper tail 0.01) guaranteed MCQ| Planning value | Calculation | n | |---|---|---| | p* = 0.7 (the nationwide figure) | 2.33² × 0.7 × 0.3 / 0.03² | 1,266.7 → 1,267 | | p* = 0.5 (no planning value available) | 2.33² × 0.25 / 0.03² | 1,508.03 → 1,509 |

    Worked example (credit card ownership by age group) — Economic Times, n = 455 per group, 95% confidence (z = 1.96) guaranteed MCQ| Age group | p̄ | Margin of error | 95% CI | |---|---|---|---| | 18–24 | 0.67 | 0.04 | 0.63 to 0.71 | | 25–34 | 0.83 | 0.03 | 0.80 to 0.86 | | 35–49 | 0.76 | 0.04 | 0.72 to 0.80 | | 50+ | 0.78 | 0.04 | 0.74 to 0.82 |

    The clever sample-size step: to guarantee E ≤ 0.03 for ALL FOUR groups with one calculation, use the p̄ CLOSEST TO 0.5 — here 0.67 (the 18–24 group), because it maximises p(1−p) among them. n = 1.96² × 0.67 × 0.33 / 0.03² = 943.75 → 944 guaranteed MCQ Worked example (Sumit Kumar, uninsured vehicles, Dainik Jagran): 46 out of 200 → p̄ = 0.23; √(0.23 × 0.77/200) = 0.03; 90% confidence (z = 1.64) → margin of error 0.05 90% CI: 0.18 to 0.28 guaranteed MCQ

    7.14 CI for the VARIANCE guaranteed MCQ

    No "± margin of error" form — the chi-square is asymmetric, so we write the bounds directly.

    The derivation: since χ²_{1−α/2} ≤ (n−1)s²/σ² ≤ χ²_{α/2}, take reciprocals (flipping the inequalities) and multiply through by (n−1)s²:

    (n−1)s² / χ²_{α/2, n−1} ≤ σ² ≤ (n−1)s² / χ²_{1−α/2, n−1}

    Worked example (Basavaraju): n = 36, s² = 40.7, df = 35 guaranteed MCQ| Confidence | χ² upper (α/2) | χ² lower (1−α/2) | σ² interval | σ interval | |---|---|---|---|---| | 80% | 46.06 (tail 0.1) | 24.80 (tail 0.9) | 30.95 to 57.49 | 5.56 to 7.58 | | 90% | 49.80 (tail 0.05) | 22.47 (tail 0.95) | 28.62 to 63.46 | 5.35 to 7.97 | | 95% | 53.20 (tail 0.025) | 20.57 (tail 0.975) | 26.79 to 69.30 | 5.18 to 8.33 |

    Worked example (Jyoti Hegde): n = 103, s = 3.66, s² = 13.39, df = 102 guaranteed MCQ χ² values: 131.84 (tail 0.025) and 75.95 (tail 0.975) 95% CI: σ² between 10.36 and 17.98 → σ between 3.22 and 4.24

    Worked example (Sunita Pandey, GE Power India, Noida) — 8 quarterly returns guaranteed MCQ| Item | Value | |---|---| | n | 8, df = 7 | | Sample mean x̄ | 3.2% (some quarters positive, some negative) | | Sum of squared deviations | 7,873.6 | | Sample variance s² = 7,873.6 / 7 | 253.37 | | Sample SD s | 15.92 | | χ² (7 df): tail 0.025 / tail 0.975 | 16.01 / 1.69 | | 95% CI for σ² | 110.76 to 1,049.54 | | 95% CI for σ | 10.52 to 32.40 |

    Worked example (Abdul Mohammad, Lucknow) — 12 stock price changes on a day the Dow rose 149.82 guaranteed MCQ| Item | Value | |---|---| | n | 12, df = 11 | | x̄ | 0.78 | | Sum of squared deviations | 5.223 | | s² = 5.223 / 11 | 0.4748 | | s | 0.6891 | | χ² (11 df): tail 0.025 / tail 0.975 | 21.92 / 3.82 | | 95% CI for σ² | 0.24 to 1.37 | | 95% CI for σ | 0.49 to 1.17 |

    1. Hypothesis testing
    31

    8.1 The two outcomes — and the wording that matters guaranteed MCQ

    The two outcomes are: "REJECT the null hypothesis" or "DO NOT REJECT the null hypothesis." We NEVER say "ACCEPT the null hypothesis."

    Outcome When Meaning
    REJECT H₀ The sample provides definitive evidence, beyond reasonable doubt, that H₀ is not true We can now claim the alternate
    DO NOT REJECT H₀ The sample casts reasonable doubt and is not conclusive "The data is INCONCLUSIVE and it is too risky to make a decision. STATUS QUO is usually the decision."

    8.2 THE LEGAL ANALOGY guaranteed MCQ — nearly certain to be tested

    H₀ = the person is INNOCENT. Hₐ = the person is NOT innocent. "In the legal setting the null hypothesis is ALWAYS that the person is innocent — that is why we say a person is innocent until proven guilty."

    The store — the party trying to prove something — files the case and puts its CLAIM in the ALTERNATE hypothesis. If the evidence is convincing beyond reasonable doubt, we reject H₀. If the evidence is weak (uncertain location, inconclusive footage, no matching fingerprints), we do not reject H₀.

    THE CRUCIAL POINT: "We did NOT PROVE INNOCENCE. We were just UNABLE TO PROVE GUILT. In the legal setting, we NEVER prove innocence."

    8.3 The TWO QUESTIONS for setting up the hypotheses guaranteed MCQ

    1. WHO is trying to make a claim about the population parameter? 2. WHAT specifically are they trying to claim?

    Whatever they are trying to CLAIM becomes the ALTERNATE hypothesis Hₐ. The OPPOSITE becomes H₀. BY CONVENTION, THE EQUALITY SIGN IS ALWAYS IN THE NULL HYPOTHESIS.

    8.4 The three forms of test guaranteed MCQ| Form | Hₐ | H₀ | p-value |

    |---|---|---|---| | LOWER TAIL | μ < A | μ ≥ A | P(test statistic ≤ observed value) | | UPPER TAIL | μ > A | μ ≤ A | P(test statistic ≥ observed value) | | TWO TAIL | μ ≠ A | μ = A | 2 × the relevant one-tail probability (by symmetry) |

    8.5 TYPE I and TYPE II ERRORS guaranteed MCQ| | H₀ is TRUE | Hₐ is TRUE |

    |---|---|---| | REJECT H₀ | TYPE I ERROR | Correct decision | | DO NOT REJECT H₀ | Correct decision | TYPE II ERROR |

    Definitions in words: guaranteed MCQ - TYPE I: wrongly REJECTING the null hypothesis when it IS true - TYPE II: NOT rejecting the null hypothesis when the ALTERNATIVE is true

    THE LEVEL OF SIGNIFICANCE α: guaranteed MCQ

    α = the probability of making a TYPE I ERROR when the null hypothesis is true AT EQUALITY. The most common choices are 0.05 and 0.1. The person conducting the test chooses α, and by doing so CONTROLS the probability of a Type I error. High cost of a Type I error → small α.

    Tests that control ONLY for Type I error are called SIGNIFICANCE TESTS. "Controlling the Type I error does not necessarily control the probability of a Type II error, so a BALANCE must be struck." guaranteed MCQ In Geeta Kumari's context (H₀: μ ≤ 48 hrs): - Type I error = claiming response time HAS exceeded 48 hours when in fact it is 48 hours or less - Type II error = concluding response time is ≤ 48 hours when in fact it is more

    8.6 THE FIVE STEPS OF A HYPOTHESIS TEST guaranteed MCQ| Step | Action |

    |---|---| | 1 | Identify H₀ and Hₐ | | 2 | Decide the significance level α — the maximum allowable Type I error | | 3 | ASSUME H₀ IS TRUE AT EQUALITY and, from the sample data, compute the TEST STATISTIC | | 4 | Either the p-VALUE approach or the CRITICAL VALUE approach (both give the same decision) | | 5 | State the MANAGERIAL IMPLICATION |

    THE DECISION RULE: REJECT H₀ if p-value ≤ α. "We reject even if the p-value is EXACTLY equal to α." guaranteed MCQ

    8.7 The three set-up examples guaranteed MCQ — the framing of each| Case | Who claims | H₀ | Hₐ | Type |

    |---|---|---|---|---| | Jalan Supermarket lentils (Santosh Mishra's complaint → Consumer Affairs Department, CAD) | The CAD, trying to show deliberate underfilling of 500 g packets | μ ≥ 500 g | μ < 500 g | LOWER TAIL | | Samsung Service Centre, Bypass Road, Bareilly (Geeta Kumari) | Geeta, checking whether the mean response time has risen above the promised 48 hours | μ ≤ 48 hrs | μ > 48 hrs | UPPER TAIL | | Petrol stations, Agra–Mathura NH44 (Ibrahim Khan) | Ibrahim, checking his pumps dispense exactly 30 litres | μ = 30 L | μ ≠ 30 L | TWO TAIL |

    Why Ibrahim's is TWO-tailed: "He should be worried about dispensing MORE and dispensing LESS. If the equipment dispenses more, he is giving petrol away for free. If it dispenses less, he could be accused of deliberately underfilling and cheating his customers." guaranteed MCQ

    8.8 HYPOTHESIS TEST FOR THE MEAN — the worked examples guaranteed MCQ

    The test statistic (σ unknown): t = (x̄ − μ₀) / (s/√n), with n − 1 degrees of freedom. (If σ IS known, the test statistic is a standard normal Z; everything else is identical.)

    (a) Jalan lentils — LOWER TAIL, α = 0.04

    Item Value
    n 50
    x̄ 497 g
    s 7 g
    s/√n 1.13
    Test statistic (497 − 500)/1.13 = −2.65, a t with 49 df
    p-value = P(t₄₉ ≤ −2.65) 0.005
    Decision 0.005 < 0.04 → REJECT H₀
    Conclusion Enough evidence to claim the supermarket is deliberately underfilling

    (b) Samsung service centre — UPPER TAIL, α = 0.03 — TWO SCENARIOS, one rejecting and one not guaranteed MCQ| | Scenario 1 | Scenario 2 | |---|---|---| | n | 40 | 40 | | x̄ | 52 hrs | 50 hrs | | s | 10 | 10 | | s/√n | 1.58 | 1.58 | | Test statistic (t₃₉) | (52 − 48)/1.58 = 2.53 | (50 − 48)/1.58 = 1.26 | | p-value | 0.008 | 0.107 | | Decision | 0.008 < 0.03 → REJECT H₀ | 0.107 > 0.03 → DO NOT REJECT H₀ |

    (c) Ibrahim's petrol pumps — TWO TAIL, α = 0.05

    Item Value
    n 32
    x̄ 30.3 L
    s 0.5 L
    s/√n 0.09
    Test statistic (t₃₁) (30.3 − 30)/0.09 = 3.39
    p-value 2 × P(t₃₁ > 3.39) ≈ 0.00
    Decision REJECT H₀ → the equipment is NOT dispensing 30 litres; recalibrate

    8.9 HYPOTHESIS TEST FOR THE PROPORTION guaranteed MCQ

    Test statistic: z = (p̄ − p₀) / √[ p₀(1 − p₀)/n ] — a STANDARD NORMAL

    Note the crucial difference from the confidence interval: in the TEST we use p₀ (the hypothesised value) in the standard error, NOT p̄ — because we assume H₀ is true at equality. guaranteed MCQ Valid as long as np₀ ≥ 5 and n(1 − p₀) ≥ 5.

    (a) Swiggy coupons (Anil Verma, Prayagraj) — UPPER TAIL, α = 0.05 guaranteed MCQ| Item | Value | |---|---| | Success criterion | more than 10% use the coupons | | H₀ / Hₐ | p ≤ 0.10 / p > 0.10 | | Sample | 12 out of 80 → p̄ = 0.15 | | σ_p̄ | √(0.1 × 0.9/80) = 0.03 | | Test statistic | (0.15 − 0.10)/0.03 = 1.49 | | p-value | P(Z > 1.49) = 0.068 | | Decision | 0.068 > 0.05 → DO NOT REJECT H₀ |

    THE TEACHING POINT: "Even though the sample shows 15% usage, why does this not carry forward to the population? Because the standard error of 0.03 is relatively high. We have to be careful making claims and decisions based on limited data." guaranteed MCQ (b) Sleeper trains (Pushpa Yadav, Jhansi) — LOWER TAIL, α = 0.03 — with a deliberate definitional trap guaranteed MCQ Claim in a study: 52% of passengers feel sleeper arrangements are INADEQUATE. She samples 510 and finds 280 said arrangements ARE ADEQUATE.

    THE TRAP: Tejas computes p̄ = 280/510 = 0.55. WRONG. "What is 'success' here based on our hypothesis? The number who feel arrangements are INADEQUATE. And 280 is the number who feel they ARE adequate." Correct: p̄ = (510 − 280)/510 = 0.45 guaranteed MCQ — watch the statements carefully| Item | Value | |---|---| | H₀ / Hₐ | p ≥ 0.50 / p < 0.50 | | σ_p̄ | √(0.5 × 0.5/510) = 0.022 | | Test statistic | (0.45 − 0.50)/0.022 = −2.21 | | p-value | P(Z < −2.21) = 0.013 | | Decision | 0.013 < 0.03 → REJECT H₀ |

    (c) Diwali hotel bookings (Dinesh Gupta / Sangeetha, Noida) — TWO TAIL, α = 0.05 guaranteed MCQ Dinesh claims 90% of hotels are fully booked. Sangeetha calls 70 hotels and finds 12 have vacancies → 58 booked → p̄ = 58/70 = 0.83

    Item Value
    H₀ / Hₐ p = 0.90 / p ≠ 0.90
    σ_p̄ √(0.9 × 0.1/70) = 0.036
    Test statistic (0.83 − 0.90)/0.036 = −1.99
    p-value 2 × P(Z < −1.99) = 0.046
    Decision 0.046 < 0.05 → REJECT H₀ — enough evidence to refute the 90% claim

    8.10 HYPOTHESIS TEST FOR THE VARIANCE guaranteed MCQ

    Test statistic: χ² = (n − 1)s² / σ₀² — a CHI-SQUARE with n − 1 degrees of freedom

    Valid only when sampling from a NORMAL population.

    (a) Bus arrival times (Rakesh Adhikari, Abu Lane market, Meerut) — α = 0.05 guaranteed MCQ He wants to guarantee a variance of 4 minutes or less.

    Item Value
    H₀ / Hₐ σ² ≥ 4 / σ² < 4 (the transcript labels this an "upper tail" test; the p-value is computed as an UPPER tail probability)
    n / s² 24 / 4.9; df = 23
    Test statistic 23 × 4.9 / 4 = 28.18
    p-value P(χ²₂₃ > 28.18) = 0.209
    Decision 0.209 > 0.05 → DO NOT REJECT H₀

    (b) Driving-licence exam scores (Ram Singh, Motor Vehicles Dept, Gorakhpur) — TWO TAIL, α = 0.05 guaranteed MCQ Historical variance 100; new exam introduced.

    Item Value
    H₀ / Hₐ σ² = 100 / σ² ≠ 100
    n / s² 30 / 162; df = 29
    Test statistic 29 × 162 / 100 = 46.98
    p-value 2 × P(χ²₂₉ > 46.98) = 0.037
    Decision 0.037 < 0.05 → REJECT H₀ — the new exam has a different variance

    8.11 The mixed "challenge" problems — done from TABLES, not templates guaranteed MCQ

    (a) EMI in Firozabad vs Gorakhpur (Ramesh Yadav, Zila Sahakari Bank) — LOWER TAIL, α = 0.05

    India Today: Gorakhpur EMI = ₹16,000/month. Sample from Firozabad: n = 40, x̄ = ₹15,837, s = ₹388

    Item Value
    Point estimate of the DIFFERENCE 15,837 − 16,000 = −163

    s/√n 388/√40 = 61.35
    Test statistic (t₃₉) (15,837 − 16,000)/61.35 = −2.66
    Table reasoning The t table has 35 df (1.69) and 40 df (1.684) but not 39. Our −2.66 is far beyond both, so the p-value is definitely < 0.05
    Decision REJECT H₀

    (d) SSV Car Bazaar used cars (Mr Dev) — TWO TAIL mean test, α = 0.05 guaranteed MCQ National average used-car price ₹3,55,000. Sample: n = 50, x̄ = ₹3,65,000, s = ₹28,500

    H₀ / Hₐ μ = 3,55,000 / μ ≠ 3,55,000

    Actual p-value (Excel) 0.017

    (e) NCR Atleos ATM error variance (Rajendra Prakash, Gurugram) — UPPER TAIL variance test, α = 0.05 guaranteed MCQ NCR Atleos is "a global leader in self-service financial access solutions" operating one of the largest independent global ATM networks. Specified variance in the error count of currency notes: 4 in 10,000 = 0.0004.

    Item Value

    Test statistic 29 × 5/4 = 36.25

    (f) AIBEA senior membership (a proportion test) — background fact: guaranteed MCQ

    The All India Bank Employees' Association (AIBEA) is the OLDEST and LARGEST national trade union of bank employees in India, FOUNDED IN 1946 IN CALCUTTA. A labour ministry report 5 years ago: 12% of bank union employees have 15 or more years of membership, granting senior membership status with special voting rights. A new sample of 400 finds 55 with senior status.

    1. Covariance and correlation
    15

    9.1 SAMPLE COVARIANCE guaranteed MCQ

    s_xy = Σ (xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / (n − 1)

    The divisor is n − 1 for the SAME degrees-of-freedom reason as the sample variance.

    THE QUADRANT INTERPRETATION — a certain MCQ: guaranteed MCQ Draw a vertical line at x̄ and a horizontal line at ȳ, creating four quadrants:

    Quadrant Condition Sign of (xᵢ−x̄)(yᵢ−ȳ)
    1 xᵢ > x̄ and yᵢ > ȳ POSITIVE
    2 xᵢ < x̄ and yᵢ > ȳ NEGATIVE
    3 xᵢ < x̄ and yᵢ < ȳ POSITIVE
    4 xᵢ > x̄ and yᵢ < ȳ NEGATIVE
    • s_xy POSITIVE → the influential points are in quadrants 1 and 3 → positive linear association
    • s_xy NEGATIVE → the influential points are in quadrants 2 and 4 → negative linear association
    • Points evenly spread across all four → s_xy ≈ 0 → little linear association

    THE SPECIAL CASE: Cov(X, X) = Var(X). "In that sense, COVARIANCE IS A GENERALISATION of the notion of VARIANCE." guaranteed MCQ THE PROBLEM WITH COVARIANCE: guaranteed MCQ

    Its value DEPENDS ON THE UNITS OF MEASUREMENT. The strength of the relationship between income and credit card spend is the same whether income is measured in rupees or in lakhs — but measuring in rupees gives much larger deviations and therefore a much larger covariance. The relationship has not changed; only the number has.

    9.2 CORRELATION guaranteed MCQ

    The measure that is NOT affected by units: the PEARSON PRODUCT MOMENT CORRELATION COEFFICIENT (a.k.a. the simple sample correlation coefficient).

    r_xy = s_xy / (s_x · s_y)

    Interpretation:

    Value of r Meaning
    +1 All points fall on a POSITIVELY sloped straight line — perfect positive LINEAR relationship
    −1 All points fall on a NEGATIVELY sloped straight line — perfect negative LINEAR relationship
    Between 0 and 1 Positive but imperfect
    Between 0 and −1 Negative but imperfect
    0 No LINEAR relationship

    9.3 Hanumantha Pai's credit card data — the running example guaranteed MCQ

    n = 55 customers; three variables: monthly amount charged (₹), annual income (lakhs), household size

    Statistic Value
    Mean monthly charge ₹3,852 (median ₹3,864)
    SD of monthly charge ₹1,454
    SD of annual household income 13.74 lakh
    SD of household size 1.76
    Cov(monthly spend, household INCOME) 16,109
    Cov(monthly spend, household SIZE) 1,610
    r(monthly spend, household INCOME) 16,109 / (13.74 × 1454) = 0.81 (Excel: 0.806)
    r(monthly spend, household SIZE) 1,610 / (1.76 × 1454) = 0.63 (Excel: 0.629)

    Conclusion: a STRONG positive linear relationship with INCOME; a positive but WEAKER relationship with household SIZE.

    9.4 THE THREE WARNINGS ABOUT CORRELATION guaranteed MCQ — all three

    WARNING 1 — CORRELATION IS NOT CAUSATION.

    "A high correlation between two variables does NOT necessarily mean that a change in one variable will CAUSE a change in the other."

    WARNING 2 — CORRELATION MEASURES ONLY LINEAR ASSOCIATION.

    The utility spend vs outside temperature example: spending is high when temperatures are very high OR very low, and low when moderate. The linear correlation would be near zero, yet the scatter diagram shows a STRONG NON-LINEAR relationship.

    The six-point proof: let x = 3, 2, 1, −1, −2, −3 and y = 1/x² = 1/9, 1/4, 1, 1, 1/4, 1/9. Excel gives covariance = 0 AND correlation = 0 — "suggesting x and y have no association. But clearly there IS an association: y = 1/x². It only implies there is no LINEAR association." guaranteed MCQ WARNING 3 — SPURIOUS CORRELATION. EXPLAINABLE correlation can be justified by logical reasoning. SPURIOUS correlation cannot. Spurious correlation is often caused by a THIRD, HIDDEN or LATENT VARIABLE that influences both.

    THE FOUR SPURIOUS-CORRELATION EXAMPLES — memorise them: guaranteed MCQ| Example | Explanation | |---|---| | Ice cream sales vs CRIME RATE (positively correlated) | The hidden variable is TEMPERATURE. Ice cream sales rise in summer; crime rises in summer because people go on holiday and leave homes empty as vulnerable targets | | Number of DOCTORS vs number of DEATHS in villages | Doctors do not cause deaths. Poor public health in villages both causes more deaths AND creates a need for more doctors | | Divorce rate in the state of MAINE vs per capita MARGARINE consumption | Data 1999–2009, correlation coefficient = 0.99. NO hidden variable has ever been found — it is purely spurious guaranteed MCQ| | The "SKIRT LENGTH THEORY" | Proposed by the economist GEORGE TAYLOR in 1926: skirts get SHORTER when the economy does WELL and LONGER when it does POORLY — his reasoning being that in a downturn women could no longer afford stockings guaranteed MCQ|

    9.5 Excel functions and the non-quantitative case guaranteed MCQ| Function | Purpose |

    |---|---| | COVARIANCE.S(array1, array2) | Sample covariance | | CORREL(array1, array2) | Correlation |

    When one or more variables is NOT quantitative (nominal or ordinal), use the SPEARMAN RANK CORRELATION COEFFICIENT or similar. Pearson assesses only the LINEAR relationship between two QUANTITATIVE variables. guaranteed MCQ

    9.6 Sample vs population correlation

    Everything computed is a SAMPLE covariance and SAMPLE correlation — point estimates of what exists in the population. To ask "what is the minimum sample correlation before we can claim there is correlation in the POPULATION?" requires a HYPOTHESIS TEST that uses the t DISTRIBUTION. guaranteed MCQ

    9.7 The bridge to regression

    The module closes by previewing SIMPLE LINEAR REGRESSION: building the model, its assumptions, the LEAST SQUARES method to estimate the parameters, interpreting the parameters under different functional forms, and model diagnostics — with confidence intervals and hypothesis tests coming together. guaranteed MCQ

    t mean / variance 0 / k/(k−2) for k > 2

    Four sampling steps Target population → sampling FRAME → sample SIZE → sampling METHOD
    Sampling frame The source/method used to IDENTIFY the elements of the target population

    Item Answer
    The four properties UNBIASED · EFFICIENT · CONSISTENT · SUFFICIENT
    Unbiased E(θ̄) = θ
    Efficient Smaller STANDARD ERROR wins. The sample MEAN is MORE efficient than the sample MEDIAN
    Consistent Gets closer to θ as n grows
    Sufficient Uses ALL n data points. The MEDIAN is NOT sufficient
    Sampling error Due to the RANDOM nature of the sample — UNAVOIDABLE
    The three non-sampling errors COVERAGE · NON-RESPONSE · MEASUREMENT
    Coverage error Research objective and sampled population are NOT ALIGNED
    Non-response error Segments systematically under/over-represented
    Measurement error Ambiguous, difficult or distorting instrument — non-anonymous forms, staff looking over shoulders, long/confusing surveys
    Four ways to reduce them Define the target population · design and TRAIN · PILOT test · choose the right method

    G. Hypothesis testing

    Item Answer
    The two outcomes REJECT H₀ or DO NOT REJECT H₀ — NEVER "accept"
    Do-not-reject means Data is inconclusive; too risky to decide; STATUS QUO
    The legal analogy H₀ = innocent. We never PROVE innocence — we only fail to prove guilt
    The two set-up questions WHO is claiming? WHAT are they claiming? — the CLAIM is the ALTERNATE
    The equality sign ALWAYS in the NULL hypothesis
    Lower tail Hₐ: μ < A; p-value = P(stat ≤ observed)
    Upper tail Hₐ: μ > A; p-value = P(stat ≥ observed)
    Two tail Hₐ: μ ≠ A; p-value = 2 × the one-tail probability
    TYPE I error REJECTING H₀ when it is TRUE
    TYPE II error NOT rejecting H₀ when the ALTERNATIVE is true
    α (level of significance) P(Type I error) when H₀ is true at EQUALITY; commonly 0.05 or 0.1; chosen by the tester
    Significance tests Tests that control ONLY the Type I error
    The five steps State H₀/Hₐ → choose α → assume H₀ true at equality and compute the test statistic → p-value or critical value → managerial implication
    Decision rule REJECT if p-value ≤ α (including exactly equal)
    Test statistic for μ (σ unknown) t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n), n−1 df
    Test statistic for μ (σ known) z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n)
    Test statistic for p z = (p̄ − p₀)/√[p₀(1−p₀)/n] — uses p₀, NOT p̄
    Test statistic for σ² χ² = (n−1)s²/σ₀², n−1 df — normal population only

    Blockchain & AI in FinTech — Complete Exam Reference

    Course instructor: Rangaraj Sriramulu

    How to use this file. The course has two halves. Part A (§1–§11) is BLOCKCHAIN: history → how it works → types → consensus → mining → crypto → smart contracts → DeFi → tokenisation → cross-border payments → CBDC → trade finance → digital identity/KYC. Part B (§12–§27) is AI: ML fundamentals → regression → classification → trees and ensembles → the ML lifecycle → unsupervised learning → deep learning → NLP and transformers → prompting → RAG → agentic AI → responsible AI. Anything marked ← guaranteed MCQ is a date, number, name or definitional distinction. The Quick-fire revision tables at the end cover both halves.

    The opening thesis of the course:

    "AI gives us the power to THINK at scale. Blockchain gives us TRUST without intermediaries. AI needs reliable data — that is where blockchain comes in. When AI runs on blockchain-verified data, you get INTELLIGENCE YOU CAN TRUST. Blockchain is the secured RECORD BOOK; AI is the intelligent ANALYST reading that record book."
