    STOPPING CRITERIA: maximum tree DEPTH · minimum number of SAMPLES in a node · NO FURTHER INFORMATION GAIN · the node is already PURE. MERGING CRITERIA / PRUNING: go back and combine branches that don't add relative value, simplifying the tree and improving generalisation.

    26.3 THE THREE SPLITTING CRITERIA guaranteed MCQ — with the worked numbers| Criterion | Used for | What it measures |

    |---|---|---| | GINI IMPURITY | CLASSIFICATION | "How often you would MISCLASSIFY a sample if you randomly labelled it based on the class distribution in the node" | | ENTROPY | CLASSIFICATION | From INFORMATION THEORY — measures DISORDER or UNCERTAINTY. The reduction is called INFORMATION GAIN | | VARIANCE | REGRESSION | How SPREAD OUT the values are in a node |

    THE WORKED VALUES — expect these exact numbers: guaranteed MCQ| Class distribution | GINI | ENTROPY | |---|---|---| | 80% not fraud / 20% fraud | 0.32 | ≈ 0.72 | | 50% / 50% | 0.5 | 1.0 |

    "LOWER gini means a PURER node. LOWER entropy means a PURER node. The tree looks for the split producing child nodes with the LOWEST COMBINED IMPURITY."

    THE VARIANCE EXAMPLE (predicting credit limits): guaranteed MCQ - Node A: $10,000, $12,000, $11,000 → mean $11,000, LOW variance — "the predictions are close to each other" - Node B: $5,000, $18,000, $25,000 → HIGH variance - The goal: split into regions where the values are TIGHTLY CLUSTERED

    THE SPLIT-EVALUATION WORKED EXAMPLE (6 transactions, split at $400): guaranteed MCQ

    Left branch (≤ $400): IDs 1, 2, 3 → 2 "no" and 1 "yes". Right branch (> $400): IDs 4, 5, 6 → 1 "no" and 2 "yes". GINI for each branch = 0.444; WEIGHTED GINI = 0.444 (equal samples on each side) ENTROPY for each branch = 0.918; WEIGHTED ENTROPY = 0.918 Conclusion: "This split gives branches that are MODERATELY MIXED — NEITHER BRANCH IS PURE. This isn't the best possible split, but it's a starting point. Try $500 or $600 and recalculate."

    26.4 DECISION TREES ARE GREEDY ALGORITHMS guaranteed MCQ

    "A GREEDY ALGORITHM makes the BEST IMMEDIATE CHOICE at each step, hoping these LOCAL choices lead to a good OVERALL solution. It DOESN'T LOOK AHEAD — it just asks, WHAT'S THE BEST THING I CAN DO RIGHT NOW?" "It's like playing a game and always taking the biggest reward in front of you without thinking about whether that move helps you WIN THE GAME in the long run."

    The tree does NOT try all possible future trees, does NOT consider how later splits interact, and does NOT explore the global best structure. IT NEVER BACKTRACKS. Consequences: it is FAST and it WORKS — but it can lead to OVERFITTING and SUBOPTIMAL TREES. Remedies: PRUNING, or better still ENSEMBLE METHODS like random forests and gradient boosting.

    26.5 THE FOUR WAYS TO PREVENT TREE OVERFITTING guaranteed MCQ| # | Technique | Detail |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | MAX DEPTH | Limit how many levels the tree can grow — "after 4 or 5 questions, stop, even if more splits are possible" | | 2 | MINIMUM SAMPLES PER LEAF / PER SPLIT | "Tiny groups lead to overly specific rules. If you're making decisions based on 1 or 2 customers, you're probably overfitting" | | 3 | MAX LEAF NODES | Cap the number of final outcomes to stop the tree creating too many MICRO-RULES | | 4 | PRUNING | PRE-PRUNING = EARLY STOPPING (max depth, min samples). POST-PRUNING = grow the full tree, then CUT BACK branches that don't improve validation accuracy guaranteed MCQ|

    THE OVERFITTING ILLUSTRATION: guaranteed MCQ

    BAD (overfitting): "If income = $5,010 AND credit score = 683 → approve. If income = $4,990 AND credit score = 684 → reject." GOOD (generalising): "If income > $5,000 AND credit score > 650 → approve."

    The overfitting story: "The tree sees one strange case — a high-value transaction at 3 a.m. from a new customer in a foreign country that happens to be NON-fraud. So it creates A VERY SPECIFIC BRANCH JUST FOR THAT CASE."

    26.6 RANDOM FOREST guaranteed MCQ

    Why: a single tree is PRONE TO OVERFITTING and UNSTABLE — "small changes in the data can lead to a completely different tree."

    "A random forest is NOT ONE TREE — it's a COLLECTION of trees. Each tree is built slightly differently, and at the end THEY ALL VOTE to make the final prediction. It's like asking NOT ONE EXPERT, but a WHOLE PANEL of experts, each trained on slightly different experiences, and then going with the MAJORITY OPINION."

    THE WISDOM OF THE CROWD — the jelly-bean story: guaranteed MCQ

    "At a country fair there's a jar full of jelly beans and everyone guesses how many are inside. If you take the AVERAGE of all the guesses, it's usually VERY CLOSE to the actual number — often BETTER than any single person's guess. Even though each individual may be wrong — some too high, others too low — THEIR ERRORS TEND TO CANCEL OUT."

    THE FOUR STEPS: guaranteed MCQ| Step | Action | |---|---| | 1. BOOTSTRAPPING the data | For each tree, randomly sample the data WITH REPLACEMENT — so each tree sees a slightly different version of the training data | | 2. RANDOM FEATURE SELECTION | At EACH SPLIT, each tree considers only a RANDOM SUBSET of features — introducing more variety among trees | | 3. Build each tree GREEDILY | Trained like a regular decision tree on its own subset of data and features | | 4. PREDICT BY VOTING | CLASSIFICATION: each tree gives a class label and the forest goes with the MAJORITY VOTE. REGRESSION: it takes the AVERAGE of all tree predictions |

    THE TECHNIQUE'S NAME: BAGGING — short for BOOTSTRAP AGGREGATING. guaranteed MCQ The fraud example: "One tree might focus on TRANSACTION AMOUNT, another on TIME OF DAY, a third on the USER'S DEVICE. When a new transaction comes in, the forest asks: OK TEAM, WHO THINKS THIS IS FRAUD?"

    Advantages Limitations
    Handles classification AND regression · great with large data sets and many features · LESS OVERFITTING than individual trees · handles missing values and categorical data · FEATURE IMPORTANCE is easy to extract SLOWER to predict (aggregates many trees) · LESS INTERPRETABLE than a single tree · may not perform as well when features are HIGHLY CORRELATED

    26.7 FEATURE IMPORTANCE guaranteed MCQ

    How it is calculated — the three steps: guaranteed MCQ 1. Every time a tree splits on a feature, calculate how much GINI IMPURITY / ENTROPY / VARIANCE IS REDUCED 2. Keep a RUNNING TOTAL of this impurity reduction for each feature ACROSS ALL THE TREES 3. The feature importance score is the total impurity reduction caused by that feature, NORMALISED SO THE SCORES ADD UP TO 1

    THE WORKED CREDIT-DEFAULT EXAMPLE — memorise the five scores: guaranteed MCQ| Feature | Importance | |---|---| | Credit score | 0.45 — "the most influential factor, used heavily in splits across the forest" | | Debt-to-income ratio | 0.25 | | Number of late payments | 0.15 | | Employment status | 0.10 | | Marital status | 0.05 — "barely mattered; may even be something you can remove in future models" |

    Three notes on feature importance: guaranteed MCQ - It is RELATIVE, not absolute - It is AGGREGATED across hundreds of trees, so it is robust - It helps with INTERPRETABILITY, FEATURE SELECTION and MODEL DEBUGGING

    Two caveats: "If features are HIGHLY CORRELATED, random forest may split on one and IGNORE THE OTHERS, giving MISLEADING SCORES." And "it does NOT capture CAUSALITY — just PREDICTIVE POWER. Always pair it with DOMAIN EXPERTISE." guaranteed MCQ

    26.8 GRADIENT BOOSTING guaranteed MCQ

    THE CONTRAST WITH RANDOM FOREST: guaranteed MCQ

    "Random forests build trees IN PARALLEL, each INDEPENDENTLY. Gradient boosting builds trees ONE AT A TIME, IN SEQUENCE, and EACH TREE TRIES TO FIX THE ERRORS MADE BY THE PREVIOUS TREES." "At its heart, gradient boosting is an ADDITIVE MODEL."

    THE WEIGHT-GUESSING ANALOGY: guaranteed MCQ

    "You're trying to guess someone's weight. Your first guess is just THE AVERAGE, say 70 kg. Someone tells you you're OFF BY 10 KG — you adjust. Then you're STILL OFF BY 2 KG — you adjust again. That's what gradient boosting does: it keeps ADJUSTING, CUTTING THE ERRORS STEP BY STEP."

    THE FOUR STEPS: guaranteed MCQ| Step | Action | |---|---| | 1 | INITIAL PREDICTION — usually just the MEAN of the target variable (for regression) | | 2 | Compute the RESIDUALS (the errors) — "how far was your prediction?" | | 3 | Train a WEAK LEARNER (a SHALLOW TREE) to predict THE RESIDUALS — NOT the actual output y, but THE ERRORS MADE BY THE PREVIOUS MODEL | | 4 | UPDATE the model, scaled by η (ETA) — the LEARNING RATE, a small number like 0.1 or 0.01 that controls HOW MUCH WE TRUST THE NEW TREE. Repeat |

    WHY IT IS CALLED "GRADIENT" BOOSTING: guaranteed MCQ

    "The model minimises a LOSS FUNCTION (log loss or squared error), and THE RESIDUALS ARE DERIVED BY COMPUTING THE GRADIENT OF THE LOSS FUNCTION with respect to the current predictions. At each step you MOVE IN THE DIRECTION OF STEEPEST DESCENT."

    The credit-scoring illustration: "The first model just guesses the average risk. The next says 'wait, you are UNDERESTIMATING the risk for LOW-INCOME applicants.' Another says 'and you are OVERESTIMATING risk for people with LONG CREDIT HISTORIES.'"

    THE THREE HYPERPARAMETERS: guaranteed MCQ| Hyperparameter | Guidance | |---|---| | LEARNING RATE | A SMALLER learning rate = SLOWER learning, but OFTEN BETTER ACCURACY if you allow more trees | | NUMBER OF TREES | More is better up to a point — too many leads to OVERFITTING | | TREE DEPTH | Often SHALLOW — a depth of 3 to 6. "Each one is WEAK on its own, but together they form a STRONG model" guaranteed MCQ|

    Why it is powerful Challenges
    Learns SEQUENTIALLY from mistakes · handles both regression and classification · often MORE ACCURATE than random forest with careful tuning SLOWER to train because it is SEQUENTIAL · sensitive to hyperparameters · can overfit if not properly regularised

    THE FIVE GRADIENT-BOOSTING FAMILY MEMBERS NAMED: AdaBoost · Stochastic Gradient Boosting · XGBoost · LightGBM · CatBoost. guaranteed MCQ On XGBoost specifically: "XGBoost is NOT A NEW ALGORITHM — it is an ENHANCED IMPLEMENTATION of gradient boosting, but with smart optimisations it is FASTER, MORE ACCURATE and often performs better RIGHT OUT OF THE BOX." guaranteed MCQ

    26.9 ADABOOST guaranteed MCQ

    "ADABOOST = ADAPTIVE BOOSTING — one of the EARLIEST and most elegant boosting algorithms. It takes many WEAK LEARNERS (shallow decision trees) and combines them cleverly. HOW cleverly? By giving MORE FOCUS TO THE MISTAKES MADE EARLIER." "Each new model is trained NOT on the full data equally, but on a RE-WEIGHTED version of the data, where MORE WEIGHT IS GIVEN TO SAMPLES THAT WERE MISCLASSIFIED EARLIER."

    Labels in AdaBoost are −1 or +1. guaranteed MCQ THE FIVE STEPS: guaranteed MCQ| Step | Action | |---|---| | 1. INITIALISE THE WEIGHTS | Assign EQUAL weights to all training examples: wᵢ = 1/m, where m is the number of samples. "Each data point starts with an EQUAL SAY" | | 2. TRAIN A WEAK LEARNER | Train h_t(x) — e.g. a DECISION STUMP, a tree with a DEPTH OF ONLY 1 ← guaranteed MCQ — on the weighted data set, then compute the WEIGHTED ERROR | | 3. COMPUTE THE LEARNER'S WEIGHT (α) | "The MORE ACCURATE the predictor, the HIGHER its weight. If it is just GUESSING RANDOMLY, its weight will be CLOSE TO ZERO. If it is MOST OFTEN WRONG — less accurate than random guessing — ITS WEIGHT WILL BE NEGATIVE" guaranteed MCQ| | 4. UPDATE THE SAMPLE WEIGHTS | MISCLASSIFIED instances are BOOSTED, then all instance weights are NORMALISED (divided by the sum of all weights) | | 5. FINAL PREDICTION | Compute the predictions of all predictors and WEIGH THEM using the predictor weights α. The predicted class is the one receiving the MAJORITY OF THE WEIGHTED VOTES |

    The loop stops when: the DESIRED NUMBER OF PREDICTORS has been trained, OR EARLY if a predictor achieves PERFECT ACCURACY on the weighted data set. guaranteed MCQ THE ANALOGY: guaranteed MCQ

    "Think of a PANEL OF JUNIOR ANALYSTS. Each reviews the data and votes. THE ONES WHO ARE MORE ACCURATE GET MORE SAY in the final decision. And as mistakes are made, the team PAYS MORE ATTENTION TO THE TRICKY CASES. Over time the group becomes better — NOT by training ONE GENIUS analyst, but by BOOSTING the performance of MANY MODEST ONES."

    Advantages Limitations
    Simple and effective · works well with weak learners · no need to tune too many hyperparameters · built-in mechanism to focus on hard cases SENSITIVE TO OUTLIERS — "because it puts too much weight on hard-to-classify points" · may not perform well on NOISY data sets · doesn't scale as well as modern boosting methods like XGBoost

    1. The end-to-end machine learning lifecycle guaranteed MCQ — the TEN steps in order
    3

    Step Detail
    1. DEFINE THE PROBLEM What are the input features? What is the output? What TYPE of ML task is it — classification, regression, clustering? "Without this step, the rest of the pipeline could be SOLVING THE WRONG PROBLEM"
    2. COLLECT THE DATA Internal databases · APIs like credit bureaus or payment gateways · external sources like scraped financial news. Check: do we have enough? Is it complete? Are there imbalances?
    3. EXPLORE THE DATA (EDA) Plot distributions and trends · look for missing values and outliers · spot correlations. "Think of this as BUILDING INTUITION — you might discover that high-value transactions occur mostly LATE AT NIGHT"
    4. PRE-PROCESS AND ENGINEER FEATURES Handle missing values · encode categories · scale/normalise · create new features like AVERAGE TRANSACTION PER DAY instead of raw counts
    5. CHOOSE THE RIGHT MODEL "NO SINGLE MODEL WORKS FOR EVERY SITUATION — experimentation is key"
    6. TRAIN THE MODEL It adjusts internal weights or rules to minimise the error on the training set
    7. EVALUATE THE MODEL On the VALIDATION set — accuracy/precision/recall for classification, RMSE/MAE/R² for regression. Catches overfitting
    8. TUNE THE HYPERPARAMETERS Number of trees, learning rate, regularisation strength — via GRID SEARCH or RANDOM SEARCH with CROSS-VALIDATION
    9. DEPLOY THE MODEL Package it into a file (.PKL — a PICKLE file — or .ONNX) · create an API or embed it into a product · ensure it works in real-time or batch mode guaranteed MCQ
    10. MONITOR AND MAINTAIN "After deployment IT IS NOT OVER — in fact it's just the beginning." Monitor performance · detect DATA DRIFT (input data changes) or CONCEPT DRIFT (the relationships change) · log predictions and feedback · RETRAIN with newer data guaranteed MCQ

    1. Data preparation
    17

    28.1 HANDLING MISSING DATA — the six strategies guaranteed MCQ| # | Strategy | When to use |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | REMOVE THE ROWS | When missing values are RARE and dropping won't significantly reduce your data. Caveat: if the data ISN'T MISSING AT RANDOM, this could BIAS your results | | 2 | REMOVE THE COLUMNS | When a feature is MOSTLY MISSING — say 80% or more — and is not essential | | 3 | IMPUTATION with a statistic | MEAN for numerical · MEDIAN for SKEWED data · MODE for CATEGORICAL. Use when data is missing at random and you want a quick fix guaranteed MCQ| | 4 | DOMAIN-BASED or CONSTANT VALUE | e.g. filling missing loan purposes with "unknown", or setting credit score to −1 if unavailable | | 5 | MODEL-BASED IMPUTATION | Train a mini ML model to PREDICT the missing values using other columns (e.g. predicting missing income from age, job type, credit history). REGRESSION for numerical, CLASSIFICATION for categorical | | 6 | FLAG the missingness / LEAVE AS IS | "An underrated trick" — create a binary column indicating whether a value was missing, because THE FACT THAT SOMETHING IS MISSING MAY ITSELF CARRY SIGNAL (e.g. not providing income could be a pattern). And DECISION TREES, XGBOOST and LIGHTGBM can handle missing values INTERNALLY guaranteed MCQ|

    28.2 ENCODING CATEGORICAL VARIABLES guaranteed MCQ

    "Most machine learning models CAN'T UNDERSTAND TEXT — they need NUMERICAL INPUT."

    Technique Method Warning
    LABEL ENCODING Map each category to a unique number — gold = 0, silver = 1, platinum = 2 "LABEL ENCODING IMPLIES ORDER OR RANKING, WHICH MAY NOT BE TRUE. Is gold really LESS THAN platinum?" → use only for ORDINAL features guaranteed MCQ
    ONE-HOT ENCODING Create a SEPARATE COLUMN FOR EACH CATEGORY. Loan type {personal, home, auto} → three columns, each with a binary indicator, 1 if the category applies and 0 otherwise. These are also called DUMMY VARIABLES In LINEAR models, keeping ALL dummy variables causes MULTICOLLINEARITY — one column can be predicted from the others guaranteed MCQ
    For HIGH CARDINALITY TARGET ENCODING · FREQUENCY ENCODING · EMBEDDINGS (especially in deep learning)

    The rule: ONE-HOT for NOMINAL (unordered) features; LABEL ENCODING for ORDINAL features.

    28.3 SCALING AND NORMALISING guaranteed MCQ

    THE MOTIVATING EXAMPLE: guaranteed MCQ

    "Customer INCOME ranges from 20,000 to 200,000. CREDIT SCORE ranges from 300 to 850. These features are on COMPLETELY DIFFERENT SCALES — and the model might COMPLETELY IGNORE THE CREDIT SCORE just because it's on a smaller range."

    WHICH MODELS NEED SCALING: LOGISTIC REGRESSION · K-NEAREST NEIGHBOURS · SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINES · NEURAL NETWORKS — "these models are DISTANCE-BASED or GRADIENT-BASED and assume all features contribute equally." guaranteed MCQ| Technique | Formula idea | Result | When used | |---|---|---|---| | STANDARDISATION (Z-SCORE SCALING) | (X − μ) ÷ σ | Mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1 | Works well even if the data is NOT BOUNDED. Used with logistic regression, SVMs, neural nets | | MIN-MAX NORMALISATION | (X − min) ÷ (max − min) | Every value between 0 and 1 — the smallest becomes 0, the largest becomes 1 | Useful when features are ALREADY BOUNDED. Common in DEEP LEARNING, where neural networks CONVERGE FASTER |

    THE THREE RULES OF SCALING: guaranteed MCQ 1. Do NOT scale the TARGET variable unless it's part of a specialised pipeline 2. ALWAYS scale AFTER splitting your data into train and test sets 3. FIT the scaler on the TRAINING SET ONLY, then APPLY to both train and test — TO PREVENT DATA LEAKAGE

    "It's like giving EVERY FEATURE A FAIR VOICE, so the model listens to each equally."

    28.4 DATA LEAKAGE guaranteed MCQ — one of the most examinable blocks

    "Data leakage happens when information from OUTSIDE the training data set — ESPECIALLY INFORMATION FROM THE FUTURE — is accidentally included during training. The model performs BRILLIANTLY in validation but COMPLETELY BREAKS DOWN IN PRODUCTION." "YOU WON'T EVEN KNOW IT HAPPENED UNTIL YOUR MODEL STARTS FAILING IN PRODUCTION."

    THE WORKED EXAMPLE: guaranteed MCQ

    Predicting whether a customer will DEFAULT on a loan, and the data set includes the field "LOAN CLOSED ON DATE". "If the loan has ALREADY BEEN CLOSED, you are using FUTURE INFORMATION to predict the outcome. YOUR MODEL IS CHEATING — IT ALREADY KNOWS HOW THINGS ENDED."

    THE TWO TYPES OF LEAKAGE: guaranteed MCQ| Type | Definition | Examples | |---|---|---| | TARGET LEAKAGE (leakage from the future) | Features include information only known AFTER the prediction is made | Including the "defaulted" column as an input feature · using account balance after three months when predicting risk today. "The model is learning FROM THE ANSWER KEY" | | TRAIN-TEST CONTAMINATION | Data from the TEST SET leaks into the TRAINING process | Accidentally using the same records in both · performing SCALING or IMPUTATION on the ENTIRE data set BEFORE splitting |

    THE FOUR PREVENTION STEPS: guaranteed MCQ 1. Understand your data deeply and what would be AVAILABLE AT PREDICTION TIME 2. Separate training, validation and test clearly 3. NEVER include target-related columns as features 4. Perform ALL pre-processing (scaling, encoding, imputation) ONLY ON THE TRAINING DATA and apply the SAME transformations to test and validation

    THE TEST QUESTION TO ASK: guaranteed MCQ

    "IS THIS INFORMATION SOMETHING I WOULD KNOW AT THE TIME OF PREDICTION? If the answer is NO, IT DOESN'T BELONG IN YOUR TRAINING DATA." "A MODEL THAT CHEATS DURING TRAINING WILL ALWAYS FAIL IN THE REAL WORLD."

    28.5 FEATURE ENGINEERING — the nine techniques guaranteed MCQ

    "The ART AND SCIENCE of creating BETTER INPUT FEATURES from raw data so the model can learn more effectively." The motivating example: "A column like TRANSACTION DATE, as is, doesn't help much. But extract the DAY OF THE WEEK, WHETHER IT'S A HOLIDAY, or TIME SINCE THE LAST TRANSACTION, and you now have MEANINGFUL FEATURES."

    # Technique Examples
    1 MATHEMATICAL TRANSFORMATIONS Taking the LOG of income to REDUCE SKEW · creating a DEBT-TO-INCOME RATIO (total debt ÷ income) · squaring or cubing variables when the data is non-linear
    2 BINNING / BUCKETING Age → under 25, 25–40, 40–60 · credit score → poor, fair, good, excellent. "Reduces noise and sometimes improves interpretability"
    3 DATE/TIME EXTRACTION "Timestamps are a GOLD MINE" — day of week · hour of the transaction · weekend vs weekday · days since last transaction. Incredibly valuable in FRAUD DETECTION
    4 ENCODING CATEGORICAL VARIABLES One-hot, label, target encoding
    5 TEXT FEATURE ENGINEERING Word counts · presence of KEYWORDS ("complaint", "urgent") · TF-IDF SCORES · SENTIMENT POLARITY. "Turns UNSTRUCTURED data into USABLE NUMBERS"
    6 INTERACTION FEATURES INCOME PER AGE (income ÷ age) · IS_HIGH_SPENDER (if the transaction amount exceeds average spending). "Captures SUBTLE PATTERNS raw features might miss"
    7 AGGREGATED / GROUP-BASED FEATURES Average spend per user · total logins per month · max loan amount by region. Useful with customer-level or transactional data
    8 MISSING VALUE INDICATORS "MISSINGNESS ITSELF CAN BE A SIGNAL — not providing income might correlate with HIGHER DEFAULT RISK"
    9 FEATURE SELECTION Removing features that don't help, are highly correlated, or cause noise or leakage. Techniques: LASSO (L1) regularisation, which drives coefficients to zero, and tree-based FEATURE IMPORTANCE from Random Forest and XGBoost

    THE CLOSING PRINCIPLE: guaranteed MCQ

    "A SIMPLE MODEL WITH GREAT FEATURES WILL ALMOST ALWAYS BEAT A COMPLEX MODEL WITH WEAK FEATURES." "Feature engineering is the BRIDGE between the raw data and smart models. You are not just CLEANING data — you're SCULPTING it."

    1. Hyperparameter tuning and cross-validation
    11

    29.1 THE FIVE KEY HYPERPARAMETERS guaranteed MCQ| Hyperparameter | Effect |

    |---|---| | LEARNING RATE | How big a step the model takes when updating weights. Too small → painfully slow. Too large → overshoot the optimal point or DIVERGE. "One of the MOST SENSITIVE hyperparameters" | | BATCH SIZE | Large → SMOOTHER training, but you MISS FINER DETAILS. Small → adds NOISE, which CAN HELP JUMP OUT OF LOCAL MINIMA, but may make training UNSTABLE. Common choices are POWERS OF TWO: 32, 64, 128 | | NUMBER OF EPOCHS | One full pass through the training data. Train for 10, 50 or hundreds until the model converges. Too many → OVERFITTING | | NUMBER OF LAYERS | More layers learn more abstract features, but make training complex and can cause VANISHING GRADIENTS and need more data. For TABULAR/STRUCTURED data, START WITH 2–3 LAYERS guaranteed MCQ| | NUMBER OF NEURONS PER LAYER | "Think of them as FEATURE DETECTORS." Too few → not expressive enough. Too many → overfits or becomes very slow |

    "Tuning these is both an ART AND A SCIENCE."

    29.2 THE FOUR TUNING TECHNIQUES guaranteed MCQ — in order of sophistication| Technique | Method | Trade-off |

    |---|---|---| | 1. MANUAL SEARCH | Try a few combinations based on intuition | Quick to set up but NOT SYSTEMATIC — you could miss better settings just because you didn't try them | | 2. GRID SEARCH | Define a GRID of possible values and try EVERY COMBINATION. "A BRUTE-FORCE approach, but it works" | Exhaustive and reliable, but gets VERY EXPENSIVE as the number of parameters grows — the COMBINATORIAL EXPLOSION problem | | 3. RANDOM SEARCH | Picks RANDOM combinations and evaluates them. "Research has shown random search OFTEN FINDS GOOD SOLUTIONS FASTER than grid search, especially when only a FEW parameters actually matter" guaranteed MCQ| Great when short on compute or time | | 4. BAYESIAN OPTIMISATION | "Doesn't blindly try values — it builds a PROBABILISTIC MODEL of the function mapping hyperparameters to performance, then uses that model to decide WHAT TO TRY NEXT, focusing on the PROMISING REGIONS." Tools: OPTUNA, HYPEROPT, SCIKIT-OPTIMIZE guaranteed MCQ| Most efficient |

    THE GRID SEARCH WORKED EXAMPLE: max_depth ∈ {3, 5, 10} and min_samples_split ∈ {2, 5, 10} → 9 COMBINATIONS, each evaluated using CROSS-VALIDATION. guaranteed MCQ The recommended real-world workflow: "Start with MANUAL tuning, move to RANDOM SEARCH, then use BAYESIAN OPTIMISATION to squeeze out the last bit of performance."

    29.3 CROSS-VALIDATION guaranteed MCQ

    WHY IT IS NEEDED: guaranteed MCQ

    "The result depends HEAVILY ON HOW WE SPLIT THE DATA. Split it differently and you might get very different accuracy numbers. Cross-validation gives us a MORE RELIABLE ESTIMATE by testing on MULTIPLE SUBSETS."

    K-FOLD CROSS-VALIDATION — the four steps: guaranteed MCQ 1. Divide the data into K equal parts called FOLDS. K is typically 5 or 10 2. For each iteration, use K−1 folds for TRAINING and the remaining fold for TESTING 3. Repeat K times, each time using a DIFFERENT fold for testing 4. AVERAGE the performance metrics across all K runs

    THE WORKED EXAMPLE (1,000 rows, K = 5): guaranteed MCQ

    Fold 1: rows 1–200 test, rows 201–1,000 train. Fold 2: rows 201–400 test, the rest train. And so on. "The model gets TESTED ON EVERY DATA POINT EXACTLY ONCE and TRAINED on different combinations."

    WHEN TO USE IT: when you have LIMITED DATA · when comparing multiple models · when tuning hyperparameters (GRID SEARCH CV) · when you're concerned your train-test split might not be representative. guaranteed MCQ "It's like putting your model through a FULL WORKOUT, not just one exercise, and checking how CONSISTENT it really is."

    1. The main challenges in machine learning guaranteed MCQ — the nine challenges
    9

    # Challenge Detail
    1 DO YOU HAVE ENOUGH DATA? Missing values · noisy/inconsistent data · IMBALANCED data sets (only 1% of transactions are fraudulent) · data stored across multiple systems or departments. "Many frauds are NOT LABELLED or are labelled INCONSISTENTLY"
    2 FEATURE ENGINEERING IS HARD Requires DOMAIN KNOWLEDGE, CREATIVITY and EXPERIMENTATION. "If you get it wrong, the model may COMPLETELY MISS THE SIGNAL"
    3 OVERFITTING AND UNDERFITTING Finding the sweet spot — trickier with new features, complex models or small data sets
    4 CONCEPT DRIFT and DATA DRIFT "Your model was working great and then suddenly the accuracy drops. WHAT HAPPENED? THE WORLD CHANGED." CONCEPT DRIFT = the RELATIONSHIP between input and output has changed over time. The example: a CREDIT SCORING MODEL TRAINED BEFORE COVID may not work during or after the pandemic — people's repayment behaviour changed drastically guaranteed MCQ
    5 FEEDBACK LOOPS AND BIAS "A fraud detection model flags someone's transaction as suspicious. That person is now LESS LIKELY TO USE THE SERVICE AGAIN — and this affects FUTURE DATA. You create a FEEDBACK LOOP THAT REINFORCES THE MODEL'S BIAS." Plus societal bias, sampling bias and labelling bias guaranteed MCQ
    6 DATA LEAKAGE "Incredibly easy to miss unless you're extremely careful"
    7 EVALUATION IS TRICKY Accuracy isn't enough — need precision/recall, F1, ROC-AUC, and BUSINESS IMPACT METRICS like FALSE POSITIVE COST or LOAN LOSS RATE. "Choosing the right metric and optimising for it is HALF THE BATTLE"
    8 MODEL INTERPRETABILITY "In high-stakes domains like FinTech, EXPLAINABILITY MATTERS. You can't just say THE MODEL SAID SO."
    9 DEPLOYMENT AND MONITORING Real-time or batch systems · versioning, retraining and scaling · "models can BREAK SILENTLY unless you actively monitor post-deployment"

    30.1 LIME and SHAP — model interpretability guaranteed MCQ — both acronyms

    "Many powerful models like Random Forest or XGBoost are often seen as BLACK BOXES. They make great predictions but they don't always tell you WHY. In FinTech, where you're handling money, trust and regulations, WHY MATTERS A LOT — to CUSTOMERS, AUDITORS, REGULATORS AND BUSINESS STAKEHOLDERS."

    LIME — LOCAL INTERPRETABLE MODEL-AGNOSTIC EXPLANATIONS guaranteed MCQ

    The core idea: "Even if your model is complex, you can understand it LOCALLY, FOR ONE PREDICTION AT A TIME."

    THE FIVE STEPS: guaranteed MCQ 1. Pick a SINGLE prediction to explain ("Customer 42 was denied a loan") 2. LIME creates MANY RANDOM VARIATIONS of that data point 3. Pass those variations to the COMPLEX MODEL to get predictions 4. Train a SIMPLE LINEAR MODEL (e.g. logistic regression) LOCALLY around that point, using those predictions as the output variable 5. The COEFFICIENTS of that simple model tell you which features influenced the prediction most

    THE WORKED OUTPUT: low income contributed −0.3 · high credit utilisation contributed −0.5 · low loan term contributed +0.1 → "You now have a HUMAN-READABLE STORY for why the customer was denied." guaranteed MCQ| Pros | Cons | |---|---| | Easy to use; works with ANY model | SENSITIVE TO DATA PERTURBATIONS — results can VARY depending on sampling |

    SHAP — SHAPLEY ADDITIVE EXPLANATIONS guaranteed MCQ

    "Based on GAME THEORY, and MORE MATHEMATICALLY RIGOROUS than LIME. SHAP answers: HOW MUCH DID EACH FEATURE CONTRIBUTE TO THIS PREDICTION COMPARED TO THE AVERAGE PREDICTION?" "It treats EACH FEATURE LIKE A PLAYER IN A TEAM GAME. The final prediction is like THE TEAM'S SCORE. SHAP calculates THE FAIR SHARE OF THE CREDIT OR BLAME each feature should get."

    THE ONE-LINE DISTINCTION: guaranteed MCQ

    "LIME helps you ZOOM IN. SHAP helps you EXPLAIN FAIRLY AND MATHEMATICALLY."

    1. Unsupervised learning in FinTech guaranteed MCQ — the four applications
    27

    # Application Detail
    1 CUSTOMER SEGMENTATION Group by spending patterns, product usage, risk profiles, preferred channels (mobile vs branch). The example segments: young digital-first savers · high-value investors · infrequent users
    2 ANOMALY DETECTION ISOLATION FORESTS or AUTOENCODERS detect sudden changes in transaction patterns, suspicious login behaviour, unusual withdrawal patterns. The example: "A customer typically spends ₹200 a week and suddenly spends ₹5,000 IN A FOREIGN COUNTRY — that's a RED FLAG, and the model catches it WITHOUT BEING EXPLICITLY TOLD" guaranteed MCQ
    3 MARKET SEGMENTATION AND PRODUCT TARGETING Cluster users by risk appetite, cash flow, transaction behaviour, LIFE STAGE (student, salaried, retiree)
    4 DIMENSIONALITY REDUCTION PCA reduces noise and simplifies training before modelling; helps VISUALISE customers or transactions on a 2D map

    "While SUPERVISED learning helps us PREDICT OUTCOMES, UNSUPERVISED learning helps us DISCOVER STRUCTURE — and in FinTech that's priceless, because OFTEN YOU DON'T EVEN KNOW WHAT PATTERNS TO LOOK FOR until the model uncovers them." guaranteed MCQ

    31.1 K-MEANS CLUSTERING guaranteed MCQ

    THE FIVE STEPS: guaranteed MCQ 1. Choose K and INITIALISE THE CENTROIDS randomly 2. ASSIGN each data point to the NEAREST centroid (using EUCLIDEAN DISTANCE) 3. RECOMPUTE the centroid of each cluster — the AVERAGE of all points in that cluster 4. REPEAT steps 2 and 3 5. STOP when the centroids stop moving significantly, or a maximum number of iterations is reached — "that's when we say the algorithm has CONVERGED"

    THE COST FUNCTION: K-means minimises the TOTAL WITHIN-CLUSTER SUM OF SQUARED DISTANCES (WCSS) — "how far each point is from its closest centre." guaranteed MCQ THE THREE POINTS TO NOTE: guaranteed MCQ 1. You must CHOOSE K IN ADVANCE, which is tricky 2. K-means works best with SPHERICAL clusters, where points are evenly spread around the centre 3. It is SENSITIVE TO OUTLIERS and to the INITIAL PLACEMENT of centroids

    THE FIVE-CUSTOMER WORKED EXAMPLE (income and spending, both in ₹'000s), K = 2: guaranteed MCQ| Step | Detail | |---|---| | Initial centroids | Customer A at (4, 4) and Customer C at (10, 8) | | Distances to centroid 1 (4,4) | A = 0 · B = 2.24 · C = 7.21 · D = 8.6 · E = 2 | | Distances to centroid 2 (10,8) | A = 7.21 · B ≈ 5 · C = 0 · D = 1.41 · E = 8.49 | | Assignment | Cluster 1 = {A, B, E}; Cluster 2 = {C, D} | | New centroid 1 | (4.67, 3.67) | | New centroid 2 | (10.5, 8.5) | | Final interpretation | Cluster 1 = LOWER income, LOWER spenders. Cluster 2 = HIGHER income, HIGHER spenders |

    Business uses: designing different credit products per segment · personalised loan or investment offers · DETECTING OUTLIERS that don't fit either cluster well.

    31.2 THE ELBOW METHOD guaranteed MCQ

    "As you INCREASE the number of clusters, the WITHIN-CLUSTER SUM OF SQUARES (WCSS) starts to DECREASE — that makes sense, the more clusters you have, the closer each point is to a centroid. BUT the IMPROVEMENT SLOWS DOWN after a certain point. THAT POINT WHERE THE CURVE BENDS LIKE AN ELBOW IS THE OPTIMAL K." Method: run K-means for K = 1 to 10, calculate WCSS for each, PLOT K vs WCSS, and look for where ADDING ANOTHER CLUSTER DOESN'T GIVE MUCH BENEFIT. In his illustration, the drop levels off around K = 3 OR 4.

    31.3 THE SIX LIMITATIONS OF K-MEANS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS guaranteed MCQ| # | Issue | Solutions |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | You must CHOOSE K MANUALLY | ELBOW METHOD · SILHOUETTE SCORE · model-based clustering methods that find the optimal K automatically | | 2 | SENSITIVITY TO INITIALISATION | K-MEANS++ INITIALISATION, which smartly picks starting centroids · run K-means MULTIPLE TIMES and take the LOWEST-COST result guaranteed MCQ| | 3 | ASSUMES SPHERICAL / ISOTROPIC CLUSTERS | GAUSSIAN MIXTURE MODELS with the EXPECTATION-MAXIMISATION algorithm (better for ELLIPTICAL clusters) · DBSCAN or SPECTRAL CLUSTERING for IRREGULAR shapes guaranteed MCQ| | 4 | SENSITIVE TO OUTLIERS — "outliers can PULL CENTROIDS FAR AWAY from the true centre" | Remove or cap outliers · robust K-means variants · DBSCAN, which can NATURALLY IDENTIFY AND IGNORE OUTLIERS | | 5 | WORKS WITH NUMERIC DATA ONLY (it relies on computing distances) | One-hot encode the categoricals · K-PROTOTYPES, which handles MIXED categorical and numerical data · hierarchical clustering with appropriate distance metrics guaranteed MCQ| | 6 | DOESN'T SCALE WELL WITH HIGH DIMENSIONS — "the CURSE OF DIMENSIONALITY" | PCA before clustering · careful feature selection |

    31.4 HIERARCHICAL CLUSTERING guaranteed MCQ

    "Builds a TREE-LIKE STRUCTURE of clusters — like a FAMILY TREE of your data. Its big advantage: IT DOESN'T REQUIRE CHOOSING K UPFRONT."

    THE TWO APPROACHES: AGGLOMERATIVE (BOTTOM-UP — THE MOST COMMON) and DIVISIVE (TOP-DOWN — less common). guaranteed MCQ THE FIVE AGGLOMERATIVE STEPS: guaranteed MCQ 1. Start with EACH DATA POINT AS ITS OWN CLUSTER 2. Compute the distance between ALL PAIRS of clusters 3. MERGE the two CLOSEST clusters 4. RECOMPUTE distances between the new cluster and all others 5. Repeat until ALL POINTS ARE MERGED INTO ONE LARGE CLUSTER

    THE FOUR LINKAGE METHODS — how "distance between clusters" is defined: guaranteed MCQ| Linkage | Definition | |---|---| | SINGLE linkage | The SHORTEST distance between points | | COMPLETE linkage | The FARTHEST distance between points | | AVERAGE linkage | The AVERAGE distance between all point pairs | | WARD'S METHOD | MINIMISES THE VARIANCE — "which often performs best" |

    THE DENDROGRAM: guaranteed MCQ

    "A TREE-LIKE DIAGRAM showing HOW CLOSE data points are to each other AND AT WHAT LEVEL THEY MERGED. Observations run along one axis; the other axis is the DISTANCE or DISSIMILARITY at which clusters merged." "YOU CAN CUT THE DENDROGRAM AT ANY HEIGHT to get the desired number of clusters. In his example, cutting at a distance of AROUND 5.5 yields THREE MAIN CLUSTERS. CUT HIGHER → FEWER clusters. CUT LOWER → MORE fine-grained groups." Observations 5 and 6 merge EARLY, "which means they're QUITE SIMILAR."

    "So instead of GUESSING K like in K-means, we just LOOK AT THE DENDROGRAM and choose the level where the clusters make the most sense."

    31.5 DIMENSIONALITY REDUCTION AND PCA guaranteed MCQ

    THE CURSE OF DIMENSIONALITY: "Too many features can actually make learning HARDER — the model becomes SLOWER, HARDER TO INTERPRET and sometimes even LESS ACCURATE."

    THE FOUR BENEFITS: 1. SIMPLIFIES the model · 2. IMPROVES PERFORMANCE and REDUCES OVERFITTING · 3. VISUALISES high-dimensional data in 2D or 3D · 4. UNCOVERS LATENT STRUCTURES or hidden patterns. guaranteed MCQ

    PCA "combines CORRELATED features into new ones while retaining as much of the VARIANCE (information) as possible. It transforms the original features into NEW AXES called PRINCIPAL COMPONENTS and RANKS THEM BY HOW MUCH VARIANCE THEY CAPTURE." "The FIRST principal component captures THE MOST VARIANCE. The SECOND captures the most variance NOT ALREADY EXPLAINED BY THE FIRST — and so on." guaranteed MCQ THE MATHEMATICS: guaranteed MCQ Z₁ = W₁X₁ + W₂X₂ + … + WₙXₙ, where Z₁ is the first principal component and W₁…Wₙ are the WEIGHTS (LOADINGS) that define the direction. The weights are chosen so that Z₁ has MAXIMUM VARIANCE, and the vector W has UNIT LENGTH to avoid arbitrary scaling.

    THE EIGENVALUE EQUATION: PCA looks at the COVARIANCE MATRIX (Σ) of the data. - W = the EIGENVECTOR — it tells us the DIRECTION of the principal component - λ (LAMBDA) = the EIGENVALUE — it tells us HOW MUCH VARIANCE is captured in that direction "The FIRST principal component corresponds to the eigenvector with the LARGEST EIGENVALUE; the second to the NEXT LARGEST."

    Each principal component is: a NEW AXIS · a LINEAR COMBINATION of your original features · UNCORRELATED with the previous components · ORDERED by how much variance it captures. guaranteed MCQ THE FOUR PCA STEPS (with the worked numbers): guaranteed MCQ 1. STANDARDISE / CENTRE the data to ZERO MEAN — subtract the mean from each feature 2. COMPUTE THE COVARIANCE MATRIX. CRITICAL DETAIL: divide by n − 1, NOT n — "we are talking about SAMPLE covariance, not POPULATION covariance." With 3 observations, divide by 3 − 1 = 2 guaranteed MCQ 3. FIND THE EIGENVALUES AND EIGENVECTORS. In his worked example: λ₁ ≈ 2.66 and λ₂ = 2 4. PROJECT the data onto the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue → the first principal component

    THE PROJECTION PICTURE: guaranteed MCQ

    "The GREEN DASHED LINE shows the direction of the first principal component — the line capturing MAXIMUM VARIANCE. The RED POINTS are the PROJECTIONS of the original points onto it. Think of it like SHINING A LIGHT PERPENDICULAR to the green line — the SHADOWS you get are your projected points. Each BLACK DASHED LINE shows the SHORTEST (PERPENDICULAR) distance from the original point to the principal component."

    "The goal of PCA isn't just to REDUCE THE NUMBER OF COLUMNS. It is to help us SEE THE SIGNAL, NOT THE NOISE." guaranteed MCQ

    1. Deep learning fundamentals
    33

    32.1 Machine learning vs deep learning guaranteed MCQ| | TRADITIONAL MACHINE LEARNING | DEEP LEARNING |

    |---|---|---| | Feature engineering | MANUAL — a human decides which features matter (e.g. average transaction size, number of failed logins) | AUTOMATIC — the network LEARNS THE FEATURES ITSELF from raw data guaranteed MCQ| | Data needs | Works with smaller data sets | Needs LARGE volumes of data | | Best for | Structured/tabular data | UNSTRUCTURED data — images, audio, text, transaction sequences |

    32.2 THE BIOLOGICAL → ARTIFICIAL NEURON MAPPING guaranteed MCQ — this table will be tested| Biological neuron | Artificial neuron |

    |---|---| | DENDRITES — receive signals from other neurons | INPUTS (X₁, X₂, … Xₙ) — features like income, credit score, transaction frequency | | SYNAPTIC STRENGTH — how strong each connection is | WEIGHTS (W₁, W₂, … Wₙ) — how important each input is | | CELL BODY (SOMA) — sums up the incoming signals | WEIGHTED SUM PLUS BIAS: Z = W₁X₁ + W₂X₂ + … + B | | FIRING THRESHOLD — the neuron fires only if the signal is strong enough | ACTIVATION FUNCTION — introduces NON-LINEARITY and decides the output | | AXON — transmits the output signal | OUTPUT — a prediction, or a signal passed to the next layer |

    "Just like the brain learns by ADJUSTING SYNAPTIC STRENGTHS, an artificial neural network learns by ADJUSTING WEIGHTS during training."

    32.3 THE PERCEPTRON guaranteed MCQ

    "The SIMPLEST form of a neural network — a SINGLE ARTIFICIAL NEURON, introduced by FRANK ROSENBLATT in the 1950s. It is the FOUNDATION of modern deep learning."

    How it works: takes multiple inputs → multiplies each by a weight → adds a bias → passes the result through a STEP FUNCTION (an ACTIVATION FUNCTION) → outputs 1 or 0. guaranteed MCQ THE FRAUD WORKED EXAMPLE: guaranteed MCQ

    X₁ = 1 if the transaction is over ₹50,000, else 0. X₂ = 1 if it's from a new device, else 0. Weights W₁ = 2, W₂ = 3, bias B = −4. A large transaction from a new device: Z = 2(1) + 3(1) − 4 = 1 → since Z > 0, the perceptron OUTPUTS 1 → FRAUD.

    THE FATAL LIMITATION: guaranteed MCQ

    "A single perceptron can only learn LINEARLY SEPARABLE patterns — it can only draw A STRAIGHT LINE to separate the data. It CANNOT solve the XOR PROBLEM." Real-world FinTech data is rarely linearly separable → we need MULTIPLE LAYERS, i.e. a MULTI-LAYER PERCEPTRON.

    32.4 THE MULTI-LAYER PERCEPTRON (MLP) guaranteed MCQ

    Structure: an INPUT LAYER → one or more HIDDEN LAYERS → an OUTPUT LAYER. Each neuron is CONNECTED TO EVERY NEURON IN THE NEXT LAYER, so it's also called a FULLY CONNECTED NETWORK.

    WHY STACKING LAYERS ALONE ISN'T ENOUGH — the key insight: guaranteed MCQ

    "If we just stack MULTIPLE LINEAR LAYERS WITHOUT ANY ACTIVATION FUNCTIONS, THE ENTIRE NETWORK STILL BEHAVES LIKE A SINGLE LINEAR MODEL. A composition of linear functions is STILL LINEAR — you gain NO ADDITIONAL POWER." The glass-sheets analogy: "Stacking multiple SHEETS OF CLEAR GLASS still gives you a FLAT SURFACE. To bend the light, you need a LENS. In neural networks, the ACTIVATION FUNCTION IS THAT LENS — it introduces NON-LINEARITY."

    32.5 THE THREE ACTIVATION FUNCTIONS guaranteed MCQ| Function | Range | Behaviour | When used |

    |---|---|---|---| | ReLU — RECTIFIED LINEAR UNIT | 0 to ∞ | Passes positive values as they are, turns NEGATIVE values into ZERO. "Simple, fast and works surprisingly well" | The DEFAULT in HIDDEN LAYERS. "Most popular in deep learning" | | SIGMOID | 0 to 1 | Squashes any value into a probability-like output | BINARY CLASSIFICATION OUTPUT LAYERS — "used when we want probabilities" | | TANH | −1 to +1 | ZERO-CENTRED — "often converges better than sigmoid" | Hidden layers where zero-centring helps |

    THE VANISHING GRADIENT PROBLEM: guaranteed MCQ

    "With SIGMOID and TANH, when values become VERY LARGE OR VERY SMALL, the GRADIENTS BECOME NEARLY ZERO, which SLOWS DOWN OR STOPS LEARNING — especially in DEEP NETWORKS. ReLU helps avoid this in most cases."

    32.6 THE FORWARD PASS — the full worked example guaranteed MCQ — memorise all the numbers

    Network: 2 inputs → 2 hidden neurons (ReLU) → 1 output neuron (sigmoid). Inputs X₁ = 1, X₂ = 2.

    Stage Calculation Result
    Hidden neuron 1 Z₁ = W₁₁X₁ + W₁₂X₂ + B₁ Z₁ = 0.6
    Hidden neuron 2 Z₂ = W₂₁X₁ + W₂₂X₂ + B₂ Z₂ = 1.2
    Apply ReLU Both are positive, so they pass through unchanged A₁ = 0.6, A₂ = 1.2
    Output neuron Z₃ = W₃₁A₁ + W₃₂A₂ + B₃ Z₃ = 1.22
    Apply SIGMOID σ(1.22) OUTPUT = 0.772
    Interpretation "There is a 77.2% chance the customer will DEFAULT"

    "This is a FORWARD PASS: raw input → weighted sum → activation → prediction. This is how EVERY neural network makes a prediction, whether it has 3 neurons or 300 million."

    32.7 BACKPROPAGATION — the worked example guaranteed MCQ — every number

    "Forward propagation is like a student ATTEMPTING an exam paper. Backpropagation is like the teacher CORRECTING it and giving FEEDBACK on where the student went wrong."

    Continuing the example — the ACTUAL LABEL is y = 0 (no default), but the model predicted 0.772.

    Stage Detail
    1. COMPUTE THE LOSS Using BINARY CROSS-ENTROPY (LOG LOSS), the loss ≈ 1.48 — "a fairly high loss, telling us the model is confidently wrong" guaranteed MCQ
    2. COMPUTE THE OUTPUT-LAYER GRADIENT ∂L/∂Z₃ = ŷ − y = 0.772 − 0 = 0.772 guaranteed MCQ — this simple form comes from sigmoid + log loss
    3. GRADIENTS FOR THE OUTPUT WEIGHTS ∂L/∂W₃₁ = 0.772 × A₁ = 0.772 × 0.6 = 0.463 and ∂L/∂W₃₂ = 0.772 × A₂ = 0.772 × 1.2 = 0.926. ∂L/∂B₃ = 0.772
    4. PROPAGATE BACK TO THE HIDDEN LAYER Using the CHAIN RULE, multiplying by the DERIVATIVE OF ReLU (which is 1 for positive inputs, 0 otherwise)
    5. UPDATE THE WEIGHTS W_new = W_old − η × gradient, with LEARNING RATE η = 0.1
    6. RESULT AFTER ONE UPDATE The new prediction drops from 0.772 to 0.7637, and the loss falls from 1.48 to 1.43 guaranteed MCQ

    "That may seem like a SMALL improvement, but over THOUSANDS of iterations these small updates accumulate and the model becomes highly accurate. THAT IS THE ESSENCE OF LEARNING IN NEURAL NETWORKS."

    The takeaway: "Backpropagation is what MAKES DEEP LEARNING POSSIBLE. Without it, we could not train networks with millions of parameters."

    32.8 THE FIVE MOST IMPORTANT NEURAL NETWORK HYPERPARAMETERS

    LEARNING RATE · BATCH SIZE · NUMBER OF EPOCHS · NUMBER OF LAYERS · NUMBER OF NEURONS PER LAYER (see §29.1 for the guidance on each).

    32.9 EARLY STOPPING AND LEARNING-RATE SCHEDULES guaranteed MCQ

    EARLY STOPPING:

    "Monitor the VALIDATION LOSS during training. If it STOPS IMPROVING FOR A FEW EPOCHS, STOP TRAINING — even if the training loss is still going down." "It's like telling a student: you have practised enough, ANY MORE AND YOU'RE JUST MEMORISING." It saves time AND prevents overfitting.

    LEARNING RATE SCHEDULING — the three types: guaranteed MCQ| Schedule | Method | |---|---| | STEP DECAY | Reduce the learning rate at fixed intervals — e.g. HALVE it every 10 epochs | | EXPONENTIAL DECAY | Multiply the learning rate by a factor like 0.96 after each epoch | | REDUCE ON PLATEAU | Cut the learning rate ONLY WHEN VALIDATION PERFORMANCE STOPS IMPROVING |

    "Start with a LARGER learning rate to make quick progress, then GRADUALLY REDUCE it so the model can settle into a good minimum."

    32.10 DROPOUT guaranteed MCQ

    "During training, RANDOMLY 'DROP' — temporarily deactivate — SOME NEURONS in a layer. Typically 30% to 50% of the neurons in a layer are dropped RANDOMLY IN EACH FORWARD PASS." guaranteed MCQ WHY IT WORKS — the two reasons: guaranteed MCQ 1. The network CANNOT RELY TOO HEAVILY ON ANY SINGLE NEURON, so it learns MORE ROBUST, DISTRIBUTED REPRESENTATIONS 2. It effectively trains an ENSEMBLE OF SMALLER SUB-NETWORKS, which reduces variance and improves generalisation

    THE CRITICAL RULE: guaranteed MCQ

    "DROPOUT IS APPLIED ONLY DURING TRAINING. At inference (test) time, ALL NEURONS ARE ACTIVE, but their outputs are SCALED APPROPRIATELY so the expected value remains consistent."

    "It's like a football team practising with random players sitting out each session, so EVERY PLAYER LEARNS TO CONTRIBUTE and the team doesn't depend on one star."

    32.11 BATCH NORMALISATION guaranteed MCQ

    THE PROBLEM IT SOLVES: INTERNAL COVARIATE SHIFT guaranteed MCQ

    "As the weights of earlier layers change during training, the DISTRIBUTION OF INPUTS TO LATER LAYERS KEEPS SHIFTING. This makes training UNSTABLE and SLOW."

    HOW IT WORKS: guaranteed MCQ

    "For each MINI-BATCH, NORMALISE the inputs to a layer so they have a MEAN OF 0 and a VARIANCE OF 1. Then the network applies TWO LEARNABLE PARAMETERS: γ (GAMMA) for SCALING and β (BETA) for SHIFTING. So the model can UNDO the normalisation if that's better for learning — it doesn't lose expressive power."

    THE FOUR BENEFITS: 1. FASTER training · 2. Allows HIGHER LEARNING RATES · 3. LESS SENSITIVE TO WEIGHT INITIALISATION · 4. Acts as a MILD REGULARISER, sometimes reducing the need for dropout. guaranteed MCQ AT INFERENCE TIME: "the network uses RUNNING AVERAGES of the mean and variance computed during training." guaranteed MCQ "Batch normalisation is like keeping all students in a class ON THE SAME PAGE, so learning progresses smoothly."

    32.12 AUTOENCODERS guaranteed MCQ

    "A special type of neural network that learns to RECONSTRUCT ITS OWN INPUT. It is an UNSUPERVISED learning technique — it does NOT need labels."

    THE THREE PARTS: guaranteed MCQ| Part | Function | |---|---| | ENCODER | COMPRESSES the input into a lower-dimensional representation | | BOTTLENECK (LATENT SPACE) | The COMPRESSED representation — "this is where the MAGIC happens." Because it is smaller than the input, the network MUST LEARN ONLY THE MOST IMPORTANT PATTERNS | | DECODER | RECONSTRUCTS the original input from the compressed representation |

    THE KEY DESIGN CONSTRAINT: guaranteed MCQ

    "If the bottleneck were AS LARGE AS THE INPUT, the network could just COPY the data — and we would learn NOTHING. So we deliberately make it SMALLER. This is called an UNDER-COMPLETE AUTOENCODER."

    The loss function: RECONSTRUCTION LOSS, typically MEAN SQUARED ERROR between input and reconstructed output. guaranteed MCQ THE PCA PARALLEL: guaranteed MCQ

    "An autoencoder with LINEAR ACTIVATIONS and MSE loss behaves SIMILARLY TO PCA. But with NON-LINEAR activations, autoencoders can capture MUCH MORE COMPLEX STRUCTURES — that's why they are considered a NON-LINEAR GENERALISATION OF PCA."

    THE FRAUD-DETECTION APPLICATION — the worked threshold: guaranteed MCQ

    1. TRAIN THE AUTOENCODER ONLY ON NORMAL (non-fraudulent) TRANSACTIONS 2. The model becomes VERY GOOD at reconstructing normal behaviour 3. When a FRAUDULENT transaction comes in, the RECONSTRUCTION ERROR IS HIGH — because the model has never seen such patterns 4. Set the THRESHOLD using the 95th or 99th PERCENTILE of reconstruction errors on normal data Example: threshold = 0.05. A transaction with a reconstruction error of 0.12 is FLAGGED AS SUSPICIOUS

    The other applications: DIMENSIONALITY REDUCTION · DENOISING (removing noise from data) · FEATURE LEARNING for downstream models.

    1. NLP, generative AI and transformers
    34

    33.1 Why NLP matters in FinTech guaranteed MCQ

    "A LARGE PORTION OF FINANCIAL DATA IS NOT NUMBERS — it's TEXT. Customer support chats, loan applications, compliance documents, financial news, regulatory filings, social media sentiment. This is UNSTRUCTURED DATA — it doesn't fit neatly into rows and columns."

    Applications: chatbots and virtual assistants · sentiment analysis on news and social media · automated document processing · compliance and regulatory monitoring · fraud detection from text patterns.

    33.2 GENERATIVE vs DISCRIMINATIVE models guaranteed MCQ| | DISCRIMINATIVE models | GENERATIVE models |

    |---|---|---| | What they learn | The BOUNDARY between classes | The UNDERLYING DISTRIBUTION of the data | | What they do | CLASSIFY or PREDICT | CREATE NEW DATA that resembles the training data | | Examples | Logistic regression, random forest, standard classifiers | GPT, image generators, autoencoders (variational), GANs |

    33.3 AUTOENCODER vs ENCODER-DECODER guaranteed MCQ — a likely trap| | AUTOENCODER | ENCODER-DECODER (sequence-to-sequence) |

    |---|---|---| | Goal | RECONSTRUCT THE SAME INPUT | TRANSFORM one sequence into a DIFFERENT one | | Output | Identical (or nearly identical) to the input | A DIFFERENT output — e.g. English → French translation, or a document → its summary |

    33.4 TOKENISATION IN NLP guaranteed MCQ — do not confuse with asset tokenisation in §16

    "Machines don't understand words — they understand NUMBERS. TOKENISATION is the process of BREAKING TEXT INTO SMALLER UNITS called TOKENS, which are then converted into numbers."

    THE THREE LEVELS: guaranteed MCQ| Level | Method | Trade-off | |---|---|---| | CHARACTER-level | Every character is a token | Very small vocabulary, but VERY LONG sequences | | WORD-level | Every word is a token | Simple, but a HUGE vocabulary, and it FAILS on words it has never seen (out-of-vocabulary) | | SUB-WORD level | Words are split into meaningful fragments | THE MODERN STANDARD — used by GPT, BERT and most LLMs |

    BPE — BYTE PAIR ENCODING: guaranteed MCQ

    "The most common sub-word algorithm. It starts with individual characters and REPEATEDLY MERGES THE MOST FREQUENT PAIRS." THE THREE RULES OF THUMB: - HIGH-FREQUENCY WORDS STAY WHOLE — "bank", "loan", "the" are single tokens - RARE WORDS ARE SPLIT INTO PIECES — "bankruptcy" might become "bank" + "rupt" + "cy" - COMPLETELY UNKNOWN WORDS FALL BACK TO CHARACTERS — an invented word like "bankzilla" gets broken into many small pieces

    "This means the model NEVER FAILS on an unseen word — it just uses more tokens to represent it."

    33.5 TOKEN COST AND CONTEXT WINDOWS guaranteed MCQ — the numbers| Fact | Figure |

    |---|---| | Typical API price | around $1.50 PER MILLION TOKENS (and INPUT and OUTPUT tokens are PRICED DIFFERENTLY — output is more expensive) | | Word-to-token conversion | 1 TOKEN ≈ 0.75 WORDS · 1 WORD ≈ 1.33 TOKENS guaranteed MCQ| | Same sentence, different tokenisers | GPT = 10 tokens · Claude = 11 tokens · Gemini = 12 tokens — "every model has its OWN tokeniser, so THE SAME TEXT COSTS DIFFERENTLY on different platforms" guaranteed MCQ| | GPT-4o context window | 128,000 tokens, with a MAXIMUM OUTPUT of 16,384 tokens guaranteed MCQ| | GPT-4.1 context window | Up to 1 MILLION tokens |

    "This is why understanding tokens matters — it directly affects BOTH COST AND CAPABILITY."

    33.6 THE EVOLUTION OF WORD REPRESENTATION guaranteed MCQ — the four stages in order| Stage | Method | Limitation / breakthrough |

    |---|---|---| | 1. ONE-HOT ENCODING | Each word is a vector of all zeros with a single 1 | HUGE, SPARSE vectors, and NO SENSE OF MEANING — "bank" and "finance" are as unrelated as "bank" and "banana" | | 2. COUNT VECTORISATION (Bag of Words) | Count how many times each word appears | Loses WORD ORDER entirely | | 3. TF-IDF | TERM FREQUENCY–INVERSE DOCUMENT FREQUENCY — weights words by how RARE and therefore how INFORMATIVE they are | Better, but still NO semantic meaning | | 4. WORD EMBEDDINGS | Dense vectors where SIMILAR WORDS ARE CLOSE TOGETHER in vector space. Named methods: WORD2VEC and GloVe | THE FAMOUS PROPERTY: KING − MAN + WOMAN ≈ QUEEN guaranteed MCQ| | 5. CONTEXTUAL EMBEDDINGS | BERT and GPT — the SAME WORD gets a DIFFERENT VECTOR DEPENDING ON CONTEXT | "'Bank' in RIVER BANK vs 'bank' in SAVINGS BANK now get DIFFERENT representations" guaranteed MCQ|

    33.7 THE ATTENTION MECHANISM guaranteed MCQ

    "Attention lets the model decide WHICH WORDS TO FOCUS ON when processing each word." The example sentence: "THE LOAN THAT THE BANK APPROVED WAS DISBURSED YESTERDAY." To understand "disbursed", the model needs to look back at "LOAN" and "BANK" — even though they are several words away. guaranteed MCQ THE THREE VECTORS — Q, K, V: guaranteed MCQ| Vector | Name | Role | |---|---|---| | Q | QUERY | "What am I looking for?" | | K | KEY | "What do I contain?" | | V | VALUE | "What information do I actually carry?" |

    THE FOUR COMPUTATION STEPS: guaranteed MCQ 1. Take the DOT PRODUCT of the query with every key → an ATTENTION SCORE for each word 2. SCALE by the SQUARE ROOT OF THE DIMENSION (√d) to keep the numbers stable guaranteed MCQ 3. Apply SOFTMAX to turn the scores into WEIGHTS THAT SUM TO 1 4. Compute the WEIGHTED SUM OF THE VALUE VECTORS — that is the output for this word

    CAUSAL / AUTO-REGRESSIVE MASKING: guaranteed MCQ

    "In a GENERATIVE model like GPT, each word can only attend to WORDS THAT CAME BEFORE IT — NOT to future words. Otherwise the model would be CHEATING BY LOOKING AT THE ANSWER. This is called CAUSAL MASKING or AUTO-REGRESSIVE generation."

    33.8 MULTI-HEAD ATTENTION guaranteed MCQ

    "Instead of computing attention ONCE, the model computes it MULTIPLE TIMES IN PARALLEL, with DIFFERENT LEARNED PROJECTIONS. Each 'head' can focus on a DIFFERENT KIND OF RELATIONSHIP — one might track GRAMMATICAL STRUCTURE, another SEMANTIC MEANING, another LONG-RANGE DEPENDENCIES. The outputs are then CONCATENATED and combined." The analogy: "Like looking at a PAINTING THROUGH MULTIPLE LENSES — each lens reveals something different, and together you get the complete picture." guaranteed MCQ

    33.9 THE TRANSFORMER BLOCK guaranteed MCQ

    The components of ONE transformer block: MULTI-HEAD ATTENTION → a FEEDFORWARD NEURAL NETWORK (applied to each position) → with RESIDUAL (SKIP) CONNECTIONS and LAYER NORMALISATION around each sub-layer. guaranteed MCQ| Component | Purpose | |---|---| | RESIDUAL CONNECTIONS | Let the gradient flow through deep networks, preventing vanishing gradients | | LAYER NORMALISATION | Stabilises training | | FEEDFORWARD NETWORK | Adds non-linear processing capacity at each position |

    WHY STACK MANY LAYERS: "EARLY layers capture BASIC PATTERNS like grammar and syntax. MIDDLE layers capture MEANING AND RELATIONSHIPS. LATER layers capture ABSTRACT REASONING and task-specific behaviour." guaranteed MCQ THE OUTPUT LAYER: guaranteed MCQ

    "The final hidden state passes through a LINEAR LAYER producing LOGITS — one score for EVERY TOKEN IN THE VOCABULARY, roughly 50,000 of them. Then SOFTMAX converts these into a PROBABILITY DISTRIBUTION over the entire vocabulary."

    33.10 THE FOUR DECODING STRATEGIES guaranteed MCQ| Strategy | Method | Character |

    |---|---|---| | GREEDY DECODING | Always pick the HIGHEST-PROBABILITY token | DETERMINISTIC and safe, but REPETITIVE AND BORING — "the same prompt always gives the same answer" | | PURE SAMPLING | Randomly sample from the full distribution | Creative, but can produce NONSENSE, because even very low-probability tokens can be picked | | TOP-K SAMPLING | Keep ONLY THE TOP K MOST LIKELY TOKENS (e.g. K = 50), renormalise, and sample from those | Blocks the truly absurd options while keeping variety. Limitation: K is FIXED regardless of how confident the model is | | TOP-P (NUCLEUS) SAMPLING | Keep the SMALLEST SET OF TOKENS whose CUMULATIVE PROBABILITY EXCEEDS P (e.g. 0.9), then sample from that set | ADAPTIVE — "when the model is CONFIDENT, the set is SMALL; when it's UNCERTAIN, the set is LARGER." Generally the preferred method guaranteed MCQ|

    THE WORKED TOP-P EXAMPLE: "Sort the tokens by probability and add them up — 0.4, then 0.65, then 0.8, then 0.92. Once you cross 0.9, you STOP. Only those four tokens are candidates."

    THE "CAPITAL OF INDIA" COMPARISON: guaranteed MCQ

    For a FACTUAL question, GREEDY DECODING is correct — you want "New Delhi" EVERY TIME. For CREATIVE writing, TOP-P sampling is better.

    33.11 TEMPERATURE guaranteed MCQ

    "Temperature RESCALES THE LOGITS BEFORE SOFTMAX by DIVIDING THEM BY T."

    Temperature Effect
    T < 1 (e.g. 0.2) SHARPENS the distribution — the model becomes MORE CONFIDENT and DETERMINISTIC
    T = 1 The model's natural distribution
    T > 1 (e.g. 1.5) FLATTENS the distribution — MORE RANDOM AND CREATIVE

    THE RECOMMENDED SETTINGS: guaranteed MCQ - 0.2 to 0.5 → FACTUAL tasks, compliance answers, financial calculations - 0.7 to 1.0 → BALANCED, general-purpose - 1.0 to 1.5+ → CREATIVE tasks, brainstorming, marketing copy

    The worked example: generating CREDIT CARD MARKETING SUBJECT LINES — a LOW temperature produces safe, similar lines; a HIGH temperature produces varied, creative, sometimes odd ones. guaranteed MCQ

    33.12 THE GPT-2 TRANSFORMER EXPLAINER DEMO guaranteed MCQ — every number

    The tool: poloclub.github.io/transformer-explainer guaranteed MCQ| Fact | Figure | |---|---| | Model used | GPT-2 (small) | | Parameters | 124 MILLION | | Vocabulary size | 50,257 tokens | | Embedding dimension | 768 |

    THE WORKED PREDICTIONS: guaranteed MCQ - "The world is beautiful" → the model predicts "PLACE" with 97.58% probability - "Data visualization empowers users to" → the top predictions are "VISUALIZE" and "CREATE" - The word "EMPOWERS" is split by the tokeniser into "EM" + "POWERS" — "an illustration of sub-word tokenisation in action"

    1. Prompt engineering guaranteed MCQ
    5

    34.1 THE THREE PARTS OF A GOOD PROMPT guaranteed MCQ

    1. THE INSTRUCTION — what you want done · 2. THE CONTEXT — the background information the model needs · 3. THE FORMAT — how you want the output structured.

    34.2 THE SIX PRINCIPLES guaranteed MCQ| # | Principle | Detail |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | BE CLEAR AND SPECIFIC | "Vague prompts give vague answers." BAD: "Tell me about loans." GOOD: "Explain the difference between SECURED and UNSECURED personal loans for a first-time borrower in India, in under 200 words" | | 2 | PROVIDE CONTEXT | Give the model the background it needs — the customer profile, the regulation, the data | | 3 | SPECIFY THE OUTPUT FORMAT | "Ask for a TABLE, BULLET POINTS, JSON, or a specific word count" | | 4 | BREAK COMPLEX TASKS INTO STEPS | "Don't ask for everything at once" | | 5 | USE ROLE-PLAY / PERSONAS | "You are a SENIOR CREDIT RISK ANALYST at an Indian bank…" — "this shifts the model's tone, vocabulary and depth" | | 6 | AVOID AMBIGUITY | Ambiguous words produce unpredictable results |

    34.3 THE FOUR PROMPTING TECHNIQUES guaranteed MCQ| Technique | Definition |

    |---|---| | ZERO-SHOT prompting | Just ask — NO EXAMPLES provided | | FEW-SHOT prompting | Give the model A FEW EXAMPLES of the input–output pattern you want, then the real question. "The model LEARNS THE PATTERN FROM THE EXAMPLES" | | CHAIN-OF-THOUGHT prompting | Ask the model to "THINK STEP BY STEP" or "SHOW YOUR REASONING." "Dramatically improves performance on MATHEMATICAL, LOGICAL AND MULTI-STEP REASONING tasks" guaranteed MCQ| | SELF-REFLECTION / SELF-CONSISTENCY | Ask the model to REVIEW AND CRITIQUE ITS OWN ANSWER, or generate multiple answers and take the most consistent one |

    1. RAG — RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION guaranteed MCQ
    8

    35.1 THE FOUR LIMITATIONS OF A PLAIN LLM guaranteed MCQ| # | Limitation | Detail |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | KNOWLEDGE CUTOFF | "The model only knows what was in its training data UP TO A CERTAIN DATE. It doesn't know YESTERDAY'S RBI CIRCULAR" | | 2 | HALLUCINATION | "When it doesn't know, it may CONFIDENTLY MAKE THINGS UP" | | 3 | CONTEXT LIMITS | "You cannot paste an ENTIRE 500-PAGE COMPLIANCE MANUAL into the prompt" | | 4 | NO PERSONALISATION | "The model knows NOTHING about YOUR company's internal policies, YOUR customer data or YOUR products" |

    35.2 FINE-TUNING vs RAG guaranteed MCQ| | FINE-TUNING | RAG |

    |---|---|---| | Method | RETRAIN the model on your data — you change the model's WEIGHTS | LEAVE the model alone — RETRIEVE the relevant information and PUT IT IN THE PROMPT | | Cost/effort | EXPENSIVE, slow, needs ML expertise, must be REDONE when the data changes | CHEAPER, FASTER, and the knowledge base can be UPDATED INSTANTLY | | Best for | Teaching the model a STYLE, TONE OR SPECIALISED SKILL | Giving the model UP-TO-DATE FACTS AND PROPRIETARY KNOWLEDGE |

    35.3 THE THREE-STAGE RAG PIPELINE guaranteed MCQ — the whole pipeline with tool names| Stage | Steps | Tools named |

    |---|---|---| | STAGE 1 — INGESTION / INDEXING (done once, offline) | 1. CHUNK the documents into pieces of typically 200 to 500 WORDS ← guaranteed MCQ — "too small and you lose context, too large and retrieval becomes imprecise" | LANGCHAIN, HAYSTACK | | | 2. EMBED each chunk into a vector | TEXT-EMBEDDING-3-SMALL and TEXT-EMBEDDING-3-LARGE (OpenAI) · ALL-MiniLM · COHERE embeddings · SENTENCE-BERT guaranteed MCQ| | | 3. STORE the vectors in a VECTOR DATABASE, along with METADATA (source, date, section, document type) | FAISS · PINECONE · WEAVIATE · CHROMA · QDRANT guaranteed MCQ| | STAGE 2 — RETRIEVAL (at query time) | The user's question is EMBEDDED using THE SAME EMBEDDING MODEL, then the system finds the TOP-K MOST SIMILAR CHUNKS by SEMANTIC SIMILARITY (cosine similarity) | | | STAGE 3 — GENERATION | The retrieved chunks are inserted into an AUGMENTED PROMPT along with the user's question, and the LLM generates the answer GROUNDED IN THOSE CHUNKS | |

    35.4 THE SIX WAYS TO IMPROVE A RAG SYSTEM guaranteed MCQ

    1. QUERY REWRITING — reformulate the user's question to retrieve better · 2. RE-RANKING — retrieve more chunks, then use a second model to rank them by relevance · 3. FILTERING OUT JUNK — remove low-quality or irrelevant chunks before they reach the prompt · 4. STREAMING CONTEXT — feed context progressively for long documents · 5. CITATIONS — make the model cite WHICH CHUNK each claim came from, so users can verify · 6. FEEDBACK LOGS — record which answers users found useful and improve retrieval over time.

    35.5 WHY RAG WORKS — IN-CONTEXT LEARNING guaranteed MCQ

    "RAG works because of IN-CONTEXT LEARNING — the ability of a large language model to USE INFORMATION PROVIDED IN ITS PROMPT, WITHOUT ANY RETRAINING. You are not teaching the model new weights; you are GIVING IT THE RIGHT MATERIAL AT THE RIGHT MOMENT."

    "RAG is like giving a brilliant analyst THE RIGHT FILE at the right time, instead of asking them to memorise every document in the company."

    1. AGENTIC AI guaranteed MCQ
    13

    36.1 The definition and the loop guaranteed MCQ

    "An AI AGENT does more than ANSWER — it PERCEIVES, PLANS, ACTS and REFLECTS. Instead of a single question-and-answer, the agent breaks a GOAL into steps, uses TOOLS to carry them out, checks the results and adjusts."

    THE FOUR-STEP LOOP: PERCEIVE → PLAN → ACT → REFLECT. guaranteed MCQ

    36.2 THE SIX COMPONENTS OF AN AI AGENT guaranteed MCQ| # | Component | Role |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | THE LLM CORE | The reasoning engine — "the BRAIN" | | 2 | THE PLANNER | Breaks the goal into a SEQUENCE OF SUB-TASKS | | 3 | TOOL INTERFACES | APIs, databases, calculators, search — "the HANDS" | | 4 | MEMORY / STATE | Keeps track of what has happened so far | | 5 | THE REFLECTION LOOP | Evaluates its own output and RETRIES OR CORRECTS if needed | | 6 | THE ENVIRONMENT INTERFACE | How the agent connects to the outside world |

    36.3 TOOL CALLING guaranteed MCQ

    "The LLM doesn't actually EXECUTE code — it OUTPUTS A STRUCTURED REQUEST, usually in JSON, saying WHICH TOOL TO CALL and WITH WHAT ARGUMENTS. The surrounding system executes it and RETURNS THE RESULT to the model." guaranteed MCQ

    36.4 THE THREE TYPES OF AGENT MEMORY guaranteed MCQ| Type | Definition |

    |---|---| | SHORT-TERM memory | The SCRATCHPAD for the current task — what has happened in this session | | LONG-TERM memory | Stored in a VECTOR DATABASE — persists ACROSS sessions | | TASK / THREAD memory | The state of a specific ongoing workflow |

    36.5 THE FOUR AGENT DESIGN PATTERNS guaranteed MCQ| Pattern | Structure |

    |---|---| | 1. SINGLE TOOL-AUGMENTED AGENT | ONE agent with access to a set of tools — the simplest pattern | | 2. MULTI-AGENT SPECIALISTS | SEVERAL agents, each with a DIFFERENT SPECIALITY, collaborating — e.g. a research agent, an analysis agent and a writing agent | | 3. AGENT-IN-A-LOOP / REFLECTION | The agent REVIEWS AND CRITIQUES ITS OWN OUTPUT and iterates until it meets the quality bar | | 4. SUPERVISOR–WORKER | A SUPERVISOR agent DELEGATES sub-tasks to WORKER agents and INTEGRATES their results |

    36.6 MCP vs A2A — THE TWO PROTOCOLS guaranteed MCQ — a certain exam item| | MCP — MODEL CONTEXT PROTOCOL | A2A — AGENT-TO-AGENT PROTOCOL |

    |---|---|---| | Purpose | Connects an AGENT TO TOOLS AND DATA SOURCES | Lets AGENTS COMMUNICATE AND COLLABORATE WITH EACH OTHER | | Direction | VERTICAL integration — agent → tool | HORIZONTAL integration — agent ↔ agent | | The analogy | "THE USB TYPE-C OF AI INTEGRATIONS" — one standard connector instead of a custom adapter for every tool guaranteed MCQ| Agents DISCOVER each other's capabilities and delegate work | | Architecture | SERVER (exposes the tools) · CLIENT (the connector) · HOST (the application running the model) guaranteed MCQ| Requires agent DISCOVERY, capability advertisement and secure messaging | | The flow | HANDSHAKE → DISCOVERY (what tools are available?) → INVOCATION → EXECUTION → RESPONSE guaranteed MCQ| | | Security | | MUTUAL TLS, authentication, and GDPR/data-protection compliance guaranteed MCQ|

    1. RESPONSIBLE AI guaranteed MCQ
    12

    37.1 BIAS — the five types guaranteed MCQ| # | Type of bias | Definition |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | HISTORICAL bias | The training data reflects PAST DISCRIMINATION. "If a bank historically approved fewer loans to a certain group, the model LEARNS THAT PATTERN AND REPEATS IT" | | 2 | REPRESENTATIONAL bias | Some groups are UNDER-REPRESENTED in the data, so the model performs poorly for them | | 3 | MEASUREMENT bias | The way a variable is MEASURED differs across groups, or a proxy variable is unfair | | 4 | LABEL bias | The LABELS THEMSELVES are biased — the "ground truth" encodes human prejudice | | 5 | ALGORITHMIC bias | The algorithm or optimisation objective AMPLIFIES existing disparities |

    THE FIVE MITIGATIONS: 1. DIVERSE AND REPRESENTATIVE training data · 2. BIAS AUDITS AND FAIRNESS METRICS measured across subgroups · 3. RE-WEIGHTING OR RE-SAMPLING under-represented groups · 4. REMOVING or carefully handling SENSITIVE ATTRIBUTES AND THEIR PROXIES · 5. HUMAN OVERSIGHT on high-stakes decisions. guaranteed MCQ

    37.2 HALLUCINATIONS — five causes and five mitigations guaranteed MCQ

    THE FIVE CAUSES: 1. The model is trained to produce PLAUSIBLE TEXT, not VERIFIED FACTS · 2. GAPS OR ERRORS in the training data · 3. The KNOWLEDGE CUTOFF · 4. AMBIGUOUS OR UNDER-SPECIFIED PROMPTS · 5. HIGH TEMPERATURE / creative decoding settings.

    THE FIVE MITIGATIONS: 1. RAG — GROUND the model in retrieved source documents · 2. Require CITATIONS so claims can be verified · 3. LOWER THE TEMPERATURE for factual tasks · 4. HUMAN REVIEW for anything high-stakes · 5. Explicitly ALLOW THE MODEL TO SAY "I DON'T KNOW". guaranteed MCQ

    37.3 SUSTAINABILITY — the five levers guaranteed MCQ

    "Training large models consumes ENORMOUS amounts of ENERGY, WATER AND COMPUTE. There is a real CARBON FOOTPRINT behind every model."

    # Lever Detail
    1 MODEL EFFICIENCY Use the SMALLEST MODEL THAT DOES THE JOB — "you don't need the biggest model for every task"
    2 DISTILLATION Train a SMALL model to MIMIC a LARGE one guaranteed MCQ
    3 QUANTISATION REDUCE THE NUMERICAL PRECISION of the weights (e.g. from 32-bit to 8-bit) to cut memory and compute guaranteed MCQ
    4 GREEN CLOUD / SMART SCHEDULING Run training in REGIONS WITH RENEWABLE ENERGY, and SCHEDULE JOBS when the grid is cleanest
    5 TRANSPARENT REPORTING Publish the energy and carbon cost of training and inference

    37.4 ETHICS — the four pillars guaranteed MCQ| Pillar | Detail |

    |---|---| | FAIRNESS | THE KEY DISTINCTION: EQUALITY means giving EVERYONE THE SAME THING. EQUITY means giving each person WHAT THEY NEED TO HAVE A FAIR CHANCE. ← guaranteed MCQ THE WORKED EXAMPLE: a loan model approves 90% OF MEN but only 60% OF WOMEN with the same financial profile — "that is not a technical bug, that's an ETHICAL FAILURE" guaranteed MCQ| | TRANSPARENCY | Document what the model does, what data it was trained on and what its limitations are — via MODEL CARDS guaranteed MCQ| | ACCOUNTABILITY | Someone must be RESPONSIBLE. Requires AUDIT TRAILS of decisions and an APPEALS PROCESS so a person denied a loan can CHALLENGE the decision guaranteed MCQ| | PRIVACY | Protect customer data; comply with data-protection law |

    "In FinTech we are not just building models — we are making decisions that AFFECT PEOPLE'S LIVES, THEIR ACCESS TO CREDIT, THEIR HOMES, THEIR BUSINESSES. RESPONSIBLE AI IS NOT OPTIONAL."

    G. AI — definitions and the learning types

    Question Answer
    Tom Mitchell's ML definition "A computer program LEARNS from EXPERIENCE E with respect to TASK T and PERFORMANCE MEASURE P if its performance at T, as measured by P, improves with E"
    ANI vs AGI ANI = WEAK AI, one specific task (exists today). AGI = STRONG AI, human-level across many tasks (DOES NOT EXIST YET)
    The nesting AI ⊃ MACHINE LEARNING ⊃ DEEP LEARNING. All DL is ML; all ML is AI; NOT all AI is ML
    The 3 reasons to use ML Traditional rule-writing can't capture subtle patterns · ML ADAPTS automatically to change · ML HELPS HUMANS LEARN (uncovers hidden patterns)
    Supervised LABELLED data. CLASSIFICATION (categorical label) vs REGRESSION (continuous label)
    Unsupervised NO labels. CLUSTERING (K-means, DBSCAN, hierarchical) and DIMENSIONALITY REDUCTION (PCA)
    Reinforcement An AGENT interacts with an ENVIRONMENT, takes ACTIONS, receives REWARDS/PENALTIES — trial and error. Example: ALGORITHMIC TRADING
    The one-line summary Supervised = teaching with ANSWER KEYS. Unsupervised = DISCOVERING hidden patterns. Reinforcement = learning FROM INTERACTION AND FEEDBACK
    ML vs DL — the key difference ML: MANUAL feature engineering. DL: AUTOMATIC feature learning

    H. AI — the worked numbers you must memorise

    Calculation Answer
    Loan = 4 × income + 20,000, income $50,000 $220,000
    Loan = 4×income + 200×credit score − 1.5×EMI + 10,000; income 5,000, score 700, EMI 1,000 $168,500
    Why raw error fails +10 and −10 average to ZERO — "it looks like no error at all"
    R² = 0 means NO BETTER than always predicting the AVERAGE
    The normal equation W = (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀ y — closed-form, no iterations; fails when features are many (inverting XᵀX is slow)
    Confusion matrix: TP 90, FN 10, FP 20, TN 880 Accuracy 97% · Precision 81.8% · Recall 90% · F1 85.7%
    Precision formula TP ÷ (TP + FP) — of those PREDICTED positive, how many were right
    Recall formula TP ÷ (TP + FN) — of the ACTUAL positives, how many were caught
    F1 The HARMONIC MEAN: 2 × (P × R) ÷ (P + R)
    The 1% fraud trap Predict "not fraud" for everything → 99% ACCURATE and COMPLETELY USELESS. Use precision/recall/F1, not accuracy
    AUC = 1 / 0.5 / < 0.5 Perfect / random guessing / worse than random (something is wrong)
    Gini for 80–20 and 50–50 0.32 and 0.5
    Entropy for 80–20 and 50–50 ≈0.72 and 1.0
    The $400 split example Gini 0.444 on both branches; entropy 0.918 — neither branch is pure
    Feature importances (credit default) Credit score 0.45 · DTI 0.25 · late payments 0.15 · employment 0.10 · marital status 0.05
    Forward pass: X₁=1, X₂=2 Z₁ = 0.6, Z₂ = 1.2 (ReLU passes both) → Z₃ = 1.22 → sigmoid → OUTPUT 0.772 = a 77.2% default probability
    Backprop from that output, true label 0 Loss (log loss) = 1.48 · ∂L/∂Z₃ = 0.772 · gradients 0.463 and 0.926 · η = 0.1 → new output 0.7637, new loss 1.43
    K-means 5-customer example Initial centroids (4,4) and (10,8) → clusters {A,B,E} and {C,D} → new centroids (4.67, 3.67) and (10.5, 8.5)
