    Token conversion 1 token ≈ 0.75 words; 1 word ≈ 1.33 tokens
    Same sentence tokenised GPT 10 · Claude 11 · Gemini 12
    GPT-4o context 128,000 tokens; max OUTPUT 16,384
    GPT-2 demo 124M parameters · 50,257 vocabulary · 768 embedding size · "the world is beautiful" → "place" at 97.58%
    TensorFlow Playground Raw X₁,X₂ stuck at loss 0.5 · adding X₁²,X₂² converges in ~10 epochs · one hidden layer of 4 neurons converges in ~162 epochs with 12 parameters · LR 0.03 optimal, LR 10 diverges · LINEAR activation stuck at 0.5 forever · ReLU under 100 epochs · spiral with 4 layers × 8 neurons in ~381 epochs

    I. AI — the "which is which" distinctions

    Pair The distinction
    MAE vs MSE vs RMSE MAE: average absolute error. MSE: squares errors, penalises large ones more, but units are SQUARED. RMSE: square root of MSE — same units as the target AND still penalises big errors
    Batch vs stochastic vs mini-batch GD Batch = entire data set, stable but slow. Stochastic = ONE example at a time, fast but noisy, CAN ESCAPE LOCAL MINIMA. Mini-batch = 32/64/128, the practical standard, uses GPU vectorisation
    Parameters vs hyperparameters Parameters (weights, biases) are LEARNED from data. Hyperparameters are SET BY YOU BEFORE TRAINING
    L1 (Lasso) vs L2 (Ridge) L1 = sum of ABSOLUTE values, drives weights TO ZERO → FEATURE SELECTION. L2 = sum of SQUARES, SHRINKS weights but keeps all features. ELASTIC NET = both
    Underfitting vs overfitting Underfitting: BOTH losses HIGH and close. Overfitting: training loss keeps falling while VALIDATION LOSS RISES — the GAP is the overfitting zone
    Overfitting fixes REDUCE COMPLEXITY (fewer parameters) or ADD MORE DATA — MORE ROWS, NOT MORE COLUMNS
    Logistic vs linear regression Logistic passes the linear output through a SIGMOID to get a value in [0,1]. Despite the name, it is a CLASSIFIER
    Log loss vs categorical cross-entropy Log loss = BINARY. Categorical cross-entropy = MULTI-CLASS (softmax)
    Label vs one-hot encoding Label encoding IMPLIES ORDER — use only for ORDINAL. One-hot for NOMINAL, but all dummies together cause MULTICOLLINEARITY in linear models
    Standardisation vs min-max Z-score → mean 0, SD 1, good for unbounded data. Min-max → 0 to 1, common in deep learning. FIT ON TRAINING DATA ONLY
    Target leakage vs train-test contamination Target leakage = FUTURE information as a feature ("loan closed on date"). Contamination = test data influencing training (e.g. scaling BEFORE splitting)
    Random forest vs gradient boosting RF builds trees IN PARALLEL, independently, and VOTES (BAGGING). GB builds trees SEQUENTIALLY, each fitting the PREVIOUS MODEL'S RESIDUALS (BOOSTING)
    Gradient boosting vs AdaBoost GB fits new trees to the RESIDUALS/GRADIENTS. AdaBoost RE-WEIGHTS THE SAMPLES, boosting misclassified points, and weights each learner by α
    XGBoost NOT a new algorithm — an OPTIMISED IMPLEMENTATION of gradient boosting
    Pre- vs post-pruning Pre-pruning = EARLY STOPPING (max depth, min samples). Post-pruning = grow the full tree then CUT BACK
    Greedy algorithm Makes the best IMMEDIATE choice, NEVER BACKTRACKS, doesn't look ahead → can produce suboptimal trees
    LIME vs SHAP LIME: local surrogate model around ONE prediction; easy but SENSITIVE TO PERTURBATIONS. SHAP: GAME THEORY (Shapley values), fair credit allocation, mathematically rigorous. "LIME helps you ZOOM IN; SHAP helps you EXPLAIN FAIRLY"
    Data drift vs concept drift Data drift: the INPUT DISTRIBUTION changes. Concept drift: the RELATIONSHIP between input and output changes (the COVID credit-scoring example)
    K-means vs hierarchical K-means REQUIRES K upfront. Hierarchical does NOT — you CUT THE DENDROGRAM at whatever height you like
    Strata vs clusters (carried from Analytics II) Strata are internally HOMOGENEOUS; clusters are internally HETEROGENEOUS
    Autoencoder vs encoder-decoder Autoencoder RECONSTRUCTS THE SAME input. Encoder-decoder produces a DIFFERENT output sequence (translation, summarisation)
    Autoencoder vs PCA A LINEAR autoencoder with MSE ≈ PCA. With NON-LINEAR activations it is a NON-LINEAR GENERALISATION of PCA
    Dropout vs batch normalisation Dropout: randomly deactivates 30–50% of neurons DURING TRAINING ONLY, an implicit ensemble. Batch norm: normalises layer inputs per MINI-BATCH to mean 0 / variance 1, with LEARNABLE γ (scale) and β (shift), fixing INTERNAL COVARIATE SHIFT
    Greedy vs top-K vs top-P decoding Greedy: always the top token, deterministic, boring. Top-K: sample from a FIXED number of top tokens. Top-P (nucleus): sample from the SMALLEST SET whose cumulative probability exceeds P — ADAPTIVE
    Temperature < 1 vs > 1 < 1 SHARPENS (more deterministic; use 0.2–0.5 for facts). > 1 FLATTENS (more creative; 1.0–1.5+ for brainstorming)
    Fine-tuning vs RAG Fine-tuning CHANGES THE WEIGHTS — expensive, redone when data changes; best for STYLE/SKILL. RAG leaves the model alone and INJECTS RETRIEVED CONTEXT — cheap, instantly updatable; best for FRESH FACTS and PROPRIETARY KNOWLEDGE
    MCP vs A2A MCP = agent-to-TOOL, VERTICAL, "the USB Type-C of AI integrations", server/client/host. A2A = agent-to-AGENT, HORIZONTAL collaboration, needs discovery and mutual TLS
    Equality vs equity Equality = everyone gets THE SAME THING. Equity = each gets WHAT THEY NEED for a fair chance
    Generative vs discriminative Discriminative learns the BOUNDARY between classes. Generative learns the DATA DISTRIBUTION and can CREATE new data

    J. AI — the ordered lists

    List The order
    The ML lifecycle (10 steps) Define the problem → collect data → EDA → pre-process & engineer features → choose the model → train → evaluate → tune hyperparameters → DEPLOY (.pkl/.onnx, API) → MONITOR for drift
    Building a decision tree Start at the ROOT with all the data → split using gini/entropy/variance (DIVIDE AND CONQUER) → repeat recursively → stop at LEAF NODES (class label for classification, AVERAGE value for regression)
    Random forest (4 steps) BOOTSTRAP the data (sample WITH REPLACEMENT) → RANDOM FEATURE SUBSET at each split → build each tree greedily → VOTE (classification) or AVERAGE (regression). The technique is BAGGING = BOOTSTRAP AGGREGATING
    Gradient boosting (4 steps) Initial prediction = the MEAN → compute RESIDUALS → train a SHALLOW TREE on the RESIDUALS → update scaled by the LEARNING RATE η. Depth typically 3–6
    AdaBoost (5 steps) Initialise weights wᵢ = 1/m → train a weak learner (a DEPTH-1 DECISION STUMP), compute the WEIGHTED ERROR → compute the learner's weight α (NEGATIVE if worse than random) → BOOST the misclassified samples and NORMALISE → final WEIGHTED MAJORITY VOTE
    K-means (5 steps) Choose K and initialise centroids → assign each point to the nearest centroid (Euclidean) → recompute centroids as the AVERAGE → repeat → stop when converged. It minimises WCSS
    Agglomerative clustering (5 steps) Each point its own cluster → compute all pairwise distances → merge the two closest → recompute → repeat until one cluster
    PCA (4 steps) Centre the data to zero mean → compute the covariance matrix (divide by n − 1) → find eigenvalues and eigenvectors → project onto the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue
    RAG pipeline (3 stages) INGEST (chunk 200–500 words → embed → store in a vector DB with metadata) → RETRIEVE (embed the query, find the top-K by semantic similarity) → GENERATE (augmented prompt → grounded answer)
    Agent loop (4 steps) PERCEIVE → PLAN → ACT → REFLECT
    Attention (4 steps) Dot product of Query with every Key → SCALE by √d → SOFTMAX → weighted sum of the VALUE vectors
    Word representation evolution One-hot → count vectorisation → TF-IDF → Word2Vec/GloVe (king − man + woman ≈ queen) → contextual embeddings (BERT, GPT)
    Tuning techniques (4, in order) Manual → GRID search (brute force, combinatorial explosion) → RANDOM search (often finds good solutions faster) → BAYESIAN optimisation (Optuna, Hyperopt, scikit-optimize)
    K-fold CV (4 steps) Split into K folds (K = 5 or 10) → train on K−1, test on 1 → repeat K times with a different test fold → AVERAGE the metrics

    K. AI — the named tools, techniques and people

    Item Answer
    The perceptron's inventor Frank Rosenblatt, 1950s
    The perceptron's fatal limitation Can only separate LINEARLY SEPARABLE data — CANNOT SOLVE XOR
    Why activation functions are needed Stacking linear layers is STILL LINEAR. "Clear glass sheets stay flat — you need a LENS"
    ReLU / sigmoid / tanh ranges 0 to ∞ (hidden layers, default) / 0 to 1 (binary output, probabilities) / −1 to +1 (zero-centred)
    Vanishing gradients Sigmoid and tanh saturate → gradients near zero → learning stalls in deep networks. ReLU mitigates it
    The imbalance fixes OVERSAMPLING (SMOTE — Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique) · UNDERSAMPLING · CLASS WEIGHTING / cost-sensitive learning (supported by logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost)
    The 6 missing-data strategies Drop rows · drop columns (if ~80%+ missing) · impute (MEAN numerical, MEDIAN skewed, MODE categorical) · domain constant · MODEL-BASED imputation · FLAG the missingness (trees/XGBoost/LightGBM handle it natively)
    The leakage test question "Is this information something I WOULD KNOW AT THE TIME OF PREDICTION?" If no, it doesn't belong in training data
    The feature-engineering principle "A SIMPLE MODEL WITH GREAT FEATURES WILL ALMOST ALWAYS BEAT A COMPLEX MODEL WITH WEAK FEATURES"
    BPE Byte Pair Encoding — sub-word tokenisation. Common words stay whole; rare words split; unknown words fall back to characters
    The 4 linkage methods SINGLE (shortest) · COMPLETE (farthest) · AVERAGE · WARD'S (minimises variance, often best)
    The elbow method Plot K vs WCSS; the OPTIMAL K is where the curve BENDS — in his example around K = 3 or 4
    K-means limitation fixes K-MEANS++ (initialisation) · GMM with EM (elliptical clusters) · DBSCAN (irregular shapes, ignores outliers) · SPECTRAL clustering · K-PROTOTYPES (mixed data types) · PCA (high dimensions)
    Vector databases FAISS · Pinecone · Weaviate · Chroma · Qdrant
    Embedding models text-embedding-3-small/large · all-MiniLM · Cohere · Sentence-BERT
    Chunking frameworks LangChain · Haystack
    Why RAG works IN-CONTEXT LEARNING — the model uses information in the prompt WITHOUT retraining
    The 5 bias types HISTORICAL · REPRESENTATIONAL · MEASUREMENT · LABEL · ALGORITHMIC
    The sustainability levers Model efficiency · DISTILLATION (small model mimics large) · QUANTISATION (lower numerical precision) · green cloud & smart scheduling · transparent reporting
    The ethics pillars FAIRNESS (equity, not just equality — the 90% men / 60% women loan example) · TRANSPARENCY (MODEL CARDS) · ACCOUNTABILITY (AUDIT TRAILS + an APPEALS PROCESS) · PRIVACY

    L. The traps most likely to catch you

    Trap The correct answer
    "Blockchain is anonymous" NO — PSEUDONYMOUS and TRACEABLE
    "Blockchain = Bitcoin" NO — Bitcoin is ONE APPLICATION, like email on the internet
    "Blockchain requires a token" NO — permissioned blockchains can have NO CRYPTO AT ALL
    The base fee in a gas fee BURNED — it is NOT paid to the validator. Only the PRIORITY FEE is the tip
    Who is the ISSUING bank in an LC? THE IMPORTER'S bank — not the exporter's
    In a COLLECTION, who is the REMITTING bank? THE EXPORTER'S bank — the reverse-sounding one
    Does a bill of lading only prove shipment? NO — it is also the TITLE OF OWNERSHIP of the goods
    Does blockchain KYC store your documents? NO — only a CRYPTOGRAPHIC PROOF
    Is CBDC a cryptocurrency? NO — it is CENTRALISED, LEGAL TENDER and government-issued
    Does CBDC need a bank account? NO. UPI DOES
    Is logistic regression a regression model? NO — it is used for CLASSIFICATION
    Is 99% accuracy on 1% fraud good? NO — it is the CLASS IMBALANCE TRAP. Use precision/recall/F1
    Does L2/ridge do feature selection? NO — that's L1/LASSO. Ridge only SHRINKS
    Fix overfitting with more columns? NO — MORE ROWS. More columns makes it worse
    Is XGBoost a new algorithm? NO — an optimised implementation of gradient boosting
    Does dropout apply at inference time? NO — TRAINING ONLY. At inference all neurons are active with scaled outputs
    Does feature importance show causality? NO — only PREDICTIVE POWER. Correlated features distort it
    Does gradient descent always find the global minimum? Only for CONVEX cost functions like MSE in linear regression. Neural networks can get STUCK IN LOCAL MINIMA
    Do you scale before or after splitting? AFTER — and fit the scaler on the TRAINING SET ONLY
    Does K-means work on categorical data? NO — numeric only. Use K-prototypes or one-hot encode
    Does PCA divide by n? NO — by n − 1, because it is the SAMPLE covariance
    Do NLP tokenisation and asset tokenisation mean the same thing? NO — one splits TEXT into tokens; the other converts a REAL-WORLD ASSET into digital ownership tokens
    Does a bigger context window mean bigger output? NO — GPT-4o has 128,000 tokens of CONTEXT but a MAXIMUM OUTPUT of only 16,384
    Does adding hidden layers fix a LINEAR activation? NO — with linear activations the network stays stuck at loss 0.5 NO MATTER HOW DEEP. NON-LINEARITY IS ESSENTIAL
